use std::io::{self, PipeReader, Read};
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::process::{Child, Command, Stdio};

Listing 1.39 Starting the commands, each with its own pipe, in Go. code/go/pipeline/main.go

// start runs the commands of a pipeline. Command i writes to pipe i and reads
// from pipe i-1; the first command reads /dev/null. It returns the commands
// and the read end of the last pipe.
func start(stages [][]string) ([]*exec.Cmd, *os.File, error) {
	var input *os.File
	commands := make([]*exec.Cmd, 0, len(stages))

	for _, stage := range stages {
		reader, writer, err := os.Pipe()

		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}

		command := exec.Command(stage[0], stage[1:]...)
		command.Stdout = writer

		if input != nil {
			command.Stdin = input
		}

		err = command.Start()

		// The child holds its own copies of both ends. Closing the parent's
		// copies leaves the child's as the only ones.
		writer.Close()

		if input != nil {
			input.Close()
		}

		if err != nil {
			reader.Close()

			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", stage[0], err)
		}

		commands, input = append(commands, command), reader
	}

	return commands, input, nil
}

Listing 1.40 Starting the commands, each with its own pipe, in Rust. code/rust/pipeline/src/main.rs

/// Runs the commands of a pipeline. Command `i` writes to pipe `i` and reads
/// from pipe `i - 1`; the first command reads /dev/null. Returns the children
/// and the read end of the last pipe.
fn start(stages: &[Vec<&str>]) -> io::Result<(Vec<Child>, PipeReader)> {
    let mut input = None;
    let mut children = Vec::with_capacity(stages.len());

    for stage in stages {
        let (reader, writer) = io::pipe()?;
        let stdin = input.take().map_or_else(Stdio::null, Stdio::from);

        // The `Command` owns the parent's copies of both ends. It is dropped
        // when this statement ends, which closes them and leaves the child's
        // copies as the only ones.
        let child = Command::new(stage[0])
            .args(&stage[1..])
            .stdin(stdin)
            .stdout(writer)
            .spawn()?;

        children.push(child);
        input = Some(reader);
    }

    let output = input.ok_or(io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput)?;

    Ok((children, output))
}

The kernel records how each process terminated: with an exit status chosen by the process, where 0 means success by convention, or by a signal. The parent retrieves the record with the wait system call.

Listing 1.41 Reporting how a command terminated, in Go. code/go/pipeline/main.go

// ending waits for a command and reports how it terminated: with an exit
// status, or by a signal.
func ending(command *exec.Cmd) string {
	command.Wait()

	state := command.ProcessState

	if status, ok := state.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && status.Signaled() {
		return fmt.Sprintf("killed by signal %d", status.Signal())
	}

	return fmt.Sprintf("exited with status %d", state.ExitCode())
}

Listing 1.42 Reporting how a command terminated, in Rust. code/rust/pipeline/src/main.rs

/// Waits for a command and reports how it terminated: with an exit status,
/// or by a signal.
fn ending(child: &mut Child) -> io::Result<String> {
    let status = child.wait()?;

    let text = match (status.signal(), status.code()) {
        (Some(signal), _) => format!("killed by signal {signal}"),
        (None, Some(code)) => format!("exited with status {code}"),
        (None, None) => status.to_string(),
    };

    Ok(text)
}

run reads the last pipe until read returns 0. That occurs when the last command has exited and no descriptor for the write end remains, which depends on start having closed the parent’s copy.

Listing 1.43 Running a pipeline, in Go. code/go/pipeline/main.go

// run starts a pipeline, reads the last command's output to the end of the
// stream, and prints the output and each command's termination.
func run(line string) error {
	var stages [][]string

	for _, stage := range strings.Split(line, " | ") {
		stages = append(stages, strings.Fields(stage))
	}

	commands, output, err := start(stages)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer output.Close()

	text, err := io.ReadAll(output)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Println(line)
	fmt.Printf("  output: %s\n", strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(text)), " "))

	for i, command := range commands {
		fmt.Printf("  %s: %s\n", stages[i][0], ending(command))
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 1.44 Running a pipeline, in Rust. code/rust/pipeline/src/main.rs

/// Starts a pipeline, reads the last command's output to the end of the
/// stream, and prints the output and each command's termination.
fn run(line: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    let stages: Vec<Vec<&str>> = line
        .split(" | ")
        .map(|stage| stage.split_whitespace().collect())
        .collect();

    let (mut children, mut output) = start(&stages)?;

    let mut text = String::new();
    output.read_to_string(&mut text)?;

    let words: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    println!("{line}");
    println!("  output: {}", words.join(" "));

    for (stage, child) in stages.iter().zip(&mut children) {
        println!("  {}: {}", stage[0], ending(child)?);
    }

    Ok(())
}
seq 1 100000 | grep 7 | wc -l
  output: 40951
  seq: exited with status 0
  grep: exited with status 0
  wc: exited with status 0
yes | head -n 3
  output: y y y
  yes: killed by signal 13
  head: exited with status 0

In the first pipeline, each command reached the end of its input when the previous command exited, and all of them exited with status 0. The result can be verified independently. Of the 100000 5-digit strings from 00000 to 99999, 95 = 59049 contain no 7. The range 1 to 100000 replaces 00000 with 100000, and neither contains a 7, so 100000 - 59049 = 40951 numbers in the range contain a 7.

The second pipeline terminates a writer that has no end of its own. yes writes the line y in a loop. head -n 3 exits after 3 lines, which closes the only read end of the pipe. The next write by yes raises SIGPIPE, signal 13, and the default action terminates the process. In a longer pipeline this propagates from right to left: each command that exits closes a read end, and the command before it is terminated on its next write.

Named pipes

The pipes so far have no name, so only processes that inherited the descriptors can use them. A named pipe, or FIFO, is the same kernel object with an entry in the file system, created by mkfifo. Unrelated processes open it by path, one for writing and one for reading, and the bytes pass through a struct pipe_inode_info exactly as before. Nothing is written to the disk. The p at the start of the permissions marks the type.

$ mkfifo /tmp/x/queue
$ ls -l /tmp/x/queue
prw-rw-r-- /tmp/x/queue
$ echo hello > /tmp/x/queue &
$ cat /tmp/x/queue
hello

An open of a FIFO for writing blocks until some process opens it for reading, and the reverse, which is why the echo above is started in the background.

Inspecting pipes on a live system

CommandShows
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fdwhich descriptors of a process are pipes, and the number of each pipe; equal numbers are the 2 ends of the same pipe
cat /proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-sizethe largest capacity an ordinary user can set with F_SETPIPE_SZ: 1048576 here
cat /proc/sys/fs/pipe-user-pages-softthe number of pages all pipes of a user may hold before new pipes are created with a single slot: 16384 here
fcntl(fd, F_GETPIPE_SZ)the capacity of a pipe, from inside a program

A pipeline that appears to hang is usually diagnosed with the first command: find the process that is blocked, read its descriptors, and look for another process that still holds the write end of the same pipe number.

The complete programs

Listing 1.45 The complete pipefacts, in Go. code/go/pipefacts/main.go

// Command pipefacts measures a kernel pipe: its capacity,
// the unit in which a read frees space, how a reader observes the end of the
// stream, and the result of a write when no reader exists.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./pipefacts
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


// block is the size of every write the program attempts: one page.
const block = 4096

// newPipe creates a pipe in non-blocking mode: a read or a write that cannot
// proceed returns EAGAIN where it would otherwise suspend the caller.
func newPipe() (reader, writer int, err error) {
	var fds [2]int

	if err := unix.Pipe2(fds[:], unix.O_NONBLOCK|unix.O_CLOEXEC); err != nil {
		return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf("pipe2: %w", err)
	}

	return fds[0], fds[1], nil
}


// fill writes whole blocks until the kernel refuses one and returns the
// number of bytes accepted.
func fill(writer int) (int, error) {
	data := make([]byte, block)
	total := 0

	for {
		n, err := unix.Write(writer, data)

		if errors.Is(err, unix.EAGAIN) {
			return total, nil
		}

		if err != nil {
			return total, fmt.Errorf("write: %w", err)
		}

		total += n
	}
}

// drain reads and discards up to n bytes.
func drain(reader, n int) error {
	_, err := unix.Read(reader, make([]byte, n))

	return err
}


// capacity fills a pipe when it is new, after 1 byte has been read, and
// after 4096 bytes have been read. Each fill reports the free space.
func capacity() error {
	reader, writer, err := newPipe()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(reader)
	defer unix.Close(writer)

	steps := []struct {
		read   int
		report string
	}{
		{0, "new pipe: %d bytes accepted\n"},
		{1, "after reading 1 byte: %d bytes accepted\n"},
		{block - 1, "after reading 4096 bytes in total: %d bytes accepted\n"},
	}

	for _, step := range steps {
		if err := drain(reader, step.read); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		accepted, err := fill(writer)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		fmt.Printf(step.report, accepted)
	}

	return nil
}


// resize changes the capacity of a pipe with fcntl and measures it after
// each change.
func resize() error {
	reader, writer, err := newPipe()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(reader)
	defer unix.Close(writer)

	for _, request := range []int{4 * block, 5000, 1 << 20} {
		granted, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(writer), unix.F_SETPIPE_SZ, request)

		if err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("F_SETPIPE_SZ: %w", err)
		}

		accepted, err := fill(writer)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		fmt.Printf("capacity of %d bytes requested: %d granted, %d bytes accepted\n", request, granted, accepted)

		if err := drain(reader, accepted); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	return nil
}


// endOfStream reads an empty pipe while a write end is open, and again after
// the write end has been closed.
func endOfStream() error {
	reader, writer, err := newPipe()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(reader)

	buf := make([]byte, block)

	_, err = unix.Read(reader, buf)
	fmt.Printf("empty pipe, write end open: read fails with %s\n", name(err))

	unix.Close(writer)

	n, err := unix.Read(reader, buf)

	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("read: %w", err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("empty pipe, write end closed: read returns %d\n", n)

	return nil
}


// brokenPipe writes to a pipe whose read end has been closed.
func brokenPipe() error {
	reader, writer, err := newPipe()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(writer)

	unix.Close(reader)

	_, err = unix.Write(writer, []byte("hello"))
	fmt.Printf("read end closed: write fails with %s\n", name(err))

	return nil
}

// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EAGAIN.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}


func main() {
	for _, experiment := range []func() error{capacity, resize, endOfStream, brokenPipe} {
		if err := experiment(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 1.46 The complete pipefacts, in Rust. code/rust/pipefacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures a kernel pipe: its capacity, the unit in which
//! a read frees space, how a reader observes the end of the stream, and the
//! result of a write when no reader exists.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p pipefacts
//! ```

use std::os::fd::OwnedFd;

use nix::errno::Errno;
use nix::fcntl::{FcntlArg, OFlag, fcntl};
use nix::unistd::{pipe2, read, write};

/// The size of every write the program attempts: one page.
const BLOCK: usize = 4096;

/// Creates a pipe in non-blocking mode: a read or a write that cannot proceed
/// returns `EAGAIN` where it would otherwise suspend the caller. The read end
/// is first.
fn new_pipe() -> nix::Result<(OwnedFd, OwnedFd)> {
    pipe2(OFlag::O_NONBLOCK | OFlag::O_CLOEXEC)
}

/// Writes whole blocks until the kernel refuses one and returns the number of
/// bytes accepted.
fn fill(writer: &OwnedFd) -> nix::Result<usize> {
    let data = [0u8; BLOCK];
    let mut total = 0;

    loop {
        match write(writer, &data) {
            Ok(n) => total += n,
            Err(Errno::EAGAIN) => return Ok(total),
            Err(error) => return Err(error),
        }
    }
}

/// Reads and discards up to `n` bytes.
fn drain(reader: &OwnedFd, n: usize) -> nix::Result<usize> {
    read(reader, &mut vec![0u8; n])
}

/// Fills a pipe when it is new, after 1 byte has been read, and after 4096
/// bytes have been read. Each fill reports the free space.
fn capacity() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (reader, writer) = new_pipe()?;

    let steps = [
        (0, "new pipe"),
        (1, "after reading 1 byte"),
        (BLOCK - 1, "after reading 4096 bytes in total"),
    ];

    for (count, label) in steps {
        drain(&reader, count)?;

        let accepted = fill(&writer)?;
        println!("{label}: {accepted} bytes accepted");
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Changes the capacity of a pipe with fcntl and measures it after each
/// change.
fn resize() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (reader, writer) = new_pipe()?;

    for request in [4 * BLOCK, 5000, 1 << 20] {
        let granted = fcntl(&writer, FcntlArg::F_SETPIPE_SZ(request as i32))?;
        let accepted = fill(&writer)?;

        println!(
            "capacity of {request} bytes requested: {granted} granted, {accepted} bytes accepted"
        );

        drain(&reader, accepted)?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Reads an empty pipe while a write end is open, and again after the write
/// end has been closed.
fn end_of_stream() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (reader, writer) = new_pipe()?;
    let mut buf = [0u8; BLOCK];

    if let Err(error) = read(&reader, &mut buf) {
        println!("empty pipe, write end open: read fails with {error:?}");
    }

    drop(writer);

    let n = read(&reader, &mut buf)?;
    println!("empty pipe, write end closed: read returns {n}");

    Ok(())
}

/// Writes to a pipe whose read end has been closed.
fn broken_pipe() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (reader, writer) = new_pipe()?;

    drop(reader);

    if let Err(error) = write(&writer, b"hello") {
        println!("read end closed: write fails with {error:?}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> nix::Result<()> {
    capacity()?;
    resize()?;
    end_of_stream()?;
    broken_pipe()
}

Listing 1.47 The complete handpipe, in Go. code/go/handpipe/main.go

// Command handpipe builds a pipe by hand, with the same parts the kernel
// uses: a ring of pages for the bytes, a lock, a place for a reader to sleep
// and a place for a writer to sleep, and a count of the open ends.
//
// It traces a small ring call by call, repeats the capacity measurement of
// pipefacts on a ring of the kernel's size, and sends 1048576 bytes from a
// writer goroutine to a reader.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./handpipe
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"sync"
)


// A page is one slot of the ring: a block of memory, and the position and
// length of the bytes in it that have not been read yet.
type page struct {
	data   []byte
	offset int
	length int
}

// A ring is the storage of a pipe. head counts the pages ever put into use
// and tail counts the pages ever emptied, so head-tail pages are in use, and
// a counter's remainder after division by the number of slots is its slot.
type ring struct {
	pages []page
	head  uint
	tail  uint
}

func newRing(slots, pageSize int) *ring {
	pages := make([]page, slots)

	for i := range pages {
		pages[i].data = make([]byte, pageSize)
	}

	return &ring{pages: pages}
}

func (r *ring) empty() bool {
	return r.head == r.tail
}

func (r *ring) full() bool {
	return r.head-r.tail == uint(len(r.pages))
}

// slot returns the page that a counter refers to.
func (r *ring) slot(counter uint) *page {
	return &r.pages[counter%uint(len(r.pages))]
}


// put copies as much of data as the ring has room for and returns the number
// of bytes it copied. The bytes go first into the unused end of the newest
// page, then into free slots, one page each.
func (r *ring) put(data []byte) int {
	copied := 0

	if !r.empty() {
		newest := r.slot(r.head - 1)
		end := newest.offset + newest.length

		n := copy(newest.data[end:], data)
		newest.length += n
		copied += n
	}

	for copied < len(data) && !r.full() {
		next := r.slot(r.head)
		next.offset = 0
		next.length = copy(next.data, data[copied:])

		copied += next.length
		r.head++
	}

	return copied
}


// take moves up to len(buf) of the oldest bytes into buf and returns the
// number it moved. A slot becomes free when the last byte of its page has
// been taken.
func (r *ring) take(buf []byte) int {
	moved := 0

	for moved < len(buf) && !r.empty() {
		oldest := r.slot(r.tail)

		n := copy(buf[moved:], oldest.data[oldest.offset:oldest.offset+oldest.length])
		oldest.offset += n
		oldest.length -= n
		moved += n

		if oldest.length == 0 {
			r.tail++
		}
	}

	return moved
}


// errBrokenPipe is what a write returns when no reader is left.
var errBrokenPipe = errors.New("EPIPE")

// A pipe is a ring shared by a reader and a writer goroutine. readable is where a reader
// sleeps while the ring is empty, and writable is where a writer sleeps while
// the ring is full. readers and writers count the open ends.
type pipe struct {
	mu       sync.Mutex
	readable *sync.Cond
	writable *sync.Cond
	ring     *ring
	readers  int
	writers  int
}

func newPipe(slots, pageSize int) *pipe {
	p := &pipe{ring: newRing(slots, pageSize), readers: 1, writers: 1}
	p.readable = sync.NewCond(&p.mu)
	p.writable = sync.NewCond(&p.mu)

	return p
}


// write returns when every byte of data is in the ring, or when no reader is
// left. While the ring is full it sleeps on writable.
func (p *pipe) write(data []byte) (int, error) {
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()

	written := 0

	for written < len(data) {
		if p.readers == 0 {
			return written, errBrokenPipe
		}

		n := p.ring.put(data[written:])
		written += n

		if n == 0 {
			p.writable.Wait()
			continue
		}

		p.readable.Broadcast()
	}

	return written, nil
}


// read returns as soon as it has moved at least one byte into buf. While the
// ring is empty and a writer exists it sleeps on readable. It returns 0 when
// the ring is empty and no writer is left: the end of the stream.
func (p *pipe) read(buf []byte) int {
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()

	for p.ring.empty() && p.writers > 0 {
		p.readable.Wait()
	}

	n := p.ring.take(buf)

	if n > 0 {
		p.writable.Broadcast()
	}

	return n
}


// closeWriter gives up a write end. A reader asleep on an empty ring wakes
// and finds that no writer is left.
func (p *pipe) closeWriter() {
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()

	p.writers--
	p.readable.Broadcast()
}

// closeReader gives up a read end. A writer asleep on a full ring wakes and
// finds that no reader is left.
func (p *pipe) closeReader() {
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()

	p.readers--
	p.writable.Broadcast()
}


// picture renders the ring as one cell per slot: the number of unread bytes
// in its page, or a dot when the slot is free.
func (r *ring) picture() string {
	cells := make([]string, len(r.pages))

	for i := range cells {
		cells[i] = "."
	}

	for counter := r.tail; counter != r.head; counter++ {
		cells[counter%uint(len(r.pages))] = fmt.Sprint(r.slot(counter).length)
	}

	return "[" + strings.Join(cells, " ") + "]"
}

// smallRing applies the calls of the trace to a ring of 4 pages of 8 bytes
// and prints the ring after each.
func smallRing() {
	r := newRing(4, 8)
	buf := make([]byte, 32)

	calls := []struct {
		op string
		n  int
	}{{"put", 12}, {"take", 3}, {"put", 30}, {"take", 5}, {"put", 30}}

	fmt.Println("ring of 4 pages of 8 bytes")

	for _, call := range calls {
		var done int

		switch call.op {
		case "put":
			done = r.put(buf[:call.n])
		case "take":
			done = r.take(buf[:call.n])
		}

		fmt.Printf("%-4s %2d: %2d bytes   head %d  tail %d   %s\n", call.op, call.n, done, r.head, r.tail, r.picture())
	}
}


// fill puts whole blocks into the ring until it accepts none and returns the
// number of bytes accepted.
func fill(r *ring, block []byte) int {
	total := 0

	for {
		n := r.put(block)

		if n == 0 {
			return total
		}

		total += n
	}
}

// kernelSize repeats the capacity measurement of pipefacts on a ring with
// the kernel's dimensions: 16 pages of 4096 bytes.
func kernelSize() {
	const pageSize = 4096

	r := newRing(16, pageSize)
	block := make([]byte, pageSize)

	steps := []struct {
		read   int
		report string
	}{
		{0, "new pipe: %d bytes accepted\n"},
		{1, "after reading 1 byte: %d bytes accepted\n"},
		{pageSize - 1, "after reading 4096 bytes in total: %d bytes accepted\n"},
	}

	for _, step := range steps {
		r.take(block[:step.read])
		fmt.Printf(step.report, fill(r, block))
	}
}


// transfer sends one megabyte through a pipe of the kernel's size. Byte i of
// the stream has the value i mod 256, which lets the reader verify the order.
func transfer() {
	const total = 1 << 20

	p := newPipe(16, 4096)

	go func() {
		defer p.closeWriter()

		chunk := make([]byte, 100_000)

		for sent := 0; sent < total; sent += len(chunk) {
			chunk = chunk[:min(len(chunk), total-sent)]

			for i := range chunk {
				chunk[i] = byte(sent + i)
			}

			if _, err := p.write(chunk); err != nil {
				return
			}
		}
	}()

	buf := make([]byte, 30_000)
	received, inOrder := 0, true

	for n := p.read(buf); n > 0; n = p.read(buf) {
		for i, b := range buf[:n] {
			inOrder = inOrder && b == byte(received+i)
		}

		received += n
	}

	fmt.Printf("1048576 bytes written: %d bytes read, in order: %v\n", received, inOrder)
	fmt.Printf("write end closed: read returns %d\n", p.read(buf))

	p.closeReader()

	_, err := p.write([]byte("hello"))
	fmt.Printf("read end closed: write fails with %v\n", err)
}


func main() {
	smallRing()
	fmt.Println()
	kernelSize()
	fmt.Println()
	transfer()
}

Listing 1.48 The complete handpipe, in Rust. code/rust/handpipe/src/main.rs

//! Builds a pipe by hand, with the same parts the kernel uses: a ring of
//! pages for the bytes, a lock, a place for a reader to sleep and a place for
//! a writer to sleep, and a count of the open ends.
//!
//! It traces a small ring call by call, repeats the capacity measurement of
//! pipefacts on a ring of the kernel's size, and sends 1048576 bytes from a
//! writer thread to a reader.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p handpipe
//! ```

use std::fmt;
use std::thread;

use parking_lot::{Condvar, Mutex};

/// One slot of the ring: a block of memory, and the position and length of
/// the bytes in it that have not been read yet.
struct Page {
    data: Vec<u8>,
    offset: usize,
    length: usize,
}

/// The storage of a pipe. `head` counts the pages ever put into use and
/// `tail` counts the pages ever emptied, so `head - tail` pages are in use,
/// and a counter's remainder after division by the number of slots is its
/// slot.
struct Ring {
    pages: Vec<Page>,
    head: usize,
    tail: usize,
}

impl Ring {
    fn new(slots: usize, page_size: usize) -> Ring {
        let pages = (0..slots)
            .map(|_| Page {
                data: vec![0; page_size],
                offset: 0,
                length: 0,
            })
            .collect();

        Ring {
            pages,
            head: 0,
            tail: 0,
        }
    }

    fn empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.head == self.tail
    }

    fn full(&self) -> bool {
        self.head - self.tail == self.pages.len()
    }

    /// The page that a counter refers to.
    fn slot(&mut self, counter: usize) -> &mut Page {
        let slots = self.pages.len();

        &mut self.pages[counter % slots]
    }
}

/// Copies as many bytes as both slices allow and returns the count.
fn copy(to: &mut [u8], from: &[u8]) -> usize {
    let n = to.len().min(from.len());
    to[..n].copy_from_slice(&from[..n]);

    n
}

impl Ring {
    /// Copies as much of `data` as the ring has room for and returns the
    /// number of bytes it copied. The bytes go first into the unused end of
    /// the newest page, then into free slots, one page each.
    fn put(&mut self, data: &[u8]) -> usize {
        let mut copied = 0;

        if !self.empty() {
            let newest = self.slot(self.head - 1);
            let end = newest.offset + newest.length;

            let n = copy(&mut newest.data[end..], data);
            newest.length += n;
            copied += n;
        }

        while copied < data.len() && !self.full() {
            let next = self.slot(self.head);
            next.offset = 0;
            next.length = copy(&mut next.data, &data[copied..]);

            copied += next.length;
            self.head += 1;
        }

        copied
    }
}

impl Ring {
    /// Moves up to `buf.len()` of the oldest bytes into `buf` and returns the
    /// number it moved. A slot becomes free when the last byte of its page
    /// has been taken.
    fn take(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> usize {
        let mut moved = 0;

        while moved < buf.len() && !self.empty() {
            let oldest = self.slot(self.tail);
            let unread = oldest.offset..oldest.offset + oldest.length;

            let n = copy(&mut buf[moved..], &oldest.data[unread]);
            oldest.offset += n;
            oldest.length -= n;
            moved += n;

            if oldest.length == 0 {
                self.tail += 1;
            }
        }

        moved
    }
}

/// What a write returns when no reader is left.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct BrokenPipe;

impl fmt::Display for BrokenPipe {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str("EPIPE")
    }
}

/// What the lock guards: the ring and the count of the open ends.
struct State {
    ring: Ring,
    readers: usize,
    writers: usize,
}

/// A ring shared by a reader and a writer thread. `readable` is where a reader sleeps while
/// the ring is empty, and `writable` is where a writer sleeps while the ring
/// is full.
struct Pipe {
    state: Mutex<State>,
    readable: Condvar,
    writable: Condvar,
}

impl Pipe {
    fn new(slots: usize, page_size: usize) -> Pipe {
        let state = State {
            ring: Ring::new(slots, page_size),
            readers: 1,
            writers: 1,
        };

        Pipe {
            state: Mutex::new(state),
            readable: Condvar::new(),
            writable: Condvar::new(),
        }
    }
}

impl Pipe {
    /// Returns when every byte of `data` is in the ring, or when no reader is
    /// left. While the ring is full it sleeps on `writable`.
    fn write(&self, data: &[u8]) -> Result<usize, BrokenPipe> {
        let mut state = self.state.lock();
        let mut written = 0;

        while written < data.len() {
            if state.readers == 0 {
                return Err(BrokenPipe);
            }

            let n = state.ring.put(&data[written..]);
            written += n;

            if n == 0 {
                self.writable.wait(&mut state);
                continue;
            }

            self.readable.notify_all();
        }

        Ok(written)
    }
}

impl Pipe {
    /// Returns as soon as it has moved at least one byte into `buf`. While
    /// the ring is empty and a writer exists it sleeps on `readable`. It
    /// returns 0 when the ring is empty and no writer is left: the end of the
    /// stream.
    fn read(&self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> usize {
        let mut state = self.state.lock();

        self.readable
            .wait_while(&mut state, |state| state.ring.empty() && state.writers > 0);

        let n = state.ring.take(buf);

        if n > 0 {
            self.writable.notify_all();
        }

        n
    }
}

impl Pipe {
    /// Gives up a write end. A reader asleep on an empty ring wakes and finds
    /// that no writer is left.
    fn close_writer(&self) {
        self.state.lock().writers -= 1;
        self.readable.notify_all();
    }

    /// Gives up a read end. A writer asleep on a full ring wakes and finds
    /// that no reader is left.
    fn close_reader(&self) {
        self.state.lock().readers -= 1;
        self.writable.notify_all();
    }
}

impl Ring {
    /// Renders the ring as one cell per slot: the unread bytes in its page,
    /// or a dot for a free slot.
    fn picture(&self) -> String {
        let slots = self.pages.len();
        let mut cells = vec![".".to_string(); slots];

        for counter in self.tail..self.head {
            cells[counter % slots] = self.pages[counter % slots].length.to_string();
        }

        format!("[{}]", cells.join(" "))
    }
}

/// Applies the calls of the trace to a ring of 4 pages of 8 bytes and prints
/// the ring after each.
fn small_ring() {
    let mut ring = Ring::new(4, 8);
    let mut buf = [0u8; 32];

    let calls = [
        ("put", 12),
        ("take", 3),
        ("put", 30),
        ("take", 5),
        ("put", 30),
    ];

    println!("ring of 4 pages of 8 bytes");

    for (op, n) in calls {
        let done = match op {
            "put" => ring.put(&buf[..n]),
            _ => ring.take(&mut buf[..n]),
        };

        println!(
            "{op:<4} {n:2}: {done:2} bytes   head {}  tail {}   {}",
            ring.head,
            ring.tail,
            ring.picture()
        );
    }
}

/// Puts whole blocks into the ring until it accepts none and returns the
/// number of bytes accepted.
fn fill(ring: &mut Ring, block: &[u8]) -> usize {
    let mut total = 0;

    loop {
        let n = ring.put(block);

        if n == 0 {
            return total;
        }

        total += n;
    }
}

/// Repeats the capacity measurement of pipefacts on a ring with the kernel's
/// dimensions: 16 pages of 4096 bytes.
fn kernel_size() {
    const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

    let mut ring = Ring::new(16, PAGE_SIZE);
    let mut block = [0u8; PAGE_SIZE];

    let steps = [
        (0, "new pipe"),
        (1, "after reading 1 byte"),
        (PAGE_SIZE - 1, "after reading 4096 bytes in total"),
    ];

    for (count, label) in steps {
        ring.take(&mut block[..count]);

        let accepted = fill(&mut ring, &block);
        println!("{label}: {accepted} bytes accepted");
    }
}

/// Sends one megabyte through a pipe of the kernel's size. Byte `i` of the
/// stream has the value `i` mod 256, which lets the reader verify the order.
fn transfer() {
    const TOTAL: usize = 1 << 20;

    let pipe = Pipe::new(16, 4096);
    let mut buf = vec![0u8; 30_000];

    thread::scope(|scope| {
        scope.spawn(|| {
            let mut chunk = vec![0u8; 100_000];

            for sent in (0..TOTAL).step_by(chunk.len()) {
                chunk.truncate(TOTAL - sent);

                for (i, byte) in chunk.iter_mut().enumerate() {
                    *byte = (sent + i) as u8;
                }

                if pipe.write(&chunk).is_err() {
                    break;
                }
            }

            pipe.close_writer();
        });

        let (mut received, mut in_order) = (0, true);

        loop {
            let n = pipe.read(&mut buf);

            if n == 0 {
                break;
            }

            for (i, byte) in buf[..n].iter().enumerate() {
                in_order = in_order && *byte == (received + i) as u8;
            }

            received += n;
        }

        println!("1048576 bytes written: {received} bytes read, in order: {in_order}");
    });

    println!("write end closed: read returns {}", pipe.read(&mut buf));

    pipe.close_reader();

    if let Err(error) = pipe.write(b"hello") {
        println!("read end closed: write fails with {error}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    small_ring();
    println!();
    kernel_size();
    println!();
    transfer();
}

Listing 1.49 The complete pipeline, in Go. code/go/pipeline/main.go

// Command pipeline runs `a | b | c` the way a shell does: each command's
// standard output is the write end of a pipe, and the next command's standard
// input is the read end of the same pipe.
//
// It runs the pipelines listed in main and prints the last command's output and how each
// command terminated.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./pipeline
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
	"syscall"
)


// start runs the commands of a pipeline. Command i writes to pipe i and reads
// from pipe i-1; the first command reads /dev/null. It returns the commands
// and the read end of the last pipe.
func start(stages [][]string) ([]*exec.Cmd, *os.File, error) {
	var input *os.File
	commands := make([]*exec.Cmd, 0, len(stages))

	for _, stage := range stages {
		reader, writer, err := os.Pipe()

		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}

		command := exec.Command(stage[0], stage[1:]...)
		command.Stdout = writer

		if input != nil {
			command.Stdin = input
		}

		err = command.Start()

		// The child holds its own copies of both ends. Closing the parent's
		// copies leaves the child's as the only ones.
		writer.Close()

		if input != nil {
			input.Close()
		}

		if err != nil {
			reader.Close()

			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", stage[0], err)
		}

		commands, input = append(commands, command), reader
	}

	return commands, input, nil
}


// ending waits for a command and reports how it terminated: with an exit
// status, or by a signal.
func ending(command *exec.Cmd) string {
	command.Wait()

	state := command.ProcessState

	if status, ok := state.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && status.Signaled() {
		return fmt.Sprintf("killed by signal %d", status.Signal())
	}

	return fmt.Sprintf("exited with status %d", state.ExitCode())
}


// run starts a pipeline, reads the last command's output to the end of the
// stream, and prints the output and each command's termination.
func run(line string) error {
	var stages [][]string

	for _, stage := range strings.Split(line, " | ") {
		stages = append(stages, strings.Fields(stage))
	}

	commands, output, err := start(stages)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer output.Close()

	text, err := io.ReadAll(output)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Println(line)
	fmt.Printf("  output: %s\n", strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(text)), " "))

	for i, command := range commands {
		fmt.Printf("  %s: %s\n", stages[i][0], ending(command))
	}

	return nil
}


func main() {
	for _, line := range []string{"seq 1 100000 | grep 7 | wc -l", "yes | head -n 3"} {
		if err := run(line); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 1.50 The complete pipeline, in Rust. code/rust/pipeline/src/main.rs

//! Runs `a | b | c` the way a shell does: each command's standard output is
//! the write end of a pipe, and the next command's standard input is the read
//! end of the same pipe.
//!
//! It runs the pipelines listed in main and prints the last command's output and how each
//! command terminated.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p pipeline
//! ```

use std::io::{self, PipeReader, Read};
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::process::{Child, Command, Stdio};

/// Runs the commands of a pipeline. Command `i` writes to pipe `i` and reads
/// from pipe `i - 1`; the first command reads /dev/null. Returns the children
/// and the read end of the last pipe.
fn start(stages: &[Vec<&str>]) -> io::Result<(Vec<Child>, PipeReader)> {
    let mut input = None;
    let mut children = Vec::with_capacity(stages.len());

    for stage in stages {
        let (reader, writer) = io::pipe()?;
        let stdin = input.take().map_or_else(Stdio::null, Stdio::from);

        // The `Command` owns the parent's copies of both ends. It is dropped
        // when this statement ends, which closes them and leaves the child's
        // copies as the only ones.
        let child = Command::new(stage[0])
            .args(&stage[1..])
            .stdin(stdin)
            .stdout(writer)
            .spawn()?;

        children.push(child);
        input = Some(reader);
    }

    let output = input.ok_or(io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput)?;

    Ok((children, output))
}

/// Waits for a command and reports how it terminated: with an exit status,
/// or by a signal.
fn ending(child: &mut Child) -> io::Result<String> {
    let status = child.wait()?;

    let text = match (status.signal(), status.code()) {
        (Some(signal), _) => format!("killed by signal {signal}"),
        (None, Some(code)) => format!("exited with status {code}"),
        (None, None) => status.to_string(),
    };

    Ok(text)
}

/// Starts a pipeline, reads the last command's output to the end of the
/// stream, and prints the output and each command's termination.
fn run(line: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    let stages: Vec<Vec<&str>> = line
        .split(" | ")
        .map(|stage| stage.split_whitespace().collect())
        .collect();

    let (mut children, mut output) = start(&stages)?;

    let mut text = String::new();
    output.read_to_string(&mut text)?;

    let words: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    println!("{line}");
    println!("  output: {}", words.join(" "));

    for (stage, child) in stages.iter().zip(&mut children) {
        println!("  {}: {}", stage[0], ending(child)?);
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    run("seq 1 100000 | grep 7 | wc -l")?;
    run("yes | head -n 3")
}

Summary

  • A pipe is a one-way byte stream between processes, buffered in kernel memory and reached through a read end and a write end.
  • The buffer is a ring of 16 slots, each referring to one page: 65536 bytes with 4096-byte pages.
  • head counts pages added and tail counts pages removed. Space is released a whole page at a time, when the last byte of the oldest page has been read.
  • A write to a full pipe blocks until a read releases a page. This limits a writer to the rate of its reader and bounds the memory between them.
  • A thread woken from a wait tests its condition again, because a wake-up reports that the state changed and says nothing about which change occurred.
  • read returns 0 when the pipe is empty and no descriptor for the write end remains.
  • write raises SIGPIPE and fails with EPIPE when no descriptor for the read end remains.
  • A program that builds a pipeline closes its own copy of each pipe end after passing it to a child. A copy left open prevents the end of the stream from being reported.

References

  • pipe(7) and pipe(2), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pipe.7.html
  • fs/pipe.c and include/linux/pipe_fs_i.h, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/fs/pipe.c
  • M. Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface, No Starch Press, 2010, chapter 44.
  • D. M. Ritchie, “The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System”, AT&T Bell Laboratories Technical Journal, 63(8), 1984.
  • Go, package os/signal, the section on SIGPIPE: https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal

File Descriptors

Every read, write and close in a program takes a small integer as its first argument. That integer is a file descriptor. It is the only handle a process has on a file, a pipe, a terminal or a network connection, and the kernel translates it on every call into the object the process means.

In this chapter, we will follow that translation from the integer to the bytes on disk. We will meet the kernel structures on the way, one at a time and in the order a read visits them: the descriptor table of the process, the open file, the directory entry, and the inode. For each structure we will look at its definition in the kernel source, say what each field is for, and confirm its behaviour with an experiment. Then we will write fdfacts, which measures all of this on a running kernel, and fdtable, a model of the same structures that gives the same results.

This chapter covers

  • why a process refers to a file by a number
  • the path of one read through the kernel
  • the descriptor table: struct fdtable, the lowest-free-number rule, and the limit on descriptors
  • the open file: struct file, the offset, and the status flags
  • names and files: directory entries, struct inode, and hard links
  • reference counts: when an open file and an inode are released
  • what dup, fork and exec do to descriptors
  • shell redirection, including 2>&1
  • how to inspect the descriptors of a running process

Why a number

A program runs in user mode, in which the processor lets it touch only its own memory. The kernel runs in kernel mode and keeps its data in memory that user-mode code cannot read or write. A system call is the controlled way from one to the other: the program puts a call number and arguments in registers and executes an instruction that switches the processor to kernel mode at a fixed entry point.

The objects that describe an open file live in kernel memory. The kernel cannot hand a process a pointer to them, because the process could not use the pointer and must not be able to forge one. It keeps a table for each process and gives the process an index into that table. The process can pass any integer it likes. The kernel looks the integer up in the caller’s own table, so a process can only ever name the files that the kernel has put there.

By convention the first 3 entries have fixed roles: descriptor 0 is the standard input, 1 the standard output, and 2 the standard error. A program started from a terminal finds all 3 referring to that terminal.

One read, step by step

Suppose a process has opened a file and received descriptor 3, and now calls read(3, buf, 100). The kernel does the following.

  1. It takes entry 3 of the calling process’s descriptor table. The entry is a pointer to a struct file, the kernel’s record of one open file. An empty entry ends the call with the error EBADF, “bad file descriptor”.
  2. It reads the current position in the file from the struct file. This position is the offset: the number of bytes from the start of the file at which the next read or write takes place.
  3. It calls the read function of whatever the file is. The struct file holds a table of functions, and a disk file, a pipe and a socket each supply their own.
  4. For a disk file, that function finds the file’s inode, the kernel’s record of the file itself, and through it the cached pages of the file. The page cache is the subject of chapter 8.
  5. It copies up to 100 bytes from those pages into buf, in the memory of the process.
  6. It adds the number of bytes copied to the offset and returns that number.

The steps name 3 objects: the table entry, the open file, and the inode. The rest of the chapter takes them in that order. The question to keep in mind for each is which state it holds, because that decides what is shared when a descriptor is duplicated or inherited.

The descriptor table

Each process has a struct files_struct, which contains its descriptor table. The table itself is a struct fdtable. These are the definitions from include/linux/fdtable.h in Linux 5.15, with the fields that concern locking left out.

struct fdtable {
        unsigned int max_fds;          /* number of entries in fd[] */
        struct file **fd;              /* the table: one pointer per descriptor */
        unsigned long *close_on_exec;  /* bitmap: descriptors closed by exec */
        unsigned long *open_fds;       /* bitmap: descriptors in use */
        /* ... */
};

struct files_struct {
        atomic_t count;                /* processes and threads sharing this table */
        struct fdtable *fdt;           /* the current table */
        unsigned int next_fd;          /* where the search for a free number starts */
        struct file *fd_array[64];     /* a first table, large enough for most programs */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
fdAn array of pointers. fd[3] is the open file behind descriptor 3, or NULL.
open_fds1 bit per descriptor, set while the number is in use.
close_on_exec1 bit per descriptor: the close-on-exec flag, described below.
max_fdsThe current length of fd. The table starts with 64 entries and is replaced by a larger one when a higher number is needed.
countHow many tasks use this table. The threads of a process share 1 table.

The table gives rise to 2 rules that every Unix program depends on.

A new descriptor gets the lowest free number. The kernel searches open_fds for the first clear bit, starting at next_fd. After a process closes descriptor 0, the next open returns 0.

The number of descriptors is limited. Each process has a resource limit, RLIMIT_NOFILE, and an open that would need a number at or above it fails with EMFILE, “too many open files”. ulimit -n shows the limit in a shell. On this machine it is 1048576 for a process started from the terminal, and many systems set 1024. The kernel as a whole has a second limit, on the number of open files in all processes together. /proc/sys/fs/file-nr shows the current number first:

$ cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr
17312	0	9223372036854775807

A server that forgets to close descriptors, a descriptor leak, eventually hits EMFILE and can accept no more connections, although memory and CPU are free.

The open file

The pointers in the table refer to struct file objects. The POSIX standard calls this object an open file description, and the name is worth learning because the manual pages use it. A struct file is created by each successful open, and also by pipe, socket and accept. This is the definition from include/linux/fs.h, reduced to the fields this chapter uses.

struct file {
        struct path f_path;                    /* the directory entry it was opened by */
        struct inode *f_inode;                 /* the file itself */
        const struct file_operations *f_op;    /* read, write, ... for this kind of file */
        atomic_long_t f_count;                 /* references to this struct file */
        unsigned int f_flags;                  /* O_APPEND, O_NONBLOCK, ... */
        fmode_t f_mode;                        /* opened for reading, writing, or both */
        loff_t f_pos;                          /* the offset */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
f_posThe offset. read and write start here and advance it. lseek sets it.
f_flagsThe status flags given to open, such as O_APPEND (every write goes to the end of the file) and O_NONBLOCK (calls return EAGAIN where they would block). fcntl with F_GETFL and F_SETFL reads and changes them.
f_modeWhether the file was opened for reading, for writing, or both. A write on a file opened read-only fails with EBADF.
f_countThe number of references to this struct file: table entries in any process, plus system calls in progress.
f_inodeThe inode of the file.
f_opA table of function pointers. read calls f_op->read_iter, write calls f_op->write_iter.

f_op is the mechanism behind the phrase “everything is a file”. The system call read contains no code for disks, pipes or sockets. It calls through f_op, and each kind of object installs its own functions when the struct file is created: ext4 for a file on disk, the pipe code of chapter 1 for a pipe, TCP for the socket of chapter 10. A program that reads descriptor 0 therefore works unchanged whether descriptor 0 is a terminal, a file or a pipe.

The important point for the rest of the chapter is where the offset lives. It is in the struct file, and neither in the table entry nor in the inode. Table entries that point to the same struct file share an offset. Separate struct file objects for the same file on disk each have their own.

Names, directory entries and inodes

A struct file refers to an inode. The inode is the file: its type, its owner, its permissions, its size, its timestamps, and the location of its data. It is identified by a number, the inode number, which is unique within a file system.

An inode contains no name. Names are kept in directories. A directory is itself a file whose contents are a list of directory entries, each a pair of a name and an inode number. Opening /tmp/x/report.txt means reading the directory /, finding the entry tmp and its inode, reading that directory, and so on to the last name. The kernel caches each step in a struct dentry, so that a path which has been used recently is resolved without reading directories from disk.

struct dentry {
        struct dentry *d_parent;       /* the directory that contains this entry */
        struct qstr d_name;            /* the name: a single component of a path */
        struct inode *d_inode;         /* the inode the name refers to */
        /* ... */
};

struct inode {
        umode_t i_mode;                /* type (file, directory, ...) and permissions */
        kuid_t i_uid;                  /* owner */
        kgid_t i_gid;                  /* group */
        unsigned long i_ino;           /* the inode number */
        unsigned int i_nlink;          /* directory entries that refer to this inode */
        loff_t i_size;                 /* size in bytes */
        struct timespec64 i_atime;     /* last access */
        struct timespec64 i_mtime;     /* last change of the contents */
        struct timespec64 i_ctime;     /* last change of the inode */
        blkcnt_t i_blocks;             /* disk space used, in 512-byte units */
        atomic_t i_count;              /* references from inside the kernel */
        const struct file_operations *i_fop;   /* copied to f_op at open */
        struct address_space *i_mapping;       /* the cached pages of the file */
        /* ... */
};

stat prints the fields of an inode, and ls -i prints inode numbers. Since the name is outside the inode, several directory entries can hold the same inode number. Such an entry is a hard link, created by ln or the link system call. On this machine:

$ echo hello > report.txt
$ ln report.txt copy.txt
$ ls -li
19927765 -rw-rw-r-- 2 jetson jetson 6 Oct 12 22:56 copy.txt
19927765 -rw-rw-r-- 2 jetson jetson 6 Oct 12 22:56 report.txt
$ stat report.txt
  File: report.txt
  Size: 6         	Blocks: 8          IO Block: 4096   regular file
Device: 10301h/66305d	Inode: 19927765    Links: 2
Access: (0664/-rw-rw-r--)  Uid: ( 1000/  jetson)   Gid: ( 1000/  jetson)

Both names show inode 19927765. The 2 after the permissions, Links: 2 in the output of stat, is i_nlink. The names are equal in every respect: neither is the original, and a change made through one is visible through the other, because there is a single inode and a single copy of the data.

Several everyday facts follow from this split.

  • Renaming a file within a file system is fast at any size. rename changes a directory entry and does not touch the inode or the data.
  • Permissions belong to the inode, so they are the same through every name.
  • Removing a file is called unlink because it removes a link: a directory entry. What happens to the inode is the subject of the next section.

Figure 2.4 puts the structures together.

What is shared

We can now answer the question a programmer has to ask: when a process has 2 descriptors, what do they share? It depends on how the second descriptor came to exist.

The second descriptor comes fromNew table entryNew struct fileThe descriptors share
dup or dup2yesnothe offset, the status flags, and the file
fork, in the childyesnothe offset, the status flags, and the file
a second open of the same nameyesyesonly the file

The reason for sharing the offset through dup and fork is sequential output. When a shell runs (date; ls) > file, both commands inherit the same struct file, and ls continues at the offset where date stopped. If each had its own offset, the second command would overwrite the output of the first. We will measure exactly that below.

The close-on-exec flag is deliberately excluded from sharing. It tells the kernel to close the descriptor when the process executes a new program, and it is stored in the close_on_exec bitmap of the table, outside the struct file. A program can therefore keep a descriptor for itself and still pass a duplicate of it to a child.

Lifetimes

An object in the kernel is released when nothing refers to it any more, and each of the objects of this chapter keeps a count for that purpose.

ObjectCountRaised byLowered byAt 0
struct filef_countopen, dup, forkclose, exit of a processthe open file is closed, and its reference to the inode is dropped
inodei_nlinklink, creating the fileunlink, rename over the namethe file has no name
inodeopen counteach struct file that refers to itclosing a struct filethe file is not open

A struct file is closed when the last descriptor for it is closed. close on a descriptor that was duplicated or inherited only lowers f_count. This is the rule that chapter 1 needed: a pipe reports the end of the stream when the last descriptor for its write end is gone, in whichever process that descriptor was.

An inode and its data are freed when it has no name and is not open. Both conditions are required. A file that is unlinked while a process has it open keeps its inode and its data until that process closes it.

The kernel shows such a file under /proc. Here a shell opens report.txt on descriptor 7 and then removes both names:

$ exec 7< report.txt
$ rm report.txt copy.txt
$ ls -l /proc/$$/fd/7
7 -> /tmp/x/report.txt (deleted)
$ cat <&7
hello

The consequences are practical. A program can create a temporary file, open it and unlink it at once, and the file disappears when the program ends, however it ends. And a large log file that is deleted while a server still writes to it continues to occupy the disk, which is the usual explanation when df reports a full disk and du cannot find the files.

A file that is deleted while a process has it open keeps its inode, its data and its disk space until that process closes it.

fork and exec

fork gives the child a copy of the parent’s descriptor table. The copy is a new struct fdtable with the same pointers, and f_count of every open file is raised by 1. Parent and child then have independent tables, so either can close or reassign a descriptor without affecting the other, and they share every open file that both still hold.

exec replaces the program and keeps the table, with 1 exception: descriptors whose close-on-exec bit is set are closed. A program sets the bit with the O_CLOEXEC flag of open, or later with fcntl and F_SETFD. Without it, every descriptor a program has open is passed to every program it starts, including descriptors for files those programs have no business with. Go’s standard library and Rust’s standard library set the flag on every descriptor they create, and pass a descriptor to a child only when the program asks for it.

Chapter 3 covers fork and exec themselves.

Measuring descriptors

fdfacts checks the statements of this chapter on a running kernel. It uses golang.org/x/sys/unix in Go and the nix crate with the fs and resource features in Rust.

$ cargo new fdfacts
$ cargo add -p fdfacts nix --features fs,resource

numbers closes descriptor 0 and opens a file.

Listing 2.3 The number of a new descriptor, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// numbers closes descriptor 0, the standard input, and opens a file. The
// kernel gives an open the lowest number that is free.
func numbers(path string) error {
	if err := unix.Close(0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fd, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns %d\n", fd)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.4 The number of a new descriptor, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Closes descriptor 0, the standard input, and opens a file. The kernel
/// gives an open the lowest number that is free.
fn numbers(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    close(0)?;

    let fd = open(path, OFlag::O_RDONLY, Mode::empty())?;
    println!(
        "descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns {}",
        fd.as_raw_fd()
    );

    Ok(())
}

limit lowers RLIMIT_NOFILE to 32 and opens a file until open fails. It reports the highest number it received and the error.

Listing 2.5 The limit on descriptors, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EMFILE.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}

// limit lowers the limit on open descriptors to 32 and opens a file until
// the kernel refuses.
func limit(path string) error {
	var saved unix.Rlimit

	if err := unix.Getrlimit(unix.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &saved); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	lowered := saved
	lowered.Cur = 32

	if err := unix.Setrlimit(unix.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &lowered); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Setrlimit(unix.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &saved)

	var opened []int
	highest := -1

	for {
		fd, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)

		if err != nil {
			fmt.Printf("limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is %d, the next open fails with %s\n",
				highest, name(err))

			break
		}

		opened, highest = append(opened, fd), max(highest, fd)
	}

	for _, fd := range opened {
		unix.Close(fd)
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 2.6 The limit on descriptors, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Lowers the limit on open descriptors to 32 and opens a file until the
/// kernel refuses.
fn limit(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let (soft, hard) = getrlimit(Resource::RLIMIT_NOFILE)?;

    setrlimit(Resource::RLIMIT_NOFILE, 32, hard)?;

    let mut opened = Vec::new();

    let error = loop {
        match open(path, OFlag::O_RDONLY, Mode::empty()) {
            Ok(fd) => opened.push(fd),
            Err(error) => break error,
        }
    };

    let highest = opened.iter().map(AsRawFd::as_raw_fd).fold(-1, i32::max);

    println!(
        "limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is {highest}, the next open fails with {error:?}"
    );

    drop(opened);
    setrlimit(Resource::RLIMIT_NOFILE, soft, hard)?;

    Ok(())
}

offsets opens a file, duplicates the descriptor, and opens the file again. It writes 5 bytes through the first descriptor and reads the offset through the other 2. lseek with a distance of 0 from the current position returns the offset without changing it.

Listing 2.7 The offset through a duplicate and through a second open, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// offset returns the file offset that a descriptor refers to.
func offset(fd int) (int64, error) {
	return unix.Seek(fd, 0, unix.SEEK_CUR)
}

// offsets writes through one descriptor and reads the offset through a
// duplicate of it and through a second open of the same file.
func offsets(path string) error {
	first, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(first)

	duplicate, err := unix.Dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(duplicate)

	second, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(second)

	if _, err := unix.Write(first, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	shared, err := offset(duplicate)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	separate, err := offset(second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate %d, through a second open %d\n",
		shared, separate)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.8 The offset through a duplicate and through a second open, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Returns the file offset that a descriptor refers to.
fn offset(fd: impl AsFd) -> nix::Result<i64> {
    lseek(fd, 0, Whence::SeekCur)
}

/// Writes through one descriptor and reads the offset through a duplicate of
/// it and through a second open of the same file.
fn offsets(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let first = open(path, OFlag::O_WRONLY, Mode::empty())?;
    let duplicate = dup(&first)?;
    let second = open(path, OFlag::O_WRONLY, Mode::empty())?;

    write(&first, b"hello")?;

    let shared = offset(&duplicate)?;
    let separate = offset(&second)?;

    println!(
        "after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate {shared}, through a second open {separate}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

flags sets O_APPEND and close-on-exec on a duplicate and reads both through the original. F_GETFL and F_SETFL address f_flags in the struct file. F_GETFD and F_SETFD address the bitmap in the table.

Listing 2.9 Status flags and descriptor flags, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// flags sets O_APPEND and close-on-exec through a duplicate and reads both
// through the original descriptor.
func flags(path string) error {
	first, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(first)

	duplicate, err := unix.Dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(duplicate)

	if _, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(duplicate), unix.F_SETFL, unix.O_APPEND); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(duplicate), unix.F_SETFD, unix.FD_CLOEXEC); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	status, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(first), unix.F_GETFL, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	descriptor, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(first), unix.F_GETFD, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND %v, close-on-exec %v\n",
		status&unix.O_APPEND != 0, descriptor&unix.FD_CLOEXEC != 0)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.10 Status flags and descriptor flags, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Sets `O_APPEND` and close-on-exec through a duplicate and reads both
/// through the original descriptor.
fn flags(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let first = open(path, OFlag::O_WRONLY, Mode::empty())?;
    let duplicate = dup(&first)?;

    fcntl(&duplicate, FcntlArg::F_SETFL(OFlag::O_APPEND))?;
    fcntl(&duplicate, FcntlArg::F_SETFD(FdFlag::FD_CLOEXEC))?;

    let status = OFlag::from_bits_truncate(fcntl(&first, FcntlArg::F_GETFL)?);
    let descriptor = FdFlag::from_bits_truncate(fcntl(&first, FcntlArg::F_GETFD)?);

    println!(
        "set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND {}, close-on-exec {}",
        status.contains(OFlag::O_APPEND),
        descriptor.contains(FdFlag::FD_CLOEXEC)
    );

    Ok(())
}

names creates a file, gives it a second name with link, and compares the inode numbers behind the names.

Listing 2.11 A second name for a file, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// inode returns the inode number and the link count of a file.
func inode(path string) (number uint64, links uint64, err error) {
	var status unix.Stat_t

	err = unix.Stat(path, &status)

	return status.Ino, uint64(status.Nlink), err
}

// names gives a file a second name and compares the inodes behind the names.
func names(path string) error {
	first, second := path+".first", path+".second"

	if err := os.WriteFile(first, []byte("hello"), 0o644); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.Remove(first)
	defer os.Remove(second)

	if err := unix.Link(first, second); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	a, _, err := inode(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	b, links, err := inode(second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("a second name for the file: same inode %v, link count %d\n", a == b, links)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.12 A second name for a file, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Gives a file a second name and compares the inodes behind the names.
fn names(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let (first, second) = (path.with_extension("first"), path.with_extension("second"));

    fs::write(&first, "hello")?;
    fs::hard_link(&first, &second)?;

    let (a, b) = (fs::metadata(&first)?, fs::metadata(&second)?);

    println!(
        "a second name for the file: same inode {}, link count {}",
        a.ino() == b.ino(),
        b.nlink()
    );

    fs::remove_file(&first)?;
    fs::remove_file(&second)
}

unlinked opens a file, removes its name, and then reads the link count and the contents through the descriptor.

Listing 2.13 A file removed while it is open, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// unlinked opens a file, removes its only name, and reads through the
// descriptor.
func unlinked(path string) error {
	file := path + ".unlinked"

	if err := os.WriteFile(file, []byte("hello"), 0o644); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fd, err := unix.Open(file, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(fd)

	if err := unix.Unlink(file); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var status unix.Stat_t

	if err := unix.Fstat(fd, &status); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	buf := make([]byte, 16)
	n, err := unix.Read(fd, buf)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the name removed, the file still open: link count %d, read through the descriptor returns %q\n",
		status.Nlink, buf[:n])

	return nil
}

Listing 2.14 A file removed while it is open, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Opens a file, removes its only name, and reads through the descriptor.
fn unlinked(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let name = path.with_extension("unlinked");

    fs::write(&name, "hello")?;

    let mut file = File::open(&name)?;

    fs::remove_file(&name)?;

    let links = file.metadata()?.nlink();
    let mut text = String::new();

    file.read_to_string(&mut text)?;

    println!(
        "the name removed, the file still open: link count {links}, read through the descriptor returns {text:?}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

redirections runs a shell command that writes out to descriptor 1 and then err to descriptor 2, with both descriptors on the same file. In the first run descriptor 2 is a duplicate of descriptor 1. In the other run the file is opened once for each.

Listing 2.15 Descriptors 1 and 2 on the same file, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// redirect runs a command that writes "out" to descriptor 1 and then "err" to
// descriptor 2, with both descriptors on the same file, and returns the
// file's contents.
func redirect(path string, stdout, stderr *os.File) (string, error) {
	command := exec.Command("sh", "-c", "echo out; echo err >&2")
	command.Stdout, command.Stderr = stdout, stderr

	if err := command.Run(); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	text, err := os.ReadFile(path)

	return strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(text)), " "), err
}

// redirections compares `> file 2>&1`, where descriptor 2 is a duplicate of
// descriptor 1, with `> file 2> file`, where the file is opened once for each.
func redirections(path string) error {
	stdout, err := os.Create(path)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer stdout.Close()

	text, err := redirect(path, stdout, stdout)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2>&1: the file holds %q\n", text)

	first, err := os.Create(path)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer first.Close()

	second, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer second.Close()

	text, err = redirect(path, first, second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2> file: the file holds %q\n", text)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.16 Descriptors 1 and 2 on the same file, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

/// Runs a command that writes "out" to descriptor 1 and then "err" to
/// descriptor 2, with both descriptors on the same file, and returns the
/// file's contents.
fn redirect(path: &Path, stdout: File, stderr: File) -> io::Result<String> {
    Command::new("sh")
        .args(["-c", "echo out; echo err >&2"])
        .stdout(stdout)
        .stderr(stderr)
        .status()?;

    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;
    let words: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    Ok(words.join(" "))
}

/// Compares `> file 2>&1`, where descriptor 2 is a duplicate of descriptor 1,
/// with `> file 2> file`, where the file is opened once for each.
fn redirections(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let stdout = File::create(path)?;
    let stderr = stdout.try_clone()?;

    let text = redirect(path, stdout, stderr)?;
    println!("> file 2>&1: the file holds {text:?}");

    let first = File::create(path)?;
    let second = OpenOptions::new().write(true).open(path)?;

    let text = redirect(path, first, second)?;
    println!("> file 2> file: the file holds {text:?}");

    Ok(())
}

Modelling the tables

fdtable implements the structures of this chapter in user space, with the same reference counts, and runs the experiments of fdfacts on them.

Low-level design: fdtable

TypeKernel structureFieldsInvariant
inodestruct inodenumber, data, links, opensfreed when links and opens are both 0
filesystema directory and the inode tablenames, inodesevery name maps to an inode in inodes
descriptionstruct filefile, offset, appendMode, refsclosed when refs is 0
descriptoran entry of fd[] and its close-on-exec bitopen, cloexecbelongs to 1 table
processstruct files_structtable, limitthe index of an entry is the descriptor number
OperationBehaviourError
create(name), link(old, new), unlink(name)add and remove names; unlink frees the inode when nothing else refers to itENOENT
install(description)places a description at the lowest free indexEMFILE at the limit
open(name)looks the name up, creates a description with offset 0, installs itENOENT, EMFILE
dup(fd), dup2(from, to)install an existing description againEBADF
close(fd)frees the entry; closes the description at the last referenceEBADF
read(fd, n), write(fd, data)use and advance the description’s offsetEBADF
fork()copies the table and counts every copy
exec()closes the entries that have cloexec set

The Go version links the objects with pointers, as the kernel does. The Rust version keeps the inodes and the open file descriptions in tables owned by a Kernel value and refers to them by number, which avoids shared mutable ownership.

An inode has its contents and its 2 counts.

Listing 2.17 The imports of fdtable, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"strings"
)

Listing 2.18 The imports of fdtable, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fmt;

Listing 2.19 The inode, and the tables that hold inodes, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
var (
	errBadDescriptor = errors.New("EBADF")
	errTooManyFiles  = errors.New("EMFILE")
	errNoEntry       = errors.New("ENOENT")
)

// An inode is a file: its number, its contents, and 2 reference counts.
// links counts the names that refer to it, and opens counts the open file
// descriptions that refer to it.
type inode struct {
	number int
	data   []byte
	links  int
	opens  int
}

// A filesystem holds the inodes and a single directory, which maps names to
// inodes.
type filesystem struct {
	names  map[string]*inode
	inodes map[int]*inode
	next   int
}

func newFilesystem() *filesystem {
	return &filesystem{names: map[string]*inode{}, inodes: map[int]*inode{}, next: 1}
}

// allocate returns a new inode with no name.
func (fs *filesystem) allocate() *inode {
	file := &inode{number: fs.next}
	fs.inodes[file.number] = file
	fs.next++

	return file
}

Listing 2.20 The inode, and the tables that hold inodes, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

/// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Error {
    BadDescriptor,
    TooManyFiles,
    NoEntry,
}

impl fmt::Display for Error {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str(match self {
            Error::BadDescriptor => "EBADF",
            Error::TooManyFiles => "EMFILE",
            Error::NoEntry => "ENOENT",
        })
    }
}

/// A file: its contents and 2 reference counts. `links` counts the names
/// that refer to it, and `opens` counts the open file descriptions that refer
/// to it. Its number is its key in the kernel's table of inodes.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Inode {
    data: Vec<u8>,
    links: u32,
    opens: u32,
}

/// The kernel's tables: a single directory that maps names to inode numbers,
/// the inodes, and every open file description.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Kernel {
    names: HashMap<&'static str, u64>,
    inodes: HashMap<u64, Inode>,
    open_files: Vec<Description>,
    next: u64,
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns the number of a new inode with no name.
    fn allocate(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.next += 1;
        self.inodes.insert(self.next, Inode::default());

        self.next
    }

    fn inode(&mut self, number: u64) -> Result<&mut Inode, Error> {
        self.inodes.get_mut(&number).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)
    }
}

create, link and unlink change the directory and the link count. release is the single place where an inode is freed, and it requires both counts to be 0.

Listing 2.21 Names: create, link, unlink, and release, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// create makes an empty file with one name.
func (fs *filesystem) create(name string) *inode {
	file := fs.allocate()
	file.links = 1
	fs.names[name] = file

	return file
}

// link adds a second name for an existing file.
func (fs *filesystem) link(existing, added string) error {
	file, ok := fs.names[existing]

	if !ok {
		return errNoEntry
	}

	file.links++
	fs.names[added] = file

	return nil
}

// unlink removes a name. The file itself is removed only when release finds
// no other reference to it.
func (fs *filesystem) unlink(name string) error {
	file, ok := fs.names[name]

	if !ok {
		return errNoEntry
	}

	delete(fs.names, name)
	file.links--
	fs.release(file)

	return nil
}

// release frees an inode that has no name and is not open.
func (fs *filesystem) release(file *inode) {
	if file.links == 0 && file.opens == 0 {
		delete(fs.inodes, file.number)
	}
}

Listing 2.22 Names: create, link, unlink, and release, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Makes an empty file with one name and returns its inode number.
    fn create(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> Result<u64, Error> {
        let number = self.allocate();

        self.inode(number)?.links = 1;
        self.names.insert(name, number);

        Ok(number)
    }

    /// Adds a second name for an existing file.
    fn link(&mut self, existing: &str, added: &'static str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let number = *self.names.get(existing).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        self.inode(number)?.links += 1;
        self.names.insert(added, number);

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Removes a name. The file itself is removed only when `release` finds
    /// no other reference to it.
    fn unlink(&mut self, name: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let number = self.names.remove(name).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        self.inode(number)?.links -= 1;
        self.release(number);

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Frees an inode that has no name and is not open.
    fn release(&mut self, number: u64) {
        if let Some(file) = self.inodes.get(&number)
            && file.links == 0
            && file.opens == 0
        {
            self.inodes.remove(&number);
        }
    }
}

The description corresponds to struct file, and the descriptor to a table entry together with its close-on-exec bit.

Listing 2.23 The description, the descriptor, and the process, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// A description is an open file description: the state created by one open.
// refs counts the descriptors, in all processes, that refer to it.
type description struct {
	file       *inode
	offset     int
	appendMode bool
	refs       int
}

// A descriptor is one entry of a process's table. The close-on-exec flag
// belongs to the entry.
type descriptor struct {
	open    *description
	cloexec bool
}

// A process is its descriptor table. The index of an entry is the file
// descriptor, a nil entry is a free number, and limit is the number of
// entries the process may use.
type process struct {
	fs    *filesystem
	table []*descriptor
	limit int
}

// newProcess returns a process with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 open on a
// terminal, which is a file without a name.
func newProcess(fs *filesystem) *process {
	p := &process{fs: fs, limit: 1024}
	terminal := &description{file: fs.allocate()}
	terminal.file.opens = 1

	for range 3 {
		p.install(terminal)
	}

	return p
}

Listing 2.24 The description, the descriptor, and the process, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

/// An open file description: the state created by one open. `file` is the
/// number of its inode, and `refs` counts the descriptors, in all processes,
/// that refer to it.
struct Description {
    file: u64,
    offset: usize,
    append_mode: bool,
    refs: u32,
}

/// One entry of a process's table. `open` is the index of a description in
/// the kernel's table. The close-on-exec flag belongs to the entry.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Descriptor {
    open: usize,
    cloexec: bool,
}

/// A process is its descriptor table. The index of an entry is the file
/// descriptor, `None` is a free number, and `limit` is the number of entries
/// the process may use.
struct Process {
    table: Vec<Option<Descriptor>>,
    limit: usize,
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Adds a description for an inode and returns its index.
    fn describe(&mut self, file: u64) -> usize {
        self.open_files.push(Description {
            file,
            offset: 0,
            append_mode: false,
            refs: 0,
        });

        self.open_files.len() - 1
    }

    /// Returns a process with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 open on a terminal,
    /// which is a file without a name.
    fn process(&mut self) -> Result<Process, Error> {
        let mut process = Process {
            table: Vec::new(),
            limit: 1024,
        };

        let terminal = self.allocate();
        let open = self.describe(terminal);

        self.inode(terminal)?.opens = 1;

        for _ in 0..3 {
            self.install(&mut process, open)?;
        }

        Ok(process)
    }
}

install implements both rules of the descriptor table: the lowest free number and the limit. open creates a description, and dup installs an existing one, which is the whole difference between them.

Listing 2.25 Creating descriptors, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// install puts a description in the lowest free entry, counts the new
// reference, and returns the number of the entry.
func (p *process) install(open *description) (int, error) {
	fd := 0

	for fd < len(p.table) && p.table[fd] != nil {
		fd++
	}

	if fd >= p.limit {
		return 0, errTooManyFiles
	}

	if fd == len(p.table) {
		p.table = append(p.table, nil)
	}

	open.refs++
	p.table[fd] = &descriptor{open: open}

	return fd, nil
}

// lookup returns the entry of a descriptor.
func (p *process) lookup(fd int) (*descriptor, error) {
	if fd < 0 || fd >= len(p.table) || p.table[fd] == nil {
		return nil, errBadDescriptor
	}

	return p.table[fd], nil
}

// open finds the inode behind a name and creates a description for it, with
// offset 0.
func (p *process) open(name string) (int, error) {
	file, ok := p.fs.names[name]

	if !ok {
		return 0, errNoEntry
	}

	fd, err := p.install(&description{file: file})

	if err == nil {
		file.opens++
	}

	return fd, err
}

// dup makes a second descriptor for an existing description.
func (p *process) dup(fd int) (int, error) {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
