	return p.install(entry.open)
}

Listing 2.26 Creating descriptors, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Puts a description in the lowest free entry, counts the new reference,
    /// and returns the number of the entry.
    fn install(&mut self, process: &mut Process, open: usize) -> Result<usize, Error> {
        let fd = process
            .table
            .iter()
            .take_while(|entry| entry.is_some())
            .count();

        if fd >= process.limit {
            return Err(Error::TooManyFiles);
        }

        if fd == process.table.len() {
            process.table.push(None);
        }

        self.open_files[open].refs += 1;
        process.table[fd] = Some(Descriptor {
            open,
            cloexec: false,
        });

        Ok(fd)
    }

    /// Finds the inode behind a name and creates a description for it, with
    /// offset 0.
    fn open(&mut self, process: &mut Process, name: &str) -> Result<usize, Error> {
        let file = *self.names.get(name).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;
        let open = self.describe(file);
        let fd = self.install(process, open)?;

        self.inode(file)?.opens += 1;

        Ok(fd)
    }

    /// Makes a second descriptor for an existing description.
    fn dup(&mut self, process: &mut Process, fd: usize) -> Result<usize, Error> {
        let entry = process.lookup(fd)?;

        self.install(process, entry.open)
    }
}

impl Process {
    /// Returns the entry of a descriptor.
    fn lookup(&self, fd: usize) -> Result<Descriptor, Error> {
        self.table
            .get(fd)
            .copied()
            .flatten()
            .ok_or(Error::BadDescriptor)
    }
}

close lowers the count of the description and, at 0, the open count of the inode. dup2 closes its target first, which is why redirecting descriptor 1 releases whatever descriptor 1 was before.

Listing 2.27 Closing a descriptor, and dup2, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// close frees an entry and drops its reference to the description. The last
// reference closes the description, which drops its reference to the inode.
func (p *process) close(fd int) error {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.table[fd] = nil
	entry.open.refs--

	if entry.open.refs == 0 {
		entry.open.file.opens--
		p.fs.release(entry.open.file)
	}

	return nil
}

// dup2 makes descriptor to refer to the description of descriptor from,
// closing whatever to referred to before.
func (p *process) dup2(from, to int) error {
	entry, err := p.lookup(from)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if from == to {
		return nil
	}

	if _, err := p.lookup(to); err == nil {
		p.close(to)
	}

	for len(p.table) <= to {
		p.table = append(p.table, nil)
	}

	entry.open.refs++
	p.table[to] = &descriptor{open: entry.open}

	return nil
}

Listing 2.28 Closing a descriptor, and dup2, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Frees an entry and drops its reference to the description. The last
    /// reference closes the description, which drops its reference to the
    /// inode.
    fn close(&mut self, process: &mut Process, fd: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let entry = process.lookup(fd)?;
        let open = &mut self.open_files[entry.open];

        process.table[fd] = None;
        open.refs -= 1;

        if open.refs == 0 {
            let file = open.file;

            self.inode(file)?.opens -= 1;
            self.release(file);
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Makes descriptor `to` refer to the description of descriptor `from`,
    /// closing whatever `to` referred to before.
    fn dup2(&mut self, process: &mut Process, from: usize, to: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let entry = process.lookup(from)?;

        if from == to {
            return Ok(());
        }

        if process.lookup(to).is_ok() {
            self.close(process, to)?;
        }

        if process.table.len() <= to {
            process.table.resize(to + 1, None);
        }

        self.open_files[entry.open].refs += 1;
        process.table[to] = Some(Descriptor {
            open: entry.open,
            cloexec: false,
        });

        Ok(())
    }
}

read and write take the offset from the description. With appendMode set, write first moves the offset to the end of the file. The kernel performs that move and the write as a single atomic step, so concurrent appends do not overwrite each other.

Listing 2.29 Reading and writing through a descriptor, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// write copies data into the file at the description's offset and advances
// the offset. In append mode the offset first moves to the end of the file.
func (p *process) write(fd int, data string) error {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	open, file := entry.open, entry.open.file

	if open.appendMode {
		open.offset = len(file.data)
	}

	end := open.offset + len(data)

	if end > len(file.data) {
		file.data = append(file.data, make([]byte, end-len(file.data))...)
	}

	copy(file.data[open.offset:], data)
	open.offset = end

	return nil
}

// read returns up to n bytes from the description's offset and advances the
// offset.
func (p *process) read(fd, n int) (string, error) {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	open := entry.open
	end := min(open.offset+n, len(open.file.data))
	data := string(open.file.data[open.offset:end])
	open.offset = end

	return data, nil
}

Listing 2.30 Reading and writing through a descriptor, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Copies `data` into the file at the description's offset and advances
    /// the offset. In append mode the offset first moves to the end of the
    /// file.
    fn write(&mut self, process: &Process, fd: usize, data: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let open = &mut self.open_files[process.lookup(fd)?.open];
        let file = self.inodes.get_mut(&open.file).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        if open.append_mode {
            open.offset = file.data.len();
        }

        let end = open.offset + data.len();

        if end > file.data.len() {
            file.data.resize(end, 0);
        }

        file.data[open.offset..end].copy_from_slice(data.as_bytes());
        open.offset = end;

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Returns up to `n` bytes from the description's offset and advances the
    /// offset.
    fn read(&mut self, process: &Process, fd: usize, n: usize) -> Result<String, Error> {
        let open = &mut self.open_files[process.lookup(fd)?.open];
        let file = self.inodes.get(&open.file).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        let end = (open.offset + n).min(file.data.len());
        let data = String::from_utf8_lossy(&file.data[open.offset..end]).into_owned();

        open.offset = end;

        Ok(data)
    }
}

fork copies the table and raises the count of every description. exec applies the close-on-exec flag.

Listing 2.31 Inheriting descriptors, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// fork returns a child whose table has a copy of every entry. The copies
// refer to the parent's descriptions, and each copy is counted.
func (p *process) fork() *process {
	child := &process{fs: p.fs, limit: p.limit, table: make([]*descriptor, len(p.table))}

	for fd, entry := range p.table {
		if entry != nil {
			entry.open.refs++
			child.table[fd] = &descriptor{open: entry.open, cloexec: entry.cloexec}
		}
	}

	return child
}

// exec closes every descriptor that has the close-on-exec flag.
func (p *process) exec() {
	for fd, entry := range p.table {
		if entry != nil && entry.cloexec {
			p.close(fd)
		}
	}
}

Listing 2.32 Inheriting descriptors, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns a child whose table has a copy of every entry. The copies
    /// refer to the parent's descriptions, and each copy is counted.
    fn fork(&mut self, parent: &Process) -> Process {
        for entry in parent.table.iter().flatten() {
            self.open_files[entry.open].refs += 1;
        }

        Process {
            table: parent.table.clone(),
            limit: parent.limit,
        }
    }

    /// Closes every descriptor that has the close-on-exec flag.
    fn exec(&mut self, process: &mut Process) -> Result<(), Error> {
        for fd in 0..process.table.len() {
            if process.table[fd].is_some_and(|entry| entry.cloexec) {
                self.close(process, fd)?;
            }
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}

The experiments repeat fdfacts on the model.

Listing 2.33 Numbers, the limit, offsets and flags on the model, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

func numbers(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)

	if err := p.close(0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fd, err := p.open("file")
	fmt.Printf("descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns %d\n", fd)

	return err
}

func limit(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	p.limit = 32
	highest := -1

	for {
		fd, err := p.open("file")

		if err != nil {
			fmt.Printf("limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is %d, the next open fails with %v\n", highest, err)

			return nil
		}

		highest = max(highest, fd)
	}
}

func offsets(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	first, err := p.open("file")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	duplicate, err := p.dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	second, err := p.open("file")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := p.write(first, "hello"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate %d, through a second open %d\n",
		p.table[duplicate].open.offset, p.table[second].open.offset)

	return nil
}

func flags(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	first, err := p.open("file")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	duplicate, err := p.dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.table[duplicate].open.appendMode = true
	p.table[duplicate].cloexec = true

	fmt.Printf("set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND %v, close-on-exec %v\n",
		p.table[first].open.appendMode, p.table[first].cloexec)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.34 Numbers, the limit, offsets and flags on the model, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

fn numbers(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;

    kernel.close(&mut process, 0)?;

    let fd = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;
    println!("descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns {fd}");

    Ok(())
}

fn limit(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;
    let mut highest = 0;

    process.limit = 32;

    let error = loop {
        match kernel.open(&mut process, "file") {
            Ok(fd) => highest = highest.max(fd),
            Err(error) => break error,
        }
    };

    println!(
        "limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is {highest}, the next open fails with {error}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn offsets(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;

    let first = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;
    let duplicate = kernel.dup(&mut process, first)?;
    let second = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;

    kernel.write(&process, first, "hello")?;

    let shared = kernel.open_files[process.lookup(duplicate)?.open].offset;
    let separate = kernel.open_files[process.lookup(second)?.open].offset;

    println!(
        "after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate {shared}, through a second open {separate}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn flags(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;

    let first = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;
    let duplicate = kernel.dup(&mut process, first)?;

    kernel.open_files[process.lookup(duplicate)?.open].append_mode = true;

    if let Some(entry) = &mut process.table[duplicate] {
        entry.cloexec = true;
    }

    let original = process.lookup(first)?;

    println!(
        "set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND {}, close-on-exec {}",
        kernel.open_files[original.open].append_mode, original.cloexec
    );

    Ok(())
}

Listing 2.35 Names and the lifetime of an inode on the model, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

func names(fs *filesystem) error {
	fs.create("first")

	if err := fs.link("first", "second"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	a, b := fs.names["first"], fs.names["second"]
	fmt.Printf("a second name for the file: same inode %v, link count %d\n", a == b, b.links)

	return nil
}

func unlinked(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	file := fs.create("unlinked")
	file.data = []byte("hello")

	fd, err := p.open("unlinked")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := fs.unlink("unlinked"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	data, err := p.read(fd, 16)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the name removed, the file still open: link count %d, read through the descriptor returns %q\n",
		file.links, data)

	return p.close(fd)
}

Listing 2.36 Names and the lifetime of an inode on the model, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

fn names(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    kernel.create("first")?;
    kernel.link("first", "second")?;

    let (a, b) = (kernel.names["first"], kernel.names["second"]);

    println!(
        "a second name for the file: same inode {}, link count {}",
        a == b,
        kernel.inode(b)?.links
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn unlinked(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;
    let file = kernel.create("unlinked")?;

    kernel.inode(file)?.data = b"hello".to_vec();

    let fd = kernel.open(&mut process, "unlinked")?;

    kernel.unlink("unlinked")?;

    let links = kernel.inode(file)?.links;
    let data = kernel.read(&process, fd, 16)?;

    println!(
        "the name removed, the file still open: link count {links}, read through the descriptor returns {data:?}"
    );

    kernel.close(&mut process, fd)
}

redirect does what a shell does between fork and exec: it rearranges the child’s descriptors 1 and 2 with dup2. The parent’s table is unchanged.

Listing 2.37 Redirection on the model, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// redirect forks a child, points its descriptors 1 and 2 at the given
// descriptors, and has it write "out" and then "err". It returns the file's
// contents.
func redirect(shell *process, file *inode, stdout, stderr int) (string, error) {
	child := shell.fork()

	if err := child.dup2(stdout, 1); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	if err := child.dup2(stderr, 2); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	child.exec()

	if err := child.write(1, "out\n"); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	if err := child.write(2, "err\n"); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	return strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(file.data)), " "), nil
}

func redirections(fs *filesystem) error {
	shell := newProcess(fs)
	file := fs.create("output")
	stdout, err := shell.open("output")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	text, err := redirect(shell, file, stdout, stdout)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2>&1: the file holds %q\n", text)

	file.data = nil
	first, err := shell.open("output")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	second, err := shell.open("output")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	text, err = redirect(shell, file, first, second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2> file: the file holds %q\n", text)

	return nil
}

Listing 2.38 Redirection on the model, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

/// Forks a child, points its descriptors 1 and 2 at the given descriptors,
/// and has it write "out" and then "err". Returns the file's contents.
fn redirect(
    kernel: &mut Kernel,
    shell: &Process,
    file: u64,
    stdout: usize,
    stderr: usize,
) -> Result<String, Error> {
    let mut child = kernel.fork(shell);

    kernel.dup2(&mut child, stdout, 1)?;
    kernel.dup2(&mut child, stderr, 2)?;
    kernel.exec(&mut child)?;

    kernel.write(&child, 1, "out\n")?;
    kernel.write(&child, 2, "err\n")?;

    let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(&kernel.inode(file)?.data).into_owned();
    let words: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    Ok(words.join(" "))
}

fn redirections(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut shell = kernel.process()?;
    let file = kernel.create("output")?;
    let stdout = kernel.open(&mut shell, "output")?;

    let text = redirect(kernel, &shell, file, stdout, stdout)?;
    println!("> file 2>&1: the file holds {text:?}");

    kernel.inode(file)?.data.clear();

    let first = kernel.open(&mut shell, "output")?;
    let second = kernel.open(&mut shell, "output")?;

    let text = redirect(kernel, &shell, file, first, second)?;
    println!("> file 2> file: the file holds {text:?}");

    Ok(())
}
descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns 0
limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is 31, the next open fails with EMFILE
after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate 5, through a second open 0
set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND true, close-on-exec false
a second name for the file: same inode true, link count 2
the name removed, the file still open: link count 0, read through the descriptor returns "hello"
> file 2>&1: the file holds "out err"
> file 2> file: the file holds "err"

The output is identical to the output of fdfacts, line for line.

Redirection

A shell applies redirections from left to right, each as a dup2 in the child before exec.

  • > file opens the file and makes descriptor 1 refer to the new struct file.
  • 2>&1 makes descriptor 2 refer to the struct file that descriptor 1 refers to at that moment.

The order of redirections therefore changes the result. In > file 2>&1, descriptor 1 is on the file when descriptor 2 is duplicated from it, and both write to the file. In 2>&1 > file, descriptor 2 is duplicated first, while descriptor 1 is still the terminal. Descriptor 1 then moves to the file, and errors continue to go to the terminal.

>> file 2>> file is safe with separate struct file objects. Both are opened with O_APPEND, so each write goes to the current end of the file regardless of the offset.

Chapter 4 builds a shell that performs these redirections.

Inspecting a running process

The kernel publishes the descriptor table of every process under /proc, which makes the structures of this chapter visible on a live system.

CommandShows
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fdeach descriptor of the process and what it refers to
cat /proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<n>the offset, the flags and the inode number of descriptor n
ulimit -nthe limit on descriptors for processes started from this shell
cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nrthe number of open files in the whole system

For descriptor 7 of the shell above, after the names were removed:

$ cat /proc/$$/fdinfo/7
pos:	0
flags:	0400000
mnt_id:	28
ino:	19927765

pos is f_pos. flags is f_flags in octal: the last digit 0 is O_RDONLY, and 0400000 is O_LARGEFILE, which the kernel sets on every open on a 64-bit system. ino is the inode number, the same 19927765 that ls -li printed while the file had names.

The complete programs

Listing 2.39 The complete fdfacts, in Go. code/go/fdfacts/main.go

// Command fdfacts measures how the kernel hands out file descriptors and what
// a pair of descriptors shares: the number an open returns, the file offset, the
// status flags, and the close-on-exec flag. It ends with the redirection
// `> file 2>&1`, done once with a shared open file description and once with
// separate ones.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./fdfacts
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


// numbers closes descriptor 0, the standard input, and opens a file. The
// kernel gives an open the lowest number that is free.
func numbers(path string) error {
	if err := unix.Close(0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fd, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns %d\n", fd)

	return nil
}


// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EMFILE.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}

// limit lowers the limit on open descriptors to 32 and opens a file until
// the kernel refuses.
func limit(path string) error {
	var saved unix.Rlimit

	if err := unix.Getrlimit(unix.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &saved); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	lowered := saved
	lowered.Cur = 32

	if err := unix.Setrlimit(unix.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &lowered); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Setrlimit(unix.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &saved)

	var opened []int
	highest := -1

	for {
		fd, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)

		if err != nil {
			fmt.Printf("limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is %d, the next open fails with %s\n",
				highest, name(err))

			break
		}

		opened, highest = append(opened, fd), max(highest, fd)
	}

	for _, fd := range opened {
		unix.Close(fd)
	}

	return nil
}


// offset returns the file offset that a descriptor refers to.
func offset(fd int) (int64, error) {
	return unix.Seek(fd, 0, unix.SEEK_CUR)
}

// offsets writes through one descriptor and reads the offset through a
// duplicate of it and through a second open of the same file.
func offsets(path string) error {
	first, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(first)

	duplicate, err := unix.Dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(duplicate)

	second, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(second)

	if _, err := unix.Write(first, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	shared, err := offset(duplicate)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	separate, err := offset(second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate %d, through a second open %d\n",
		shared, separate)

	return nil
}


// flags sets O_APPEND and close-on-exec through a duplicate and reads both
// through the original descriptor.
func flags(path string) error {
	first, err := unix.Open(path, unix.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(first)

	duplicate, err := unix.Dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(duplicate)

	if _, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(duplicate), unix.F_SETFL, unix.O_APPEND); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(duplicate), unix.F_SETFD, unix.FD_CLOEXEC); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	status, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(first), unix.F_GETFL, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	descriptor, err := unix.FcntlInt(uintptr(first), unix.F_GETFD, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND %v, close-on-exec %v\n",
		status&unix.O_APPEND != 0, descriptor&unix.FD_CLOEXEC != 0)

	return nil
}


// inode returns the inode number and the link count of a file.
func inode(path string) (number uint64, links uint64, err error) {
	var status unix.Stat_t

	err = unix.Stat(path, &status)

	return status.Ino, uint64(status.Nlink), err
}

// names gives a file a second name and compares the inodes behind the names.
func names(path string) error {
	first, second := path+".first", path+".second"

	if err := os.WriteFile(first, []byte("hello"), 0o644); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.Remove(first)
	defer os.Remove(second)

	if err := unix.Link(first, second); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	a, _, err := inode(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	b, links, err := inode(second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("a second name for the file: same inode %v, link count %d\n", a == b, links)

	return nil
}


// unlinked opens a file, removes its only name, and reads through the
// descriptor.
func unlinked(path string) error {
	file := path + ".unlinked"

	if err := os.WriteFile(file, []byte("hello"), 0o644); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fd, err := unix.Open(file, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(fd)

	if err := unix.Unlink(file); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var status unix.Stat_t

	if err := unix.Fstat(fd, &status); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	buf := make([]byte, 16)
	n, err := unix.Read(fd, buf)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the name removed, the file still open: link count %d, read through the descriptor returns %q\n",
		status.Nlink, buf[:n])

	return nil
}


// redirect runs a command that writes "out" to descriptor 1 and then "err" to
// descriptor 2, with both descriptors on the same file, and returns the
// file's contents.
func redirect(path string, stdout, stderr *os.File) (string, error) {
	command := exec.Command("sh", "-c", "echo out; echo err >&2")
	command.Stdout, command.Stderr = stdout, stderr

	if err := command.Run(); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	text, err := os.ReadFile(path)

	return strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(text)), " "), err
}

// redirections compares `> file 2>&1`, where descriptor 2 is a duplicate of
// descriptor 1, with `> file 2> file`, where the file is opened once for each.
func redirections(path string) error {
	stdout, err := os.Create(path)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer stdout.Close()

	text, err := redirect(path, stdout, stdout)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2>&1: the file holds %q\n", text)

	first, err := os.Create(path)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer first.Close()

	second, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_WRONLY, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer second.Close()

	text, err = redirect(path, first, second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2> file: the file holds %q\n", text)

	return nil
}


func run() error {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "fdfacts")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)

	path := filepath.Join(dir, "file")

	if err := os.WriteFile(path, nil, 0o644); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for _, experiment := range []func(string) error{numbers, limit, offsets, flags, names, unlinked, redirections} {
		if err := experiment(path); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	return nil
}

func main() {
	if err := run(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

Listing 2.40 The complete fdfacts, in Rust. code/rust/fdfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures how the kernel hands out file descriptors and what a pair of
//! descriptors shares: the number an open returns, the file offset, the
//! status flags, and the close-on-exec flag. It ends with the redirection
//! `> file 2>&1`, done once with a shared open file description and once with
//! separate ones.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p fdfacts
//! ```

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, Read};
use std::os::fd::{AsFd, AsRawFd};
use std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt;
use std::path::Path;
use std::process::Command;

use nix::fcntl::{FcntlArg, FdFlag, OFlag, fcntl, open};
use nix::sys::resource::{Resource, getrlimit, setrlimit};
use nix::sys::stat::Mode;
use nix::unistd::{Whence, close, dup, lseek, write};

/// Closes descriptor 0, the standard input, and opens a file. The kernel
/// gives an open the lowest number that is free.
fn numbers(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    close(0)?;

    let fd = open(path, OFlag::O_RDONLY, Mode::empty())?;
    println!(
        "descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns {}",
        fd.as_raw_fd()
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Lowers the limit on open descriptors to 32 and opens a file until the
/// kernel refuses.
fn limit(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let (soft, hard) = getrlimit(Resource::RLIMIT_NOFILE)?;

    setrlimit(Resource::RLIMIT_NOFILE, 32, hard)?;

    let mut opened = Vec::new();

    let error = loop {
        match open(path, OFlag::O_RDONLY, Mode::empty()) {
            Ok(fd) => opened.push(fd),
            Err(error) => break error,
        }
    };

    let highest = opened.iter().map(AsRawFd::as_raw_fd).fold(-1, i32::max);

    println!(
        "limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is {highest}, the next open fails with {error:?}"
    );

    drop(opened);
    setrlimit(Resource::RLIMIT_NOFILE, soft, hard)?;

    Ok(())
}

/// Returns the file offset that a descriptor refers to.
fn offset(fd: impl AsFd) -> nix::Result<i64> {
    lseek(fd, 0, Whence::SeekCur)
}

/// Writes through one descriptor and reads the offset through a duplicate of
/// it and through a second open of the same file.
fn offsets(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let first = open(path, OFlag::O_WRONLY, Mode::empty())?;
    let duplicate = dup(&first)?;
    let second = open(path, OFlag::O_WRONLY, Mode::empty())?;

    write(&first, b"hello")?;

    let shared = offset(&duplicate)?;
    let separate = offset(&second)?;

    println!(
        "after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate {shared}, through a second open {separate}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Sets `O_APPEND` and close-on-exec through a duplicate and reads both
/// through the original descriptor.
fn flags(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let first = open(path, OFlag::O_WRONLY, Mode::empty())?;
    let duplicate = dup(&first)?;

    fcntl(&duplicate, FcntlArg::F_SETFL(OFlag::O_APPEND))?;
    fcntl(&duplicate, FcntlArg::F_SETFD(FdFlag::FD_CLOEXEC))?;

    let status = OFlag::from_bits_truncate(fcntl(&first, FcntlArg::F_GETFL)?);
    let descriptor = FdFlag::from_bits_truncate(fcntl(&first, FcntlArg::F_GETFD)?);

    println!(
        "set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND {}, close-on-exec {}",
        status.contains(OFlag::O_APPEND),
        descriptor.contains(FdFlag::FD_CLOEXEC)
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Gives a file a second name and compares the inodes behind the names.
fn names(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let (first, second) = (path.with_extension("first"), path.with_extension("second"));

    fs::write(&first, "hello")?;
    fs::hard_link(&first, &second)?;

    let (a, b) = (fs::metadata(&first)?, fs::metadata(&second)?);

    println!(
        "a second name for the file: same inode {}, link count {}",
        a.ino() == b.ino(),
        b.nlink()
    );

    fs::remove_file(&first)?;
    fs::remove_file(&second)
}

/// Opens a file, removes its only name, and reads through the descriptor.
fn unlinked(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let name = path.with_extension("unlinked");

    fs::write(&name, "hello")?;

    let mut file = File::open(&name)?;

    fs::remove_file(&name)?;

    let links = file.metadata()?.nlink();
    let mut text = String::new();

    file.read_to_string(&mut text)?;

    println!(
        "the name removed, the file still open: link count {links}, read through the descriptor returns {text:?}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Runs a command that writes "out" to descriptor 1 and then "err" to
/// descriptor 2, with both descriptors on the same file, and returns the
/// file's contents.
fn redirect(path: &Path, stdout: File, stderr: File) -> io::Result<String> {
    Command::new("sh")
        .args(["-c", "echo out; echo err >&2"])
        .stdout(stdout)
        .stderr(stderr)
        .status()?;

    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;
    let words: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    Ok(words.join(" "))
}

/// Compares `> file 2>&1`, where descriptor 2 is a duplicate of descriptor 1,
/// with `> file 2> file`, where the file is opened once for each.
fn redirections(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let stdout = File::create(path)?;
    let stderr = stdout.try_clone()?;

    let text = redirect(path, stdout, stderr)?;
    println!("> file 2>&1: the file holds {text:?}");

    let first = File::create(path)?;
    let second = OpenOptions::new().write(true).open(path)?;

    let text = redirect(path, first, second)?;
    println!("> file 2> file: the file holds {text:?}");

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("fdfacts-{}", std::process::id()));
    let path = dir.join("file");

    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;
    fs::write(&path, "")?;

    let result = numbers(&path)
        .and_then(|()| limit(&path))
        .and_then(|()| offsets(&path))
        .and_then(|()| flags(&path))
        .and_then(|()| names(&path))
        .and_then(|()| unlinked(&path))
        .and_then(|()| redirections(&path));

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)?;

    result
}

Listing 2.41 The complete fdtable, in Go. code/go/fdtable/main.go

// Command fdtable models the kernel's file tables in user space: names that
// refer to inodes, open file descriptions that refer to an inode and hold an
// offset, and a descriptor table for each process. Every object counts the
// references to it and is released when the count reaches 0. The program
// repeats the experiments of fdfacts on the model and prints the same lines.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./fdtable
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"strings"
)


// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
var (
	errBadDescriptor = errors.New("EBADF")
	errTooManyFiles  = errors.New("EMFILE")
	errNoEntry       = errors.New("ENOENT")
)

// An inode is a file: its number, its contents, and 2 reference counts.
// links counts the names that refer to it, and opens counts the open file
// descriptions that refer to it.
type inode struct {
	number int
	data   []byte
	links  int
	opens  int
}

// A filesystem holds the inodes and a single directory, which maps names to
// inodes.
type filesystem struct {
	names  map[string]*inode
	inodes map[int]*inode
	next   int
}

func newFilesystem() *filesystem {
	return &filesystem{names: map[string]*inode{}, inodes: map[int]*inode{}, next: 1}
}

// allocate returns a new inode with no name.
func (fs *filesystem) allocate() *inode {
	file := &inode{number: fs.next}
	fs.inodes[file.number] = file
	fs.next++

	return file
}


// create makes an empty file with one name.
func (fs *filesystem) create(name string) *inode {
	file := fs.allocate()
	file.links = 1
	fs.names[name] = file

	return file
}

// link adds a second name for an existing file.
func (fs *filesystem) link(existing, added string) error {
	file, ok := fs.names[existing]

	if !ok {
		return errNoEntry
	}

	file.links++
	fs.names[added] = file

	return nil
}

// unlink removes a name. The file itself is removed only when release finds
// no other reference to it.
func (fs *filesystem) unlink(name string) error {
	file, ok := fs.names[name]

	if !ok {
		return errNoEntry
	}

	delete(fs.names, name)
	file.links--
	fs.release(file)

	return nil
}

// release frees an inode that has no name and is not open.
func (fs *filesystem) release(file *inode) {
	if file.links == 0 && file.opens == 0 {
		delete(fs.inodes, file.number)
	}
}


// A description is an open file description: the state created by one open.
// refs counts the descriptors, in all processes, that refer to it.
type description struct {
	file       *inode
	offset     int
	appendMode bool
	refs       int
}

// A descriptor is one entry of a process's table. The close-on-exec flag
// belongs to the entry.
type descriptor struct {
	open    *description
	cloexec bool
}

// A process is its descriptor table. The index of an entry is the file
// descriptor, a nil entry is a free number, and limit is the number of
// entries the process may use.
type process struct {
	fs    *filesystem
	table []*descriptor
	limit int
}

// newProcess returns a process with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 open on a
// terminal, which is a file without a name.
func newProcess(fs *filesystem) *process {
	p := &process{fs: fs, limit: 1024}
	terminal := &description{file: fs.allocate()}
	terminal.file.opens = 1

	for range 3 {
		p.install(terminal)
	}

	return p
}


// install puts a description in the lowest free entry, counts the new
// reference, and returns the number of the entry.
func (p *process) install(open *description) (int, error) {
	fd := 0

	for fd < len(p.table) && p.table[fd] != nil {
		fd++
	}

	if fd >= p.limit {
		return 0, errTooManyFiles
	}

	if fd == len(p.table) {
		p.table = append(p.table, nil)
	}

	open.refs++
	p.table[fd] = &descriptor{open: open}

	return fd, nil
}

// lookup returns the entry of a descriptor.
func (p *process) lookup(fd int) (*descriptor, error) {
	if fd < 0 || fd >= len(p.table) || p.table[fd] == nil {
		return nil, errBadDescriptor
	}

	return p.table[fd], nil
}

// open finds the inode behind a name and creates a description for it, with
// offset 0.
func (p *process) open(name string) (int, error) {
	file, ok := p.fs.names[name]

	if !ok {
		return 0, errNoEntry
	}

	fd, err := p.install(&description{file: file})

	if err == nil {
		file.opens++
	}

	return fd, err
}

// dup makes a second descriptor for an existing description.
func (p *process) dup(fd int) (int, error) {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return p.install(entry.open)
}


// close frees an entry and drops its reference to the description. The last
// reference closes the description, which drops its reference to the inode.
func (p *process) close(fd int) error {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.table[fd] = nil
	entry.open.refs--

	if entry.open.refs == 0 {
		entry.open.file.opens--
		p.fs.release(entry.open.file)
	}

	return nil
}

// dup2 makes descriptor to refer to the description of descriptor from,
// closing whatever to referred to before.
func (p *process) dup2(from, to int) error {
	entry, err := p.lookup(from)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if from == to {
		return nil
	}

	if _, err := p.lookup(to); err == nil {
		p.close(to)
	}

	for len(p.table) <= to {
		p.table = append(p.table, nil)
	}

	entry.open.refs++
	p.table[to] = &descriptor{open: entry.open}

	return nil
}


// write copies data into the file at the description's offset and advances
// the offset. In append mode the offset first moves to the end of the file.
func (p *process) write(fd int, data string) error {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	open, file := entry.open, entry.open.file

	if open.appendMode {
		open.offset = len(file.data)
	}

	end := open.offset + len(data)

	if end > len(file.data) {
		file.data = append(file.data, make([]byte, end-len(file.data))...)
	}

	copy(file.data[open.offset:], data)
	open.offset = end

	return nil
}

// read returns up to n bytes from the description's offset and advances the
// offset.
func (p *process) read(fd, n int) (string, error) {
	entry, err := p.lookup(fd)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	open := entry.open
	end := min(open.offset+n, len(open.file.data))
	data := string(open.file.data[open.offset:end])
	open.offset = end

	return data, nil
}


// fork returns a child whose table has a copy of every entry. The copies
// refer to the parent's descriptions, and each copy is counted.
func (p *process) fork() *process {
	child := &process{fs: p.fs, limit: p.limit, table: make([]*descriptor, len(p.table))}

	for fd, entry := range p.table {
		if entry != nil {
			entry.open.refs++
			child.table[fd] = &descriptor{open: entry.open, cloexec: entry.cloexec}
		}
	}

	return child
}

// exec closes every descriptor that has the close-on-exec flag.
func (p *process) exec() {
	for fd, entry := range p.table {
		if entry != nil && entry.cloexec {
			p.close(fd)
		}
	}
}


func numbers(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)

	if err := p.close(0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fd, err := p.open("file")
	fmt.Printf("descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns %d\n", fd)

	return err
}

func limit(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	p.limit = 32
	highest := -1

	for {
		fd, err := p.open("file")

		if err != nil {
			fmt.Printf("limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is %d, the next open fails with %v\n", highest, err)

			return nil
		}

		highest = max(highest, fd)
	}
}

func offsets(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	first, err := p.open("file")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	duplicate, err := p.dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	second, err := p.open("file")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := p.write(first, "hello"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate %d, through a second open %d\n",
		p.table[duplicate].open.offset, p.table[second].open.offset)

	return nil
}

func flags(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	first, err := p.open("file")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	duplicate, err := p.dup(first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.table[duplicate].open.appendMode = true
	p.table[duplicate].cloexec = true

	fmt.Printf("set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND %v, close-on-exec %v\n",
		p.table[first].open.appendMode, p.table[first].cloexec)

	return nil
}


func names(fs *filesystem) error {
	fs.create("first")

	if err := fs.link("first", "second"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	a, b := fs.names["first"], fs.names["second"]
	fmt.Printf("a second name for the file: same inode %v, link count %d\n", a == b, b.links)

	return nil
}

func unlinked(fs *filesystem) error {
	p := newProcess(fs)
	file := fs.create("unlinked")
	file.data = []byte("hello")

	fd, err := p.open("unlinked")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := fs.unlink("unlinked"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	data, err := p.read(fd, 16)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the name removed, the file still open: link count %d, read through the descriptor returns %q\n",
		file.links, data)

	return p.close(fd)
}


// redirect forks a child, points its descriptors 1 and 2 at the given
// descriptors, and has it write "out" and then "err". It returns the file's
// contents.
func redirect(shell *process, file *inode, stdout, stderr int) (string, error) {
	child := shell.fork()

	if err := child.dup2(stdout, 1); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	if err := child.dup2(stderr, 2); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	child.exec()

	if err := child.write(1, "out\n"); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	if err := child.write(2, "err\n"); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	return strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(file.data)), " "), nil
}

func redirections(fs *filesystem) error {
	shell := newProcess(fs)
	file := fs.create("output")
	stdout, err := shell.open("output")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	text, err := redirect(shell, file, stdout, stdout)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2>&1: the file holds %q\n", text)

	file.data = nil
	first, err := shell.open("output")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	second, err := shell.open("output")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	text, err = redirect(shell, file, first, second)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("> file 2> file: the file holds %q\n", text)

	return nil
}


func main() {
	experiments := []func(*filesystem) error{numbers, limit, offsets, flags, names, unlinked, redirections}

	for _, experiment := range experiments {
		fs := newFilesystem()
		fs.create("file")

		if err := experiment(fs); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 2.42 The complete fdtable, in Rust. code/rust/fdtable/src/main.rs

//! Models the kernel's file tables in user space: names that refer to inodes,
//! open file descriptions that refer to an inode and hold an offset, and a
//! descriptor table for each process. Every object counts the references to
//! it and is released when the count reaches 0. The program repeats the
//! experiments of fdfacts on the model and prints the same lines.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p fdtable
//! ```

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fmt;

/// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Error {
    BadDescriptor,
    TooManyFiles,
    NoEntry,
}

impl fmt::Display for Error {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str(match self {
            Error::BadDescriptor => "EBADF",
            Error::TooManyFiles => "EMFILE",
            Error::NoEntry => "ENOENT",
        })
    }
}

/// A file: its contents and 2 reference counts. `links` counts the names
/// that refer to it, and `opens` counts the open file descriptions that refer
/// to it. Its number is its key in the kernel's table of inodes.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Inode {
    data: Vec<u8>,
    links: u32,
    opens: u32,
}

/// The kernel's tables: a single directory that maps names to inode numbers,
/// the inodes, and every open file description.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Kernel {
    names: HashMap<&'static str, u64>,
    inodes: HashMap<u64, Inode>,
    open_files: Vec<Description>,
    next: u64,
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns the number of a new inode with no name.
    fn allocate(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.next += 1;
        self.inodes.insert(self.next, Inode::default());

        self.next
    }

    fn inode(&mut self, number: u64) -> Result<&mut Inode, Error> {
        self.inodes.get_mut(&number).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Makes an empty file with one name and returns its inode number.
    fn create(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> Result<u64, Error> {
        let number = self.allocate();

        self.inode(number)?.links = 1;
        self.names.insert(name, number);

        Ok(number)
    }

    /// Adds a second name for an existing file.
    fn link(&mut self, existing: &str, added: &'static str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let number = *self.names.get(existing).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        self.inode(number)?.links += 1;
        self.names.insert(added, number);

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Removes a name. The file itself is removed only when `release` finds
    /// no other reference to it.
    fn unlink(&mut self, name: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let number = self.names.remove(name).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        self.inode(number)?.links -= 1;
        self.release(number);

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Frees an inode that has no name and is not open.
    fn release(&mut self, number: u64) {
        if let Some(file) = self.inodes.get(&number)
            && file.links == 0
            && file.opens == 0
        {
            self.inodes.remove(&number);
        }
    }
}

/// An open file description: the state created by one open. `file` is the
/// number of its inode, and `refs` counts the descriptors, in all processes,
/// that refer to it.
struct Description {
    file: u64,
    offset: usize,
    append_mode: bool,
    refs: u32,
}

/// One entry of a process's table. `open` is the index of a description in
/// the kernel's table. The close-on-exec flag belongs to the entry.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Descriptor {
    open: usize,
    cloexec: bool,
}

/// A process is its descriptor table. The index of an entry is the file
/// descriptor, `None` is a free number, and `limit` is the number of entries
/// the process may use.
struct Process {
    table: Vec<Option<Descriptor>>,
    limit: usize,
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Adds a description for an inode and returns its index.
    fn describe(&mut self, file: u64) -> usize {
        self.open_files.push(Description {
            file,
            offset: 0,
            append_mode: false,
            refs: 0,
        });

        self.open_files.len() - 1
    }

    /// Returns a process with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 open on a terminal,
    /// which is a file without a name.
    fn process(&mut self) -> Result<Process, Error> {
        let mut process = Process {
            table: Vec::new(),
            limit: 1024,
        };

        let terminal = self.allocate();
        let open = self.describe(terminal);

        self.inode(terminal)?.opens = 1;

        for _ in 0..3 {
            self.install(&mut process, open)?;
        }

        Ok(process)
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Puts a description in the lowest free entry, counts the new reference,
    /// and returns the number of the entry.
    fn install(&mut self, process: &mut Process, open: usize) -> Result<usize, Error> {
        let fd = process
            .table
            .iter()
            .take_while(|entry| entry.is_some())
            .count();

        if fd >= process.limit {
            return Err(Error::TooManyFiles);
        }

        if fd == process.table.len() {
            process.table.push(None);
        }

        self.open_files[open].refs += 1;
        process.table[fd] = Some(Descriptor {
            open,
            cloexec: false,
        });

        Ok(fd)
    }

    /// Finds the inode behind a name and creates a description for it, with
    /// offset 0.
    fn open(&mut self, process: &mut Process, name: &str) -> Result<usize, Error> {
        let file = *self.names.get(name).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;
        let open = self.describe(file);
        let fd = self.install(process, open)?;

        self.inode(file)?.opens += 1;

        Ok(fd)
    }

    /// Makes a second descriptor for an existing description.
    fn dup(&mut self, process: &mut Process, fd: usize) -> Result<usize, Error> {
        let entry = process.lookup(fd)?;

        self.install(process, entry.open)
    }
}

impl Process {
    /// Returns the entry of a descriptor.
    fn lookup(&self, fd: usize) -> Result<Descriptor, Error> {
        self.table
            .get(fd)
            .copied()
            .flatten()
            .ok_or(Error::BadDescriptor)
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Frees an entry and drops its reference to the description. The last
    /// reference closes the description, which drops its reference to the
    /// inode.
    fn close(&mut self, process: &mut Process, fd: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let entry = process.lookup(fd)?;
        let open = &mut self.open_files[entry.open];

        process.table[fd] = None;
        open.refs -= 1;

        if open.refs == 0 {
            let file = open.file;

            self.inode(file)?.opens -= 1;
            self.release(file);
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Makes descriptor `to` refer to the description of descriptor `from`,
    /// closing whatever `to` referred to before.
    fn dup2(&mut self, process: &mut Process, from: usize, to: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let entry = process.lookup(from)?;

        if from == to {
            return Ok(());
        }

        if process.lookup(to).is_ok() {
            self.close(process, to)?;
        }

        if process.table.len() <= to {
            process.table.resize(to + 1, None);
        }

        self.open_files[entry.open].refs += 1;
        process.table[to] = Some(Descriptor {
            open: entry.open,
            cloexec: false,
        });

        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Copies `data` into the file at the description's offset and advances
    /// the offset. In append mode the offset first moves to the end of the
    /// file.
    fn write(&mut self, process: &Process, fd: usize, data: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let open = &mut self.open_files[process.lookup(fd)?.open];
        let file = self.inodes.get_mut(&open.file).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        if open.append_mode {
            open.offset = file.data.len();
        }

        let end = open.offset + data.len();

        if end > file.data.len() {
            file.data.resize(end, 0);
        }

        file.data[open.offset..end].copy_from_slice(data.as_bytes());
        open.offset = end;

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Returns up to `n` bytes from the description's offset and advances the
    /// offset.
    fn read(&mut self, process: &Process, fd: usize, n: usize) -> Result<String, Error> {
        let open = &mut self.open_files[process.lookup(fd)?.open];
        let file = self.inodes.get(&open.file).ok_or(Error::NoEntry)?;

        let end = (open.offset + n).min(file.data.len());
        let data = String::from_utf8_lossy(&file.data[open.offset..end]).into_owned();

        open.offset = end;

        Ok(data)
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns a child whose table has a copy of every entry. The copies
    /// refer to the parent's descriptions, and each copy is counted.
    fn fork(&mut self, parent: &Process) -> Process {
        for entry in parent.table.iter().flatten() {
            self.open_files[entry.open].refs += 1;
        }

        Process {
            table: parent.table.clone(),
            limit: parent.limit,
        }
    }

    /// Closes every descriptor that has the close-on-exec flag.
    fn exec(&mut self, process: &mut Process) -> Result<(), Error> {
        for fd in 0..process.table.len() {
            if process.table[fd].is_some_and(|entry| entry.cloexec) {
                self.close(process, fd)?;
            }
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}

fn numbers(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;

    kernel.close(&mut process, 0)?;

    let fd = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;
    println!("descriptor 0 closed: the next open returns {fd}");

    Ok(())
}

fn limit(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;
    let mut highest = 0;

    process.limit = 32;

    let error = loop {
        match kernel.open(&mut process, "file") {
            Ok(fd) => highest = highest.max(fd),
            Err(error) => break error,
        }
    };

    println!(
        "limit of 32 descriptors: the highest number obtained is {highest}, the next open fails with {error}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn offsets(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;

    let first = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;
    let duplicate = kernel.dup(&mut process, first)?;
    let second = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;

    kernel.write(&process, first, "hello")?;

    let shared = kernel.open_files[process.lookup(duplicate)?.open].offset;
    let separate = kernel.open_files[process.lookup(second)?.open].offset;

    println!(
        "after a write of 5 bytes: offset through the duplicate {shared}, through a second open {separate}"
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn flags(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;

    let first = kernel.open(&mut process, "file")?;
    let duplicate = kernel.dup(&mut process, first)?;

    kernel.open_files[process.lookup(duplicate)?.open].append_mode = true;

    if let Some(entry) = &mut process.table[duplicate] {
        entry.cloexec = true;
    }

    let original = process.lookup(first)?;

    println!(
        "set on the duplicate, read on the original: O_APPEND {}, close-on-exec {}",
        kernel.open_files[original.open].append_mode, original.cloexec
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn names(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    kernel.create("first")?;
    kernel.link("first", "second")?;

    let (a, b) = (kernel.names["first"], kernel.names["second"]);

    println!(
        "a second name for the file: same inode {}, link count {}",
        a == b,
        kernel.inode(b)?.links
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn unlinked(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut process = kernel.process()?;
    let file = kernel.create("unlinked")?;

    kernel.inode(file)?.data = b"hello".to_vec();

    let fd = kernel.open(&mut process, "unlinked")?;

    kernel.unlink("unlinked")?;

    let links = kernel.inode(file)?.links;
    let data = kernel.read(&process, fd, 16)?;

    println!(
        "the name removed, the file still open: link count {links}, read through the descriptor returns {data:?}"
    );

    kernel.close(&mut process, fd)
}

/// Forks a child, points its descriptors 1 and 2 at the given descriptors,
/// and has it write "out" and then "err". Returns the file's contents.
fn redirect(
    kernel: &mut Kernel,
    shell: &Process,
    file: u64,
    stdout: usize,
    stderr: usize,
) -> Result<String, Error> {
    let mut child = kernel.fork(shell);

    kernel.dup2(&mut child, stdout, 1)?;
    kernel.dup2(&mut child, stderr, 2)?;
    kernel.exec(&mut child)?;

    kernel.write(&child, 1, "out\n")?;
    kernel.write(&child, 2, "err\n")?;

    let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(&kernel.inode(file)?.data).into_owned();
    let words: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    Ok(words.join(" "))
}

fn redirections(kernel: &mut Kernel) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut shell = kernel.process()?;
    let file = kernel.create("output")?;
    let stdout = kernel.open(&mut shell, "output")?;

    let text = redirect(kernel, &shell, file, stdout, stdout)?;
    println!("> file 2>&1: the file holds {text:?}");

    kernel.inode(file)?.data.clear();

    let first = kernel.open(&mut shell, "output")?;
    let second = kernel.open(&mut shell, "output")?;

    let text = redirect(kernel, &shell, file, first, second)?;
    println!("> file 2> file: the file holds {text:?}");

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let experiments = [
        numbers,
        limit,
        offsets,
        flags,
        names,
        unlinked,
        redirections,
    ];

    for experiment in experiments {
        let mut kernel = Kernel::default();

        kernel.create("file")?;
        experiment(&mut kernel)?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

Summary

  • A file descriptor is an index into a per-process table, struct fdtable. A process can name only the objects in its own table.
  • A new descriptor gets the lowest free number. RLIMIT_NOFILE limits the numbers, and open fails with EMFILE at the limit.
  • A table entry points to a struct file, the open file description. It holds the offset f_pos, the status flags f_flags, and the function table f_op through which read and write reach a file, a pipe or a socket.
  • A struct file refers to an inode. The inode holds the type, owner, permissions, size and data location of a file, and no name.
  • Names are directory entries. Several entries may refer to the same inode, and i_nlink counts them.
  • dup and fork create table entries for an existing struct file, so the offset and the status flags are shared. Each open creates a new struct file.
  • A struct file is closed when its last descriptor is closed. An inode is freed when it has no name and is not open.
  • The close-on-exec flag belongs to the table entry. exec closes the descriptors that have it.
  • 2>&1 duplicates descriptor 1 onto descriptor 2. The descriptors then share an offset, and their output appears in order.

References

  • open(2), dup(2), fcntl(2), link(2), unlink(2), stat(2) and inode(7), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inode.7.html
  • M. Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface, No Starch Press, 2010, chapters 4, 5 and 18.
  • include/linux/fdtable.h, include/linux/fs.h, include/linux/dcache.h and fs/file.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/include/linux/fs.h
  • Overview of the Linux Virtual File System, Linux kernel documentation: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v5.15/filesystems/vfs.html

Processes

A process is a program in execution, together with everything the kernel keeps for it: its memory, its open files, its identity for permission checks, and its place in the scheduler. The kernel represents each process by a record, struct task_struct, and identifies it by a number, the process ID or pid.

In this chapter, we will follow a process through its whole life: how it is created, how it comes to run a different program, how it ends, and how the process that created it learns the result. We will read the kernel’s record of a process field by field and find the same information under /proc. Then we will write procfacts, which measures each step on a running kernel, and proctable, a model of the kernel’s process table.

This chapter covers

  • what happens when a shell runs a command, step by step
  • struct task_struct: the kernel’s record of a process
  • process states, and how to read them from /proc
  • fork: what the child copies, what it shares, and what is new
  • exec: what is replaced and what survives
  • exit and wait, and the integer that carries the result
  • zombies, orphans, and the process that adopts them
  • how the kernel chooses a pid
  • threads, and the difference between a process and a task

A shell runs a command

When we type ls in a shell, 4 system calls do the work, 2 in the shell and 2 in a new process.

  1. The shell calls fork. The kernel creates a second process that is a copy of the shell: the same program, the same memory contents, the same open files. The new process is the child, and the shell is its parent. fork returns in both processes. In the parent it returns the pid of the child, and in the child it returns 0, which is how each of them knows which one it is.
  2. The child calls exec with the path of the ls program. The kernel discards the memory of the child, loads ls in its place, and starts it. The pid does not change. It is the same process running a different program.
  3. ls does its work and calls exit with a status, 0 for success.
  4. Meanwhile the parent has called wait, which puts it to sleep until a child ends. wait now returns the pid of the child and its status, and the shell prints the next prompt.

Creating a process and loading a program are separate calls, and that is deliberate. Between fork and exec the child is still running the shell’s code, with the shell’s descriptors. The shell uses that interval to prepare the environment of the new program: it redirects descriptors with dup2, changes the working directory, or adjusts signal handling. Then it calls exec. The new program starts in the prepared environment and contains no code for the preparation. The redirections of chapter 2 are performed in this interval, and chapter 4 builds a shell that does it.

The kernel’s record of a process

Every process has a struct task_struct. It is one of the largest structures in the kernel, about 700 lines in include/linux/sched.h. These are the fields that this chapter and the following chapters use, as they appear in Linux 5.15.

struct task_struct {
        unsigned int __state;                  /* running, sleeping, stopped, ... */
        struct sched_entity se;                /* scheduling data, chapter 6 */
        struct mm_struct *mm;                  /* the address space, chapter 7 */
        int exit_state;                        /* EXIT_ZOMBIE after exit */
        int exit_code;                         /* the status for the parent */
        pid_t pid;                             /* the number of this task */
        pid_t tgid;                            /* the number of its process */
        struct task_struct *real_parent;       /* the process that created it */
        struct list_head children;             /* its children */
        struct list_head sibling;              /* its place in the parent's list */
        const struct cred *cred;               /* user and group, capabilities */
        char comm[TASK_COMM_LEN];              /* the name of the program */
        struct files_struct *files;            /* the descriptor table, chapter 2 */
        struct nsproxy *nsproxy;               /* its namespaces, chapter 11 */
        struct signal_struct *signal;          /* signal state, chapter 5 */
        struct sighand_struct *sighand;        /* signal handlers, chapter 5 */
        struct css_set *cgroups;               /* its control groups, chapter 12 */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
pidThe number by which system calls and /proc name the task.
real_parentThe process that is told when this one ends and that collects its status.
children, siblingThe children of a process form a linked list. children is the head of the list in the parent, and sibling links a child into it.
__stateWhether the task is runnable, sleeping or stopped.
exit_state, exit_codeSet when the task ends, and kept until the parent has read them.
commThe name of the program, at most 15 characters. ps and /proc/<pid>/comm show it.
credThe user and group the process runs as. The kernel checks these when the process opens a file or sends a signal.
mm, files, signal, nsproxy, cgroupsPointers to the other resources of the process. Each is the subject of a later chapter.

The resources are separate structures reached through pointers, and this is what makes fork and threads possible with the same code. A new task can receive a copy of a resource or a pointer to the same one, resource by resource.

Reading the record from /proc

The kernel publishes the record of every process as text files in /proc/<pid>. This is a sleep started from a shell with pid 565533:

$ ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm
    PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
 565533  565532 S    sh
 565534  565533 S    sleep
$ grep -E 'Name|State|Tgid|Pid|PPid|Threads' /proc/565534/status
Name:	sleep
State:	S (sleeping)
Tgid:	565534
Pid:	565534
PPid:	565533
Threads:	1

Name is comm, Pid and Tgid are pid and tgid, and PPid is the pid of real_parent. State is a letter derived from __state and exit_state.

LetterStateMeaning
RrunningThe task is on a CPU or waiting in the run queue for one.
SsleepingThe task waits for an event, such as input or a timer, and a signal can wake it.
Duninterruptible sleepThe task waits for an event, usually disk I/O, and signals are held back until it arrives.
TstoppedThe task was stopped by a signal such as SIGSTOP and continues on SIGCONT.
ZzombieThe task has ended, and its parent has not yet collected its status.

Most processes on a system are in state S at any moment. A process in state R uses CPU time, and chapter 6 describes how the kernel divides the CPUs among them.

fork

fork creates a new struct task_struct and decides, for each resource of the parent, whether the child gets a copy.

ResourceIn the child
pidnew
parentthe process that called fork
memorya copy, made lazily: the pages are shared until one side writes (chapter 7)
descriptor tablea copy; the entries refer to the same open files (chapter 2)
signal handlersa copy
pending signalsnone
working directory, user and groupthe same
namespaces and control groupthe same

A way to remember the table: the child starts as a photograph of the parent, taken at the moment of the call. Everything that is true of the parent at that moment is true of the child, with 2 differences that let them tell each other apart: the pid, and the return value of fork. From then on they are separate processes, and a change in one is invisible to the other, except through the open files they still share.

The copy of the memory is what makes fork look expensive and why it is cheap in practice. The kernel copies the page table and leaves the pages themselves shared and read-only. A page is copied only when one of the processes writes to it. A child that calls exec immediately, the usual case, discards the address space before it has written to more than a few pages.

On Linux, fork is a special case of a more general call, clone, which takes a flag for each resource: with the flag, the child shares the parent’s structure, and without it the child gets a copy. fork is clone with no sharing flags.

exec

exec keeps the task_struct and replaces what the process runs. The kernel reads the header of the program file, which is in the ELF format on Linux, to learn which parts of the file to map into memory and at which address execution starts. It builds a new address space, places the arguments and the environment variables on a new stack, and sets the processor to the entry point.

Kept across execReplaced or reset
pid, parent, childrenthe address space: code, data, heap and stack
open descriptors without the close-on-exec flagdescriptors with the flag are closed
working directory, user and groupsignal handlers return to the default action
ignored signals stay ignoredcomm becomes the name of the new program
namespaces and control group

The table explains why the preparation between fork and exec works. Everything the shell arranges in that interval is in the left column.

exit and wait

A process ends by calling exit with a status, or because a signal ends it. In both cases the kernel releases its memory and closes its descriptors at once. The task_struct remains, with exit_state set to EXIT_ZOMBIE and the result in exit_code, because the parent has not yet asked for the result. A process in this condition is a zombie. It uses no memory and no CPU. It occupies a task_struct and a pid.

The parent collects the result with wait or waitpid, and the kernel then frees the task_struct. This is called reaping the child. wait delivers both kinds of ending in a single integer.

The exit status has 8 bits. A program that calls exit(300) is reported with status 44, the low 8 bits of 300. A shell folds the integer into its own $?: the exit status itself, or 128 + n for a process ended by signal n, so a process ended by SIGTERM, signal 15, appears as 143.

A parent that does not call wait leaves a zombie for each child that ends. The zombies disappear when the parent itself ends, for the reason given next.

A zombie cannot be ended with kill. It has already ended, and only its parent can remove it, by calling wait.

Orphans

A zombie can be reaped only by its parent, so every process needs a living parent. When a process ends before its children, the children are orphans, and the kernel gives them a new parent at once. The new parent is process 1, the first process of the system, unless a closer ancestor has asked for the role: a process can declare itself a subreaper with prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER), and it then adopts the orphans among its descendants. Process 1 and every subreaper call wait in a loop for exactly this purpose.

Processes and threads

task_struct has 2 numbers, pid and tgid, because the kernel schedules tasks, and a process can consist of several. A thread is a task that shares the address space, the descriptor table and the signal handlers of another task. It is created by clone with the sharing flags set, where fork sets none.

All threads of a process have the same tgid, the thread group ID, and each has its own pid. The number that getpid returns, and that we call the pid of a process, is the tgid. The number of each thread is visible under /proc/<pid>/task, and the Threads line of /proc/<pid>/status counts them. The sleep above has 1. A Go program always has several, because the Go runtime starts threads of its own to run goroutines.

Measuring processes

procfacts starts child processes with the standard libraries, os/exec in Go and std::process in Rust. Both perform the creation of the child and the exec in a single call, since a program with several threads cannot safely run arbitrary code between fork and exec. The Rust version uses the nix crate with the signal feature to send a signal.

$ cargo new procfacts
$ cargo add -p procfacts nix --features signal

field reads a field of /proc/<pid>/stat, a single line with the same information as status in a fixed order. Field 3 is the state letter and field 4 is the parent’s pid.

Listing 3.1 The imports of procfacts, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

Listing 3.2 The imports of procfacts, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::path::Path;
use std::process::{self, Command};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

use nix::sys::signal::{Signal, kill};

Listing 3.3 Reading a field of a process's record, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// field returns one field of /proc/<pid>/stat, counted from 1. The second
// field, the command name, is in parentheses and may contain spaces, so the
// fields after it are counted from the closing parenthesis.
func field(pid, n int) (string, error) {
	stat, err := os.ReadFile(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/stat", pid))

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	end := strings.LastIndexByte(string(stat), ')')
	rest := strings.Fields(string(stat[end+1:]))

	return rest[n-3], nil
}

// output runs a shell command and returns what it printed, without the final
// newline.
func output(script string) (string, error) {
	text, err := exec.Command("sh", "-c", script).Output()

	return strings.TrimSpace(string(text)), err
}

Listing 3.4 Reading a field of a process's record, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

/// Returns one field of `/proc/<pid>/stat`, counted from 1. The second field,
/// the command name, is in parentheses and may contain spaces, so the fields
/// after it are counted from the closing parenthesis.
fn field(pid: u32, n: usize) -> io::Result<String> {
    let stat = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/stat"))?;
    let rest = stat.rsplit_once(')').map_or("", |(_, rest)| rest);

    rest.split_whitespace()
        .nth(n - 3)
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into())
}

/// Runs a shell command and returns what it printed, without the final
/// newline.
fn output(script: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let output = Command::new("sh").args(["-c", script]).output()?;

    Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).trim().to_owned())
}

parent runs a shell that prints $PPID, the pid of its parent, and compares it with the pid of the program.

Listing 3.5 The parent of a child, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// parent asks a child for the number of its parent process.
func parent() error {
	text, err := output("echo $PPID")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the child's parent is this process: %v\n", text == strconv.Itoa(os.Getpid()))

	return nil
}

Listing 3.6 The parent of a child, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

/// Asks a child for the number of its parent process.
fn parent() -> io::Result<()> {
    let text = output("echo $PPID")?;

    println!(
        "the child's parent is this process: {}",
        text == process::id().to_string()
    );

    Ok(())
