status runs a script and reports how it ended. The program calls it with exit 7, with exit 300, and with a script that sends itself SIGTERM.

Listing 3.7 Exit status and signal, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// status runs a script and reports how it terminated.
func status(script string) error {
	err := exec.Command("sh", "-c", script).Run()

	var exit *exec.ExitError

	if !errors.As(err, &exit) {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %v", script, err)
	}

	wait, ok := exit.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus)

	switch {
	case ok && wait.Signaled():
		fmt.Printf("%s: killed by signal %d\n", script, wait.Signal())
	default:
		fmt.Printf("%s: exited with status %d\n", script, exit.ExitCode())
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 3.8 Exit status and signal, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

/// Runs a script and reports how it terminated.
fn status(script: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    let status = Command::new("sh").args(["-c", script]).status()?;

    match (status.signal(), status.code()) {
        (Some(signal), _) => println!("{script}: killed by signal {signal}"),
        (None, Some(code)) => println!("{script}: exited with status {code}"),
        (None, None) => println!("{script}: {status}"),
    }

    Ok(())
}

execKeepsPid runs a shell that prints its pid, replaces itself with another shell by exec, and prints the pid again.

Listing 3.9 The pid before and after exec, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// execKeepsPid prints the process number of a shell before and after the
// shell replaces its program with exec.
func execKeepsPid() error {
	text, err := output(`echo $$; exec sh -c 'echo $$'`)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pids := strings.Fields(text)

	fmt.Printf("pid before and after exec: equal %v\n", len(pids) == 2 && pids[0] == pids[1])

	return nil
}

Listing 3.10 The pid before and after exec, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

/// Prints the process number of a shell before and after the shell replaces
/// its program with exec.
fn exec_keeps_pid() -> io::Result<()> {
    let text = output("echo $$; exec sh -c 'echo $$'")?;
    let pids: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    println!(
        "pid before and after exec: equal {}",
        pids.len() == 2 && pids[0] == pids[1]
    );

    Ok(())
}

zombie starts true, which exits immediately, and polls the state field until the child has ended. Then it waits for the child and checks whether the /proc entry still exists.

Listing 3.11 A child between exit and wait, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// zombie starts a child that exits at once, and reads its state before and
// after waiting for it.
func zombie() error {
	child := exec.Command("true")

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid := child.Process.Pid
	state, err := field(pid, 3)

	for err == nil && state != "Z" {
		time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)
		state, err = field(pid, 3)
	}

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := child.Wait(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	_, err = os.Stat(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d", pid))

	fmt.Printf("exited child: state %s before wait, /proc entry present after wait: %v\n", state, err == nil)

	return nil
}

Listing 3.12 A child between exit and wait, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

/// Starts a child that exits at once, and reads its state before and after
/// waiting for it.
fn zombie() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut child = Command::new("true").spawn()?;
    let pid = child.id();

    let mut state = field(pid, 3)?;

    while state != "Z" {
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
        state = field(pid, 3)?;
    }

    child.wait()?;

    let present = Path::new(&format!("/proc/{pid}")).exists();
    println!("exited child: state {state} before wait, /proc entry present after wait: {present}");

    Ok(())
}

orphan runs a shell that starts sleep 30 in the background, prints the pid of the sleep, and exits. The sleep is then an orphan. The program reads the pid of its new parent and the name of that process.

Listing 3.13 The new parent of an orphan, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// orphan starts a shell that starts a background sleep and exits. The sleep
// outlives its parent, and the kernel gives it a new one.
func orphan() error {
	text, err := output("sleep 30 >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo $!")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid, err := strconv.Atoi(text)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGKILL)

	adopter, err := field(pid, 4)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	name, err := os.ReadFile("/proc/" + adopter + "/comm")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("orphan adopted by: %s\n", strings.TrimSpace(string(name)))

	return nil
}

Listing 3.14 The new parent of an orphan, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

/// Starts a shell that starts a background sleep and exits. The sleep
/// outlives its parent, and the kernel gives it a new one.
fn orphan() -> io::Result<()> {
    let text = output("sleep 30 >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo $!")?;

    let pid: u32 = text
        .parse()
        .map_err(|_| io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData))?;

    let adopter = field(pid, 4);
    kill(Pid::from_raw(pid as i32), Signal::SIGKILL)?;

    let name = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{}/comm", adopter?))?;
    println!("orphan adopted by: {}", name.trim());

    Ok(())
}
the child's parent is this process: true
exit 7: exited with status 7
exit 300: exited with status 44
kill -TERM $$: killed by signal 15
pid before and after exec: equal true
exited child: state Z before wait, /proc entry present after wait: false
orphan adopted by: systemd
OutputConclusion
the child’s parent is this processreal_parent of a child is the process that created it.
exit 7: status 7The status passed to exit reaches the parent.
exit 300: status 44Only the low 8 bits are kept: 300 - 256 = 44.
kill -TERM $$: signal 15A process ended by a signal has no exit status. The parent receives the signal number.
the pid is equal before and after execexec replaces the program inside the same task_struct.
state Z before wait, no entry afterA process that has ended is a zombie until its parent reaps it.
the orphan is adopted by systemdThe kernel gave the orphan a new parent.

The process named systemd in the last line is the service manager of the user’s session, which has registered as a subreaper. On a system without one, the line would name process 1.

Modelling the process table

proctable is a model of the part of the kernel that this chapter describes: the table of processes, the allocation of pids, the zombie state, and the adoption of orphans.

Low-level design: proctable

TypeKernel structureFieldsInvariant
processstruct task_structparent, state, statusstate is running or zombie; status is meaningful for a zombie
tablethe kernel’s table of pidsprocs, last, pidMaxevery parent except that of process 1 is a pid in procs
OperationBehaviourError
allocate()returns the first free pid after last, wrapping at pidMaxEAGAIN when every pid is in use
fork(parent)adds a running child of parentESRCH when parent does not exist
exit(pid, status)marks pid a zombie, stores status, gives its children to process 1ESRCH
wait(parent)removes a zombie child and returns its pid and statusECHILD when parent has no children

The table maps a pid to an entry. last remembers the pid allocated most recently.

Listing 3.15 The imports of proctable, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"slices"
	"strings"
)

Listing 3.16 The imports of proctable, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::fmt;

Listing 3.17 The process table, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
var (
	errAgain   = errors.New("EAGAIN: no process number is free")
	errNoChild = errors.New("ECHILD: the caller has no child to wait for")
	errSearch  = errors.New("ESRCH: no such process")
)

// initPid is the process that adopts orphans.
const initPid = 1

type state byte

const (
	running state = 'R'
	zombie  state = 'Z'
)

// A process is one entry of the table.
type process struct {
	parent int
	state  state
	status int
}

// A table maps process numbers to entries. last is the number given out most
// recently, and pidMax is the largest number allowed.
type table struct {
	procs  map[int]*process
	last   int
	pidMax int
}

func newTable(pidMax int) *table {
	return &table{
		procs:  map[int]*process{initPid: {state: running}},
		last:   initPid,
		pidMax: pidMax,
	}
}

Listing 3.18 The process table, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

/// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Error {
    Again,
    NoChild,
    Search,
}

impl fmt::Display for Error {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str(match self {
            Error::Again => "EAGAIN: no process number is free",
            Error::NoChild => "ECHILD: the caller has no child to wait for",
            Error::Search => "ESRCH: no such process",
        })
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for Error {}

/// The process that adopts orphans.
const INIT_PID: u32 = 1;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum State {
    Running,
    Zombie,
}

/// One entry of the table.
struct Process {
    parent: u32,
    state: State,
    status: i32,
}

/// Maps process numbers to entries. `last` is the number given out most
/// recently, and `pid_max` is the largest number allowed.
struct Table {
    procs: BTreeMap<u32, Process>,
    last: u32,
    pid_max: u32,
}

impl Table {
    fn new(pid_max: u32) -> Table {
        let init = Process {
            parent: 0,
            state: State::Running,
            status: 0,
        };

        Table {
            procs: BTreeMap::from([(INIT_PID, init)]),
            last: INIT_PID,
            pid_max,
        }
    }
}

allocate searches upward from last and wraps around at pidMax. A pid that has been freed is therefore reused only after all higher numbers have been tried. The delay protects programs that hold a pid: a process that stored the pid of another, to send it a signal later, would otherwise reach an unrelated new process if the number were reused quickly. /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max sets the limit, 4194304 on this machine.

Listing 3.19 Allocating a pid and creating a child, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

// allocate returns the first free number after last, wrapping around from
// pidMax to the number after initPid.
func (t *table) allocate() (int, error) {
	pid := t.last

	for range t.pidMax {
		pid++

		if pid > t.pidMax {
			pid = initPid + 1
		}

		if _, used := t.procs[pid]; !used {
			t.last = pid

			return pid, nil
		}
	}

	return 0, errAgain
}

// fork creates a child of parent and returns the child's number.
func (t *table) fork(parent int) (int, error) {
	if _, ok := t.procs[parent]; !ok {
		return 0, errSearch
	}

	pid, err := t.allocate()

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	t.procs[pid] = &process{parent: parent, state: running}

	return pid, nil
}

Listing 3.20 Allocating a pid and creating a child, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

impl Table {
    /// Returns the first free number after `last`, wrapping around from
    /// `pid_max` to the number after `INIT_PID`.
    fn allocate(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Error> {
        let mut pid = self.last;

        for _ in 0..self.pid_max {
            pid += 1;

            if pid > self.pid_max {
                pid = INIT_PID + 1;
            }

            if !self.procs.contains_key(&pid) {
                self.last = pid;

                return Ok(pid);
            }
        }

        Err(Error::Again)
    }

    /// Creates a child of `parent` and returns the child's number.
    fn fork(&mut self, parent: u32) -> Result<u32, Error> {
        if !self.procs.contains_key(&parent) {
            return Err(Error::Search);
        }

        let pid = self.allocate()?;

        let child = Process {
            parent,
            state: State::Running,
            status: 0,
        };

        self.procs.insert(pid, child);

        Ok(pid)
    }
}

exit keeps the entry and changes its state. It then gives every child of the ended process to process 1.

Listing 3.21 Ending a process, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

// exit ends a process. The entry stays in the table as a zombie that holds
// the exit status, and the children of the process become children of init.
func (t *table) exit(pid, status int) error {
	p, ok := t.procs[pid]

	if !ok {
		return errSearch
	}

	p.state, p.status = zombie, status

	for _, child := range t.procs {
		if child.parent == pid {
			child.parent = initPid
		}
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 3.22 Ending a process, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

impl Table {
    /// Ends a process. The entry stays in the table as a zombie that holds
    /// the exit status, and the children of the process become children of
    /// init.
    fn exit(&mut self, pid: u32, status: i32) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let process = self.procs.get_mut(&pid).ok_or(Error::Search)?;

        process.state = State::Zombie;
        process.status = status;

        for child in self.procs.values_mut() {
            if child.parent == pid {
                child.parent = INIT_PID;
            }
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}

wait has 3 outcomes. A zombie child exists, and it is removed and returned. Children exist and none has ended, where the kernel would put the caller to sleep. Or the caller has no children, which is the error ECHILD.

Listing 3.23 Collecting a child, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

// wait removes a zombie child of parent from the table and returns its number
// and exit status. ok is false when parent has children and none of them has
// exited, the case in which the kernel suspends the caller.
func (t *table) wait(parent int) (pid, status int, ok bool, err error) {
	children := 0

	for _, pid := range t.pids() {
		child := t.procs[pid]

		if child.parent != parent {
			continue
		}

		children++

		if child.state == zombie {
			delete(t.procs, pid)

			return pid, child.status, true, nil
		}
	}

	if children == 0 {
		return 0, 0, false, errNoChild
	}

	return 0, 0, false, nil
}

// pids returns the process numbers in use, in increasing order.
func (t *table) pids() []int {
	pids := make([]int, 0, len(t.procs))

	for pid := range t.procs {
		pids = append(pids, pid)
	}

	slices.Sort(pids)

	return pids
}

Listing 3.24 Collecting a child, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

impl Table {
    /// Removes a zombie child of `parent` from the table and returns its
    /// number and exit status. The result is `None` when `parent` has
    /// children and none of them has exited, the case in which the kernel
    /// suspends the caller.
    fn wait(&mut self, parent: u32) -> Result<Option<(u32, i32)>, Error> {
        let mut children = self
            .procs
            .iter()
            .filter(|(_, child)| child.parent == parent)
            .peekable();

        if children.peek().is_none() {
            return Err(Error::NoChild);
        }

        let Some((&pid, child)) = children.find(|(_, child)| child.state == State::Zombie) else {
            return Ok(None);
        };

        let status = child.status;
        self.procs.remove(&pid);

        Ok(Some((pid, status)))
    }
}

The program applies a sequence of calls to a table with pidMax set to 6 and prints the table after each call. An entry is printed as pid(parent)state.

Listing 3.25 The trace, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

// String renders the table as pid(parent)state for each entry.
func (t *table) String() string {
	var cells []string

	for _, pid := range t.pids() {
		p := t.procs[pid]
		cells = append(cells, fmt.Sprintf("%d(%d)%c", pid, p.parent, p.state))
	}

	return strings.Join(cells, " ")
}

// A call is one step of the trace: an operation, the process it applies to,
// and for exit the status.
type call struct {
	op     string
	pid    int
	status int
}

// apply performs a call and describes its result.
func (t *table) apply(c call) (string, error) {
	switch c.op {
	case "fork":
		child, err := t.fork(c.pid)

		return fmt.Sprintf("fork by %d: pid %d", c.pid, child), err

	case "exit":
		return fmt.Sprintf("exit of %d, status %d", c.pid, c.status), t.exit(c.pid, c.status)

	default:
		child, status, ok, err := t.wait(c.pid)

		if !ok {
			return fmt.Sprintf("wait by %d: would block", c.pid), err
		}

		return fmt.Sprintf("wait by %d: pid %d, status %d", c.pid, child, status), nil
	}
}

func main() {
	t := newTable(6)

	calls := []call{
		{op: "fork", pid: 1},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
		{op: "fork", pid: 3},
		{op: "wait", pid: 2},
		{op: "exit", pid: 3},
		{op: "wait", pid: 2},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
		{op: "exit", pid: 4, status: 7},
		{op: "wait", pid: 1},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
	}

	fmt.Printf("%-30s %s\n", "start", t)

	for _, c := range calls {
		result, err := t.apply(c)

		if err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}

		fmt.Printf("%-30s %s\n", result, t)
	}
}

Listing 3.26 The trace, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

/// Renders the table as pid(parent)state for each entry.
impl fmt::Display for Table {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        let cells: Vec<String> = self
            .procs
            .iter()
            .map(|(pid, process)| {
                let state = match process.state {
                    State::Running => 'R',
                    State::Zombie => 'Z',
                };

                format!("{pid}({}){state}", process.parent)
            })
            .collect();

        f.write_str(&cells.join(" "))
    }
}

/// One step of the trace.
enum Call {
    Fork(u32),
    Exit(u32, i32),
    Wait(u32),
}

impl Table {
    /// Performs a call and describes its result.
    fn apply(&mut self, call: &Call) -> Result<String, Error> {
        match *call {
            Call::Fork(parent) => {
                let child = self.fork(parent)?;

                Ok(format!("fork by {parent}: pid {child}"))
            }
            Call::Exit(pid, status) => {
                self.exit(pid, status)?;

                Ok(format!("exit of {pid}, status {status}"))
            }
            Call::Wait(parent) => match self.wait(parent)? {
                Some((child, status)) => {
                    Ok(format!("wait by {parent}: pid {child}, status {status}"))
                }
                None => Ok(format!("wait by {parent}: would block")),
            },
        }
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut table = Table::new(6);

    let calls = [
        Call::Fork(1),
        Call::Fork(2),
        Call::Fork(3),
        Call::Wait(2),
        Call::Exit(3, 0),
        Call::Wait(2),
        Call::Fork(2),
        Call::Exit(4, 7),
        Call::Wait(1),
        Call::Fork(2),
        Call::Fork(2),
    ];

    println!("{:<30} {table}", "start");

    for call in &calls {
        let result = table.apply(call)?;
        println!("{result:<30} {table}");
    }

    Ok(())
}
start                          1(0)R
fork by 1: pid 2               1(0)R 2(1)R
fork by 2: pid 3               1(0)R 2(1)R 3(2)R
fork by 3: pid 4               1(0)R 2(1)R 3(2)R 4(3)R
wait by 2: would block         1(0)R 2(1)R 3(2)R 4(3)R
exit of 3, status 0            1(0)R 2(1)R 3(2)Z 4(1)R
wait by 2: pid 3, status 0     1(0)R 2(1)R 4(1)R
fork by 2: pid 5               1(0)R 2(1)R 4(1)R 5(2)R
exit of 4, status 7            1(0)R 2(1)R 4(1)Z 5(2)R
wait by 1: pid 4, status 7     1(0)R 2(1)R 5(2)R
fork by 2: pid 6               1(0)R 2(1)R 5(2)R 6(2)R
fork by 2: pid 3               1(0)R 2(1)R 3(2)R 5(2)R 6(2)R
LineWhat it shows
wait by 2: would blockProcess 2 has a child, 3, which is still running.
exit of 3Entry 3 becomes Z and stays. Its child 4 now has parent 1.
wait by 2: pid 3The zombie is removed and its status is returned.
fork by 2: pid 5Pid 3 is free, and the search continues upward from last, which is 4.
wait by 1: pid 4, status 7Process 1 reaps the orphan it adopted.
fork by 2: pid 3After pid 6 the search wraps around. Pid 2 is in use, and 3 is the first free number.

Correspondence with the kernel source. kernel/fork.c contains copy_process, which builds the new task_struct and calls a copy_ function for each resource (copy_mm, copy_files, copy_sighand, and others), each of which copies or shares according to the clone flags. alloc_pid in kernel/pid.c allocates numbers with idr_alloc_cyclic, the cyclic search that allocate models. do_exit in kernel/exit.c sets EXIT_ZOMBIE and calls forget_original_parent, which chooses the new parent of each child with find_new_reaper. The kernel keeps a list of children in each task, where proctable scans the whole table.

Inspecting processes on a live system

CommandShows
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,commpid, parent, state and name of the processes of the terminal
ps -ef --forest or pstree -pevery process, drawn as a tree of parents and children
cat /proc/<pid>/statusthe record of a process: state, parent, threads, memory, user
ls /proc/<pid>/taskthe threads of a process
cat /proc/sys/kernel/pid_maxthe largest pid
ps -eo stat,pid,ppid,comm | grep '^Z'the zombies of the system, with the parent that has not reaped them

A zombie cannot be removed with kill, since it has already ended. The last command gives the pid of the parent, and the remedy is there: the parent has to call wait, or end.

The complete programs

Listing 3.27 The complete procfacts, in Go. code/go/procfacts/main.go

// Command procfacts measures the life cycle of a process: who its parent is,
// how its termination is reported, what exec keeps, what remains of a child
// that has exited and has not been waited for, and who becomes the parent of
// an orphan.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./procfacts
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)


// field returns one field of /proc/<pid>/stat, counted from 1. The second
// field, the command name, is in parentheses and may contain spaces, so the
// fields after it are counted from the closing parenthesis.
func field(pid, n int) (string, error) {
	stat, err := os.ReadFile(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/stat", pid))

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	end := strings.LastIndexByte(string(stat), ')')
	rest := strings.Fields(string(stat[end+1:]))

	return rest[n-3], nil
}

// output runs a shell command and returns what it printed, without the final
// newline.
func output(script string) (string, error) {
	text, err := exec.Command("sh", "-c", script).Output()

	return strings.TrimSpace(string(text)), err
}


// parent asks a child for the number of its parent process.
func parent() error {
	text, err := output("echo $PPID")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the child's parent is this process: %v\n", text == strconv.Itoa(os.Getpid()))

	return nil
}


// status runs a script and reports how it terminated.
func status(script string) error {
	err := exec.Command("sh", "-c", script).Run()

	var exit *exec.ExitError

	if !errors.As(err, &exit) {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %v", script, err)
	}

	wait, ok := exit.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus)

	switch {
	case ok && wait.Signaled():
		fmt.Printf("%s: killed by signal %d\n", script, wait.Signal())
	default:
		fmt.Printf("%s: exited with status %d\n", script, exit.ExitCode())
	}

	return nil
}


// execKeepsPid prints the process number of a shell before and after the
// shell replaces its program with exec.
func execKeepsPid() error {
	text, err := output(`echo $$; exec sh -c 'echo $$'`)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pids := strings.Fields(text)

	fmt.Printf("pid before and after exec: equal %v\n", len(pids) == 2 && pids[0] == pids[1])

	return nil
}


// zombie starts a child that exits at once, and reads its state before and
// after waiting for it.
func zombie() error {
	child := exec.Command("true")

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid := child.Process.Pid
	state, err := field(pid, 3)

	for err == nil && state != "Z" {
		time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)
		state, err = field(pid, 3)
	}

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := child.Wait(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	_, err = os.Stat(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d", pid))

	fmt.Printf("exited child: state %s before wait, /proc entry present after wait: %v\n", state, err == nil)

	return nil
}


// orphan starts a shell that starts a background sleep and exits. The sleep
// outlives its parent, and the kernel gives it a new one.
func orphan() error {
	text, err := output("sleep 30 >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo $!")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid, err := strconv.Atoi(text)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGKILL)

	adopter, err := field(pid, 4)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	name, err := os.ReadFile("/proc/" + adopter + "/comm")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("orphan adopted by: %s\n", strings.TrimSpace(string(name)))

	return nil
}


func main() {
	experiments := []func() error{
		parent,
		func() error { return status("exit 7") },
		func() error { return status("exit 300") },
		func() error { return status("kill -TERM $$") },
		execKeepsPid,
		zombie,
		orphan,
	}

	for _, experiment := range experiments {
		if err := experiment(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 3.28 The complete procfacts, in Rust. code/rust/procfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures the life cycle of a process: who its parent is, how its
//! termination is reported, what exec keeps, what remains of a child that has
//! exited and has not been waited for, and who becomes the parent of an
//! orphan.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p procfacts
//! ```

use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::path::Path;
use std::process::{self, Command};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

use nix::sys::signal::{Signal, kill};
use nix::unistd::Pid;

/// Returns one field of `/proc/<pid>/stat`, counted from 1. The second field,
/// the command name, is in parentheses and may contain spaces, so the fields
/// after it are counted from the closing parenthesis.
fn field(pid: u32, n: usize) -> io::Result<String> {
    let stat = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/stat"))?;
    let rest = stat.rsplit_once(')').map_or("", |(_, rest)| rest);

    rest.split_whitespace()
        .nth(n - 3)
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into())
}

/// Runs a shell command and returns what it printed, without the final
/// newline.
fn output(script: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let output = Command::new("sh").args(["-c", script]).output()?;

    Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).trim().to_owned())
}

/// Asks a child for the number of its parent process.
fn parent() -> io::Result<()> {
    let text = output("echo $PPID")?;

    println!(
        "the child's parent is this process: {}",
        text == process::id().to_string()
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Runs a script and reports how it terminated.
fn status(script: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    let status = Command::new("sh").args(["-c", script]).status()?;

    match (status.signal(), status.code()) {
        (Some(signal), _) => println!("{script}: killed by signal {signal}"),
        (None, Some(code)) => println!("{script}: exited with status {code}"),
        (None, None) => println!("{script}: {status}"),
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Prints the process number of a shell before and after the shell replaces
/// its program with exec.
fn exec_keeps_pid() -> io::Result<()> {
    let text = output("echo $$; exec sh -c 'echo $$'")?;
    let pids: Vec<&str> = text.split_whitespace().collect();

    println!(
        "pid before and after exec: equal {}",
        pids.len() == 2 && pids[0] == pids[1]
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Starts a child that exits at once, and reads its state before and after
/// waiting for it.
fn zombie() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut child = Command::new("true").spawn()?;
    let pid = child.id();

    let mut state = field(pid, 3)?;

    while state != "Z" {
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
        state = field(pid, 3)?;
    }

    child.wait()?;

    let present = Path::new(&format!("/proc/{pid}")).exists();
    println!("exited child: state {state} before wait, /proc entry present after wait: {present}");

    Ok(())
}

/// Starts a shell that starts a background sleep and exits. The sleep
/// outlives its parent, and the kernel gives it a new one.
fn orphan() -> io::Result<()> {
    let text = output("sleep 30 >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo $!")?;

    let pid: u32 = text
        .parse()
        .map_err(|_| io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData))?;

    let adopter = field(pid, 4);
    kill(Pid::from_raw(pid as i32), Signal::SIGKILL)?;

    let name = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{}/comm", adopter?))?;
    println!("orphan adopted by: {}", name.trim());

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    parent()?;
    status("exit 7")?;
    status("exit 300")?;
    status("kill -TERM $$")?;
    exec_keeps_pid()?;
    zombie()?;
    orphan()
}

Listing 3.29 The complete proctable, in Go. code/go/proctable/main.go

// Command proctable models the kernel's process table: process numbers handed
// out in a cycle, a parent for every process, a zombie state between exit and
// wait, and a new parent for orphans. It applies a sequence of calls and
// prints the table after each.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./proctable
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"slices"
	"strings"
)


// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
var (
	errAgain   = errors.New("EAGAIN: no process number is free")
	errNoChild = errors.New("ECHILD: the caller has no child to wait for")
	errSearch  = errors.New("ESRCH: no such process")
)

// initPid is the process that adopts orphans.
const initPid = 1

type state byte

const (
	running state = 'R'
	zombie  state = 'Z'
)

// A process is one entry of the table.
type process struct {
	parent int
	state  state
	status int
}

// A table maps process numbers to entries. last is the number given out most
// recently, and pidMax is the largest number allowed.
type table struct {
	procs  map[int]*process
	last   int
	pidMax int
}

func newTable(pidMax int) *table {
	return &table{
		procs:  map[int]*process{initPid: {state: running}},
		last:   initPid,
		pidMax: pidMax,
	}
}


// allocate returns the first free number after last, wrapping around from
// pidMax to the number after initPid.
func (t *table) allocate() (int, error) {
	pid := t.last

	for range t.pidMax {
		pid++

		if pid > t.pidMax {
			pid = initPid + 1
		}

		if _, used := t.procs[pid]; !used {
			t.last = pid

			return pid, nil
		}
	}

	return 0, errAgain
}

// fork creates a child of parent and returns the child's number.
func (t *table) fork(parent int) (int, error) {
	if _, ok := t.procs[parent]; !ok {
		return 0, errSearch
	}

	pid, err := t.allocate()

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	t.procs[pid] = &process{parent: parent, state: running}

	return pid, nil
}


// exit ends a process. The entry stays in the table as a zombie that holds
// the exit status, and the children of the process become children of init.
func (t *table) exit(pid, status int) error {
	p, ok := t.procs[pid]

	if !ok {
		return errSearch
	}

	p.state, p.status = zombie, status

	for _, child := range t.procs {
		if child.parent == pid {
			child.parent = initPid
		}
	}

	return nil
}


// wait removes a zombie child of parent from the table and returns its number
// and exit status. ok is false when parent has children and none of them has
// exited, the case in which the kernel suspends the caller.
func (t *table) wait(parent int) (pid, status int, ok bool, err error) {
	children := 0

	for _, pid := range t.pids() {
		child := t.procs[pid]

		if child.parent != parent {
			continue
		}

		children++

		if child.state == zombie {
			delete(t.procs, pid)

			return pid, child.status, true, nil
		}
	}

	if children == 0 {
		return 0, 0, false, errNoChild
	}

	return 0, 0, false, nil
}

// pids returns the process numbers in use, in increasing order.
func (t *table) pids() []int {
	pids := make([]int, 0, len(t.procs))

	for pid := range t.procs {
		pids = append(pids, pid)
	}

	slices.Sort(pids)

	return pids
}


// String renders the table as pid(parent)state for each entry.
func (t *table) String() string {
	var cells []string

	for _, pid := range t.pids() {
		p := t.procs[pid]
		cells = append(cells, fmt.Sprintf("%d(%d)%c", pid, p.parent, p.state))
	}

	return strings.Join(cells, " ")
}

// A call is one step of the trace: an operation, the process it applies to,
// and for exit the status.
type call struct {
	op     string
	pid    int
	status int
}

// apply performs a call and describes its result.
func (t *table) apply(c call) (string, error) {
	switch c.op {
	case "fork":
		child, err := t.fork(c.pid)

		return fmt.Sprintf("fork by %d: pid %d", c.pid, child), err

	case "exit":
		return fmt.Sprintf("exit of %d, status %d", c.pid, c.status), t.exit(c.pid, c.status)

	default:
		child, status, ok, err := t.wait(c.pid)

		if !ok {
			return fmt.Sprintf("wait by %d: would block", c.pid), err
		}

		return fmt.Sprintf("wait by %d: pid %d, status %d", c.pid, child, status), nil
	}
}

func main() {
	t := newTable(6)

	calls := []call{
		{op: "fork", pid: 1},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
		{op: "fork", pid: 3},
		{op: "wait", pid: 2},
		{op: "exit", pid: 3},
		{op: "wait", pid: 2},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
		{op: "exit", pid: 4, status: 7},
		{op: "wait", pid: 1},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
		{op: "fork", pid: 2},
	}

	fmt.Printf("%-30s %s\n", "start", t)

	for _, c := range calls {
		result, err := t.apply(c)

		if err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}

		fmt.Printf("%-30s %s\n", result, t)
	}
}

Listing 3.30 The complete proctable, in Rust. code/rust/proctable/src/main.rs

//! Models the kernel's process table: process numbers handed out in a cycle,
//! a parent for every process, a zombie state between exit and wait, and a
//! new parent for orphans. It applies a sequence of calls and prints the
//! table after each.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p proctable
//! ```

use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::fmt;

/// The errors carry the names of the kernel's error codes for the same cases.
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Error {
    Again,
    NoChild,
    Search,
}

impl fmt::Display for Error {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str(match self {
            Error::Again => "EAGAIN: no process number is free",
            Error::NoChild => "ECHILD: the caller has no child to wait for",
            Error::Search => "ESRCH: no such process",
        })
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for Error {}

/// The process that adopts orphans.
const INIT_PID: u32 = 1;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum State {
    Running,
    Zombie,
}

/// One entry of the table.
struct Process {
    parent: u32,
    state: State,
    status: i32,
}

/// Maps process numbers to entries. `last` is the number given out most
/// recently, and `pid_max` is the largest number allowed.
struct Table {
    procs: BTreeMap<u32, Process>,
    last: u32,
    pid_max: u32,
}

impl Table {
    fn new(pid_max: u32) -> Table {
        let init = Process {
            parent: 0,
            state: State::Running,
            status: 0,
        };

        Table {
            procs: BTreeMap::from([(INIT_PID, init)]),
            last: INIT_PID,
            pid_max,
        }
    }
}

impl Table {
    /// Returns the first free number after `last`, wrapping around from
    /// `pid_max` to the number after `INIT_PID`.
    fn allocate(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Error> {
        let mut pid = self.last;

        for _ in 0..self.pid_max {
            pid += 1;

            if pid > self.pid_max {
                pid = INIT_PID + 1;
            }

            if !self.procs.contains_key(&pid) {
                self.last = pid;

                return Ok(pid);
            }
        }

        Err(Error::Again)
    }

    /// Creates a child of `parent` and returns the child's number.
    fn fork(&mut self, parent: u32) -> Result<u32, Error> {
        if !self.procs.contains_key(&parent) {
            return Err(Error::Search);
        }

        let pid = self.allocate()?;

        let child = Process {
            parent,
            state: State::Running,
            status: 0,
        };

        self.procs.insert(pid, child);

        Ok(pid)
    }
}

impl Table {
    /// Ends a process. The entry stays in the table as a zombie that holds
    /// the exit status, and the children of the process become children of
    /// init.
    fn exit(&mut self, pid: u32, status: i32) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let process = self.procs.get_mut(&pid).ok_or(Error::Search)?;

        process.state = State::Zombie;
        process.status = status;

        for child in self.procs.values_mut() {
            if child.parent == pid {
                child.parent = INIT_PID;
            }
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Table {
    /// Removes a zombie child of `parent` from the table and returns its
    /// number and exit status. The result is `None` when `parent` has
    /// children and none of them has exited, the case in which the kernel
    /// suspends the caller.
    fn wait(&mut self, parent: u32) -> Result<Option<(u32, i32)>, Error> {
        let mut children = self
            .procs
            .iter()
            .filter(|(_, child)| child.parent == parent)
            .peekable();

        if children.peek().is_none() {
            return Err(Error::NoChild);
        }

        let Some((&pid, child)) = children.find(|(_, child)| child.state == State::Zombie) else {
            return Ok(None);
        };

        let status = child.status;
        self.procs.remove(&pid);

        Ok(Some((pid, status)))
    }
}

/// Renders the table as pid(parent)state for each entry.
impl fmt::Display for Table {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        let cells: Vec<String> = self
            .procs
            .iter()
            .map(|(pid, process)| {
                let state = match process.state {
                    State::Running => 'R',
                    State::Zombie => 'Z',
                };

                format!("{pid}({}){state}", process.parent)
            })
            .collect();

        f.write_str(&cells.join(" "))
    }
}

/// One step of the trace.
enum Call {
    Fork(u32),
    Exit(u32, i32),
    Wait(u32),
}

impl Table {
    /// Performs a call and describes its result.
    fn apply(&mut self, call: &Call) -> Result<String, Error> {
        match *call {
            Call::Fork(parent) => {
                let child = self.fork(parent)?;

                Ok(format!("fork by {parent}: pid {child}"))
            }
            Call::Exit(pid, status) => {
                self.exit(pid, status)?;

                Ok(format!("exit of {pid}, status {status}"))
            }
            Call::Wait(parent) => match self.wait(parent)? {
                Some((child, status)) => {
                    Ok(format!("wait by {parent}: pid {child}, status {status}"))
                }
                None => Ok(format!("wait by {parent}: would block")),
            },
        }
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut table = Table::new(6);

    let calls = [
        Call::Fork(1),
        Call::Fork(2),
        Call::Fork(3),
        Call::Wait(2),
        Call::Exit(3, 0),
        Call::Wait(2),
        Call::Fork(2),
        Call::Exit(4, 7),
        Call::Wait(1),
        Call::Fork(2),
        Call::Fork(2),
    ];

    println!("{:<30} {table}", "start");

    for call in &calls {
        let result = table.apply(call)?;
        println!("{result:<30} {table}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

Summary

  • A process is a struct task_struct and the resources it points to: an address space, a descriptor table, signal state, namespaces and control groups.
  • fork creates a child with a new pid and copies of the parent’s resources. Memory is copied lazily. exec replaces the program and keeps the task_struct.
  • The code that runs between fork and exec prepares the environment of the new program.
  • A process ends with an 8-bit exit status or by a signal, and wait reports which in a single integer.
  • A process that has ended is a zombie until its parent reaps it with wait.
  • An orphan is adopted by the nearest subreaper among its ancestors, or by process 1.
  • Pids are allocated in a cycle, so a freed pid is reused as late as possible.
  • A thread is a task that shares the resources of another. The pid of a process is the thread group ID of its tasks.

References

  • fork(2), clone(2), execve(2), wait(2), prctl(2) and proc(5), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html
  • M. Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface, No Starch Press, 2010, chapters 6 and 24 to 28.
  • include/linux/sched.h, kernel/fork.c, kernel/exit.c and kernel/pid.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/kernel/fork.c

Building a Shell

A shell is a user program that reads command lines and converts each into the system calls of the previous chapters: pipe, fork, dup2, exec and wait. It has no special privileges and no private interface to the kernel. Everything a shell does, any program can do.

In this chapter, we will write msh, a shell that runs pipelines with input and output redirection and has the built-in commands cd and exit. We will first watch a real shell at work, by tracing the system calls it makes for a single line. Then we will build msh in stages: the parser, the redirections, the launch of a pipeline, the collection of statuses, and the built-in commands.

This chapter covers

  • the loop of a shell: read, parse, start, wait
  • a system call trace of a shell running a pipeline
  • how a shell finds a program: the PATH variable
  • the environment, and how it reaches a new program
  • the system calls behind |, <, > and >>
  • why the shell closes its own copies of every descriptor it hands to a child
  • the status a shell reports for a pipeline, a signal, and a missing command
  • why cd and exit cannot be separate programs
  • what a full shell adds: expansion, quoting, and job control

The loop of a shell

A shell repeats 4 steps. It reads a line. It parses the line into commands. It starts a process for each command, with the descriptors of each process arranged as the line asks. It waits for the processes to end and remembers the status of the last one. A few commands, the built-in commands, are carried out by the shell itself in place of the third step.

Each element of a command line corresponds to a small number of system calls.

SyntaxWhat the shell does
cmd argsstarts a child process that executes cmd, then waits for it
a | bcreates a pipe; starts a with descriptor 1 on the write end and b with descriptor 0 on the read end
cmd < fileopens file for reading and makes it descriptor 0 of the child
cmd > fileopens file with O_CREAT and O_TRUNC and makes it descriptor 1 of the child
cmd >> filethe same with O_APPEND in place of O_TRUNC
cd dircalls chdir in the shell process
exit nends the shell process with status n

A real shell, traced

strace prints the system calls of a process as it makes them. With -f it follows the children as well. This is the system shell, sh, running the line seq 1 3 | wc -l > count.txt on our machine. The first column is the pid of the caller. The calls that load shared libraries are removed, and calls that were interleaved are shown in order.

$ strace -f -e trace=pipe2,clone,dup3,execve,wait4,close,openat sh -c 'seq 1 3 | wc -l > count.txt'
570272 pipe2([3, 4], 0)                                  = 0
570272 clone(... flags=...|SIGCHLD ...)                  = 570273
570272 close(4)                                          = 0
570273 close(3)                                          = 0
570273 dup3(4, 1, 0)                                     = 1
570273 close(4)                                          = 0
570273 execve("/usr/bin/seq", ["seq", "1", "3"], ...)    = 0
570272 clone(... flags=...|SIGCHLD ...)                  = 570274
570272 close(3)                                          = 0
570272 wait4(-1, ...
570274 dup3(3, 0, 0)                                     = 0
570274 close(3)                                          = 0
570274 openat(AT_FDCWD, "count.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666) = 3
570274 close(1)                                          = 0
570274 dup3(3, 1, 0)                                     = 1
570274 close(3)                                          = 0
570274 execve("/usr/bin/wc", ["wc", "-l"], ...)          = 0
570273 +++ exited with 0 +++
570272 ... wait4 resumed                                 = 570273
570274 +++ exited with 0 +++
570272 wait4(-1, ...)                                    = 570274

Every line of the trace is something we have already met.

CallMeaning
pipe2([3, 4], 0)The shell creates the pipe. Descriptor 3 is the read end and 4 the write end (chapter 1).
clone(...)The shell creates a child. On Linux, fork is implemented by clone (chapter 3). The return value is the pid of the child.
570273 dup3(4, 1, 0)The first child makes descriptor 1 refer to the write end. dup3 is dup2 with a flags argument (chapter 2).
570273 close(3), close(4)The child closes the pipe descriptors it does not need under their old numbers.
570273 execve("/usr/bin/seq", ...)The child becomes seq. Its descriptor 1 is the pipe, and seq does not know it.
570272 close(4), close(3)The shell closes its own copies of both ends.
570274 openat("count.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666)The second child opens the output file. The file is truncated here, before wc runs.
570272 wait4(-1, ...)The shell waits for any child, 2 times.

A trace is easier to read one process at a time. Follow the lines that begin with 570273 and ignore the rest: it closes 3, makes 4 its descriptor 1, closes 4, and becomes seq. The whole preparation is 3 calls. Figure 4.3 shows the result as descriptor tables.

The redirections are carried out in the children, between clone and execve. The shell’s own descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are untouched, so the next command line starts from the same state.

Finding the program, and the environment

The trace shows execve("/usr/bin/seq", ...), although the line said seq. execve takes a path, and the shell has to find one. It looks the name up in each directory listed in the variable PATH, in order, and uses the first match. A name that contains a / is used as it is.

$ type seq cd
seq is /usr/bin/seq
cd is a shell builtin

PATH is an environment variable. The environment is a list of strings of the form NAME=value that every process has. It is the third argument of execve: the trace shows /* 92 vars */ where strace abbreviated it. A program started without special arrangement receives a copy of the environment of the process that started it, which is how settings such as PATH, HOME and LANG reach every program in a session. The environment lives in the memory of the process, so a change in a child is invisible to the parent.

msh leaves the lookup to the standard library. Go’s exec.Command and Rust’s Command::new search PATH when the name has no /, and both pass the environment of msh on to the child.

Setting up

msh uses only the standard libraries.

$ cargo new msh

Low-level design: msh

TypeFieldsMeaning
commandargs, input, output, appendOutputa stage of a pipeline and its redirections
shelllast, exitingthe status of the previous line; whether exit has run
FunctionBehaviour
parse(line)splits a line into commands; fails on an empty command or a missing file name
redirect(command)opens the files named by <, > and >>
launch(pipeline)starts every command with its descriptors; closes the shell’s copies
run(pipeline)launches, waits for every child, returns the status of the last
execute(line)runs cd and exit in the shell; passes everything else to run

Parsing

A pipeline is a list of commands, and a command is a list of arguments with optional file names for its input and output. parse reads the words of a line from left to right. A | ends the current command, a redirection operator consumes the next word as a file name, and every other word is an argument.

msh requires spaces around operators and has no quoting, which keeps the parser to a single loop.

Listing 4.1 The imports of msh, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

import (
	"bufio"
	"errors"
	"fmt"

	"strconv"

)

Listing 4.2 The imports of msh, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

use std::env;
use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, BufRead, PipeReader, Write};
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::process::{self, Child, Stdio};

Listing 4.3 Parsing a line into a pipeline, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// A command is one stage of a pipeline: its arguments and the files that
// replace its standard input and output, when the line names any.
type command struct {
	args         []string
	input        string
	output       string
	appendOutput bool
}

var errSyntax = errors.New("syntax error")

// parse splits a line into the commands of a pipeline. Words and operators
// are separated by spaces. The operators are | < > and >>.
func parse(line string) ([]command, error) {
	pipeline := []command{{}}
	words := strings.Fields(line)

	for i := 0; i < len(words); i++ {
		current := &pipeline[len(pipeline)-1]

		switch word := words[i]; word {
		case "|":
			if len(current.args) == 0 {
				return nil, errSyntax
			}

			pipeline = append(pipeline, command{})

		case "<", ">", ">>":
			i++

			if i == len(words) {
				return nil, errSyntax
			}

			if word == "<" {
				current.input = words[i]
			} else {
				current.output, current.appendOutput = words[i], word == ">>"
			}

		default:
			current.args = append(current.args, word)
		}
	}

	if len(pipeline[len(pipeline)-1].args) == 0 {
		return nil, errSyntax
	}

	return pipeline, nil
}

Listing 4.4 Parsing a line into a pipeline, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

/// One stage of a pipeline: its arguments and the files that replace its
/// standard input and output, when the line names any.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Command {
    args: Vec<String>,
    input: Option<String>,
    output: Option<String>,
    append_output: bool,
}

struct SyntaxError;

/// Splits a line into the commands of a pipeline. Words and operators are
/// separated by spaces. The operators are | < > and >>.
fn parse(line: &str) -> Result<Vec<Command>, SyntaxError> {
    let mut pipeline = Vec::new();
    let mut current = Command::default();
    let mut words = line.split_whitespace();

    while let Some(word) = words.next() {
        match word {
            "|" => {
                if current.args.is_empty() {
                    return Err(SyntaxError);
                }

                pipeline.push(std::mem::take(&mut current));
            }
            "<" | ">" | ">>" => {
                let file = words.next().ok_or(SyntaxError)?.to_owned();

                if word == "<" {
                    current.input = Some(file);
                } else {
                    current.output = Some(file);
                    current.append_output = word == ">>";
                }
            }
            _ => current.args.push(word.to_owned()),
        }
    }

    if current.args.is_empty() {
        return Err(SyntaxError);
    }

    pipeline.push(current);

    Ok(pipeline)
}

Redirections

redirect opens the files a command names. > truncates the file when it is opened, which is before the command runs, as the trace showed. For this reason sort < numbers > numbers empties the file before sort reads it. >> opens with O_APPEND and keeps the contents.

Listing 4.5 Opening the files of a redirection, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// redirect opens the files a command names and returns the files to use as
// its standard input and output. A nil result means "keep the default".
func redirect(c command) (input, output *os.File, err error) {
	if c.input != "" {
		input, err = os.Open(c.input)

		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}
	}

	if c.output != "" {
		flags := os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREATE | os.O_TRUNC

		if c.appendOutput {
			flags = os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREATE | os.O_APPEND
		}

		output, err = os.OpenFile(c.output, flags, 0o644)

		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}
	}

	return input, output, nil
}

Listing 4.6 Opening the files of a redirection, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

/// Opens the files a command names and returns the files to use as its
/// standard input and output. `None` means "keep the default".
fn redirect(command: &Command) -> io::Result<(Option<File>, Option<File>)> {
    let input = command.input.as_ref().map(File::open).transpose()?;

    let output = command
        .output
        .as_ref()
        .map(|path| {
            OpenOptions::new()
                .write(true)
                .create(true)
                .append(command.append_output)
                .truncate(!command.append_output)
                .open(path)
        })
        .transpose()?;

    Ok((input, output))
}

Launching a pipeline

launch walks the pipeline from left to right. For each command except the last it creates a pipe, gives the write end to this command as descriptor 1, and carries the read end to the next iteration, where it becomes descriptor 0 of the next command. A redirection takes precedence over the pipe: when a command names a file for a descriptor, the file replaces the pipe end on that descriptor.

After a child has started, the shell closes every descriptor it opened for that child, as sh did in the trace. The rule from chapter 1 applies: a write end that stays open in the shell keeps the write count of the pipe above 0, and the next command waits for an end of the stream that is not reported.

The standard libraries perform the clone, the dup3 calls and the execve in a single call, Start in Go and spawn in Rust. We name the files for descriptors 0 and 1 of the child, and the library arranges them in the child.

Listing 4.7 Starting the commands of a pipeline, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// launch starts every command of a pipeline and returns the commands that
// started. Command i reads from the pipe that command i-1 writes to, unless
// a redirection replaces that descriptor.
func launch(pipeline []command) []*exec.Cmd {
	var started []*exec.Cmd
	var fromPrevious *os.File

	for i, c := range pipeline {
		stdin, stdout := os.Stdin, os.Stdout
		var toNext, nextInput *os.File

		if fromPrevious != nil {
			stdin = fromPrevious
		}

		if i < len(pipeline)-1 {
			reader, writer, err := os.Pipe()

			if err != nil {
				fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)

				break
			}

			stdout, toNext, nextInput = writer, writer, reader
		}

		input, output, err := redirect(c)

		if input != nil {
			stdin = input
		}

		if output != nil {
			stdout = output
		}

		if err == nil {
			child := exec.Command(c.args[0], c.args[1:]...)
			child.Stdin, child.Stdout, child.Stderr = stdin, stdout, os.Stderr
			err = child.Start()

			if err == nil {
				started = append(started, child)
			}
		}

		if errors.Is(err, exec.ErrNotFound) {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "msh: %s: command not found\n", c.args[0])
		} else if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)
		}

		// The child has its own copies. The shell closes every descriptor it
		// opened for this command.
		for _, file := range []*os.File{input, output, toNext, fromPrevious} {
			if file != nil {
				file.Close()
			}
		}

		fromPrevious = nextInput
	}

	return started
}

Listing 4.8 Starting the commands of a pipeline, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

/// Starts every command of a pipeline and returns the children that started.
/// Command `i` reads from the pipe that command `i - 1` writes to, unless a
/// redirection replaces that descriptor.
fn launch(pipeline: &[Command]) -> Vec<Child> {
    let mut started = Vec::new();
    let mut from_previous: Option<PipeReader> = None;

    for (i, command) in pipeline.iter().enumerate() {
        let mut stdin = from_previous
            .take()
            .map_or_else(Stdio::inherit, Stdio::from);
        let mut stdout = Stdio::inherit();

        if i + 1 < pipeline.len() {
            let Ok((reader, writer)) = io::pipe() else {
                eprintln!("msh: cannot create a pipe");

                break;
            };

            stdout = writer.into();
            from_previous = Some(reader);
        }

        let (input, output) = match redirect(command) {
            Ok(files) => files,
            Err(error) => {
                eprintln!("msh: {error}");

                continue;
            }
        };

        if let Some(file) = input {
            stdin = file.into();
        }

        if let Some(file) = output {
            stdout = file.into();
        }

        // The `Command` owns the shell's copies of the descriptors. It is
        // dropped when the statement ends, which closes them.
        let child = process::Command::new(&command.args[0])
            .args(&command.args[1..])
            .stdin(stdin)
            .stdout(stdout)
            .spawn();

        match child {
            Ok(child) => started.push(child),
            Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound => {
                eprintln!("msh: {}: command not found", command.args[0]);
            }
            Err(error) => eprintln!("msh: {error}"),
        }
    }

    started
}

Collecting statuses

The shell waits for every child. A child that is not waited for remains a zombie, as chapter 3 showed. The status of a pipeline is the status of its last command. status applies the conventions of a shell.

Ending of the last commandStatus
it called exit(n)n
it was ended by signal n128 + n
it could not be started127

By convention 0 means success and any other value means failure, and the commands if and while of a full shell test exactly this number.

Listing 4.9 Waiting for the pipeline, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// status converts a wait status to the number a shell reports: the exit
// status, or 128 plus the signal number.
func status(child *exec.Cmd) int {
	child.Wait()

	if wait, ok := child.ProcessState.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && wait.Signaled() {
		return 128 + int(wait.Signal())
	}

	return child.ProcessState.ExitCode()
}

// run starts a pipeline, waits for every command, and returns the status of
// the last command, or 127 when the last command did not start.
func run(pipeline []command) int {
	started := launch(pipeline)
	last := 127

	for _, child := range started {
		last = status(child)
	}

	if len(started) < len(pipeline) {
		return 127
	}

	return last
}

Listing 4.10 Waiting for the pipeline, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

/// Converts a wait status to the number a shell reports: the exit status, or
/// 128 plus the signal number.
fn status(child: &mut Child) -> i32 {
    let Ok(status) = child.wait() else {
        return 127;
    };

    match (status.signal(), status.code()) {
        (Some(signal), _) => 128 + signal,
        (None, Some(code)) => code,
        (None, None) => 127,
    }
}

/// Starts a pipeline, waits for every command, and returns the status of the
/// last command, or 127 when the last command did not start.
fn run(pipeline: &[Command]) -> i32 {
    let mut started = launch(pipeline);
    let mut last = 127;

    for child in &mut started {
        last = status(child);
    }

    if started.len() < pipeline.len() {
        return 127;
    }

    last
}

Built-in commands

The working directory is an attribute of a process, kept by the kernel, and a child receives a copy of it. If cd were a separate program, it would change the directory of its own process and exit, and the directory of the shell would be unchanged. The same reasoning applies to exit. Both therefore run inside the shell process.

Listing 4.11 Running a line: built-in commands and pipelines, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// A shell holds the state that outlives a command line.
type shell struct {
	last    int
	exiting bool
}

// execute runs one command line. cd and exit change the shell process
// itself, so they run inside it. Everything else runs in child processes.
func (s *shell) execute(line string) {
	pipeline, err := parse(line)

	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)
		s.last = 2

		return
	}

	switch first := pipeline[0]; {
	case len(pipeline) == 1 && first.args[0] == "cd" && len(first.args) == 2:
		s.last = 0

		if err := os.Chdir(first.args[1]); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)
			s.last = 1
		}

	case len(pipeline) == 1 && first.args[0] == "exit":
		s.exiting = true

		if len(first.args) == 2 {
			s.last, _ = strconv.Atoi(first.args[1])
		}

	default:
		s.last = run(pipeline)
	}
}

Listing 4.12 Running a line: built-in commands and pipelines, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

/// The state that outlives a command line.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Shell {
    last: i32,
    exiting: bool,
}

impl Shell {
    /// Runs one command line. cd and exit change the shell process itself, so
    /// they run inside it. Everything else runs in child processes.
    fn execute(&mut self, line: &str) {
        let Ok(pipeline) = parse(line) else {
            eprintln!("msh: syntax error");
            self.last = 2;

            return;
        };

        let args: Vec<&str> = pipeline[0].args.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();

        match (pipeline.len(), args.as_slice()) {
            (1, ["cd", directory]) => {
                self.last = 0;

                if let Err(error) = env::set_current_dir(directory) {
                    eprintln!("msh: {error}");
                    self.last = 1;
                }
            }
            (1, ["exit", rest @ ..]) => {
                self.exiting = true;

                if let [code] = rest
                    && let Ok(code) = code.parse()
                {
                    self.last = code;
                }
            }
            _ => self.last = run(&pipeline),
        }
    }
}

cd works because it runs inside the shell. A separate cd program would change its own directory and exit.

Running a script

Without arguments, msh runs a fixed script in a temporary directory and prints the status after each line. With -i, it reads lines from standard input.

Listing 4.13 The script, and the interactive loop, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// script is the demonstration that msh runs without arguments.
var script = []string{
	"seq 1 5 > numbers",
	"wc -l < numbers",
	"sort -rn < numbers | head -n 2 >> numbers",
	"paste -sd, numbers",
	"false",
	"nosuchcommand",
	"cd /",
	"pwd",
	"exit 3",
	"echo not reached",
}

// demonstrate runs the script in a new temporary directory and prints the
// status after each line.
func demonstrate() error {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "msh")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)

	if err := os.Chdir(dir); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	s := &shell{}

	for _, line := range script {
		fmt.Println("$", line)
		s.execute(line)

		if s.exiting {
			fmt.Printf("[the shell exits with status %d]\n", s.last)

			return nil
		}

		fmt.Printf("[status %d]\n", s.last)
	}

	return nil
}

// interact reads command lines from standard input until exit or the end of
// the input, and ends the process with the last status.
func interact() {
	s := &shell{}
	lines := bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)

	for !s.exiting {
		fmt.Print("msh$ ")

		if !lines.Scan() {
			break
		}

		if strings.TrimSpace(lines.Text()) != "" {
			s.execute(lines.Text())
		}
	}

	os.Exit(s.last)
}

func main() {
	if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "-i" {
		interact()
	}

	if err := demonstrate(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

Listing 4.14 The script, and the interactive loop, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

/// The demonstration that msh runs without arguments.
const SCRIPT: [&str; 10] = [
    "seq 1 5 > numbers",
    "wc -l < numbers",
    "sort -rn < numbers | head -n 2 >> numbers",
    "paste -sd, numbers",
    "false",
    "nosuchcommand",
    "cd /",
    "pwd",
    "exit 3",
    "echo not reached",
];

/// Runs the script in a new temporary directory and prints the status after
/// each line.
fn demonstrate() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = env::temp_dir().join(format!("msh-{}", process::id()));

    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;
    env::set_current_dir(&dir)?;

    let mut shell = Shell::default();

    for line in SCRIPT {
        println!("$ {line}");
        shell.execute(line);

        if shell.exiting {
            println!("[the shell exits with status {}]", shell.last);

            break;
        }

        println!("[status {}]", shell.last);
    }

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)
}

/// Reads command lines from standard input until exit or the end of the
/// input, and ends the process with the last status.
fn interact() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut shell = Shell::default();
    let mut lines = io::stdin().lock().lines();

    while !shell.exiting {
        print!("msh$ ");
        io::stdout().flush()?;

        let Some(line) = lines.next().transpose()? else {
            break;
        };

        if !line.trim().is_empty() {
            shell.execute(&line);
        }
    }

    process::exit(shell.last);
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    if env::args().nth(1).as_deref() == Some("-i") {
        interact()?;
    }

    demonstrate()
}

[status 0]
$ wc -l < numbers
5
[status 0]
$ sort -rn < numbers | head -n 2 >> numbers
[status 0]
$ paste -sd, numbers
1,2,3,4,5,5,4
[status 0]
$ false
[status 1]
$ nosuchcommand
msh: nosuchcommand: command not found
[status 127]
$ cd /
[status 0]
$ pwd

[status 0]
$ exit 3
