LineWhat it shows
seq 1 5 > numbersDescriptor 1 of seq is the file. Nothing is printed.
wc -l < numbersDescriptor 0 of wc is the file.
sort -rn < numbers | head -n 2 >> numberssort reads its whole input before writing, so the 2 lines that head appends are 5 and 4.
paste -sd, numbersThe file now has 7 lines.
falseThe status is the exit status of the command, 1.
nosuchcommandThe command could not be started. The status is 127.
cd / then pwdThe child pwd inherits the directory that the built-in cd set in the shell.
exit 3The shell ends, and the last line of the script is not run.

What a full shell adds

msh passes each word of a line to the program unchanged. A shell such as bash or dash processes the words first, and it is useful to know that these steps happen in the shell, before any program starts.

FeatureWhat the shell does before exec
variablesreplaces $HOME with the value of the variable
wildcardsreplaces *.txt with the list of matching file names; the program receives the names and does not see the *
command substitutionruns the command inside $(...) with its output on a pipe, and inserts what it reads
quoting'...' and "..." keep spaces and operators from being treated as separators
a && b, a || bruns b depending on whether the status of a was 0
cmd &starts the command and does not wait for it

The last row leads to job control. A shell places each pipeline in a process group, a set of processes that can be signalled together, and tells the terminal which group is in the foreground. When we press Ctrl-C, the terminal driver in the kernel sends SIGINT to every process of the foreground group, and the shell itself, which is in a different group, is unaffected. Signals are the subject of chapter 5.

Inspecting a shell at work

CommandShows
strace -f -e trace=process,pipe2,dup3 sh -c '...'the system calls of a shell and its children for a line
type namewhether a name is a built-in command or a program, and which file
echo $?the status of the previous command
set -xeach command, after expansion, as the shell runs it
echo $PATHthe directories searched for programs

The complete program

Listing 4.15 The complete msh, in Go. code/go/msh/main.go

// Command msh is a small shell. It parses a command line into a pipeline of
// commands with redirections, starts each command with its descriptors
// arranged, waits for all of them, and reports the status of the last. The
// commands cd and exit are built in.
//
// Without arguments it runs a fixed script in a temporary directory. With -i
// it reads command lines from standard input.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./msh
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"syscall"
)


// A command is one stage of a pipeline: its arguments and the files that
// replace its standard input and output, when the line names any.
type command struct {
	args         []string
	input        string
	output       string
	appendOutput bool
}

var errSyntax = errors.New("syntax error")

// parse splits a line into the commands of a pipeline. Words and operators
// are separated by spaces. The operators are | < > and >>.
func parse(line string) ([]command, error) {
	pipeline := []command{{}}
	words := strings.Fields(line)

	for i := 0; i < len(words); i++ {
		current := &pipeline[len(pipeline)-1]

		switch word := words[i]; word {
		case "|":
			if len(current.args) == 0 {
				return nil, errSyntax
			}

			pipeline = append(pipeline, command{})

		case "<", ">", ">>":
			i++

			if i == len(words) {
				return nil, errSyntax
			}

			if word == "<" {
				current.input = words[i]
			} else {
				current.output, current.appendOutput = words[i], word == ">>"
			}

		default:
			current.args = append(current.args, word)
		}
	}

	if len(pipeline[len(pipeline)-1].args) == 0 {
		return nil, errSyntax
	}

	return pipeline, nil
}


// redirect opens the files a command names and returns the files to use as
// its standard input and output. A nil result means "keep the default".
func redirect(c command) (input, output *os.File, err error) {
	if c.input != "" {
		input, err = os.Open(c.input)

		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}
	}

	if c.output != "" {
		flags := os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREATE | os.O_TRUNC

		if c.appendOutput {
			flags = os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREATE | os.O_APPEND
		}

		output, err = os.OpenFile(c.output, flags, 0o644)

		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}
	}

	return input, output, nil
}


// launch starts every command of a pipeline and returns the commands that
// started. Command i reads from the pipe that command i-1 writes to, unless
// a redirection replaces that descriptor.
func launch(pipeline []command) []*exec.Cmd {
	var started []*exec.Cmd
	var fromPrevious *os.File

	for i, c := range pipeline {
		stdin, stdout := os.Stdin, os.Stdout
		var toNext, nextInput *os.File

		if fromPrevious != nil {
			stdin = fromPrevious
		}

		if i < len(pipeline)-1 {
			reader, writer, err := os.Pipe()

			if err != nil {
				fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)

				break
			}

			stdout, toNext, nextInput = writer, writer, reader
		}

		input, output, err := redirect(c)

		if input != nil {
			stdin = input
		}

		if output != nil {
			stdout = output
		}

		if err == nil {
			child := exec.Command(c.args[0], c.args[1:]...)
			child.Stdin, child.Stdout, child.Stderr = stdin, stdout, os.Stderr
			err = child.Start()

			if err == nil {
				started = append(started, child)
			}
		}

		if errors.Is(err, exec.ErrNotFound) {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "msh: %s: command not found\n", c.args[0])
		} else if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)
		}

		// The child has its own copies. The shell closes every descriptor it
		// opened for this command.
		for _, file := range []*os.File{input, output, toNext, fromPrevious} {
			if file != nil {
				file.Close()
			}
		}

		fromPrevious = nextInput
	}

	return started
}


// status converts a wait status to the number a shell reports: the exit
// status, or 128 plus the signal number.
func status(child *exec.Cmd) int {
	child.Wait()

	if wait, ok := child.ProcessState.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && wait.Signaled() {
		return 128 + int(wait.Signal())
	}

	return child.ProcessState.ExitCode()
}

// run starts a pipeline, waits for every command, and returns the status of
// the last command, or 127 when the last command did not start.
func run(pipeline []command) int {
	started := launch(pipeline)
	last := 127

	for _, child := range started {
		last = status(child)
	}

	if len(started) < len(pipeline) {
		return 127
	}

	return last
}


// A shell holds the state that outlives a command line.
type shell struct {
	last    int
	exiting bool
}

// execute runs one command line. cd and exit change the shell process
// itself, so they run inside it. Everything else runs in child processes.
func (s *shell) execute(line string) {
	pipeline, err := parse(line)

	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)
		s.last = 2

		return
	}

	switch first := pipeline[0]; {
	case len(pipeline) == 1 && first.args[0] == "cd" && len(first.args) == 2:
		s.last = 0

		if err := os.Chdir(first.args[1]); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "msh:", err)
			s.last = 1
		}

	case len(pipeline) == 1 && first.args[0] == "exit":
		s.exiting = true

		if len(first.args) == 2 {
			s.last, _ = strconv.Atoi(first.args[1])
		}

	default:
		s.last = run(pipeline)
	}
}


// script is the demonstration that msh runs without arguments.
var script = []string{
	"seq 1 5 > numbers",
	"wc -l < numbers",
	"sort -rn < numbers | head -n 2 >> numbers",
	"paste -sd, numbers",
	"false",
	"nosuchcommand",
	"cd /",
	"pwd",
	"exit 3",
	"echo not reached",
}

// demonstrate runs the script in a new temporary directory and prints the
// status after each line.
func demonstrate() error {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "msh")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)

	if err := os.Chdir(dir); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	s := &shell{}

	for _, line := range script {
		fmt.Println("$", line)
		s.execute(line)

		if s.exiting {
			fmt.Printf("[the shell exits with status %d]\n", s.last)

			return nil
		}

		fmt.Printf("[status %d]\n", s.last)
	}

	return nil
}

// interact reads command lines from standard input until exit or the end of
// the input, and ends the process with the last status.
func interact() {
	s := &shell{}
	lines := bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)

	for !s.exiting {
		fmt.Print("msh$ ")

		if !lines.Scan() {
			break
		}

		if strings.TrimSpace(lines.Text()) != "" {
			s.execute(lines.Text())
		}
	}

	os.Exit(s.last)
}

func main() {
	if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "-i" {
		interact()
	}

	if err := demonstrate(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

Listing 4.16 The complete msh, in Rust. code/rust/msh/src/main.rs

//! A small shell. It parses a command line into a pipeline of commands with
//! redirections, starts each command with its descriptors arranged, waits for
//! all of them, and reports the status of the last. The commands cd and exit
//! are built in.
//!
//! Without arguments it runs a fixed script in a temporary directory. With -i
//! it reads command lines from standard input.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p msh
//! ```

use std::env;
use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, BufRead, PipeReader, Write};
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::process::{self, Child, Stdio};

/// One stage of a pipeline: its arguments and the files that replace its
/// standard input and output, when the line names any.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Command {
    args: Vec<String>,
    input: Option<String>,
    output: Option<String>,
    append_output: bool,
}

struct SyntaxError;

/// Splits a line into the commands of a pipeline. Words and operators are
/// separated by spaces. The operators are | < > and >>.
fn parse(line: &str) -> Result<Vec<Command>, SyntaxError> {
    let mut pipeline = Vec::new();
    let mut current = Command::default();
    let mut words = line.split_whitespace();

    while let Some(word) = words.next() {
        match word {
            "|" => {
                if current.args.is_empty() {
                    return Err(SyntaxError);
                }

                pipeline.push(std::mem::take(&mut current));
            }
            "<" | ">" | ">>" => {
                let file = words.next().ok_or(SyntaxError)?.to_owned();

                if word == "<" {
                    current.input = Some(file);
                } else {
                    current.output = Some(file);
                    current.append_output = word == ">>";
                }
            }
            _ => current.args.push(word.to_owned()),
        }
    }

    if current.args.is_empty() {
        return Err(SyntaxError);
    }

    pipeline.push(current);

    Ok(pipeline)
}

/// Opens the files a command names and returns the files to use as its
/// standard input and output. `None` means "keep the default".
fn redirect(command: &Command) -> io::Result<(Option<File>, Option<File>)> {
    let input = command.input.as_ref().map(File::open).transpose()?;

    let output = command
        .output
        .as_ref()
        .map(|path| {
            OpenOptions::new()
                .write(true)
                .create(true)
                .append(command.append_output)
                .truncate(!command.append_output)
                .open(path)
        })
        .transpose()?;

    Ok((input, output))
}

/// Starts every command of a pipeline and returns the children that started.
/// Command `i` reads from the pipe that command `i - 1` writes to, unless a
/// redirection replaces that descriptor.
fn launch(pipeline: &[Command]) -> Vec<Child> {
    let mut started = Vec::new();
    let mut from_previous: Option<PipeReader> = None;

    for (i, command) in pipeline.iter().enumerate() {
        let mut stdin = from_previous
            .take()
            .map_or_else(Stdio::inherit, Stdio::from);
        let mut stdout = Stdio::inherit();

        if i + 1 < pipeline.len() {
            let Ok((reader, writer)) = io::pipe() else {
                eprintln!("msh: cannot create a pipe");

                break;
            };

            stdout = writer.into();
            from_previous = Some(reader);
        }

        let (input, output) = match redirect(command) {
            Ok(files) => files,
            Err(error) => {
                eprintln!("msh: {error}");

                continue;
            }
        };

        if let Some(file) = input {
            stdin = file.into();
        }

        if let Some(file) = output {
            stdout = file.into();
        }

        // The `Command` owns the shell's copies of the descriptors. It is
        // dropped when the statement ends, which closes them.
        let child = process::Command::new(&command.args[0])
            .args(&command.args[1..])
            .stdin(stdin)
            .stdout(stdout)
            .spawn();

        match child {
            Ok(child) => started.push(child),
            Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound => {
                eprintln!("msh: {}: command not found", command.args[0]);
            }
            Err(error) => eprintln!("msh: {error}"),
        }
    }

    started
}

/// Converts a wait status to the number a shell reports: the exit status, or
/// 128 plus the signal number.
fn status(child: &mut Child) -> i32 {
    let Ok(status) = child.wait() else {
        return 127;
    };

    match (status.signal(), status.code()) {
        (Some(signal), _) => 128 + signal,
        (None, Some(code)) => code,
        (None, None) => 127,
    }
}

/// Starts a pipeline, waits for every command, and returns the status of the
/// last command, or 127 when the last command did not start.
fn run(pipeline: &[Command]) -> i32 {
    let mut started = launch(pipeline);
    let mut last = 127;

    for child in &mut started {
        last = status(child);
    }

    if started.len() < pipeline.len() {
        return 127;
    }

    last
}

/// The state that outlives a command line.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Shell {
    last: i32,
    exiting: bool,
}

impl Shell {
    /// Runs one command line. cd and exit change the shell process itself, so
    /// they run inside it. Everything else runs in child processes.
    fn execute(&mut self, line: &str) {
        let Ok(pipeline) = parse(line) else {
            eprintln!("msh: syntax error");
            self.last = 2;

            return;
        };

        let args: Vec<&str> = pipeline[0].args.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();

        match (pipeline.len(), args.as_slice()) {
            (1, ["cd", directory]) => {
                self.last = 0;

                if let Err(error) = env::set_current_dir(directory) {
                    eprintln!("msh: {error}");
                    self.last = 1;
                }
            }
            (1, ["exit", rest @ ..]) => {
                self.exiting = true;

                if let [code] = rest
                    && let Ok(code) = code.parse()
                {
                    self.last = code;
                }
            }
            _ => self.last = run(&pipeline),
        }
    }
}

/// The demonstration that msh runs without arguments.
const SCRIPT: [&str; 10] = [
    "seq 1 5 > numbers",
    "wc -l < numbers",
    "sort -rn < numbers | head -n 2 >> numbers",
    "paste -sd, numbers",
    "false",
    "nosuchcommand",
    "cd /",
    "pwd",
    "exit 3",
    "echo not reached",
];

/// Runs the script in a new temporary directory and prints the status after
/// each line.
fn demonstrate() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = env::temp_dir().join(format!("msh-{}", process::id()));

    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;
    env::set_current_dir(&dir)?;

    let mut shell = Shell::default();

    for line in SCRIPT {
        println!("$ {line}");
        shell.execute(line);

        if shell.exiting {
            println!("[the shell exits with status {}]", shell.last);

            break;
        }

        println!("[status {}]", shell.last);
    }

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)
}

/// Reads command lines from standard input until exit or the end of the
/// input, and ends the process with the last status.
fn interact() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut shell = Shell::default();
    let mut lines = io::stdin().lock().lines();

    while !shell.exiting {
        print!("msh$ ");
        io::stdout().flush()?;

        let Some(line) = lines.next().transpose()? else {
            break;
        };

        if !line.trim().is_empty() {
            shell.execute(&line);
        }
    }

    process::exit(shell.last);
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    if env::args().nth(1).as_deref() == Some("-i") {
        interact()?;
    }

    demonstrate()
}

Summary

  • A shell is an ordinary program built on pipe, fork, dup2, exec and wait.
  • | becomes a pipe between descriptor 1 of one child and descriptor 0 of the next. <, > and >> become an open whose result replaces descriptor 0 or 1.
  • Redirections are performed in the child, between its creation and exec. The shell’s own descriptors do not change.
  • > truncates its file before the command starts.
  • The shell finds a program by searching the directories of PATH, and the environment is passed to the program by exec.
  • The shell closes its own copies of pipe ends and redirected files after starting each child, and waits for every child.
  • The status of a pipeline is the status of its last command; a signal is reported as 128 + n, and a command that cannot be started as 127.
  • cd and exit act on the shell process and are built in for that reason.
  • Variables, wildcards and quoting are processed by the shell before a program starts.

References

  • The Open Group Base Specifications, Shell Command Language: https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/V3_chap02.html
  • execve(2), environ(7), chdir(2) and strace(1), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html
  • M. Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface, No Starch Press, 2010, chapters 6, 27, 34 and 44.

Signals

A signal is a notification that the kernel delivers to a process at a moment the process did not choose. Each signal is identified by a small number and a name. The kernel sends signals to report events: a key pressed on the terminal, a write to a pipe with no reader, the end of a child, an invalid memory access. Processes send them to each other with the kill system call.

In this chapter, we will learn what state the kernel keeps for signals and at which moment a signal takes effect. We will follow Ctrl-C from the keyboard to the end of a program, read the kernel’s structures, and see how a handler function is run. Then we will measure signal handling from outside a process with sigfacts, and write sigmodel, a model of the kernel’s signal state.

This chapter covers

  • the common signals, what sends them, and what they do by default
  • the path of Ctrl-C from the terminal to a process
  • the pending mask, the blocked mask, and the action of a signal
  • the kernel structures: struct sigpending, struct sighand_struct, struct k_sigaction
  • why sending a signal and delivering it are separate events
  • why several sends of the same signal can result in a single delivery
  • how the kernel runs a handler, and what a handler may safely do
  • which dispositions survive exec
  • why SIGKILL cannot be blocked, ignored or handled
  • EINTR and SA_RESTART: a signal during a blocking system call

The common signals

Linux has 64 signals. Numbers 1 to 31 are the standard signals, each with a fixed meaning, and numbers 32 to 64 are the real-time signals, which programs may use for their own purposes. kill -l lists them. These are the ones a programmer meets.

NumberNameSent whenDefault action
2SIGINTCtrl-C is pressed on the terminalend the process
3SIGQUITCtrl-\ is pressedend the process and write a core dump
9SIGKILLa program calls kill with itend the process; cannot be changed
11SIGSEGVthe process accesses memory it has no mapping for (chapter 7)end the process and write a core dump
13SIGPIPEthe process writes to a pipe or socket with no reader (chapter 1)end the process
15SIGTERMa program calls kill; the default of the kill commandend the process
17SIGCHLDa child of the process ends or stops (chapter 3)ignore
19SIGSTOPa program calls kill with itstop the process; cannot be changed
20SIGTSTPCtrl-Z is pressedstop the process
18SIGCONTfg, bg, or killcontinue a stopped process

For each signal a process has a disposition, also called its action: what happens when the signal is delivered. There are 3 possibilities. The default action is the one in the table. Ignore discards the signal. A handler is a function of the program that the kernel calls when the signal arrives. SIGTERM is the polite request to end, which a program can handle to save its work, and SIGKILL is the request that cannot be refused.

From Ctrl-C to the end of a program

Suppose a program is running in a terminal, blocked in a read, and we press Ctrl-C.

  1. The terminal passes the byte 0x03 to the kernel’s terminal driver.
  2. The driver recognises it as the interrupt character and does not put it in the input of the program. It sends SIGINT to every process of the terminal’s foreground process group, the set of processes the shell started for the current command line.
  3. Sending means setting a bit: the kernel sets the bit for SIGINT in the pending mask of each of those processes. Nothing else has happened to them yet.
  4. A process that is sleeping in a system call is woken so that it can notice.
  5. When the process is next about to return from the kernel to user mode, the kernel checks its pending mask, finds SIGINT, clears the bit, and performs the action. The default action ends the process.

Steps 3 and 5 are separate events. Sending a signal runs in the sender, or in the kernel on behalf of a device, and only records that the signal is wanted. Delivery runs later, in the target, at the boundary between kernel mode and user mode. Every property of signals in this chapter follows from that split.

The state behind a signal

The kernel keeps 3 pieces of signal state.

StateContentsChanged by
Pending mask1 bit per signal: the signal has been sent and not yet deliveredkill sets a bit; delivery clears it
Blocked mask1 bit per signal: delivery of the signal is postponedsigprocmask
Actionper signal: the default, ignore, or the address of a handler functionsigaction

Blocking a signal is different from ignoring it. An ignored signal is discarded. A blocked signal stays pending and is delivered when the program unblocks it. A program blocks a signal around a piece of code that must not be interrupted by its handler.

These are the kernel’s definitions in Linux 5.15, from include/linux/signal_types.h, include/linux/sched/signal.h and include/linux/sched.h, reduced to the fields we use.

struct sigpending {
        struct list_head list;         /* queued details of pending signals */
        sigset_t signal;               /* the pending mask: 64 bits */
};

struct sigaction {
        __sighandler_t sa_handler;     /* SIG_DFL, SIG_IGN, or a function */
        unsigned long sa_flags;        /* SA_RESTART, ... */
        sigset_t sa_mask;              /* signals blocked while the handler runs */
};

struct sighand_struct {
        struct k_sigaction action[_NSIG];      /* one action per signal, _NSIG is 64 */
        /* ... */
};

struct signal_struct {
        struct sigpending shared_pending;      /* signals sent to the process */
        /* ... */
};

struct task_struct {
        struct signal_struct *signal;
        struct sighand_struct *sighand;
        sigset_t blocked;                      /* the blocked mask */
        struct sigpending pending;             /* signals sent to this thread */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
sigset_tA set of signals as a bit mask of 64 bits. Signal n is bit n - 1.
sigpending.signalThe pending mask.
sighand_struct.actionThe table of actions, indexed by signal number.
sa_handlerThe action: the constant SIG_DFL for the default, SIG_IGN for ignore, or the address of a handler.
sa_flags, sa_maskOptions for a handler, set by the program with sigaction.
task_struct.blockedThe blocked mask. Each thread has its own.
task_struct.pending and signal_struct.shared_pendingThere are 2 pending sets. A signal sent to a process with kill goes into shared_pending, and any thread of the process that does not block it may take it. A signal aimed at a single thread, such as SIGSEGV for the thread that made the invalid access, goes into that thread’s pending.

The kernel shows these masks in /proc/<pid>/status. This is a shell after trap '' INT and trap 'echo x' USR1:

$ grep -E 'SigPnd|ShdPnd|SigBlk|SigIgn|SigCgt' /proc/$$/status
SigPnd:	0000000000000000
ShdPnd:	0000000000000000
SigBlk:	0000000000000000
SigIgn:	0000000000000002
SigCgt:	0000000000010200

SigPnd is the thread’s pending mask and ShdPnd is shared_pending. SigBlk is blocked. SigIgn and SigCgt are derived from the action table: the signals that are ignored and the signals that have a handler. The values are hexadecimal. 0x2 is bit 1, signal 2, SIGINT. 0x10200 is bit 9, signal 10, SIGUSR1, and bit 16, signal 17, SIGCHLD, which the shell handles for its own purposes.

The masks are easier to read after decoding one by hand. Take SigCgt, 0000000000010200.

  1. Drop the leading zeros: 0x10200.
  2. Write each hexadecimal digit as 4 bits: 1 0000 0010 0000 0000.
  3. Number the bits from the right, starting at 0. The bits that are 1 are bit 9 and bit 16.
  4. Add 1 to each: signals 10 and 17, SIGUSR1 and SIGCHLD.

SigIgn, 0x2, is the single bit 1, signal 2, SIGINT. A mask of all zeros, as for SigPnd and SigBlk here, means that no signal is pending and none is blocked.

The design has direct consequences, and the measurements below confirm each of them.

  • The pending mask has 1 bit per signal, so it cannot count. A signal that is sent again while its bit is set leaves the mask unchanged.
  • A blocked signal stays pending for as long as it is blocked.
  • A handler is an address inside the current program. exec replaces the program, so a handled signal returns to the default action. Ignore and default are independent of the program and are kept.
  • SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are exempt from all 3 mechanisms. The kernel guarantees that an administrator can always end or stop a process.

SIGKILL cannot be blocked, ignored or handled. A process that receives it gets no chance to clean up.

How a handler is run

A handler is a function in the program, and the kernel has to make the program call it at a moment the program did not plan for. It does so by editing the state it is about to return to.

  1. The process is in the kernel, about to return to user mode, with its user-mode registers saved.
  2. The kernel copies those saved registers to the user stack of the process, in a signal frame.
  3. It changes the saved program counter to the address of the handler, and arranges the return address of the handler to point at a small piece of code that makes the system call sigreturn.
  4. It returns to user mode. The process now executes the handler, as if the handler had been called at the point of interruption.
  5. When the handler returns, sigreturn enters the kernel, which restores the registers from the signal frame. The program continues at the instruction where it was interrupted.

The handler can run between any 2 instructions of the program. If the program was in the middle of malloc, with the allocator’s data structures half updated, and the handler calls malloc too, the structures are corrupted. A handler may therefore call only functions that are async-signal-safe, a short list that includes write and excludes malloc and printf. The usual practice is a handler that does almost nothing: it sets a flag, or writes a byte to a pipe that the main loop of the program reads.

The runtimes of both languages do this for us. The Go runtime installs handlers for all signals and forwards them to the program through a channel registered with signal.Notify. Rust libraries such as signal-hook use the pipe technique. In both, the code we write for a signal runs in ordinary program context and may call anything.

Measuring signals

A program that changed its own signal handling would measure its language runtime as much as the kernel. sigfacts therefore observes other processes. It starts shell scripts that set dispositions with trap, sends them signals, and reads their masks from /proc/<pid>/status. The Rust version uses the nix crate with the signal feature.

$ cargo new sigfacts
$ cargo add -p sigfacts nix --features signal

mask reads a mask from the status file as a hexadecimal number. await waits until a process has reached a given state.
