use std::fs;
use std::io::{self, Read};
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::process::{Child, Command, Stdio};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

use nix::sys::signal::{Signal, kill};
use nix::unistd::Pid;

Listing 5.3 Reading the signal masks of another process, in Go. code/go/sigfacts/main.go

// mask returns one of the signal masks in /proc/<pid>/status: ShdPnd
// (pending), SigBlk (blocked), SigIgn (ignored) or SigCgt (caught).
func mask(pid int, name string) (uint64, error) {
	status, err := os.Open(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/status", pid))

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	defer status.Close()

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(status); lines.Scan(); {
		if value, ok := strings.CutPrefix(lines.Text(), name+":"); ok {
			return strconv.ParseUint(strings.TrimSpace(value), 16, 64)
		}
	}

	return 0, fmt.Errorf("%s: not in /proc/%d/status", name, pid)
}

// has reports whether a mask contains a signal. Signal n is bit n-1.
func has(mask uint64, signal syscall.Signal) bool {
	return mask&(1<<(signal-1)) != 0
}

// await polls /proc/<pid>/stat until the process has the given command name
// and state. State T is "stopped" and S is "sleeping".
func await(pid int, command string, state byte) error {
	want := fmt.Sprintf("(%s) %c", command, state)

	for {
		stat, err := os.ReadFile(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/stat", pid))

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if strings.Contains(string(stat), want) {
			return nil
		}

		time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)
	}
}

Listing 5.4 Reading the signal masks of another process, in Rust. code/rust/sigfacts/src/main.rs

/// Returns one of the signal masks in `/proc/<pid>/status`: `ShdPnd`
/// (pending), `SigBlk` (blocked), `SigIgn` (ignored) or `SigCgt` (caught).
fn mask(pid: Pid, name: &str) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let status = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/status"))?;

    status
        .lines()
        .find_map(|line| line.strip_prefix(name)?.strip_prefix(':'))
        .and_then(|value| u64::from_str_radix(value.trim(), 16).ok())
        .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into())
}

/// Reports whether a mask contains a signal. Signal `n` is bit `n - 1`.
fn has(mask: u64, signal: Signal) -> bool {
    mask & (1 << (signal as i32 - 1)) != 0
}

/// Polls `/proc/<pid>/stat` until the process has the given command name and
/// state. State `T` is "stopped" and `S` is "sleeping".
fn wait_for(pid: Pid, command: &str, state: char) -> io::Result<()> {
    let want = format!("({command}) {state}");

    while !fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/stat"))?.contains(&want) {
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Starts a shell script and returns the child with its process number.
fn shell(script: &str, stdout: Stdio) -> io::Result<(Child, Pid)> {
    let child = Command::new("sh")
        .args(["-c", script])
        .stdout(stdout)
        .spawn()?;
    let pid = Pid::from_raw(child.id() as i32);

    Ok((child, pid))
}

A stopped process does not return to user mode, so nothing is delivered to it. pending uses that to observe the pending mask. The script installs a handler for SIGUSR1 and stops itself. The program sends SIGUSR1 3 times, reads the mask, and lets the script continue with SIGCONT.

Listing 5.5 Sending a signal 3 times to a stopped process, in Go. code/go/sigfacts/main.go

// pending sends SIGUSR1 3 times to a stopped process that has a handler for
// it, reads the pending mask, and counts how often the handler runs after
// the process continues.
func pending() error {
	child := exec.Command("sh", "-c", `trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$; echo done`)
	stdout, err := child.StdoutPipe()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid := child.Process.Pid

	if err := await(pid, "sh", 'T'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for range 3 {
		syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGUSR1)
	}

	waiting, err := mask(pid, "ShdPnd")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGCONT)

	text, err := io.ReadAll(stdout)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("SIGUSR1 sent 3 times to a stopped process: pending mask %#x\n", waiting)
	fmt.Printf("after SIGCONT the handler ran %d time(s)\n", strings.Count(string(text), "caught"))

	return child.Wait()
}

Listing 5.6 Sending a signal 3 times to a stopped process, in Rust. code/rust/sigfacts/src/main.rs

/// Sends `SIGUSR1` 3 times to a stopped process that has a handler for it,
/// reads the pending mask, and counts how often the handler runs after the
/// process continues.
fn pending() -> io::Result<()> {
    let script = "trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$; echo done";
    let (mut child, pid) = shell(script, Stdio::piped())?;

    wait_for(pid, "sh", 'T')?;

    for _ in 0..3 {
        kill(pid, Signal::SIGUSR1)?;
    }

    let waiting = mask(pid, "ShdPnd")?;

    kill(pid, Signal::SIGCONT)?;

    let mut text = String::new();

    if let Some(stdout) = child.stdout.as_mut() {
        stdout.read_to_string(&mut text)?;
    }

    child.wait()?;

    println!("SIGUSR1 sent 3 times to a stopped process: pending mask {waiting:#x}");
    println!(
        "after SIGCONT the handler ran {} time(s)",
        text.matches("caught").count()
    );

    Ok(())
}

dispositions reads the ignored and caught masks of a shell that ignores SIGINT and handles SIGUSR1.

Listing 5.7 The actions of a process, read from outside, in Go. code/go/sigfacts/main.go

// dispositions reads the ignored and caught masks of a shell that ignores
// SIGINT and handles SIGUSR1.
func dispositions() error {
	child := exec.Command("sh", "-c", `trap '' INT; trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$`)

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer child.Wait()
	defer child.Process.Kill()

	pid := child.Process.Pid

	if err := await(pid, "sh", 'T'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	ignored, err := mask(pid, "SigIgn")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	caught, err := mask(pid, "SigCgt")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("shell with 2 traps: SIGINT ignored %v, SIGUSR1 caught %v, SIGTERM ignored %v\n",
		has(ignored, syscall.SIGINT), has(caught, syscall.SIGUSR1), has(ignored, syscall.SIGTERM))

	return nil
}

Listing 5.8 The actions of a process, read from outside, in Rust. code/rust/sigfacts/src/main.rs

/// Reads the ignored and caught masks of a shell that ignores `SIGINT` and
/// handles `SIGUSR1`.
fn dispositions() -> io::Result<()> {
    let script = "trap '' INT; trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$";
    let (mut child, pid) = shell(script, Stdio::inherit())?;

    wait_for(pid, "sh", 'T')?;

    let ignored = mask(pid, "SigIgn")?;
    let caught = mask(pid, "SigCgt")?;

    child.kill()?;
    child.wait()?;

    println!(
        "shell with 2 traps: SIGINT ignored {}, SIGUSR1 caught {}, SIGTERM ignored {}",
        has(ignored, Signal::SIGINT),
        has(caught, Signal::SIGUSR1),
        has(ignored, Signal::SIGTERM)
    );

    Ok(())
}

acrossExec starts a shell that ignores SIGTERM, handles SIGUSR1, and then replaces itself with sleep by exec. It reads the masks of the sleep process, sends it SIGTERM and then SIGKILL, and reports how it ended.

Listing 5.9 Dispositions after exec, and SIGKILL, in Go. code/go/sigfacts/main.go

// acrossExec reads the masks of a process after exec, sends it a signal it
// ignores, and then SIGKILL.
func acrossExec() error {
	child := exec.Command("sh", "-c", `trap '' TERM; trap 'echo caught' USR1; exec sleep 30`)

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid := child.Process.Pid

	if err := await(pid, "sleep", 'S'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	ignored, err := mask(pid, "SigIgn")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	caught, err := mask(pid, "SigCgt")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after exec: SIGTERM ignored %v, SIGUSR1 caught %v\n",
		has(ignored, syscall.SIGTERM), has(caught, syscall.SIGUSR1))

	syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGTERM)
	syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGKILL)
	child.Wait()

	if status, ok := child.ProcessState.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && status.Signaled() {
		fmt.Printf("SIGTERM, then SIGKILL: killed by signal %d\n", status.Signal())
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 5.10 Dispositions after exec, and SIGKILL, in Rust. code/rust/sigfacts/src/main.rs

/// Reads the masks of a process after exec, sends it a signal it ignores, and
/// then `SIGKILL`.
fn across_exec() -> io::Result<()> {
    let script = "trap '' TERM; trap 'echo caught' USR1; exec sleep 30";
    let (mut child, pid) = shell(script, Stdio::inherit())?;

    wait_for(pid, "sleep", 'S')?;

    let ignored = mask(pid, "SigIgn")?;
    let caught = mask(pid, "SigCgt")?;

    println!(
        "after exec: SIGTERM ignored {}, SIGUSR1 caught {}",
        has(ignored, Signal::SIGTERM),
        has(caught, Signal::SIGUSR1)
    );

    kill(pid, Signal::SIGTERM)?;
    kill(pid, Signal::SIGKILL)?;

    if let Some(signal) = child.wait()?.signal() {
        println!("SIGTERM, then SIGKILL: killed by signal {signal}");
    }

    Ok(())
}
SIGUSR1 sent 3 times to a stopped process: pending mask 0x200
after SIGCONT the handler ran 1 time(s)
shell with 2 traps: SIGINT ignored true, SIGUSR1 caught true, SIGTERM ignored false
after exec: SIGTERM ignored true, SIGUSR1 caught false
SIGTERM, then SIGKILL: killed by signal 9
OutputConclusion
pending mask 0x200 after 3 sends0x200 is bit 9, signal 10, SIGUSR1. The mask records that the signal is pending and holds no count.
the handler ran 1 time3 sends were merged into a single delivery.
SIGINT ignored, SIGUSR1 caught, SIGTERM not ignoredEach signal has its own entry in the action table.
after exec: SIGTERM ignored, SIGUSR1 not caughtIgnore survives exec. A handler is reset to the default.
killed by signal 9SIGTERM was discarded. SIGKILL ended the process.

Line 4 explains a detail from chapter 1. A Rust program starts with SIGPIPE ignored, and an ignored signal stays ignored across exec. Rust’s Command therefore resets SIGPIPE to the default in each child before it calls exec, and yes in the pipeline was ended by the signal as intended.

The merging of signals has a consequence for every program that handles SIGCHLD. A handler for it calls wait in a loop until no ended child remains, because several children may have ended behind a single delivery.

Modelling signal state

Low-level design: sigmodel

Field of processKernel fieldMeaning
pendingshared_pending.signalmask of 64 bits; signal n is bit n - 1
blockedtask_struct.blockedmask of 64 bits
actions, restartsighand->action[n]default, ignore or handle; the SA_RESTART flag
handled, killedByhow many handlers have run; the signal that ended the process
call, outcomethe system call the process is blocked in; what a signal did to it
OperationSystem callBehaviour
setAction(signal, action, restart)sigactioninstalls an action; fails with EINVAL for SIGKILL
block(mask), unblock(mask)sigprocmaskchanges the blocked mask; SIGKILL cannot be added
send(signal)killdiscards an ignored signal, otherwise sets its pending bit
deliver()performs the action of each pending, unblocked signal, lowest number first

The state of a process is the 2 masks and a table of actions.

Listing 5.11 The imports of sigmodel, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
)

Listing 5.12 The imports of sigmodel, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

use std::fmt;

Listing 5.13 The signal state of a process, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

const (
	sigKill = 9
	sigUsr1 = 10
	sigTerm = 15
	sigChld = 17
	sigLast = 64
)

type action int

const (
	byDefault action = iota
	ignore
	handle
)

var errInvalid = errors.New("EINVAL")

// A process holds the signal state of one process. Signal n is bit n-1 of
// the masks.
type process struct {
	pending  uint64
	blocked  uint64
	actions  [sigLast + 1]action
	restart  [sigLast + 1]bool
	handled  int
	killedBy int

	// call is the system call the process is blocked in, or "" when it is
	// running. outcome records what a signal did to that call.
	call    string
	outcome string
}

func bit(signal int) uint64 {
	return 1 << (signal - 1)
}

Listing 5.14 The signal state of a process, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

const SIGKILL: usize = 9;
const SIGUSR1: usize = 10;
const SIGTERM: usize = 15;
const SIGCHLD: usize = 17;
const SIGLAST: usize = 64;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum Action {
    Default,
    Ignore,
    Handle,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Invalid;

impl fmt::Display for Invalid {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str("EINVAL")
    }
}

/// The signal state of one process. Signal `n` is bit `n - 1` of the masks.
struct Process {
    pending: u64,
    blocked: u64,
    actions: [Action; SIGLAST + 1],
    restart: [bool; SIGLAST + 1],
    handled: u32,
    killed_by: Option<usize>,

    /// The system call the process is blocked in, or `None` when it is
    /// running. `outcome` records what a signal did to that call.
    call: Option<&'static str>,
    outcome: String,
}

fn bit(signal: usize) -> u64 {
    1 << (signal - 1)
}

impl Process {
    fn new(call: Option<&'static str>) -> Process {
        Process {
            pending: 0,
            blocked: 0,
            actions: [Action::Default; SIGLAST + 1],
            restart: [false; SIGLAST + 1],
            handled: 0,
            killed_by: None,
            call,
            outcome: String::new(),
        }
    }
}

setAction and block enforce the exemption of SIGKILL. Changing its action is an error, and a request to block it is reduced silently.

Listing 5.15 Installing actions and changing the blocked mask, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

// setAction installs an action for a signal. restart is the SA_RESTART flag
// of a handler. The action of SIGKILL cannot be changed.
func (p *process) setAction(signal int, a action, restart bool) error {
	if signal == sigKill {
		return errInvalid
	}

	p.actions[signal], p.restart[signal] = a, restart

	return nil
}

// block adds signals to the blocked mask. SIGKILL is removed from the
// request without an error, as the kernel does.
func (p *process) block(mask uint64) {
	p.blocked |= mask &^ bit(sigKill)
}

// unblock removes signals from the blocked mask and delivers what was
// waiting for it.
func (p *process) unblock(mask uint64) {
	p.blocked &^= mask
	p.deliver()
}

Listing 5.16 Installing actions and changing the blocked mask, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

impl Process {
    /// Installs an action for a signal. `restart` is the `SA_RESTART` flag of
    /// a handler. The action of `SIGKILL` cannot be changed.
    fn set_action(&mut self, signal: usize, action: Action, restart: bool) -> Result<(), Invalid> {
        if signal == SIGKILL {
            return Err(Invalid);
        }

        self.actions[signal] = action;
        self.restart[signal] = restart;

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Adds signals to the blocked mask. `SIGKILL` is removed from the
    /// request without an error, as the kernel does.
    fn block(&mut self, mask: u64) {
        self.blocked |= mask & !bit(SIGKILL);
    }

    /// Removes signals from the blocked mask and delivers what was waiting
    /// for it.
    fn unblock(&mut self, mask: u64) {
        self.blocked &= !mask;
        self.deliver();
    }
}

send is the half that runs in the sender. A signal that the target ignores is discarded at this point and does not become pending, unless it is blocked: a blocked signal is kept, because its action may have changed by the time it is unblocked. Setting a bit that is already set has no effect, which is the merging we measured.

Listing 5.17 Sending: setting a pending bit, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

// ignored reports whether a signal would be discarded on delivery: its
// action is ignore, or its action is the default and the default is to
// ignore, which is the case for SIGCHLD.
func (p *process) ignored(signal int) bool {
	return p.actions[signal] == ignore || p.actions[signal] == byDefault && signal == sigChld
}

// send is the sender's half. It discards a signal that the target ignores
// and does not block. Otherwise it sets the pending bit, which is already
// set when the same signal is waiting.
func (p *process) send(signal int) {
	if p.ignored(signal) && p.blocked&bit(signal) == 0 {
		return
	}

	p.pending |= bit(signal)
}

Listing 5.18 Sending: setting a pending bit, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

impl Process {
    /// Reports whether a signal would be discarded on delivery: its action is
    /// ignore, or its action is the default and the default is to ignore,
    /// which is the case for `SIGCHLD`.
    fn ignored(&self, signal: usize) -> bool {
        match self.actions[signal] {
            Action::Ignore => true,
            Action::Default => signal == SIGCHLD,
            Action::Handle => false,
        }
    }

    /// The sender's half. It discards a signal that the target ignores and
    /// does not block. Otherwise it sets the pending bit, which is already
    /// set when the same signal is waiting.
    fn send(&mut self, signal: usize) {
        if self.ignored(signal) && self.blocked & bit(signal) == 0 {
            return;
        }

        self.pending |= bit(signal);
    }
}

deliver is the half that runs in the target. It considers the signals that are pending and not blocked. For a handler it also decides the fate of a system call that the process was blocked in.

Listing 5.19 Delivering: performing the action, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

// deliver is the target's half. The kernel runs it when the process is about
// to return to user mode. It takes each pending signal that is not blocked,
// lowest number first, and performs its action.
func (p *process) deliver() {
	for signal := 1; signal <= sigLast && p.killedBy == 0; signal++ {
		if p.pending&^p.blocked&bit(signal) == 0 {
			continue
		}

		p.pending &^= bit(signal)

		switch {
		case p.actions[signal] == handle:
			p.handled++
			p.interrupt(signal)

		case !p.ignored(signal):
			p.killedBy = signal
		}
	}
}

// interrupt decides what happens to a blocking system call when a handler
// has run: the call is restarted, or it fails with EINTR.
func (p *process) interrupt(signal int) {
	if p.call == "" {
		return
	}

	if p.restart[signal] {
		p.outcome = "the " + p.call + " is restarted"

		return
	}

	p.outcome = "the " + p.call + " fails with EINTR"
	p.call = ""
}

Listing 5.20 Delivering: performing the action, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

impl Process {
    /// The target's half. The kernel runs it when the process is about to
    /// return to user mode. It takes each pending signal that is not blocked,
    /// lowest number first, and performs its action.
    fn deliver(&mut self) {
        for signal in 1..=SIGLAST {
            if self.killed_by.is_some() {
                break;
            }

            if self.pending & !self.blocked & bit(signal) == 0 {
                continue;
            }

            self.pending &= !bit(signal);

            if self.actions[signal] == Action::Handle {
                self.handled += 1;
                self.interrupt(signal);
            } else if !self.ignored(signal) {
                self.killed_by = Some(signal);
            }
        }
    }

    /// Decides what happens to a blocking system call when a handler has run:
    /// the call is restarted, or it fails with `EINTR`.
    fn interrupt(&mut self, signal: usize) {
        let Some(call) = self.call else {
            return;
        };

        if self.restart[signal] {
            self.outcome = format!("the {call} is restarted");

            return;
        }

        self.outcome = format!("the {call} fails with EINTR");
        self.call = None;
    }
}

A signal during a blocking call

A process that is blocked in a system call is inside the kernel and is not about to return to user mode. If signals waited for the call to finish, a process blocked in a read on a terminal could not be interrupted by Ctrl-C. The kernel therefore wakes the process, abandons the call, and runs the handler. After the handler returns there are 2 possible outcomes, selected by a flag given to sigaction when the handler was installed.

Without SA_RESTART, the call returns the error EINTR, “interrupted system call”, and the program has to call it again. A loop that retries on EINTR around every blocking call is the standard defence. Go’s standard library and Rust’s std::io helpers such as read_to_end contain that loop.

Listing 5.21 The trace, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

func coalescing() error {
	p := &process{}

	if err := p.setAction(sigUsr1, handle, false); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.block(bit(sigUsr1))

	for range 3 {
		p.send(sigUsr1)
		p.deliver()
	}

	fmt.Printf("SIGUSR1 blocked and sent 3 times: pending mask %#x\n", p.pending)

	p.unblock(bit(sigUsr1))
	fmt.Printf("after unblocking the handler ran %d time(s)\n", p.handled)

	return nil
}

func ignoring() error {
	p := &process{}

	if err := p.setAction(sigTerm, ignore, false); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.send(sigTerm)
	fmt.Printf("SIGTERM ignored and sent: pending mask %#x\n", p.pending)

	fmt.Printf("installing a handler for SIGKILL: %v\n", p.setAction(sigKill, handle, false))

	p.block(^uint64(0))
	p.send(sigKill)
	p.deliver()
	fmt.Printf("every signal blocked, SIGKILL sent: killed by signal %d\n", p.killedBy)

	return nil
}

func interrupting(restart bool) error {
	p := &process{call: "read"}

	if err := p.setAction(sigUsr1, handle, restart); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.send(sigUsr1)
	p.deliver()
	fmt.Printf("handler runs during a blocking read, SA_RESTART %v: %s\n", restart, p.outcome)

	return nil
}

func main() {
	steps := []func() error{
		coalescing,
		ignoring,
		func() error { return interrupting(false) },
		func() error { return interrupting(true) },
	}

	for _, step := range steps {
		if err := step(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 5.22 The trace, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

fn coalescing() -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    let mut process = Process::new(None);

    process.set_action(SIGUSR1, Action::Handle, false)?;
    process.block(bit(SIGUSR1));

    for _ in 0..3 {
        process.send(SIGUSR1);
        process.deliver();
    }

    println!(
        "SIGUSR1 blocked and sent 3 times: pending mask {:#x}",
        process.pending
    );

    process.unblock(bit(SIGUSR1));
    println!(
        "after unblocking the handler ran {} time(s)",
        process.handled
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn ignoring() -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    let mut process = Process::new(None);

    process.set_action(SIGTERM, Action::Ignore, false)?;
    process.send(SIGTERM);
    println!(
        "SIGTERM ignored and sent: pending mask {:#x}",
        process.pending
    );

    if let Err(error) = process.set_action(SIGKILL, Action::Handle, false) {
        println!("installing a handler for SIGKILL: {error}");
    }

    process.block(u64::MAX);
    process.send(SIGKILL);
    process.deliver();

    if let Some(signal) = process.killed_by {
        println!("every signal blocked, SIGKILL sent: killed by signal {signal}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn interrupting(restart: bool) -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    let mut process = Process::new(Some("read"));

    process.set_action(SIGUSR1, Action::Handle, restart)?;
    process.send(SIGUSR1);
    process.deliver();

    println!(
        "handler runs during a blocking read, SA_RESTART {restart}: {}",
        process.outcome
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    coalescing()?;
    ignoring()?;
    interrupting(false)?;
    interrupting(true)
}
SIGUSR1 blocked and sent 3 times: pending mask 0x200
after unblocking the handler ran 1 time(s)
SIGTERM ignored and sent: pending mask 0x0
installing a handler for SIGKILL: EINVAL
every signal blocked, SIGKILL sent: killed by signal 9
handler runs during a blocking read, SA_RESTART false: the read fails with EINTR
handler runs during a blocking read, SA_RESTART true: the read is restarted

Lines 1 and 2 reproduce the pending mask and the single delivery that sigfacts measured.

Correspondence with the kernel source. __send_signal in kernel/signal.c sets the bit, and prepare_signal discards ignored signals. Delivery starts in get_signal, called on the way back to user mode, and the signal frame of an arm64 process is built by setup_rt_frame in arch/arm64/kernel/signal.c. Real-time signals, numbers 32 to 64, are an exception to merging: the kernel queues each send of those separately, in the list of struct sigpending.

Inspecting signals on a live system

CommandShows
kill -lthe names and numbers of all signals
grep Sig /proc/<pid>/statusthe pending, blocked, ignored and caught masks of a process
kill -TERM <pid>, kill -KILL <pid>sends a signal to a process
kill -STOP <pid>, kill -CONT <pid>stops and continues a process
strace -e trace=signal -p <pid>the signals a process receives and the signal system calls it makes

A process that does not react to kill is diagnosed with the second command. If SIGTERM, bit 14, is set in SigIgn or SigBlk, the process has ignored or blocked it, and only SIGKILL will end it.

The complete programs

Listing 5.23 The complete sigfacts, in Go. code/go/sigfacts/main.go

// Command sigfacts measures signal handling from outside a process. It starts
// shell scripts that set signal dispositions, sends them signals, and reads
// their signal masks from /proc/<pid>/status.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./sigfacts
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)


// mask returns one of the signal masks in /proc/<pid>/status: ShdPnd
// (pending), SigBlk (blocked), SigIgn (ignored) or SigCgt (caught).
func mask(pid int, name string) (uint64, error) {
	status, err := os.Open(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/status", pid))

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	defer status.Close()

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(status); lines.Scan(); {
		if value, ok := strings.CutPrefix(lines.Text(), name+":"); ok {
			return strconv.ParseUint(strings.TrimSpace(value), 16, 64)
		}
	}

	return 0, fmt.Errorf("%s: not in /proc/%d/status", name, pid)
}

// has reports whether a mask contains a signal. Signal n is bit n-1.
func has(mask uint64, signal syscall.Signal) bool {
	return mask&(1<<(signal-1)) != 0
}

// await polls /proc/<pid>/stat until the process has the given command name
// and state. State T is "stopped" and S is "sleeping".
func await(pid int, command string, state byte) error {
	want := fmt.Sprintf("(%s) %c", command, state)

	for {
		stat, err := os.ReadFile(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/stat", pid))

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if strings.Contains(string(stat), want) {
			return nil
		}

		time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)
	}
}


// pending sends SIGUSR1 3 times to a stopped process that has a handler for
// it, reads the pending mask, and counts how often the handler runs after
// the process continues.
func pending() error {
	child := exec.Command("sh", "-c", `trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$; echo done`)
	stdout, err := child.StdoutPipe()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid := child.Process.Pid

	if err := await(pid, "sh", 'T'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for range 3 {
		syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGUSR1)
	}

	waiting, err := mask(pid, "ShdPnd")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGCONT)

	text, err := io.ReadAll(stdout)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("SIGUSR1 sent 3 times to a stopped process: pending mask %#x\n", waiting)
	fmt.Printf("after SIGCONT the handler ran %d time(s)\n", strings.Count(string(text), "caught"))

	return child.Wait()
}


// dispositions reads the ignored and caught masks of a shell that ignores
// SIGINT and handles SIGUSR1.
func dispositions() error {
	child := exec.Command("sh", "-c", `trap '' INT; trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$`)

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer child.Wait()
	defer child.Process.Kill()

	pid := child.Process.Pid

	if err := await(pid, "sh", 'T'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	ignored, err := mask(pid, "SigIgn")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	caught, err := mask(pid, "SigCgt")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("shell with 2 traps: SIGINT ignored %v, SIGUSR1 caught %v, SIGTERM ignored %v\n",
		has(ignored, syscall.SIGINT), has(caught, syscall.SIGUSR1), has(ignored, syscall.SIGTERM))

	return nil
}


// acrossExec reads the masks of a process after exec, sends it a signal it
// ignores, and then SIGKILL.
func acrossExec() error {
	child := exec.Command("sh", "-c", `trap '' TERM; trap 'echo caught' USR1; exec sleep 30`)

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	pid := child.Process.Pid

	if err := await(pid, "sleep", 'S'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	ignored, err := mask(pid, "SigIgn")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	caught, err := mask(pid, "SigCgt")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after exec: SIGTERM ignored %v, SIGUSR1 caught %v\n",
		has(ignored, syscall.SIGTERM), has(caught, syscall.SIGUSR1))

	syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGTERM)
	syscall.Kill(pid, syscall.SIGKILL)
	child.Wait()

	if status, ok := child.ProcessState.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && status.Signaled() {
		fmt.Printf("SIGTERM, then SIGKILL: killed by signal %d\n", status.Signal())
	}

	return nil
}


func main() {
	for _, experiment := range []func() error{pending, dispositions, acrossExec} {
		if err := experiment(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 5.24 The complete sigfacts, in Rust. code/rust/sigfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures signal handling from outside a process. It starts shell scripts
//! that set signal dispositions, sends them signals, and reads their signal
//! masks from `/proc/<pid>/status`.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p sigfacts
//! ```

use std::fs;
use std::io::{self, Read};
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::process::{Child, Command, Stdio};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

use nix::sys::signal::{Signal, kill};
use nix::unistd::Pid;

/// Returns one of the signal masks in `/proc/<pid>/status`: `ShdPnd`
/// (pending), `SigBlk` (blocked), `SigIgn` (ignored) or `SigCgt` (caught).
fn mask(pid: Pid, name: &str) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let status = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/status"))?;

    status
        .lines()
        .find_map(|line| line.strip_prefix(name)?.strip_prefix(':'))
        .and_then(|value| u64::from_str_radix(value.trim(), 16).ok())
        .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into())
}

/// Reports whether a mask contains a signal. Signal `n` is bit `n - 1`.
fn has(mask: u64, signal: Signal) -> bool {
    mask & (1 << (signal as i32 - 1)) != 0
}

/// Polls `/proc/<pid>/stat` until the process has the given command name and
/// state. State `T` is "stopped" and `S` is "sleeping".
fn wait_for(pid: Pid, command: &str, state: char) -> io::Result<()> {
    let want = format!("({command}) {state}");

    while !fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/stat"))?.contains(&want) {
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Starts a shell script and returns the child with its process number.
fn shell(script: &str, stdout: Stdio) -> io::Result<(Child, Pid)> {
    let child = Command::new("sh")
        .args(["-c", script])
        .stdout(stdout)
        .spawn()?;
    let pid = Pid::from_raw(child.id() as i32);

    Ok((child, pid))
}

/// Sends `SIGUSR1` 3 times to a stopped process that has a handler for it,
/// reads the pending mask, and counts how often the handler runs after the
/// process continues.
fn pending() -> io::Result<()> {
    let script = "trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$; echo done";
    let (mut child, pid) = shell(script, Stdio::piped())?;

    wait_for(pid, "sh", 'T')?;

    for _ in 0..3 {
        kill(pid, Signal::SIGUSR1)?;
    }

    let waiting = mask(pid, "ShdPnd")?;

    kill(pid, Signal::SIGCONT)?;

    let mut text = String::new();

    if let Some(stdout) = child.stdout.as_mut() {
        stdout.read_to_string(&mut text)?;
    }

    child.wait()?;

    println!("SIGUSR1 sent 3 times to a stopped process: pending mask {waiting:#x}");
    println!(
        "after SIGCONT the handler ran {} time(s)",
        text.matches("caught").count()
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Reads the ignored and caught masks of a shell that ignores `SIGINT` and
/// handles `SIGUSR1`.
fn dispositions() -> io::Result<()> {
    let script = "trap '' INT; trap 'echo caught' USR1; kill -STOP $$";
    let (mut child, pid) = shell(script, Stdio::inherit())?;

    wait_for(pid, "sh", 'T')?;

    let ignored = mask(pid, "SigIgn")?;
    let caught = mask(pid, "SigCgt")?;

    child.kill()?;
    child.wait()?;

    println!(
        "shell with 2 traps: SIGINT ignored {}, SIGUSR1 caught {}, SIGTERM ignored {}",
        has(ignored, Signal::SIGINT),
        has(caught, Signal::SIGUSR1),
        has(ignored, Signal::SIGTERM)
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Reads the masks of a process after exec, sends it a signal it ignores, and
/// then `SIGKILL`.
fn across_exec() -> io::Result<()> {
    let script = "trap '' TERM; trap 'echo caught' USR1; exec sleep 30";
    let (mut child, pid) = shell(script, Stdio::inherit())?;

    wait_for(pid, "sleep", 'S')?;

    let ignored = mask(pid, "SigIgn")?;
    let caught = mask(pid, "SigCgt")?;

    println!(
        "after exec: SIGTERM ignored {}, SIGUSR1 caught {}",
        has(ignored, Signal::SIGTERM),
        has(caught, Signal::SIGUSR1)
    );

    kill(pid, Signal::SIGTERM)?;
    kill(pid, Signal::SIGKILL)?;

    if let Some(signal) = child.wait()?.signal() {
        println!("SIGTERM, then SIGKILL: killed by signal {signal}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    pending()?;
    dispositions()?;
    across_exec()
}

Listing 5.25 The complete sigmodel, in Go. code/go/sigmodel/main.go

// Command sigmodel models the signal state the kernel keeps for a process: a
// pending mask, a blocked mask, and an action for each signal. It separates
// sending a signal from delivering it, and shows what a delivered signal
// does to a process that is blocked in a system call.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./sigmodel
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
)


const (
	sigKill = 9
	sigUsr1 = 10
	sigTerm = 15
	sigChld = 17
	sigLast = 64
)

type action int

const (
	byDefault action = iota
	ignore
	handle
)

var errInvalid = errors.New("EINVAL")

// A process holds the signal state of one process. Signal n is bit n-1 of
// the masks.
type process struct {
	pending  uint64
	blocked  uint64
	actions  [sigLast + 1]action
	restart  [sigLast + 1]bool
	handled  int
	killedBy int

	// call is the system call the process is blocked in, or "" when it is
	// running. outcome records what a signal did to that call.
	call    string
	outcome string
}

func bit(signal int) uint64 {
	return 1 << (signal - 1)
}


// setAction installs an action for a signal. restart is the SA_RESTART flag
// of a handler. The action of SIGKILL cannot be changed.
func (p *process) setAction(signal int, a action, restart bool) error {
	if signal == sigKill {
		return errInvalid
	}

	p.actions[signal], p.restart[signal] = a, restart

	return nil
}

// block adds signals to the blocked mask. SIGKILL is removed from the
// request without an error, as the kernel does.
func (p *process) block(mask uint64) {
	p.blocked |= mask &^ bit(sigKill)
}

// unblock removes signals from the blocked mask and delivers what was
// waiting for it.
func (p *process) unblock(mask uint64) {
	p.blocked &^= mask
	p.deliver()
}


// ignored reports whether a signal would be discarded on delivery: its
// action is ignore, or its action is the default and the default is to
// ignore, which is the case for SIGCHLD.
func (p *process) ignored(signal int) bool {
	return p.actions[signal] == ignore || p.actions[signal] == byDefault && signal == sigChld
}

// send is the sender's half. It discards a signal that the target ignores
// and does not block. Otherwise it sets the pending bit, which is already
// set when the same signal is waiting.
func (p *process) send(signal int) {
	if p.ignored(signal) && p.blocked&bit(signal) == 0 {
		return
	}

	p.pending |= bit(signal)
}


// deliver is the target's half. The kernel runs it when the process is about
// to return to user mode. It takes each pending signal that is not blocked,
// lowest number first, and performs its action.
func (p *process) deliver() {
	for signal := 1; signal <= sigLast && p.killedBy == 0; signal++ {
		if p.pending&^p.blocked&bit(signal) == 0 {
			continue
		}

		p.pending &^= bit(signal)

		switch {
		case p.actions[signal] == handle:
			p.handled++
			p.interrupt(signal)

		case !p.ignored(signal):
			p.killedBy = signal
		}
	}
}

// interrupt decides what happens to a blocking system call when a handler
// has run: the call is restarted, or it fails with EINTR.
func (p *process) interrupt(signal int) {
	if p.call == "" {
		return
	}

	if p.restart[signal] {
		p.outcome = "the " + p.call + " is restarted"

		return
	}

	p.outcome = "the " + p.call + " fails with EINTR"
	p.call = ""
}


func coalescing() error {
	p := &process{}

	if err := p.setAction(sigUsr1, handle, false); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.block(bit(sigUsr1))

	for range 3 {
		p.send(sigUsr1)
		p.deliver()
	}

	fmt.Printf("SIGUSR1 blocked and sent 3 times: pending mask %#x\n", p.pending)

	p.unblock(bit(sigUsr1))
	fmt.Printf("after unblocking the handler ran %d time(s)\n", p.handled)

	return nil
}

func ignoring() error {
	p := &process{}

	if err := p.setAction(sigTerm, ignore, false); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.send(sigTerm)
	fmt.Printf("SIGTERM ignored and sent: pending mask %#x\n", p.pending)

	fmt.Printf("installing a handler for SIGKILL: %v\n", p.setAction(sigKill, handle, false))

	p.block(^uint64(0))
	p.send(sigKill)
	p.deliver()
	fmt.Printf("every signal blocked, SIGKILL sent: killed by signal %d\n", p.killedBy)

	return nil
}

func interrupting(restart bool) error {
	p := &process{call: "read"}

	if err := p.setAction(sigUsr1, handle, restart); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	p.send(sigUsr1)
	p.deliver()
	fmt.Printf("handler runs during a blocking read, SA_RESTART %v: %s\n", restart, p.outcome)

	return nil
}

func main() {
	steps := []func() error{
		coalescing,
		ignoring,
		func() error { return interrupting(false) },
		func() error { return interrupting(true) },
	}

	for _, step := range steps {
		if err := step(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 5.26 The complete sigmodel, in Rust. code/rust/sigmodel/src/main.rs

//! Models the signal state the kernel keeps for a process: a pending mask, a
//! blocked mask, and an action for each signal. It separates sending a signal
//! from delivering it, and shows what a delivered signal does to a process
//! that is blocked in a system call.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p sigmodel
//! ```

use std::fmt;

const SIGKILL: usize = 9;
const SIGUSR1: usize = 10;
const SIGTERM: usize = 15;
const SIGCHLD: usize = 17;
const SIGLAST: usize = 64;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum Action {
    Default,
    Ignore,
    Handle,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Invalid;

impl fmt::Display for Invalid {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str("EINVAL")
    }
}

/// The signal state of one process. Signal `n` is bit `n - 1` of the masks.
struct Process {
    pending: u64,
    blocked: u64,
    actions: [Action; SIGLAST + 1],
    restart: [bool; SIGLAST + 1],
    handled: u32,
    killed_by: Option<usize>,

    /// The system call the process is blocked in, or `None` when it is
    /// running. `outcome` records what a signal did to that call.
    call: Option<&'static str>,
    outcome: String,
}

fn bit(signal: usize) -> u64 {
    1 << (signal - 1)
}

impl Process {
    fn new(call: Option<&'static str>) -> Process {
        Process {
            pending: 0,
            blocked: 0,
            actions: [Action::Default; SIGLAST + 1],
            restart: [false; SIGLAST + 1],
            handled: 0,
            killed_by: None,
            call,
            outcome: String::new(),
        }
    }
}

impl Process {
    /// Installs an action for a signal. `restart` is the `SA_RESTART` flag of
    /// a handler. The action of `SIGKILL` cannot be changed.
    fn set_action(&mut self, signal: usize, action: Action, restart: bool) -> Result<(), Invalid> {
        if signal == SIGKILL {
            return Err(Invalid);
        }

        self.actions[signal] = action;
        self.restart[signal] = restart;

        Ok(())
    }

    /// Adds signals to the blocked mask. `SIGKILL` is removed from the
    /// request without an error, as the kernel does.
    fn block(&mut self, mask: u64) {
        self.blocked |= mask & !bit(SIGKILL);
    }

    /// Removes signals from the blocked mask and delivers what was waiting
    /// for it.
    fn unblock(&mut self, mask: u64) {
        self.blocked &= !mask;
        self.deliver();
    }
}

impl Process {
    /// Reports whether a signal would be discarded on delivery: its action is
    /// ignore, or its action is the default and the default is to ignore,
    /// which is the case for `SIGCHLD`.
    fn ignored(&self, signal: usize) -> bool {
        match self.actions[signal] {
            Action::Ignore => true,
            Action::Default => signal == SIGCHLD,
            Action::Handle => false,
        }
    }

    /// The sender's half. It discards a signal that the target ignores and
    /// does not block. Otherwise it sets the pending bit, which is already
    /// set when the same signal is waiting.
    fn send(&mut self, signal: usize) {
        if self.ignored(signal) && self.blocked & bit(signal) == 0 {
            return;
        }

        self.pending |= bit(signal);
    }
}

impl Process {
    /// The target's half. The kernel runs it when the process is about to
    /// return to user mode. It takes each pending signal that is not blocked,
    /// lowest number first, and performs its action.
    fn deliver(&mut self) {
        for signal in 1..=SIGLAST {
            if self.killed_by.is_some() {
                break;
            }

            if self.pending & !self.blocked & bit(signal) == 0 {
                continue;
            }

            self.pending &= !bit(signal);

            if self.actions[signal] == Action::Handle {
                self.handled += 1;
                self.interrupt(signal);
            } else if !self.ignored(signal) {
                self.killed_by = Some(signal);
            }
        }
    }

    /// Decides what happens to a blocking system call when a handler has run:
    /// the call is restarted, or it fails with `EINTR`.
    fn interrupt(&mut self, signal: usize) {
        let Some(call) = self.call else {
            return;
        };

        if self.restart[signal] {
            self.outcome = format!("the {call} is restarted");

            return;
        }

        self.outcome = format!("the {call} fails with EINTR");
        self.call = None;
    }
}

fn coalescing() -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    let mut process = Process::new(None);

    process.set_action(SIGUSR1, Action::Handle, false)?;
    process.block(bit(SIGUSR1));

    for _ in 0..3 {
        process.send(SIGUSR1);
        process.deliver();
    }

    println!(
        "SIGUSR1 blocked and sent 3 times: pending mask {:#x}",
        process.pending
    );

    process.unblock(bit(SIGUSR1));
    println!(
        "after unblocking the handler ran {} time(s)",
        process.handled
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn ignoring() -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    let mut process = Process::new(None);

    process.set_action(SIGTERM, Action::Ignore, false)?;
    process.send(SIGTERM);
    println!(
        "SIGTERM ignored and sent: pending mask {:#x}",
        process.pending
    );

    if let Err(error) = process.set_action(SIGKILL, Action::Handle, false) {
        println!("installing a handler for SIGKILL: {error}");
    }

    process.block(u64::MAX);
    process.send(SIGKILL);
    process.deliver();

    if let Some(signal) = process.killed_by {
        println!("every signal blocked, SIGKILL sent: killed by signal {signal}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn interrupting(restart: bool) -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    let mut process = Process::new(Some("read"));

    process.set_action(SIGUSR1, Action::Handle, restart)?;
    process.send(SIGUSR1);
    process.deliver();

    println!(
        "handler runs during a blocking read, SA_RESTART {restart}: {}",
        process.outcome
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Invalid> {
    coalescing()?;
    ignoring()?;
    interrupting(false)?;
    interrupting(true)
}

Summary

  • A signal is sent by setting a bit in the pending mask of the target. Its action is performed later, when the target is about to return to user mode and the signal is not blocked.
  • Each signal has an action: the default, ignore, or a handler function. The actions are in struct sighand_struct, and the masks are visible in /proc/<pid>/status.
  • The pending mask holds 1 bit per signal, so repeated sends of a pending signal are merged into a single delivery.
  • The kernel runs a handler by saving the program’s registers on its stack and redirecting it to the handler. A handler may call only async-signal-safe functions.
  • exec resets handlers to the default action and keeps ignored signals ignored.
  • SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be blocked, ignored or handled.
  • A handler that runs during a blocking system call makes the call fail with EINTR, or restart when the handler was installed with SA_RESTART.

References

  • signal(7), sigaction(2), sigprocmask(2), signal-safety(7) and sigreturn(2), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html
  • M. Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface, No Starch Press, 2010, chapters 20 to 22.
  • kernel/signal.c and include/linux/sched/signal.h, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/kernel/signal.c

CPU Scheduling

A machine has a fixed number of CPUs and usually many more tasks that want to run. The scheduler is the part of the kernel that decides, for each CPU and at each moment, which task runs. A task is the unit it schedules: a process with a single thread, or one thread of a process with several (chapter 3).

In this chapter, we will learn how the Completely Fair Scheduler, the default of Linux 5.15, makes that decision. We will first see how the scheduler gets control of a CPU at all, and follow a switch from one task to the next. Then we will measure how it divides a CPU between busy processes of different priorities with schedfacts, and write cfs, a model of its central rule that produces the measured shares.

This chapter covers

  • when the scheduler runs: system calls, sleeping, and the timer interrupt
  • a context switch, step by step
  • scheduling classes and policies, and where ordinary tasks fit
  • the requirement a fair scheduler has to meet
  • nice values, weights, and shares of a CPU
  • virtual runtime, and the rule “run the task with the smallest”
  • the kernel structures: struct sched_entity and struct cfs_rq
  • the length of a time slice
  • what the scheduler does with a task that wakes after a long sleep
  • several CPUs: a run queue for each, load balancing, and affinity

When the scheduler runs

A task that is running holds its CPU, and the kernel is not executing. The scheduler can act only when control passes to the kernel. That happens in 3 ways.

EventWhat happens
The task makes a system call that has to waitA read with no data puts the task to sleep. The task gives up the CPU voluntarily, and the scheduler picks another.
The task endsexit releases the CPU.
An interrupt arrivesThe processor stops the task and enters the kernel. The most important one for scheduling is the timer interrupt, which a hardware timer raises at a fixed rate.

The timer interrupt is what makes it impossible for a task to keep a CPU for ever. A program in an endless loop makes no system calls, and it is still interrupted, 250 times per second on our machine. Taking the CPU from a task that did not offer it is called preemption.

The kernel counts both kinds of switch for every task. This is a shell loop that had been running for a second on a busy machine:

$ grep ctxt /proc/577022/status
voluntary_ctxt_switches:	0
nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches:	37

The loop did not sleep once, and was preempted 37 times. A program that waits for input shows the opposite pattern.

From one task to the next

  1. Task A is running on a CPU. The timer interrupt arrives, and the processor enters the kernel on A’s behalf.
  2. The kernel charges A for the time it has run since it was last charged.
  3. It checks whether A has had its share for now. If so, it sets a flag on A that asks for a reschedule.
  4. On the way back to user mode, the kernel sees the flag and calls the scheduler.
  5. The scheduler picks the next task, B, from the run queue: the set of tasks that are ready to run on this CPU.
  6. The kernel performs a context switch. It saves the registers of A in A’s task_struct, loads the registers of B, and switches to B’s address space. A’s state remains complete, so it will continue later as if nothing had happened.
  7. The return to user mode now resumes B. A waits in the run queue.

Steps 2, 3 and 5 are the scheduling policy: how much each task is charged, when it has had enough, and who is next. The rest of the chapter is about those 3 decisions.

Classes and policies

Linux has several schedulers side by side, called scheduling classes. Each task belongs to one, selected by its policy. When a CPU needs a task, the kernel asks the classes in a fixed order and takes the first task offered.

$ chrt -p 577022
pid 577022's current scheduling policy: SCHED_OTHER
pid 577022's current scheduling priority: 0

SCHED_OTHER is the policy of every task that has not asked for something else, and it belongs to the fair class. The real-time policies are for tasks that must run within a bounded time of becoming runnable, such as audio processing, and they require privilege, because a real-time task in an endless loop keeps its CPU from every ordinary task. The rest of this chapter concerns the fair class.

The requirement

The goal of the fair class is stated in terms of an ideal: if n tasks of equal priority are runnable on a CPU, each should receive 1/n of it, and a task of higher priority should receive a proportionally larger part. A real CPU runs a single task at a time, so the scheduler approximates the ideal by switching between tasks and keeping account of what each has received.

The priority of a task in the fair class is its nice value, an integer from -20 to 19. A higher value means a lower priority: the task is “nicer” to the others. The nice command and the setpriority system call set it, and only a privileged process may set a negative value. The kernel converts the nice value to a weight with a fixed table, in which nice 0 has weight 1024 and each step changes the weight by about 25%. The share of a task is its weight divided by the sum of the weights of all runnable tasks on the CPU.

A share is relative. A task of nice 19 that is alone on a CPU receives all of it. The nice value has an effect only when tasks compete.

Measuring shares

schedfacts starts 2 busy processes, restricts both to CPU 0 with taskset, and sets their nice values with nice. Restricting them to the same CPU makes them compete: on an idle machine with 8 CPUs each would otherwise get a CPU of its own. After 2 seconds the program reads the CPU time of each from /proc/<pid>/stat. It needs only the standard libraries.

$ cargo new schedfacts

spin starts a busy shell loop, and cpuTime reads the time a process has spent on a CPU. The kernel reports it in clock ticks of 10 ms, in separate fields for the time spent in user mode and in kernel mode.

Listing 6.1 The imports of schedfacts, in Go. code/go/schedfacts/main.go

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

Listing 6.2 The imports of schedfacts, in Rust. code/rust/schedfacts/src/main.rs

use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::process::{Child, Command};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

Listing 6.3 Starting a busy process on CPU 0, and reading its CPU time, in Go. code/go/schedfacts/main.go

// spin starts a busy shell loop, restricted to CPU 0 and with
// the given nice value.
func spin(nice int) (*exec.Cmd, error) {
	child := exec.Command("taskset", "-c", "0", "nice", "-n", strconv.Itoa(nice), "sh", "-c", "while :; do :; done")

	return child, child.Start()
}

// cpuTime returns the CPU time a process has used, in clock ticks: fields 14
// and 15 of /proc/<pid>/stat, the time in user mode and in kernel mode.
func cpuTime(pid int) (int, error) {
	stat, err := os.ReadFile(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/stat", pid))

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	fields := strings.Fields(string(stat[strings.LastIndexByte(string(stat), ')')+1:]))

	if len(fields) < 13 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("/proc/%d/stat: too few fields", pid)
	}

	var user, kernel int

	if _, err := fmt.Sscan(fields[11], &user); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	if _, err := fmt.Sscan(fields[12], &kernel); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return user + kernel, nil
}

Listing 6.4 Starting a busy process on CPU 0, and reading its CPU time, in Rust. code/rust/schedfacts/src/main.rs

/// Starts a busy shell loop, restricted to CPU 0 and with the
/// given nice value.
fn spin(nice: i32) -> io::Result<Child> {
    Command::new("taskset")
        .args(["-c", "0", "nice", "-n", &nice.to_string()])
        .args(["sh", "-c", "while :; do :; done"])
        .spawn()
}

/// Returns the CPU time a process has used, in clock ticks: fields 14 and 15
/// of `/proc/<pid>/stat`, the time in user mode and in kernel mode.
fn cpu_time(pid: u32) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stat = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/stat"))?;
    let rest = stat.rsplit_once(')').map_or("", |(_, rest)| rest);

    let ticks: Vec<u64> = rest
        .split_whitespace()
        .skip(11)
        .take(2)
        .filter_map(|field| field.parse().ok())
        .collect();

    match ticks.as_slice() {
        [user, kernel] => Ok(user + kernel),
        _ => Err(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into()),
    }
}

share lets a process of nice 0 compete with a process of a given nice value, and prints the percentage each received. The percentages are rounded to the nearest 5, since a measurement over 2 seconds varies by a few ticks between runs.

Listing 6.5 Measuring the division of a CPU, in Go. code/go/schedfacts/main.go

// stop ends a busy process and collects it.
func stop(child *exec.Cmd) {
	child.Process.Kill()
	child.Wait()
}

// share lets a process of nice 0 and a process of the given nice value
// compete for CPU 0 for 2 seconds and prints the share of CPU time each
// received, rounded to the nearest 5%.
func share(nice int) error {
	first, err := spin(0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer stop(first)

	second, err := spin(nice)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer stop(second)

	time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)

	a, err := cpuTime(first.Process.Pid)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	b, err := cpuTime(second.Process.Pid)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	percent := (200*a/(a+b) + 5) / 10 * 5
	fmt.Printf("nice 0 and nice %d on 1 CPU: %d%% and %d%%\n", nice, percent, 100-percent)

	return nil
}

Listing 6.6 Measuring the division of a CPU, in Rust. code/rust/schedfacts/src/main.rs

/// Ends a busy process and collects it.
fn stop(mut child: Child) -> io::Result<()> {
    child.kill()?;
    child.wait()?;

    Ok(())
}

/// Lets a process of nice 0 and a process of the given nice value compete for
/// CPU 0 for 2 seconds and prints the share of CPU time each received,
/// rounded to the nearest 5%.
fn share(nice: i32) -> io::Result<()> {
    let first = spin(0)?;
    let second = spin(nice)?;

    thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2));

    let times = cpu_time(first.id()).and_then(|a| Ok((a, cpu_time(second.id())?)));

    stop(first)?;
    stop(second)?;

    let (a, b) = times?;
    let percent = (200 * a / (a + b) + 5) / 10 * 5;

    println!(
        "nice 0 and nice {nice} on 1 CPU: {percent}% and {}%",
        100 - percent
    );

    Ok(())
}
nice 0 and nice 0 on 1 CPU: 50% and 50%
nice 0 and nice 5 on 1 CPU: 75% and 25%
nice 0 and nice 10 on 1 CPU: 90% and 10%

The shares predicted from the table are 1024/2048 = 50%, 1024/1359 = 75.3% and 1024/1134 = 90.3%. The measurement agrees with all of them.

Virtual runtime

The scheduler needs a rule that produces these shares without computing them. It keeps a number for each task, the virtual runtime or vruntime, and follows 2 rules.

  1. When a task has run for a time t, its vruntime increases by t × 1024 / weight.
  2. The task with the smallest vruntime runs next.

For a task of weight 1024, vruntime is the real time it has run. A task of weight 335 is charged about 3.06 ms for each millisecond, and a task of weight 3121 is charged about 0.33 ms.

To see why this produces the shares, take a task A of weight 1024 and a task C of weight 335. Rule 2 always runs the one that is behind, so their vruntimes stay close together. Suppose both have advanced by 300 ms of vruntime. A was charged at the real rate, so it ran for 300 ms. C was charged 3.06 ms per millisecond, so it ran for 98 ms. The ratio 300 to 98 is the ratio of the weights, 1024 to 335. Equal progress in virtual time means weighted progress in real time.

The kernel’s structures

The scheduling data of a task is a struct sched_entity, embedded in its task_struct as the field se. Each CPU has a struct cfs_rq, the run queue of the fair class. These are the definitions in Linux 5.15, from include/linux/sched.h and kernel/sched/sched.h, reduced to the fields we use.

struct load_weight {
        unsigned long weight;                  /* 1024 for nice 0 */
        u32 inv_weight;                        /* precomputed 2^32 / weight */
};

struct sched_entity {
        struct load_weight load;
        struct rb_node run_node;               /* its node in the run queue's tree */
        unsigned int on_rq;                    /* 1 while it is in the run queue */
        u64 exec_start;                        /* when it was last put on a CPU */
        u64 sum_exec_runtime;                  /* real CPU time received, in ns */
        u64 vruntime;                          /* virtual runtime, in ns */
        /* ... */
};

struct cfs_rq {
        struct load_weight load;               /* sum of the weights in the queue */
        unsigned int nr_running;               /* number of runnable entities */
        u64 min_vruntime;                      /* a floor that only increases */
        struct rb_root_cached tasks_timeline;  /* the tree, ordered by vruntime */
        struct sched_entity *curr;             /* the entity on the CPU */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
load.weightThe weight from the nice table.
inv_weightA precomputed reciprocal, so that the division in rule 1 becomes a multiplication.
vruntimeThe virtual runtime of the task.
sum_exec_runtimeThe real CPU time, the number behind the measurement of schedfacts.
tasks_timelineA red-black tree, a balanced search tree, with the runnable entities ordered by vruntime.
run_nodeThe place of the entity in that tree.
min_vruntimeThe smallest vruntime in the queue, kept so that it only increases. It is used when a task wakes up.

Rule 2 needs a data structure that returns its smallest element and accepts insertions, both quickly. A red-black tree does each in time proportional to the logarithm of the number of tasks, and the kernel keeps a pointer to the leftmost node, so finding the next task takes constant time.

The length of a slice

How long a task runs before the scheduler chooses again is also derived from the weights. The scheduler aims to run every runnable task once within a period called the scheduling latency, and gives each task the part of the period that corresponds to its weight. With more tasks the parts become shorter, down to a minimum, so that the cost of switching does not dominate. The defaults in Linux 5.15 are a latency of 6 ms and a minimum of 0.75 ms, both multiplied by a factor that grows with the number of CPUs: 4 on a machine with 8 or more CPUs, giving 24 ms and 3 ms here.

An example with the 3 tasks of this chapter makes the rule concrete. A and B have weight 1024 and C has weight 335, a total of 2383. In a period of 24 ms, A receives 24 × 1024 / 2383 = 10.3 ms, B the same, and C receives 24 × 335 / 2383 = 3.4 ms.

Low-level design: cfs

TypeKernel structureFieldsInvariant
taskstruct sched_entityname, weight, vruntime, slicesvruntime only increases
schedulerstruct cfs_rqrunnable, minVruntimerunnable is ordered by vruntime; minVruntime only increases
OperationKernel functionBehaviour
tick()update_curr, pick_next_entityremoves the task with the smallest vruntime, charges it for 1 slice, inserts it again
wake(task, place)place_entity, enqueue_entityinserts a task; with place, first raises its vruntime to minVruntime

Modelling the scheduler

The weights are the kernel’s table sched_prio_to_weight. The model uses a fixed slice of 1 ms, which is enough to reproduce the shares.

use std::collections::BTreeSet;

// weights is the kernel's table sched_prio_to_weight: the weight of each nice
// value from -20 to 19. Each step of nice changes the weight by about 25%.
var weights = [40]int64{
	88761, 71755, 56483, 46273, 36291, 29154, 23254, 18705, 14949, 11916,
	9548, 7620, 6100, 4904, 3906, 3121, 2501, 1991, 1586, 1277,
	1024, 820, 655, 526, 423, 335, 272, 215, 172, 137,
	110, 87, 70, 56, 45, 36, 29, 23, 18, 15,
}

// slice is the time a task runs before the scheduler chooses again, in
// nanoseconds.
const slice = 1_000_000

// A task is one schedulable entity. vruntime is its virtual runtime in
// nanoseconds, and slices counts how often it has run.
type task struct {
	name     string
	weight   int64
	vruntime int64
	slices   int
}

func newTask(name string, nice int) *task {
	return &task{name: name, weight: weights[nice+20]}
}

Listing 6.10 Weights and tasks, in Rust. code/rust/cfs/src/main.rs

/// The kernel's table `sched_prio_to_weight`: the weight of each nice value
/// from -20 to 19. Each step of nice changes the weight by about 25%.
const WEIGHTS: [u64; 40] = [
    88761, 71755, 56483, 46273, 36291, 29154, 23254, 18705, 14949, 11916, 9548, 7620, 6100, 4904,
    3906, 3121, 2501, 1991, 1586, 1277, 1024, 820, 655, 526, 423, 335, 272, 215, 172, 137, 110, 87,
    70, 56, 45, 36, 29, 23, 18, 15,
];

/// The time a task runs before the scheduler chooses again, in nanoseconds.
const SLICE: u64 = 1_000_000;

/// One schedulable entity. `vruntime` is its virtual runtime in nanoseconds,
/// and `slices` counts how often it has run.
struct Task {
    name: &'static str,
    weight: u64,
    vruntime: u64,
    slices: u64,
}

impl Task {
    fn new(name: &'static str, nice: i32) -> Task {
        Task {
            name,
            weight: WEIGHTS[(nice + 20) as usize],
            vruntime: 0,
            slices: 0,
        }
    }
}

The run queue orders tasks by vruntime. The Go version is a binary heap from container/heap, and the Rust version is a BTreeSet of keys. Both give the operations rule 2 needs.

Listing 6.11 The run queue, in Go. code/go/cfs/main.go

// A queue holds the runnable tasks ordered by virtual runtime, with the name
// as a tie-break. It implements heap.Interface. The kernel keeps the same
// order in a red-black tree and takes the leftmost node.
type queue []*task

func (q queue) Len() int      { return len(q) }
func (q queue) Swap(i, j int) { q[i], q[j] = q[j], q[i] }
func (q *queue) Push(t any)   { *q = append(*q, t.(*task)) }

func (q queue) Less(i, j int) bool {
	if q[i].vruntime != q[j].vruntime {
		return q[i].vruntime < q[j].vruntime
	}

	return q[i].name < q[j].name
}

func (q *queue) Pop() any {
	old := *q
	last := old[len(old)-1]
	*q = old[:len(old)-1]

	return last
}

Listing 6.12 The run queue, in Rust. code/rust/cfs/src/main.rs

/// The runnable tasks, ordered by virtual runtime with the name as a
/// tie-break. `runnable` holds the order and `tasks` holds the tasks, indexed
/// by the number in the key. The kernel keeps the same order in a red-black
/// tree and takes the leftmost node.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Scheduler {
    tasks: Vec<Task>,
    runnable: BTreeSet<(u64, &'static str, usize)>,
    min_vruntime: u64,
}

impl Scheduler {
    fn enqueue(&mut self, id: usize) {
        let task = &self.tasks[id];

        self.runnable.insert((task.vruntime, task.name, id));
    }
}

tick applies both rules. minVruntime follows the vruntime of the task at the front of the queue.

Listing 6.13 Running the task with the smallest vruntime, in Go. code/go/cfs/main.go

// A scheduler is a run queue and the smallest virtual runtime it has seen,
// which only increases.
type scheduler struct {
	runnable    queue
	minVruntime int64
}

// tick runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime for one slice and
// returns it. The task is charged slice * 1024 / weight, so a task of weight
// 1024 is charged real time and a heavier task is charged less.
func (s *scheduler) tick() *task {
	t := heap.Pop(&s.runnable).(*task)

	t.vruntime += slice * 1024 / t.weight
	t.slices++

	heap.Push(&s.runnable, t)
	s.minVruntime = max(s.minVruntime, s.runnable[0].vruntime)

	return t
}

// wake makes a task runnable. With place set, a task that slept is moved
// forward to the queue's minimum, so that it cannot claim the time it did
// not use while it slept.
func (s *scheduler) wake(t *task, place bool) {
	if place {
		t.vruntime = max(t.vruntime, s.minVruntime)
	}

	heap.Push(&s.runnable, t)
}

Listing 6.14 Running the task with the smallest vruntime, in Rust. code/rust/cfs/src/main.rs

impl Scheduler {
    /// Runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime for one slice and
    /// returns its number. The task is charged `SLICE * 1024 / weight`, so a
    /// task of weight 1024 is charged real time and a heavier task is charged
    /// less.
    fn tick(&mut self) -> Option<usize> {
        let (_, _, id) = self.runnable.pop_first()?;
        let task = &mut self.tasks[id];

        task.vruntime += SLICE * 1024 / task.weight;
        task.slices += 1;

        self.enqueue(id);

        if let Some(&(leftmost, _, _)) = self.runnable.first() {
            self.min_vruntime = self.min_vruntime.max(leftmost);
        }

        Some(id)
    }

    /// Makes a task runnable and returns its number. With `place` set, a task
    /// that slept is moved forward to the queue's minimum, so that it cannot
    /// claim the time it did not use while it slept.
    fn wake(&mut self, mut task: Task, place: bool) -> usize {
        if place {
            task.vruntime = task.vruntime.max(self.min_vruntime);
        }

        self.tasks.push(task);
        self.enqueue(self.tasks.len() - 1);

        self.tasks.len() - 1
    }
}

share repeats the measurement on the model: a task of nice 0 against a task of another nice value, for 2000 slices.

Listing 6.15 The shares on the model, in Go. code/go/cfs/main.go

// share runs a task of nice 0 against a task of the given nice value for
// 2000 slices and prints each task's share, rounded to the nearest 5%.
func share(nice int) {
	s := &scheduler{}
	first, second := newTask("A", 0), newTask("B", nice)

	s.wake(first, true)
	s.wake(second, true)

	for range 2000 {
		s.tick()
	}

	percent := (200*first.slices/(first.slices+second.slices) + 5) / 10 * 5
	fmt.Printf("nice 0 and nice %d on 1 CPU: %d%% and %d%%\n", nice, percent, 100-percent)
}

Listing 6.16 The shares on the model, in Rust. code/rust/cfs/src/main.rs

/// Runs a task of nice 0 against a task of the given nice value for 2000
/// slices and prints each task's share, rounded to the nearest 5%.
fn share(nice: i32) {
    let mut scheduler = Scheduler::default();

    let first = scheduler.wake(Task::new("A", 0), true);
    let second = scheduler.wake(Task::new("B", nice), true);

    for _ in 0..2000 {
        scheduler.tick();
    }

    let (a, b) = (
        scheduler.tasks[first].slices,
        scheduler.tasks[second].slices,
    );
    let percent = (200 * a / (a + b) + 5) / 10 * 5;

    println!(
        "nice 0 and nice {nice} on 1 CPU: {percent}% and {}%",
        100 - percent
    );
}
