/// Prints which task runs in each of the first 12 slices.
fn order() {
    let mut scheduler = Scheduler::default();

    for task in [Task::new("A", 0), Task::new("B", 0), Task::new("C", 5)] {
        scheduler.wake(task, true);
    }

    let mut names = Vec::new();

    for _ in 0..12 {
        if let Some(id) = scheduler.tick() {
            names.push(scheduler.tasks[id].name);
        }
    }

    println!("A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5: {}", names.join(" "));
}

A task that wakes up

A task that sleeps is removed from the run queue, and its vruntime stops increasing. After a long sleep its vruntime is far below that of the tasks that kept running. Under rule 2 alone it would then run without interruption until it had caught up, and every other task would stop for that time. A task that had slept for an hour could claim the CPU for many minutes.

The scheduler prevents this when the task wakes: it raises the task’s vruntime to the min_vruntime of the queue. The task is treated as if it had kept pace while it slept. It competes on equal terms from the moment it wakes and receives no credit for the time it did not use.

Listing 6.19 Waking a task with and without placement, in Go. code/go/cfs/main.go

// sleeper lets A and B run for 200 slices, wakes C with a virtual runtime of
// 0, and counts how many of the next 30 slices C receives.
func sleeper(place bool) int {
	s := &scheduler{}

	s.wake(newTask("A", 0), true)
	s.wake(newTask("B", 0), true)

	for range 200 {
		s.tick()
	}

	c := newTask("C", 0)
	s.wake(c, place)

	for range 30 {
		s.tick()
	}

	return c.slices
}

Listing 6.20 Waking a task with and without placement, in Rust. code/rust/cfs/src/main.rs

/// Lets A and B run for 200 slices, wakes C with a virtual runtime of 0, and
/// counts how many of the next 30 slices C receives.
fn sleeper(place: bool) -> u64 {
    let mut scheduler = Scheduler::default();

    scheduler.wake(Task::new("A", 0), true);
    scheduler.wake(Task::new("B", 0), true);

    for _ in 0..200 {
        scheduler.tick();
    }

    let c = scheduler.wake(Task::new("C", 0), place);

    for _ in 0..30 {
        scheduler.tick();
    }

    scheduler.tasks[c].slices
}
nice 0 and nice 0 on 1 CPU: 50% and 50%
nice 0 and nice 5 on 1 CPU: 75% and 25%
nice 0 and nice 10 on 1 CPU: 90% and 10%
A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5: A B C A B A B A B C A B
C wakes with its old virtual runtime: it receives 30 of the next 30 slices
C wakes and is placed at the minimum: it receives 10 of the next 30 slices
LineWhat it shows
lines 1 to 3The model gives the shares that schedfacts measured.
A B C A B A B A B C A BC runs in slices 3 and 10: 2 slices of 12, against 5 each for A and B.
30 of the next 30 slicesWith its old vruntime, the woken task monopolises the CPU.
10 of the next 30 slicesPlaced at the minimum, it receives the same share as A and B.

A task that sleeps for an hour is placed at the minimum vruntime when it wakes. It gets its fair share from that moment, and no credit for the hour.

Several CPUs

Everything so far concerned a single CPU. A machine with several CPUs has a run queue for each, with its own tree and its own lock, so that the CPUs can schedule without waiting for each other. A task is in the queue of exactly 1 CPU at a time.

Separate queues can become uneven, with tasks waiting on one CPU while another is idle. Load balancing corrects this: periodically, and whenever a CPU runs out of tasks, the kernel compares the queues and moves tasks from a loaded CPU to a lighter one. Moving has a cost, because the task’s data is in the caches of the CPU it leaves, so the balancer prefers to leave a task where it last ran.

A program can restrict the CPUs a task may use, its affinity, with sched_setaffinity or the taskset command. schedfacts used this to force its 2 processes onto the same CPU.

$ taskset -p 577022
pid 577022's current affinity mask: ff

The mask ff has 8 bits set: the task may run on any of the 8 CPUs.

Correspondence with the kernel source. The model corresponds to kernel/sched/fair.c. update_curr charges the running task with calc_delta_fair, pick_next_entity takes the leftmost node of tasks_timeline, and place_entity sets the vruntime of a waking task from min_vruntime. The model simplifies 2 points. The kernel computes the length of a slice in sched_slice, where the model uses 1 ms. And place_entity grants a waking task a small bonus below min_vruntime, so that interactive tasks respond quickly. Linux 6.6 replaced this policy with EEVDF, which keeps weights and virtual time and changes how the next task is selected.

Inspecting the scheduler on a live system

CommandShows
top or ps -eo pid,ni,pcpu,comm --sort=-pcputhe nice value and CPU use of each process
chrt -p <pid>the scheduling policy and real-time priority of a task
taskset -p <pid>the CPUs a task may run on
grep ctxt /proc/<pid>/statusvoluntary and involuntary context switches
cat /proc/loadavgthe average number of runnable tasks over 1, 5 and 15 minutes
nice -n 10 cmd, renice 10 -p <pid>starts a command with a nice value, or changes one

A high count of involuntary switches means the task wants more CPU than it gets. A high count of voluntary switches means it mostly waits.

The complete programs

Listing 6.21 The complete schedfacts, in Go. code/go/schedfacts/main.go

// Command schedfacts measures how the scheduler divides a CPU between busy
// processes of different nice values. It starts the processes on the same
// CPU, lets them compete, and reads the CPU time each one received.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./schedfacts
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"time"
)


// spin starts a busy shell loop, restricted to CPU 0 and with
// the given nice value.
func spin(nice int) (*exec.Cmd, error) {
	child := exec.Command("taskset", "-c", "0", "nice", "-n", strconv.Itoa(nice), "sh", "-c", "while :; do :; done")

	return child, child.Start()
}

// cpuTime returns the CPU time a process has used, in clock ticks: fields 14
// and 15 of /proc/<pid>/stat, the time in user mode and in kernel mode.
func cpuTime(pid int) (int, error) {
	stat, err := os.ReadFile(fmt.Sprintf("/proc/%d/stat", pid))

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	fields := strings.Fields(string(stat[strings.LastIndexByte(string(stat), ')')+1:]))

	if len(fields) < 13 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("/proc/%d/stat: too few fields", pid)
	}

	var user, kernel int

	if _, err := fmt.Sscan(fields[11], &user); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	if _, err := fmt.Sscan(fields[12], &kernel); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return user + kernel, nil
}


// stop ends a busy process and collects it.
func stop(child *exec.Cmd) {
	child.Process.Kill()
	child.Wait()
}

// share lets a process of nice 0 and a process of the given nice value
// compete for CPU 0 for 2 seconds and prints the share of CPU time each
// received, rounded to the nearest 5%.
func share(nice int) error {
	first, err := spin(0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer stop(first)

	second, err := spin(nice)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer stop(second)

	time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)

	a, err := cpuTime(first.Process.Pid)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	b, err := cpuTime(second.Process.Pid)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	percent := (200*a/(a+b) + 5) / 10 * 5
	fmt.Printf("nice 0 and nice %d on 1 CPU: %d%% and %d%%\n", nice, percent, 100-percent)

	return nil
}


func main() {
	for _, nice := range []int{0, 5, 10} {
		if err := share(nice); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 6.22 The complete schedfacts, in Rust. code/rust/schedfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures how the scheduler divides a CPU between busy processes of
//! different nice values. It starts the processes on the same CPU, lets them
//! compete, and reads the CPU time each one received.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p schedfacts
//! ```

use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::process::{Child, Command};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

/// Starts a busy shell loop, restricted to CPU 0 and with the
/// given nice value.
fn spin(nice: i32) -> io::Result<Child> {
    Command::new("taskset")
        .args(["-c", "0", "nice", "-n", &nice.to_string()])
        .args(["sh", "-c", "while :; do :; done"])
        .spawn()
}

/// Returns the CPU time a process has used, in clock ticks: fields 14 and 15
/// of `/proc/<pid>/stat`, the time in user mode and in kernel mode.
fn cpu_time(pid: u32) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stat = fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/stat"))?;
    let rest = stat.rsplit_once(')').map_or("", |(_, rest)| rest);

    let ticks: Vec<u64> = rest
        .split_whitespace()
        .skip(11)
        .take(2)
        .filter_map(|field| field.parse().ok())
        .collect();

    match ticks.as_slice() {
        [user, kernel] => Ok(user + kernel),
        _ => Err(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into()),
    }
}

/// Ends a busy process and collects it.
fn stop(mut child: Child) -> io::Result<()> {
    child.kill()?;
    child.wait()?;

    Ok(())
}

/// Lets a process of nice 0 and a process of the given nice value compete for
/// CPU 0 for 2 seconds and prints the share of CPU time each received,
/// rounded to the nearest 5%.
fn share(nice: i32) -> io::Result<()> {
    let first = spin(0)?;
    let second = spin(nice)?;

    thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2));

    let times = cpu_time(first.id()).and_then(|a| Ok((a, cpu_time(second.id())?)));

    stop(first)?;
    stop(second)?;

    let (a, b) = times?;
    let percent = (200 * a / (a + b) + 5) / 10 * 5;

    println!(
        "nice 0 and nice {nice} on 1 CPU: {percent}% and {}%",
        100 - percent
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    for nice in [0, 5, 10] {
        share(nice)?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

Listing 6.23 The complete cfs, in Go. code/go/cfs/main.go

// Command cfs models the Completely Fair Scheduler: every runnable task has a
// virtual runtime, the scheduler always runs the task with the smallest one,
// and a task's virtual runtime advances more slowly the larger its weight.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./cfs
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)


// weights is the kernel's table sched_prio_to_weight: the weight of each nice
// value from -20 to 19. Each step of nice changes the weight by about 25%.
var weights = [40]int64{
	88761, 71755, 56483, 46273, 36291, 29154, 23254, 18705, 14949, 11916,
	9548, 7620, 6100, 4904, 3906, 3121, 2501, 1991, 1586, 1277,
	1024, 820, 655, 526, 423, 335, 272, 215, 172, 137,
	110, 87, 70, 56, 45, 36, 29, 23, 18, 15,
}

// slice is the time a task runs before the scheduler chooses again, in
// nanoseconds.
const slice = 1_000_000

// A task is one schedulable entity. vruntime is its virtual runtime in
// nanoseconds, and slices counts how often it has run.
type task struct {
	name     string
	weight   int64
	vruntime int64
	slices   int
}

func newTask(name string, nice int) *task {
	return &task{name: name, weight: weights[nice+20]}
}


// A queue holds the runnable tasks ordered by virtual runtime, with the name
// as a tie-break. It implements heap.Interface. The kernel keeps the same
// order in a red-black tree and takes the leftmost node.
type queue []*task

func (q queue) Len() int      { return len(q) }
func (q queue) Swap(i, j int) { q[i], q[j] = q[j], q[i] }
func (q *queue) Push(t any)   { *q = append(*q, t.(*task)) }

func (q queue) Less(i, j int) bool {
	if q[i].vruntime != q[j].vruntime {
		return q[i].vruntime < q[j].vruntime
	}

	return q[i].name < q[j].name
}

func (q *queue) Pop() any {
	old := *q
	last := old[len(old)-1]
	*q = old[:len(old)-1]

	return last
}


// A scheduler is a run queue and the smallest virtual runtime it has seen,
// which only increases.
type scheduler struct {
	runnable    queue
	minVruntime int64
}

// tick runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime for one slice and
// returns it. The task is charged slice * 1024 / weight, so a task of weight
// 1024 is charged real time and a heavier task is charged less.
func (s *scheduler) tick() *task {
	t := heap.Pop(&s.runnable).(*task)

	t.vruntime += slice * 1024 / t.weight
	t.slices++

	heap.Push(&s.runnable, t)
	s.minVruntime = max(s.minVruntime, s.runnable[0].vruntime)

	return t
}

// wake makes a task runnable. With place set, a task that slept is moved
// forward to the queue's minimum, so that it cannot claim the time it did
// not use while it slept.
func (s *scheduler) wake(t *task, place bool) {
	if place {
		t.vruntime = max(t.vruntime, s.minVruntime)
	}

	heap.Push(&s.runnable, t)
}


// share runs a task of nice 0 against a task of the given nice value for
// 2000 slices and prints each task's share, rounded to the nearest 5%.
func share(nice int) {
	s := &scheduler{}
	first, second := newTask("A", 0), newTask("B", nice)

	s.wake(first, true)
	s.wake(second, true)

	for range 2000 {
		s.tick()
	}

	percent := (200*first.slices/(first.slices+second.slices) + 5) / 10 * 5
	fmt.Printf("nice 0 and nice %d on 1 CPU: %d%% and %d%%\n", nice, percent, 100-percent)
}


// order prints which task runs in each of the first 12 slices.
func order() {
	s := &scheduler{}

	for _, t := range []*task{newTask("A", 0), newTask("B", 0), newTask("C", 5)} {
		s.wake(t, true)
	}

	var names []string

	for range 12 {
		names = append(names, s.tick().name)
	}

	fmt.Printf("A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5: %s\n", strings.Join(names, " "))
}


// sleeper lets A and B run for 200 slices, wakes C with a virtual runtime of
// 0, and counts how many of the next 30 slices C receives.
func sleeper(place bool) int {
	s := &scheduler{}

	s.wake(newTask("A", 0), true)
	s.wake(newTask("B", 0), true)

	for range 200 {
		s.tick()
	}

	c := newTask("C", 0)
	s.wake(c, place)

	for range 30 {
		s.tick()
	}

	return c.slices
}


func main() {
	for _, nice := range []int{0, 5, 10} {
		share(nice)
	}

	order()

	fmt.Printf("C wakes with its old virtual runtime: it receives %d of the next 30 slices\n", sleeper(false))
	fmt.Printf("C wakes and is placed at the minimum: it receives %d of the next 30 slices\n", sleeper(true))
}

Listing 6.24 The complete cfs, in Rust. code/rust/cfs/src/main.rs

//! Models the Completely Fair Scheduler: every runnable task has a virtual
//! runtime, the scheduler always runs the task with the smallest one, and a
//! task's virtual runtime advances more slowly the larger its weight.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p cfs
//! ```

use std::collections::BTreeSet;

/// The kernel's table `sched_prio_to_weight`: the weight of each nice value
/// from -20 to 19. Each step of nice changes the weight by about 25%.
const WEIGHTS: [u64; 40] = [
    88761, 71755, 56483, 46273, 36291, 29154, 23254, 18705, 14949, 11916, 9548, 7620, 6100, 4904,
    3906, 3121, 2501, 1991, 1586, 1277, 1024, 820, 655, 526, 423, 335, 272, 215, 172, 137, 110, 87,
    70, 56, 45, 36, 29, 23, 18, 15,
];

/// The time a task runs before the scheduler chooses again, in nanoseconds.
const SLICE: u64 = 1_000_000;

/// One schedulable entity. `vruntime` is its virtual runtime in nanoseconds,
/// and `slices` counts how often it has run.
struct Task {
    name: &'static str,
    weight: u64,
    vruntime: u64,
    slices: u64,
}

impl Task {
    fn new(name: &'static str, nice: i32) -> Task {
        Task {
            name,
            weight: WEIGHTS[(nice + 20) as usize],
            vruntime: 0,
            slices: 0,
        }
    }
}

/// The runnable tasks, ordered by virtual runtime with the name as a
/// tie-break. `runnable` holds the order and `tasks` holds the tasks, indexed
/// by the number in the key. The kernel keeps the same order in a red-black
/// tree and takes the leftmost node.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Scheduler {
    tasks: Vec<Task>,
    runnable: BTreeSet<(u64, &'static str, usize)>,
    min_vruntime: u64,
}

impl Scheduler {
    fn enqueue(&mut self, id: usize) {
        let task = &self.tasks[id];

        self.runnable.insert((task.vruntime, task.name, id));
    }
}

impl Scheduler {
    /// Runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime for one slice and
    /// returns its number. The task is charged `SLICE * 1024 / weight`, so a
    /// task of weight 1024 is charged real time and a heavier task is charged
    /// less.
    fn tick(&mut self) -> Option<usize> {
        let (_, _, id) = self.runnable.pop_first()?;
        let task = &mut self.tasks[id];

        task.vruntime += SLICE * 1024 / task.weight;
        task.slices += 1;

        self.enqueue(id);

        if let Some(&(leftmost, _, _)) = self.runnable.first() {
            self.min_vruntime = self.min_vruntime.max(leftmost);
        }

        Some(id)
    }

    /// Makes a task runnable and returns its number. With `place` set, a task
    /// that slept is moved forward to the queue's minimum, so that it cannot
    /// claim the time it did not use while it slept.
    fn wake(&mut self, mut task: Task, place: bool) -> usize {
        if place {
            task.vruntime = task.vruntime.max(self.min_vruntime);
        }

        self.tasks.push(task);
        self.enqueue(self.tasks.len() - 1);

        self.tasks.len() - 1
    }
}

/// Runs a task of nice 0 against a task of the given nice value for 2000
/// slices and prints each task's share, rounded to the nearest 5%.
fn share(nice: i32) {
    let mut scheduler = Scheduler::default();

    let first = scheduler.wake(Task::new("A", 0), true);
    let second = scheduler.wake(Task::new("B", nice), true);

    for _ in 0..2000 {
        scheduler.tick();
    }

    let (a, b) = (
        scheduler.tasks[first].slices,
        scheduler.tasks[second].slices,
    );
    let percent = (200 * a / (a + b) + 5) / 10 * 5;

    println!(
        "nice 0 and nice {nice} on 1 CPU: {percent}% and {}%",
        100 - percent
    );
}

/// Prints which task runs in each of the first 12 slices.
fn order() {
    let mut scheduler = Scheduler::default();

    for task in [Task::new("A", 0), Task::new("B", 0), Task::new("C", 5)] {
        scheduler.wake(task, true);
    }

    let mut names = Vec::new();

    for _ in 0..12 {
        if let Some(id) = scheduler.tick() {
            names.push(scheduler.tasks[id].name);
        }
    }

    println!("A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5: {}", names.join(" "));
}

/// Lets A and B run for 200 slices, wakes C with a virtual runtime of 0, and
/// counts how many of the next 30 slices C receives.
fn sleeper(place: bool) -> u64 {
    let mut scheduler = Scheduler::default();

    scheduler.wake(Task::new("A", 0), true);
    scheduler.wake(Task::new("B", 0), true);

    for _ in 0..200 {
        scheduler.tick();
    }

    let c = scheduler.wake(Task::new("C", 0), place);

    for _ in 0..30 {
        scheduler.tick();
    }

    scheduler.tasks[c].slices
}

fn main() {
    for nice in [0, 5, 10] {
        share(nice);
    }

    order();

    println!(
        "C wakes with its old virtual runtime: it receives {} of the next 30 slices",
        sleeper(false)
    );
    println!(
        "C wakes and is placed at the minimum: it receives {} of the next 30 slices",
        sleeper(true)
    );
}

Summary

  • The scheduler runs when a task sleeps, ends, or is interrupted. The timer interrupt lets the kernel take a CPU from a task that does not give it up.
  • A context switch saves the registers of one task and loads those of another.
  • Tasks belong to scheduling classes. Ordinary tasks are in the fair class and are ordered by nice value.
  • A nice value maps to a weight through a fixed table. Nice 0 is 1024, and each step changes the weight by about 25%.
  • Each task has a virtual runtime that grows by t × 1024 / weight when the task runs for a time t. The task with the smallest virtual runtime runs next, which divides the CPU in proportion to the weights.
  • The run queue is a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime, one for each CPU.
  • A waking task is placed at the minimum virtual runtime of the queue, so a long sleep does not turn into a long uninterrupted run.
  • Load balancing moves tasks between the queues of the CPUs, and affinity restricts where a task may run.

References

  • sched(7), nice(2), sched_setaffinity(2) and chrt(1), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html
  • CFS Scheduler, Linux kernel documentation: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v5.15/scheduler/sched-design-CFS.html
  • kernel/sched/fair.c, kernel/sched/core.c and include/linux/sched.h, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/kernel/sched/fair.c

Virtual Memory

The address space of a process is the set of memory addresses the process can use and the meaning the kernel has given to each. The addresses are virtual: they are translated to locations in physical memory by the processor, through a table that the kernel maintains for each process. Different processes can use the same virtual address for different memory, and neither can reach the memory of the other.

In this chapter, we will learn how the kernel fills an address space. We will first measure with vmfacts when a mapped page receives physical memory and where a write through a file mapping ends up. Then we will write vmmodel, a model with mappings, a page table and a page fault handler, and use it to follow copy-on-write after fork.

This chapter covers

  • the layout of a process’s address space, read from /proc/self/maps
  • pages, frames, and how the processor translates an address
  • the kernel structures: struct mm_struct, struct vm_area_struct, struct page
  • mappings, and what mmap does and leaves undone
  • demand paging: a page receives memory when it is first used
  • the shared zero page
  • private and shared file mappings
  • copy-on-write, and why fork does not copy the memory of a process
  • which accesses end in SIGSEGV
  • how much memory a process uses: virtual size, resident size, and overcommit

Why addresses are virtual

Suppose programs used the addresses of physical memory directly. A program compiled to keep a variable at address 0x1000 could run only when that memory was free, and 2 copies of it could not run together. Any program could read or overwrite the memory of any other by using its addresses. And a program could use no more memory than was physically free at the moment it started.

Virtual addresses remove all 3 problems with a single idea: the addresses a program uses are private to it, and a table per process says which physical memory, if any, stands behind each of them.

With this arrangement every program can be built as if it had the machine to itself. The kernel decides which physical memory each address reaches, and it can decide late, at the moment the address is first used. The rest of the chapter is about how the table is organised and when it is filled in.

The layout of an address space

Before the mechanism, we look at what an address space contains. The kernel lists the address ranges a process can use in /proc/<pid>/maps. This is the listing of a cat process on our machine, with 3 of its columns removed.

$ cat /proc/self/maps
aaaab7c80000-aaaab7c86000 r-xp 00000000 /usr/bin/cat
aaaab7c95000-aaaab7c96000 r--p 00005000 /usr/bin/cat
aaaab7c96000-aaaab7c97000 rw-p 00006000 /usr/bin/cat
aaaacae31000-aaaacae52000 rw-p 00000000 [heap]
ffffaa650000-ffffaa7d8000 r-xp 00000000 /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
ffffaa7e7000-ffffaa7eb000 r--p 00187000 /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
ffffaa7eb000-ffffaa7ed000 rw-p 0018b000 /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
ffffaa80b000-ffffaa82d000 rw-p 00000000
ffffaa82d000-ffffaa858000 r-xp 00000000 /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1
ffffaa866000-ffffaa867000 r-xp 00000000 [vdso]
fffff2ebe000-fffff2ee0000 rw-p 00000000 [stack]

The numbers are addresses in hexadecimal, and they are less forbidding than they look. A line gives a start and an end, and the size of the range is the difference. For the first line, 0xaaaab7c86000 - 0xaaaab7c80000 = 0x6000, which is 6 × 4096 bytes: the code of cat occupies 6 pages. Only the differences carry information. The absolute values change on every run.

Each line is a mapping: a range of addresses with the same permissions and the same source.

ColumnMeaning
aaaab7c80000-aaaab7c86000the first address of the range, and the first address after it
r-xpread, write and execute permission, then p for a private mapping or s for a shared one
00005000for a mapping of a file: the offset in the file at which the range starts
the last columnthe file that is mapped, a name in brackets for a special region, or nothing for anonymous memory
RegionContents
/usr/bin/cat, r-xpthe instructions of the program, read from the program file; executable and read-only
/usr/bin/cat, rw-pthe global variables of the program
[heap]memory for small allocations by malloc, grown with the brk system call
libc.so.6, ld-linux-aarch64.so.1shared libraries, each with its own code and data ranges
no nameanonymous memory: not backed by a file, and filled with zeros when first used
[vdso]a small library that the kernel maps into every process, which lets calls such as clock_gettime run without entering the kernel
[stack]the stack of the main thread: local variables and return addresses

The ranges are far apart, and most of the space between them is unmapped. An access to an unmapped address ends the process with SIGSEGV. The addresses differ from run to run, because the kernel chooses the positions of the regions at random for each new program, which makes attacks that depend on known addresses harder.

Pages, mappings and the page table

Virtual and physical memory are both divided into units of the same size, 4096 bytes on this machine. A unit of virtual memory is a page, and a unit of physical memory is a frame. The address space is described at 2 levels.

LevelKept byContents
Mappingsthe kernela list of address ranges; for each, the permitted access and where its contents come from: a file, or nothing (anonymous memory, initially zero)
Page tablethe kernel, read by the processorfor each page that is in use: the frame that holds it, and whether writing is allowed

Translating an address

Translation is easiest to follow on a machine small enough to work by hand. Imagine addresses of 16 bits and pages of 256 bytes. An address then has 2 hexadecimal digits for the page number and 2 for the offset within the page. To translate 0x1234, split it into page 0x12 and offset 0x34, look up entry 0x12 of the page table, find frame 0x7A there, and attach the offset: the physical address is 0x7A34.

A real machine does exactly this, with larger numbers and with a table that is split into several levels to save space.

The processor translates every address a program uses, in hardware. An address of this machine has 48 significant bits. The low 12 bits are the offset within a page, since a page has 4096 = 212 bytes. The remaining 36 bits are the page number, and they are used in 4 groups of 9 bits.

The page table is a tree of tables, each a page of 512 entries. The processor starts at the root table of the process, uses the first 9 bits to select an entry, follows it to a table of the next level, and repeats this 4 times. The last entry holds the number of the frame and the permission bits. The frame number and the offset together are the physical address.

A tree is used because the address space is almost empty. A flat table for 236 pages would need 512 GiB for each process. In the tree, a table exists only for the regions that are in use, and the cat process above needs a few dozen kilobytes.

Walking 4 tables for every memory access would be slow, so the processor keeps the results of recent translations in a cache, the translation lookaside buffer or TLB. Most accesses are answered from the TLB. When the kernel changes a page table entry, it tells the processor to discard the cached translation.

mmap adds a mapping. It writes no page table entry and allocates no frame. A mapping is a promise: these addresses are valid, and this is what they contain.

The promise is kept later. When the program uses an address whose page has no entry, or writes where the entry forbids writing, the processor cannot complete the instruction. It raises a page fault, which transfers control to the kernel. The kernel looks up the address in the mappings. If a mapping permits the access, the kernel provides a frame, writes the entry, and returns, and the processor repeats the instruction. If no mapping permits it, the kernel sends the process the signal SIGSEGV.

Filling the table on demand means that memory is spent only on pages that are used. A program can map a large range and touch a small part of it, and a large program starts quickly because its code is read from disk page by page as it runs.

The kernel’s structures

The kernel describes an address space with 3 structures. These are the definitions in include/linux/mm_types.h of Linux 5.15, reduced to the fields we use.

struct mm_struct {
        struct vm_area_struct *mmap;           /* the mappings, as a list */
        struct rb_root mm_rb;                  /* the mappings, as a tree by address */
        pgd_t *pgd;                            /* the root of the page table */
        int map_count;                         /* number of mappings */
        unsigned long total_vm;                /* pages mapped */
        unsigned long start_brk, brk;          /* the heap */
        unsigned long start_stack;             /* the stack */
        /* ... */
};

struct vm_area_struct {
        unsigned long vm_start;                /* first address of the mapping */
        unsigned long vm_end;                  /* first address after it */
        struct vm_area_struct *vm_next, *vm_prev;
        struct mm_struct *vm_mm;               /* the address space it belongs to */
        unsigned long vm_flags;                /* VM_READ, VM_WRITE, VM_EXEC, VM_SHARED */
        unsigned long vm_pgoff;                /* offset in the file, in pages */
        struct file *vm_file;                  /* the mapped file, or NULL */
        /* ... */
};

struct page {
        unsigned long flags;                   /* dirty, locked, ... */
        struct address_space *mapping;         /* the file this frame caches, if any */
        pgoff_t index;                         /* its page number in that file */
        atomic_t _mapcount;                    /* page table entries that map it */
        atomic_t _refcount;                    /* users of the frame */
        /* ... */
};
StructureExistsMeaning
struct mm_structonce per processThe address space. task_struct.mm points to it, and the threads of a process share it.
struct vm_area_structonce per mappingA line of /proc/<pid>/maps. The kernel calls it a VMA.
struct pageonce per frame of physical memoryThe kernel’s record of a frame: who uses it and what it contains.
FieldMeaning
mmap, mm_rbThe mappings of the process, as a list in address order and as a tree for fast lookup of the mapping that contains an address.
pgdThe address of the root table that the processor walks. A context switch loads it into the processor (chapter 6).
vm_start, vm_endThe 2 addresses in the first column of maps.
vm_flagsThe permissions in the second column.
vm_file, vm_pgoffThe file and the offset in the last columns. vm_file is a struct file (chapter 2).
_refcount, _mapcountCounts that decide when a frame is free and whether it is shared, used for copy-on-write below.

There are 2 descriptions of the same address space, and the difference between them is the subject of this chapter. The list of VMAs says what the process is allowed to use. The page table says what has actually been given a frame. mmap changes only the first.

mmap of 1 GiB allocates no memory. The frames arrive page by page, at the first access to each page.

Measuring an address space

vmfacts uses golang.org/x/sys/unix in Go and the memmap2 crate in Rust.

$ cargo new vmfacts
$ cargo add -p vmfacts memmap2

The kernel publishes the page table of a process in /proc/self/pagemap: 8 bytes for each virtual page, in which bit 63 is set when the page has a frame. resident counts those pages for a mapping.

Listing 7.1 The imports of vmfacts, in Go. code/go/vmfacts/main.go

import (
	"bufio"
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"reflect"
	"strings"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"

Listing 7.2 The imports of vmfacts, in Rust. code/rust/vmfacts/src/main.rs

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io;
use std::os::unix::fs::FileExt;
use std::path::Path;

use memmap2::{MmapMut, MmapOptions};

Listing 7.3 Counting the pages of a mapping that have a frame, in Go. code/go/vmfacts/main.go

const pageSize = 4096

// address returns the virtual address of the first byte of a mapping.
func address(mapping []byte) uintptr {
	return reflect.ValueOf(mapping).Pointer()
}

// resident counts the pages of a mapping that have physical memory. The
// kernel publishes 8 bytes per virtual page in /proc/self/pagemap, and bit 63
// of an entry is set when the page is present in memory.
func resident(mapping []byte) (int, error) {
	pagemap, err := os.Open("/proc/self/pagemap")

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	defer pagemap.Close()

	entries := make([]byte, 8*len(mapping)/pageSize)

	if _, err := pagemap.ReadAt(entries, int64(address(mapping)/pageSize*8)); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	count := 0

	for i := 0; i < len(entries); i += 8 {
		if binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(entries[i:])>>63 == 1 {
			count++
		}
	}

	return count, nil
}

Listing 7.4 Counting the pages of a mapping that have a frame, in Rust. code/rust/vmfacts/src/main.rs

const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

/// Counts the pages of a mapping that have physical memory. The kernel
/// publishes 8 bytes per virtual page in `/proc/self/pagemap`, and bit 63 of
/// an entry is set when the page is present in memory.
fn resident(mapping: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let pagemap = File::open("/proc/self/pagemap")?;
    let mut entries = vec![0u8; 8 * mapping.len() / PAGE_SIZE];
    let offset = mapping.as_ptr() as usize / PAGE_SIZE * 8;

    pagemap.read_exact_at(&mut entries, offset as u64)?;

    let (entries, _) = entries.as_chunks::<8>();
    let count = entries.iter().filter(|entry| entry[7] >> 7 == 1).count();

    Ok(count)
}

demand maps 64 pages of anonymous memory and counts the resident pages 3 times: after mmap, after writing to 10 pages, and after reading 1 further page.

Listing 7.5 When a page receives memory, in Go. code/go/vmfacts/main.go

// demand maps 64 pages of anonymous memory, writes to 10 of them, reads 1
// more, and counts the resident pages after each step.
func demand() error {
	mapping, err := unix.Mmap(-1, 0, 64*pageSize, unix.PROT_READ|unix.PROT_WRITE, unix.MAP_PRIVATE|unix.MAP_ANONYMOUS)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Munmap(mapping)

	before, err := resident(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for page := range 10 {
		mapping[page*pageSize] = 1
	}

	written, err := resident(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	value := mapping[20*pageSize]
	read, err := resident(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("64 pages mapped: %d resident\n", before)
	fmt.Printf("after writing to 10 pages: %d resident\n", written)
	fmt.Printf("after reading 1 more page: %d resident, the byte read is %d\n", read, value)

	return nil
}

Listing 7.6 When a page receives memory, in Rust. code/rust/vmfacts/src/main.rs

/// Maps 64 pages of anonymous memory, writes to 10 of them, reads 1 more, and
/// counts the resident pages after each step.
fn demand() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut mapping = MmapMut::map_anon(64 * PAGE_SIZE)?;

    let before = resident(&mapping)?;

    for page in 0..10 {
        mapping[page * PAGE_SIZE] = 1;
    }

    let written = resident(&mapping)?;

    let value = mapping[20 * PAGE_SIZE];
    let read = resident(&mapping)?;

    println!("64 pages mapped: {before} resident");
    println!("after writing to 10 pages: {written} resident");
    println!("after reading 1 more page: {read} resident, the byte read is {value}");

    Ok(())
}

protect reads the permissions of a mapping from /proc/self/maps before and after mprotect removes the permission to write.

Listing 7.7 The permissions of a mapping, in Go. code/go/vmfacts/main.go

// permissions returns the permission column of the line in /proc/self/maps
// that starts at the address of a mapping.
func permissions(mapping []byte) (string, error) {
	maps, err := os.Open("/proc/self/maps")

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	defer maps.Close()

	start := fmt.Sprintf("%x-", address(mapping))

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(maps); lines.Scan(); {
		if fields := strings.Fields(lines.Text()); strings.HasPrefix(fields[0], start) {
			return fields[1], nil
		}
	}

	return "", fmt.Errorf("mapping at %s not found", start)
}

// protect reads the permissions of a mapping before and after mprotect
// removes the permission to write.
func protect() error {
	mapping, err := unix.Mmap(-1, 0, pageSize, unix.PROT_READ|unix.PROT_WRITE, unix.MAP_PRIVATE|unix.MAP_ANONYMOUS)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Munmap(mapping)

	before, err := permissions(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := unix.Mprotect(mapping, unix.PROT_READ); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	after, err := permissions(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("permissions of the mapping: %s, after mprotect: %s\n", before, after)

	return nil
}

Listing 7.8 The permissions of a mapping, in Rust. code/rust/vmfacts/src/main.rs

/// Returns the permission column of the line in `/proc/self/maps` that starts
/// at the address of a mapping.
fn permissions(mapping: &[u8]) -> io::Result<String> {
    let start = format!("{:x}-", mapping.as_ptr() as usize);

    fs::read_to_string("/proc/self/maps")?
        .lines()
        .filter(|line| line.starts_with(&start))
        .find_map(|line| line.split_whitespace().nth(1))
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::NotFound.into())
}

/// Reads the permissions of a mapping before and after mprotect removes the
/// permission to write.
fn protect() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mapping = MmapMut::map_anon(PAGE_SIZE)?;
    let before = permissions(&mapping)?;

    let mapping = mapping.make_read_only()?;
    let after = permissions(&mapping)?;

    println!("permissions of the mapping: {before}, after mprotect: {after}");

    Ok(())
}

throughMapping maps a file that contains hello, writes HELLO into the mapped memory, and reads the file again. It does this with a private mapping and with a shared one. Mapping a file is an unsafe operation in Rust, because another process could change the file while the program holds a slice of it. The comment in the listing states why the use is sound here.

Listing 7.9 Writing through a private and a shared file mapping, in Go. code/go/vmfacts/main.go

// throughMapping maps a file that holds "hello", writes "HELLO" through the
// mapping, unmaps it, and returns the contents of the file.
func throughMapping(path string, flags int) (string, error) {
	if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte("hello"), 0o644); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	file, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_RDWR, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	defer file.Close()

	mapping, err := unix.Mmap(int(file.Fd()), 0, 5, unix.PROT_READ|unix.PROT_WRITE, flags)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	copy(mapping, "HELLO")

	if err := unix.Munmap(mapping); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	text, err := os.ReadFile(path)

	return string(text), err
}

// files compares a private file mapping with a shared one.
func files() error {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "vmfacts")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)

	path := filepath.Join(dir, "file")

	for _, kind := range []struct {
		name  string
		flags int
	}{{"private", unix.MAP_PRIVATE}, {"shared", unix.MAP_SHARED}} {
		text, err := throughMapping(path, kind.flags)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		fmt.Printf("HELLO written through a %s file mapping: the file holds %q\n", kind.name, text)
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 7.10 Writing through a private and a shared file mapping, in Rust. code/rust/vmfacts/src/main.rs

/// Maps a file that holds "hello", writes "HELLO" through the mapping, unmaps
/// it, and returns the contents of the file.
fn through_mapping(path: &Path, shared: bool) -> io::Result<String> {
    fs::write(path, "hello")?;

    let file = OpenOptions::new().read(true).write(true).open(path)?;
    let options = MmapOptions::new();

    // SAFETY: mapping a file is unsafe in Rust because another process could
    // change the file while the slice exists. This file is in a directory the
    // program has just created, and nothing else opens it.
    let mut mapping = unsafe {
        if shared {
            options.map_mut(&file)?
        } else {
            options.map_copy(&file)?
        }
    };

    mapping.copy_from_slice(b"HELLO");
    drop(mapping);

    fs::read_to_string(path)
}

/// Compares a private file mapping with a shared one.
fn files() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("vmfacts-{}", std::process::id()));
    let path = dir.join("file");

    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;

    for (name, shared) in [("private", false), ("shared", true)] {
        let text = through_mapping(&path, shared)?;
        println!("HELLO written through a {name} file mapping: the file holds {text:?}");
    }

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)
}
