Modelling an address space

Low-level design: vmmodel

TypeFieldsMeaning
framedata, refsa page of physical memory and the number of entries that refer to it
memoryframes, zerothe count of allocated frames; the shared frame of zeros
mappingstart, pages, writablea range of virtual pages and its permission
entryframe, writablea page table entry
spacemappings, table, faultsan address space
OperationBehaviour
mmap(pages, writable)adds a mapping; returns its address
read(address), write(address, value)use the entry when it permits the access; otherwise call fault and repeat
fault(page, write)fails with SIGSEGV, or installs an entry
fork()returns a space with the same mappings and entries, all read-only on both sides

In the Rust version, a frame is an Rc of an array, and the reference count of the Rc is the refs field of the Go version.

Listing 7.11 The imports of vmmodel, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
)

Listing 7.12 The imports of vmmodel, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

use std::cell::Cell;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fmt;
use std::rc::Rc;

Listing 7.13 Frames, mappings, entries and the address space, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

const pageSize = 4096

// errSegv is the result of an access that no mapping allows. The kernel
// sends the process the signal SIGSEGV.
var errSegv = errors.New("SIGSEGV")

// A frame is a page of physical memory. refs counts the page table entries
// that refer to it.
type frame struct {
	data [pageSize]byte
	refs int
}

// memory is the physical memory shared by all address spaces: the number of
// frames allocated, and the frame of zeros that every read of an untouched
// page maps.
type memory struct {
	frames int
	zero   *frame
}

func (m *memory) allocate() *frame {
	m.frames++

	return &frame{refs: 1}
}

// A mapping is a range of virtual pages and the access it permits.
type mapping struct {
	start, pages int
	writable     bool
}

// An entry is a page table entry: the frame behind a virtual page, and
// whether the processor may write to it without a fault.
type entry struct {
	frame    *frame
	writable bool
}

// A space is the address space of a process.
type space struct {
	memory   *memory
	mappings []mapping
	table    map[int]entry
	faults   int
	nextPage int
}

func newSpace() *space {
	return &space{
		memory:   &memory{zero: &frame{refs: 1}},
		table:    map[int]entry{},
		nextPage: 16,
	}
}

Listing 7.14 Frames, mappings, entries and the address space, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

/// The result of an access that no mapping allows. The kernel sends the
/// process the signal `SIGSEGV`.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Segv;

impl fmt::Display for Segv {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str("SIGSEGV")
    }
}

/// A page of physical memory. The reference count of the `Rc` is the number
/// of page table entries that refer to it.
type Frame = Rc<[u8; PAGE_SIZE]>;

/// The physical memory shared by all address spaces: the number of frames
/// allocated, and the frame of zeros that every read of an untouched page
/// maps.
struct Memory {
    frames: Cell<usize>,
    zero: Frame,
}

impl Memory {
    fn allocate(&self, contents: [u8; PAGE_SIZE]) -> Frame {
        self.frames.set(self.frames.get() + 1);

        Rc::new(contents)
    }
}

/// A range of virtual pages and the access it permits.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Mapping {
    start: usize,
    pages: usize,
    writable: bool,
}

/// A page table entry: the frame behind a virtual page, and whether the
/// processor may write to it without a fault.
#[derive(Clone)]
struct Entry {
    frame: Frame,
    writable: bool,
}

/// The address space of a process.
struct Space {
    memory: Rc<Memory>,
    mappings: Vec<Mapping>,
    table: HashMap<usize, Entry>,
    faults: usize,
    next_page: usize,
}

impl Space {
    fn new() -> Space {
        let memory = Memory {
            frames: Cell::new(0),
            zero: Rc::new([0; PAGE_SIZE]),
        };

        Space {
            memory: Rc::new(memory),
            mappings: Vec::new(),
            table: HashMap::new(),
            faults: 0,
            next_page: 16,
        }
    }
}

mmap only records the range.

Listing 7.15 Adding a mapping, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

// mmap records a new mapping and returns its address. It allocates no frame
// and writes no page table entry.
func (s *space) mmap(pages int, writable bool) int {
	start := s.nextPage
	s.mappings = append(s.mappings, mapping{start: start, pages: pages, writable: writable})
	s.nextPage += pages + 1

	return start * pageSize
}

// find returns the mapping that contains a page.
func (s *space) find(page int) (mapping, bool) {
	for _, m := range s.mappings {
		if page >= m.start && page < m.start+m.pages {
			return m, true
		}
	}

	return mapping{}, false
}

Listing 7.16 Adding a mapping, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

impl Space {
    /// Records a new mapping and returns its address. It allocates no frame
    /// and writes no page table entry.
    fn mmap(&mut self, pages: usize, writable: bool) -> usize {
        let start = self.next_page;

        self.mappings.push(Mapping {
            start,
            pages,
            writable,
        });
        self.next_page += pages + 1;

        start * PAGE_SIZE
    }

    /// Returns the mapping that contains a page.
    fn find(&self, page: usize) -> Option<Mapping> {
        self.mappings
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .find(|mapping| (mapping.start..mapping.start + mapping.pages).contains(&page))
    }
}

read and write play the part of the processor. They consult the page table and call fault when the entry is missing or forbids the access.

Listing 7.17 An access through the page table, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

// read returns the byte at an address. The processor uses the page table
// entry when one exists, and faults when none does.
func (s *space) read(address int) (byte, error) {
	page, offset := address/pageSize, address%pageSize

	if _, present := s.table[page]; !present {
		if err := s.fault(page, false); err != nil {
			return 0, err
		}
	}

	return s.table[page].frame.data[offset], nil
}

// write stores a byte at an address. It faults when the page has no entry or
// the entry does not permit writing.
func (s *space) write(address int, value byte) error {
	page, offset := address/pageSize, address%pageSize

	if !s.table[page].writable {
		if err := s.fault(page, true); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	s.table[page].frame.data[offset] = value

	return nil
}

Listing 7.18 An access through the page table, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

impl Space {
    /// Returns the byte at an address. The processor uses the page table
    /// entry when one exists, and faults when none does.
    fn read(&mut self, address: usize) -> Result<u8, Segv> {
        let (page, offset) = (address / PAGE_SIZE, address % PAGE_SIZE);

        if !self.table.contains_key(&page) {
            self.fault(page, false)?;
        }

        self.table
            .get(&page)
            .map(|entry| entry.frame[offset])
            .ok_or(Segv)
    }

    /// Stores a byte at an address. It faults when the page has no entry or
    /// the entry does not permit writing.
    fn write(&mut self, address: usize, value: u8) -> Result<(), Segv> {
        let (page, offset) = (address / PAGE_SIZE, address % PAGE_SIZE);

        if !self.table.get(&page).is_some_and(|entry| entry.writable) {
            self.fault(page, true)?;
        }

        let entry = self.table.get_mut(&page).ok_or(Segv)?;

        // A writable entry is the only user of its frame, so `make_mut`
        // returns the frame itself.
        Rc::make_mut(&mut entry.frame)[offset] = value;

        Ok(())
    }
}

fault is the kernel’s handler. After the check against the mappings it has 4 cases.

AccessEntryAction
readnonemap the shared zero frame, read-only
writenoneallocate a frame of zeros, writable
writeread-only, and the frame has no other usermake the entry writable
writeread-only, and the frame is sharedallocate a frame, copy the contents, map the copy writable

Case 1 explains the measurement of 11 resident pages. Every read of an untouched anonymous page maps the same frame of zeros, so reading costs no memory. The frame is mapped read-only, and the first write replaces it with a private frame through case 4.

Listing 7.19 The page fault handler, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

// fault is the kernel's page fault handler. It checks the access against
// the mappings and then repairs the page table entry so that the access can
// be repeated.
func (s *space) fault(page int, write bool) error {
	m, ok := s.find(page)

	if !ok || write && !m.writable {
		return errSegv
	}

	s.faults++
	e, present := s.table[page]

	switch {
	case !write:
		// A read of an untouched page maps the shared zero frame.
		s.memory.zero.refs++
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: s.memory.zero}

	case !present:
		// A write to an untouched page gets a new frame of zeros.
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: s.memory.allocate(), writable: true}

	case e.frame.refs == 1:
		// The frame has no other user. Writing is enabled in place.
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: e.frame, writable: true}

	default:
		// The frame is shared. The writer gets a private copy.
		private := s.memory.allocate()
		private.data = e.frame.data
		e.frame.refs--
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: private, writable: true}
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 7.20 The page fault handler, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

impl Space {
    /// The kernel's page fault handler. It checks the access against the
    /// mappings and then repairs the page table entry so that the access can
    /// be repeated.
    fn fault(&mut self, page: usize, write: bool) -> Result<(), Segv> {
        let mapping = self.find(page).ok_or(Segv)?;

        if write && !mapping.writable {
            return Err(Segv);
        }

        self.faults += 1;

        let entry = match (write, self.table.remove(&page)) {
            // A read of an untouched page maps the shared zero frame.
            (false, _) => Entry {
                frame: Rc::clone(&self.memory.zero),
                writable: false,
            },

            // A write to an untouched page gets a new frame of zeros.
            (true, None) => Entry {
                frame: self.memory.allocate([0; PAGE_SIZE]),
                writable: true,
            },

            // The frame has no other user. Writing is enabled in place.
            (true, Some(entry)) if Rc::strong_count(&entry.frame) == 1 => Entry {
                frame: entry.frame,
                writable: true,
            },

            // The frame is shared. The writer gets a private copy.
            (true, Some(entry)) => Entry {
                frame: self.memory.allocate(*entry.frame),
                writable: true,
            },
        };

        self.table.insert(page, entry);

        Ok(())
    }
}

Copy-on-write

fork gives the child a copy of the parent’s address space. Copying every frame would be slow, and most of the work would be wasted, since the usual next step of the child is exec, which discards the address space. The kernel therefore copies only the page table. Parent and child refer to the same frames, and every entry is made read-only in both.

Listing 7.21 Forking an address space, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

// fork returns a child with the same mappings and a page table that refers
// to the same frames. Every entry is made read-only in the parent and in the
// child, so that the first write by either causes a fault.
func (s *space) fork() *space {
	child := &space{
		memory:   s.memory,
		mappings: append([]mapping(nil), s.mappings...),
		table:    map[int]entry{},
		nextPage: s.nextPage,
	}

	for page, e := range s.table {
		e.frame.refs++
		e.writable = false
		s.table[page], child.table[page] = e, e
	}

	return child
}

Listing 7.22 Forking an address space, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

impl Space {
    /// Returns a child with the same mappings and a page table that refers to
    /// the same frames. Every entry is made read-only in the parent and in
    /// the child, so that the first write by either causes a fault.
    fn fork(&mut self) -> Space {
        for entry in self.table.values_mut() {
            entry.writable = false;
        }

        Space {
            memory: Rc::clone(&self.memory),
            mappings: self.mappings.clone(),
            table: self.table.clone(),
            faults: 0,
            next_page: self.next_page,
        }
    }
}

Reads continue without faults. The first write to a page by either process faults. The handler sees a read-only entry in a writable mapping, copies the frame for the writer, and the processes diverge on that page only.

A private file mapping uses the same mechanism. Its pages initially refer to the file’s frames, read-only, and a write copies the page. The file is unchanged, as vmfacts measured.

Listing 7.23 The trace, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

// report prints a step with the fault count of a space and the number of
// frames allocated.
func (s *space) report(step string) {
	fmt.Printf("%-34s faults %d, frames %d\n", step, s.faults, s.memory.frames)
}

func run() error {
	parent := newSpace()
	base := parent.mmap(4, true)
	parent.report("mmap of 4 pages:")

	if err := parent.write(base, 'a'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report("write to page 0:")

	value, err := parent.read(base + pageSize)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report(fmt.Sprintf("read of page 1, value %d:", value))

	if err := parent.write(base+pageSize, 'x'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report("write to page 1:")

	child := parent.fork()
	child.report("fork, in the child:")

	if err := child.write(base, 'b'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	child.report("child writes page 0:")

	if err := parent.write(base, 'c'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report("parent writes page 0:")

	inParent, err := parent.read(base)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	inChild, err := child.read(base)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("page 0 holds %q in the parent and %q in the child\n", inParent, inChild)

	fmt.Printf("write outside every mapping: %v\n", parent.write(base+100*pageSize, 1))

	readOnly := parent.mmap(1, false)
	fmt.Printf("write to a read-only mapping: %v\n", parent.write(readOnly, 1))

	return nil
}

func main() {
	if err := run(); err != nil {
		fmt.Println(err)
	}
}

Listing 7.24 The trace, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

impl Space {
    /// Prints a step with the fault count of a space and the number of frames
    /// allocated.
    fn report(&self, step: &str) {
        println!(
            "{step:<34} faults {}, frames {}",
            self.faults,
            self.memory.frames.get()
        );
    }
}

fn run() -> Result<(), Segv> {
    let mut parent = Space::new();
    let base = parent.mmap(4, true);
    parent.report("mmap of 4 pages:");

    parent.write(base, b'a')?;
    parent.report("write to page 0:");

    let value = parent.read(base + PAGE_SIZE)?;
    parent.report(&format!("read of page 1, value {value}:"));

    parent.write(base + PAGE_SIZE, b'x')?;
    parent.report("write to page 1:");

    let mut child = parent.fork();
    child.report("fork, in the child:");

    child.write(base, b'b')?;
    child.report("child writes page 0:");

    parent.write(base, b'c')?;
    parent.report("parent writes page 0:");

    println!(
        "page 0 holds {:?} in the parent and {:?} in the child",
        char::from(parent.read(base)?),
        char::from(child.read(base)?)
    );

    if let Err(error) = parent.write(base + 100 * PAGE_SIZE, 1) {
        println!("write outside every mapping: {error}");
    }

    let read_only = parent.mmap(1, false);

    if let Err(error) = parent.write(read_only, 1) {
        println!("write to a read-only mapping: {error}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    if let Err(error) = run() {
        println!("{error}");
    }
}
mmap of 4 pages:                   faults 0, frames 0
write to page 0:                   faults 1, frames 1
read of page 1, value 0:           faults 2, frames 1
write to page 1:                   faults 3, frames 2
fork, in the child:                faults 0, frames 2
child writes page 0:               faults 1, frames 3
parent writes page 0:              faults 4, frames 3
page 0 holds 'c' in the parent and 'b' in the child
write outside every mapping: SIGSEGV
write to a read-only mapping: SIGSEGV
LineWhat it shows
mmap of 4 pagesNo fault and no frame.
write to page 0A write to an untouched page allocates frame 1.
read of page 1A read maps the zero frame: a fault, and no new frame.
write to page 1The zero frame is shared, so the write copies it into frame 2.
fork, in the childThe child starts with the parent’s 2 frames and none of its own.
child writes page 0The child faults and receives a copy, frame 3.
parent writes page 0The parent also faults, because its entry is read-only. It is now the only user of frame 1, so no copy is made.
the last 2 linesAn address outside every mapping, and a write to a read-only mapping, end in SIGSEGV.

Correspondence with the kernel source. A mapping is struct vm_area_struct in include/linux/mm_types.h, and the list of mappings is in struct mm_struct. On arm64 the page table is a tree of 4 levels that the processor walks itself; the model replaces the tree by a map from page number to entry. The fault handler is handle_mm_fault in mm/memory.c, where do_anonymous_page handles the first 2 cases of the table and do_wp_page the last 2. /proc/self/maps prints a line for each vm_area_struct.

How much memory a process uses

Since mapping and allocating are separate, a process has 2 sizes.

$ ps -o pid,vsz,rss,min_flt,maj_flt,comm -p 580844
    PID    VSZ   RSS  MINFL  MAJFL COMMAND
 580844  11204   776    114      0 sleep
ColumnMeaning
VSZVirtual size: the total of all mappings, 11204 kB. It is total_vm.
RSSResident set size: the pages that have a frame, 776 kB.
MINFLMinor faults: page faults that the kernel resolved without reading from a disk, 114.
MAJFLMajor faults: page faults that had to wait for a page to be read from a disk, 0.

The sleep process has mapped 11 MB and uses under 1 MB, because most of the pages of its libraries have not been touched. It took 114 page faults to start, each bringing in a single page or a few. RSS is the number to look at when asking how much memory a process costs, with the reservation that pages shared with other processes, such as the code of libc, are counted in the RSS of each.

Because memory is given out at the first access, the kernel can promise more than it has. This is overcommit: the sum of the mappings of all processes may exceed physical memory and swap, on the assumption that not all of it will be touched. The policy is in /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory, and the value 1 on this machine means that mmap does not refuse a request for lack of memory. When the promises are called in and no frame is free, the kernel first reclaims frames, by discarding page cache pages (chapter 8) and by writing anonymous pages to swap space on disk. When that is not enough, the OOM killer ends a process to free its memory. Chapter 12 shows it at work inside a memory limit.

The heap and the stack

malloc is a library function, and the kernel knows nothing about individual allocations. The allocator asks the kernel for memory in large pieces and divides them itself. It has 2 ways to ask. brk moves the end of the [heap] mapping, which suits many small allocations. For a large request, 128 KiB or more in the allocator of glibc, it calls mmap for an anonymous mapping of its own, which can be returned to the kernel independently. Both give addresses without frames, so memory that a program allocates and does not touch costs nothing.

The stack is a mapping that the kernel extends on demand. An access directly below its current end causes a page fault, and the handler enlarges the mapping, up to the limit shown by ulimit -s.

Inspecting memory on a live system

CommandShows
cat /proc/<pid>/mapsthe mappings of a process
cat /proc/<pid>/smapsfor each mapping: resident, shared, private and swapped pages
ps -o pid,vsz,rss,min_flt,maj_flt,commvirtual size, resident size and page faults
grep Vm /proc/<pid>/statusthe sizes by kind: data, stack, code, libraries, page tables
free -mmemory of the whole system: used, free, and used for the page cache
cat /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memorythe overcommit policy

The complete programs

Listing 7.25 The complete vmfacts, in Go. code/go/vmfacts/main.go

// Command vmfacts measures how the kernel fills an address space: when a
// mapped page receives physical memory, what an untouched page contains, how
// a mapping's permissions appear in /proc/self/maps, and where a write
// through a private or a shared file mapping ends up.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./vmfacts
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"reflect"
	"strings"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


const pageSize = 4096

// address returns the virtual address of the first byte of a mapping.
func address(mapping []byte) uintptr {
	return reflect.ValueOf(mapping).Pointer()
}

// resident counts the pages of a mapping that have physical memory. The
// kernel publishes 8 bytes per virtual page in /proc/self/pagemap, and bit 63
// of an entry is set when the page is present in memory.
func resident(mapping []byte) (int, error) {
	pagemap, err := os.Open("/proc/self/pagemap")

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	defer pagemap.Close()

	entries := make([]byte, 8*len(mapping)/pageSize)

	if _, err := pagemap.ReadAt(entries, int64(address(mapping)/pageSize*8)); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	count := 0

	for i := 0; i < len(entries); i += 8 {
		if binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(entries[i:])>>63 == 1 {
			count++
		}
	}

	return count, nil
}


// demand maps 64 pages of anonymous memory, writes to 10 of them, reads 1
// more, and counts the resident pages after each step.
func demand() error {
	mapping, err := unix.Mmap(-1, 0, 64*pageSize, unix.PROT_READ|unix.PROT_WRITE, unix.MAP_PRIVATE|unix.MAP_ANONYMOUS)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Munmap(mapping)

	before, err := resident(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for page := range 10 {
		mapping[page*pageSize] = 1
	}

	written, err := resident(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	value := mapping[20*pageSize]
	read, err := resident(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("64 pages mapped: %d resident\n", before)
	fmt.Printf("after writing to 10 pages: %d resident\n", written)
	fmt.Printf("after reading 1 more page: %d resident, the byte read is %d\n", read, value)

	return nil
}


// permissions returns the permission column of the line in /proc/self/maps
// that starts at the address of a mapping.
func permissions(mapping []byte) (string, error) {
	maps, err := os.Open("/proc/self/maps")

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	defer maps.Close()

	start := fmt.Sprintf("%x-", address(mapping))

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(maps); lines.Scan(); {
		if fields := strings.Fields(lines.Text()); strings.HasPrefix(fields[0], start) {
			return fields[1], nil
		}
	}

	return "", fmt.Errorf("mapping at %s not found", start)
}

// protect reads the permissions of a mapping before and after mprotect
// removes the permission to write.
func protect() error {
	mapping, err := unix.Mmap(-1, 0, pageSize, unix.PROT_READ|unix.PROT_WRITE, unix.MAP_PRIVATE|unix.MAP_ANONYMOUS)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Munmap(mapping)

	before, err := permissions(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := unix.Mprotect(mapping, unix.PROT_READ); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	after, err := permissions(mapping)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("permissions of the mapping: %s, after mprotect: %s\n", before, after)

	return nil
}


// throughMapping maps a file that holds "hello", writes "HELLO" through the
// mapping, unmaps it, and returns the contents of the file.
func throughMapping(path string, flags int) (string, error) {
	if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte("hello"), 0o644); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	file, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_RDWR, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	defer file.Close()

	mapping, err := unix.Mmap(int(file.Fd()), 0, 5, unix.PROT_READ|unix.PROT_WRITE, flags)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	copy(mapping, "HELLO")

	if err := unix.Munmap(mapping); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	text, err := os.ReadFile(path)

	return string(text), err
}

// files compares a private file mapping with a shared one.
func files() error {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "vmfacts")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)

	path := filepath.Join(dir, "file")

	for _, kind := range []struct {
		name  string
		flags int
	}{{"private", unix.MAP_PRIVATE}, {"shared", unix.MAP_SHARED}} {
		text, err := throughMapping(path, kind.flags)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		fmt.Printf("HELLO written through a %s file mapping: the file holds %q\n", kind.name, text)
	}

	return nil
}


func main() {
	for _, experiment := range []func() error{demand, protect, files} {
		if err := experiment(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 7.26 The complete vmfacts, in Rust. code/rust/vmfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures how the kernel fills an address space: when a mapped page
//! receives physical memory, what an untouched page contains, how a mapping's
//! permissions appear in `/proc/self/maps`, and where a write through a
//! private or a shared file mapping ends up.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p vmfacts
//! ```

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io;
use std::os::unix::fs::FileExt;
use std::path::Path;

use memmap2::{MmapMut, MmapOptions};

const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

/// Counts the pages of a mapping that have physical memory. The kernel
/// publishes 8 bytes per virtual page in `/proc/self/pagemap`, and bit 63 of
/// an entry is set when the page is present in memory.
fn resident(mapping: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let pagemap = File::open("/proc/self/pagemap")?;
    let mut entries = vec![0u8; 8 * mapping.len() / PAGE_SIZE];
    let offset = mapping.as_ptr() as usize / PAGE_SIZE * 8;

    pagemap.read_exact_at(&mut entries, offset as u64)?;

    let (entries, _) = entries.as_chunks::<8>();
    let count = entries.iter().filter(|entry| entry[7] >> 7 == 1).count();

    Ok(count)
}

/// Maps 64 pages of anonymous memory, writes to 10 of them, reads 1 more, and
/// counts the resident pages after each step.
fn demand() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut mapping = MmapMut::map_anon(64 * PAGE_SIZE)?;

    let before = resident(&mapping)?;

    for page in 0..10 {
        mapping[page * PAGE_SIZE] = 1;
    }

    let written = resident(&mapping)?;

    let value = mapping[20 * PAGE_SIZE];
    let read = resident(&mapping)?;

    println!("64 pages mapped: {before} resident");
    println!("after writing to 10 pages: {written} resident");
    println!("after reading 1 more page: {read} resident, the byte read is {value}");

    Ok(())
}

/// Returns the permission column of the line in `/proc/self/maps` that starts
/// at the address of a mapping.
fn permissions(mapping: &[u8]) -> io::Result<String> {
    let start = format!("{:x}-", mapping.as_ptr() as usize);

    fs::read_to_string("/proc/self/maps")?
        .lines()
        .filter(|line| line.starts_with(&start))
        .find_map(|line| line.split_whitespace().nth(1))
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::NotFound.into())
}

/// Reads the permissions of a mapping before and after mprotect removes the
/// permission to write.
fn protect() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mapping = MmapMut::map_anon(PAGE_SIZE)?;
    let before = permissions(&mapping)?;

    let mapping = mapping.make_read_only()?;
    let after = permissions(&mapping)?;

    println!("permissions of the mapping: {before}, after mprotect: {after}");

    Ok(())
}

/// Maps a file that holds "hello", writes "HELLO" through the mapping, unmaps
/// it, and returns the contents of the file.
fn through_mapping(path: &Path, shared: bool) -> io::Result<String> {
    fs::write(path, "hello")?;

    let file = OpenOptions::new().read(true).write(true).open(path)?;
    let options = MmapOptions::new();

    // SAFETY: mapping a file is unsafe in Rust because another process could
    // change the file while the slice exists. This file is in a directory the
    // program has just created, and nothing else opens it.
    let mut mapping = unsafe {
        if shared {
            options.map_mut(&file)?
        } else {
            options.map_copy(&file)?
        }
    };

    mapping.copy_from_slice(b"HELLO");
    drop(mapping);

    fs::read_to_string(path)
}

/// Compares a private file mapping with a shared one.
fn files() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("vmfacts-{}", std::process::id()));
    let path = dir.join("file");

    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;

    for (name, shared) in [("private", false), ("shared", true)] {
        let text = through_mapping(&path, shared)?;
        println!("HELLO written through a {name} file mapping: the file holds {text:?}");
    }

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    demand()?;
    protect()?;
    files()
}

Listing 7.27 The complete vmmodel, in Go. code/go/vmmodel/main.go

// Command vmmodel models an address space: a list of mappings, a page table
// that is filled on demand by page faults, a shared zero page, and
// copy-on-write after fork.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./vmmodel
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
)


const pageSize = 4096

// errSegv is the result of an access that no mapping allows. The kernel
// sends the process the signal SIGSEGV.
var errSegv = errors.New("SIGSEGV")

// A frame is a page of physical memory. refs counts the page table entries
// that refer to it.
type frame struct {
	data [pageSize]byte
	refs int
}

// memory is the physical memory shared by all address spaces: the number of
// frames allocated, and the frame of zeros that every read of an untouched
// page maps.
type memory struct {
	frames int
	zero   *frame
}

func (m *memory) allocate() *frame {
	m.frames++

	return &frame{refs: 1}
}

// A mapping is a range of virtual pages and the access it permits.
type mapping struct {
	start, pages int
	writable     bool
}

// An entry is a page table entry: the frame behind a virtual page, and
// whether the processor may write to it without a fault.
type entry struct {
	frame    *frame
	writable bool
}

// A space is the address space of a process.
type space struct {
	memory   *memory
	mappings []mapping
	table    map[int]entry
	faults   int
	nextPage int
}

func newSpace() *space {
	return &space{
		memory:   &memory{zero: &frame{refs: 1}},
		table:    map[int]entry{},
		nextPage: 16,
	}
}


// mmap records a new mapping and returns its address. It allocates no frame
// and writes no page table entry.
func (s *space) mmap(pages int, writable bool) int {
	start := s.nextPage
	s.mappings = append(s.mappings, mapping{start: start, pages: pages, writable: writable})
	s.nextPage += pages + 1

	return start * pageSize
}

// find returns the mapping that contains a page.
func (s *space) find(page int) (mapping, bool) {
	for _, m := range s.mappings {
		if page >= m.start && page < m.start+m.pages {
			return m, true
		}
	}

	return mapping{}, false
}


// read returns the byte at an address. The processor uses the page table
// entry when one exists, and faults when none does.
func (s *space) read(address int) (byte, error) {
	page, offset := address/pageSize, address%pageSize

	if _, present := s.table[page]; !present {
		if err := s.fault(page, false); err != nil {
			return 0, err
		}
	}

	return s.table[page].frame.data[offset], nil
}

// write stores a byte at an address. It faults when the page has no entry or
// the entry does not permit writing.
func (s *space) write(address int, value byte) error {
	page, offset := address/pageSize, address%pageSize

	if !s.table[page].writable {
		if err := s.fault(page, true); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	s.table[page].frame.data[offset] = value

	return nil
}


// fault is the kernel's page fault handler. It checks the access against
// the mappings and then repairs the page table entry so that the access can
// be repeated.
func (s *space) fault(page int, write bool) error {
	m, ok := s.find(page)

	if !ok || write && !m.writable {
		return errSegv
	}

	s.faults++
	e, present := s.table[page]

	switch {
	case !write:
		// A read of an untouched page maps the shared zero frame.
		s.memory.zero.refs++
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: s.memory.zero}

	case !present:
		// A write to an untouched page gets a new frame of zeros.
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: s.memory.allocate(), writable: true}

	case e.frame.refs == 1:
		// The frame has no other user. Writing is enabled in place.
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: e.frame, writable: true}

	default:
		// The frame is shared. The writer gets a private copy.
		private := s.memory.allocate()
		private.data = e.frame.data
		e.frame.refs--
		s.table[page] = entry{frame: private, writable: true}
	}

	return nil
}


// fork returns a child with the same mappings and a page table that refers
// to the same frames. Every entry is made read-only in the parent and in the
// child, so that the first write by either causes a fault.
func (s *space) fork() *space {
	child := &space{
		memory:   s.memory,
		mappings: append([]mapping(nil), s.mappings...),
		table:    map[int]entry{},
		nextPage: s.nextPage,
	}

	for page, e := range s.table {
		e.frame.refs++
		e.writable = false
		s.table[page], child.table[page] = e, e
	}

	return child
}


// report prints a step with the fault count of a space and the number of
// frames allocated.
func (s *space) report(step string) {
	fmt.Printf("%-34s faults %d, frames %d\n", step, s.faults, s.memory.frames)
}

func run() error {
	parent := newSpace()
	base := parent.mmap(4, true)
	parent.report("mmap of 4 pages:")

	if err := parent.write(base, 'a'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report("write to page 0:")

	value, err := parent.read(base + pageSize)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report(fmt.Sprintf("read of page 1, value %d:", value))

	if err := parent.write(base+pageSize, 'x'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report("write to page 1:")

	child := parent.fork()
	child.report("fork, in the child:")

	if err := child.write(base, 'b'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	child.report("child writes page 0:")

	if err := parent.write(base, 'c'); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	parent.report("parent writes page 0:")

	inParent, err := parent.read(base)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	inChild, err := child.read(base)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("page 0 holds %q in the parent and %q in the child\n", inParent, inChild)

	fmt.Printf("write outside every mapping: %v\n", parent.write(base+100*pageSize, 1))

	readOnly := parent.mmap(1, false)
	fmt.Printf("write to a read-only mapping: %v\n", parent.write(readOnly, 1))

	return nil
}

func main() {
	if err := run(); err != nil {
		fmt.Println(err)
	}
}

Listing 7.28 The complete vmmodel, in Rust. code/rust/vmmodel/src/main.rs

//! Models an address space: a list of mappings, a page table that is filled
//! on demand by page faults, a shared zero page, and copy-on-write after
//! fork.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p vmmodel
//! ```

use std::cell::Cell;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fmt;
use std::rc::Rc;

const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

/// The result of an access that no mapping allows. The kernel sends the
/// process the signal `SIGSEGV`.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Segv;

impl fmt::Display for Segv {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str("SIGSEGV")
    }
}

/// A page of physical memory. The reference count of the `Rc` is the number
/// of page table entries that refer to it.
type Frame = Rc<[u8; PAGE_SIZE]>;

/// The physical memory shared by all address spaces: the number of frames
/// allocated, and the frame of zeros that every read of an untouched page
/// maps.
struct Memory {
    frames: Cell<usize>,
    zero: Frame,
}

impl Memory {
    fn allocate(&self, contents: [u8; PAGE_SIZE]) -> Frame {
        self.frames.set(self.frames.get() + 1);

        Rc::new(contents)
    }
}

/// A range of virtual pages and the access it permits.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Mapping {
    start: usize,
    pages: usize,
    writable: bool,
}

/// A page table entry: the frame behind a virtual page, and whether the
/// processor may write to it without a fault.
#[derive(Clone)]
struct Entry {
    frame: Frame,
    writable: bool,
}

/// The address space of a process.
struct Space {
    memory: Rc<Memory>,
    mappings: Vec<Mapping>,
    table: HashMap<usize, Entry>,
    faults: usize,
    next_page: usize,
}

impl Space {
    fn new() -> Space {
        let memory = Memory {
            frames: Cell::new(0),
            zero: Rc::new([0; PAGE_SIZE]),
        };

        Space {
            memory: Rc::new(memory),
            mappings: Vec::new(),
            table: HashMap::new(),
            faults: 0,
            next_page: 16,
        }
    }
}

impl Space {
    /// Records a new mapping and returns its address. It allocates no frame
    /// and writes no page table entry.
    fn mmap(&mut self, pages: usize, writable: bool) -> usize {
        let start = self.next_page;

        self.mappings.push(Mapping {
            start,
            pages,
            writable,
        });
        self.next_page += pages + 1;

        start * PAGE_SIZE
    }

    /// Returns the mapping that contains a page.
    fn find(&self, page: usize) -> Option<Mapping> {
        self.mappings
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .find(|mapping| (mapping.start..mapping.start + mapping.pages).contains(&page))
    }
}

impl Space {
    /// Returns the byte at an address. The processor uses the page table
    /// entry when one exists, and faults when none does.
    fn read(&mut self, address: usize) -> Result<u8, Segv> {
        let (page, offset) = (address / PAGE_SIZE, address % PAGE_SIZE);

        if !self.table.contains_key(&page) {
            self.fault(page, false)?;
        }

        self.table
            .get(&page)
            .map(|entry| entry.frame[offset])
            .ok_or(Segv)
    }

    /// Stores a byte at an address. It faults when the page has no entry or
    /// the entry does not permit writing.
    fn write(&mut self, address: usize, value: u8) -> Result<(), Segv> {
        let (page, offset) = (address / PAGE_SIZE, address % PAGE_SIZE);

        if !self.table.get(&page).is_some_and(|entry| entry.writable) {
            self.fault(page, true)?;
        }

        let entry = self.table.get_mut(&page).ok_or(Segv)?;

        // A writable entry is the only user of its frame, so `make_mut`
        // returns the frame itself.
        Rc::make_mut(&mut entry.frame)[offset] = value;

        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Space {
    /// The kernel's page fault handler. It checks the access against the
    /// mappings and then repairs the page table entry so that the access can
    /// be repeated.
    fn fault(&mut self, page: usize, write: bool) -> Result<(), Segv> {
        let mapping = self.find(page).ok_or(Segv)?;

        if write && !mapping.writable {
            return Err(Segv);
        }

        self.faults += 1;

        let entry = match (write, self.table.remove(&page)) {
            // A read of an untouched page maps the shared zero frame.
            (false, _) => Entry {
                frame: Rc::clone(&self.memory.zero),
                writable: false,
            },

            // A write to an untouched page gets a new frame of zeros.
            (true, None) => Entry {
                frame: self.memory.allocate([0; PAGE_SIZE]),
                writable: true,
            },

            // The frame has no other user. Writing is enabled in place.
            (true, Some(entry)) if Rc::strong_count(&entry.frame) == 1 => Entry {
                frame: entry.frame,
                writable: true,
            },

            // The frame is shared. The writer gets a private copy.
            (true, Some(entry)) => Entry {
                frame: self.memory.allocate(*entry.frame),
                writable: true,
            },
        };

        self.table.insert(page, entry);

        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Space {
    /// Returns a child with the same mappings and a page table that refers to
    /// the same frames. Every entry is made read-only in the parent and in
    /// the child, so that the first write by either causes a fault.
    fn fork(&mut self) -> Space {
        for entry in self.table.values_mut() {
            entry.writable = false;
        }

        Space {
            memory: Rc::clone(&self.memory),
            mappings: self.mappings.clone(),
            table: self.table.clone(),
            faults: 0,
            next_page: self.next_page,
        }
    }
}

impl Space {
    /// Prints a step with the fault count of a space and the number of frames
    /// allocated.
    fn report(&self, step: &str) {
        println!(
            "{step:<34} faults {}, frames {}",
            self.faults,
            self.memory.frames.get()
        );
    }
}

fn run() -> Result<(), Segv> {
    let mut parent = Space::new();
    let base = parent.mmap(4, true);
    parent.report("mmap of 4 pages:");

    parent.write(base, b'a')?;
    parent.report("write to page 0:");

    let value = parent.read(base + PAGE_SIZE)?;
    parent.report(&format!("read of page 1, value {value}:"));

    parent.write(base + PAGE_SIZE, b'x')?;
    parent.report("write to page 1:");

    let mut child = parent.fork();
    child.report("fork, in the child:");

    child.write(base, b'b')?;
    child.report("child writes page 0:");

    parent.write(base, b'c')?;
    parent.report("parent writes page 0:");

    println!(
        "page 0 holds {:?} in the parent and {:?} in the child",
        char::from(parent.read(base)?),
        char::from(child.read(base)?)
    );

    if let Err(error) = parent.write(base + 100 * PAGE_SIZE, 1) {
        println!("write outside every mapping: {error}");
    }

    let read_only = parent.mmap(1, false);

    if let Err(error) = parent.write(read_only, 1) {
        println!("write to a read-only mapping: {error}");
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    if let Err(error) = run() {
        println!("{error}");
    }
}

Summary

  • Each process has its own virtual addresses, translated to physical frames through a page table.
  • mmap records a mapping and allocates nothing. A page receives a frame at its first access, through a page fault.
  • A read of an untouched anonymous page maps a shared frame of zeros. The first write replaces it with a private frame.
  • A write through a shared file mapping reaches the file. A write through a private mapping changes a copy.
  • fork copies the page table and shares the frames read-only. A frame is copied when one side first writes to it.
  • An access that no mapping permits ends in SIGSEGV.

References

  • mmap(2), mprotect(2) and proc(5) for pagemap and maps, Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html
  • Examining Process Page Tables, Linux kernel documentation: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v5.15/admin-guide/mm/pagemap.html
  • M. Gorman, Understanding the Linux Virtual Memory Manager, Prentice Hall, 2004.
  • mm/memory.c and mm/mmap.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/mm/memory.c

The Page Cache

The page cache is the kernel’s in-memory copy of file contents. It holds frames of file data, indexed by file and by page number within the file. read copies from these frames and write copies into them. The disk is involved only when a page is missing from the cache, or when a changed page is written back.

In this chapter, we will learn when file data moves between the cache and the disk. We will first measure with cachefacts how many pages of a file are cached after writes and reads of different kinds. Then we will write pagecache, a model with readahead, dirty pages and eviction, and compare its behaviour with the measurements.

This chapter covers

  • why reads and writes go through memory
  • one read, step by step, with the page cached and with it missing
  • the kernel structure of the cache: struct address_space
  • how much of a machine’s memory is page cache, and why that memory still counts as available
  • readahead: how a read of 1 byte brings several pages into the cache
  • dirty pages, writeback and fsync
  • eviction of the page used least recently
  • posix_fadvise: telling the kernel how a file will be used
  • the settings that control writeback, and how to observe the cache on a running system

Why a cache

A disk request takes far longer than a copy in memory: roughly 100 microseconds for a fast solid-state drive against well under 1 microsecond for a page that is already in memory. The kernel therefore keeps file pages in frames that no process currently needs and serves file operations from them.

OperationWith the page cachedWith the page missing
readcopies from the cached pagereads the page from the disk into the cache, then copies
writecopies into the cached page and marks it dirtycreates the page in the cache, copies, and marks it dirty

A dirty page is newer than the disk. The kernel writes dirty pages to the disk in the background, a process called writeback, typically within 30 seconds. write therefore returns before the data is on the disk, and data written shortly before a power failure can be lost. A program that needs the data to be durable calls fsync, which returns when the file’s dirty pages have reached the disk.

The cache uses memory that is otherwise free, and gives it up when processes need it. A clean page can be discarded at any time, because the disk has the same contents. A dirty page has to be written first.

One read, step by step

A process calls read(fd, buf, 4096) on a file whose offset is 8192.

  1. The kernel finds the struct file for the descriptor and, through it, the inode of the file (chapter 2).
  2. It divides the offset by the page size. Offset 8192 is the start of page number 2 of the file.
  3. It looks page 2 up in the cache of this file. Each inode has its own index of cached pages.
  4. If the page is there, the kernel copies 4096 bytes from it to buf, advances the offset, and returns. No request reaches the disk.
  5. If the page is missing, the kernel allocates a frame, asks the file system to read the block from the disk into it, and inserts the frame in the index. The process sleeps until the disk has answered. Then step 4 follows.

A read that finds its page is a cache hit, and one that has to go to the disk is a cache miss. The page fault of chapter 7 that reads a page of a mapped file takes the same path from step 3 on, and the frame it maps is the frame in the cache. read and mmap therefore see the same copy of a file.

The kernel’s structure

The index of cached pages of a file is a struct address_space, embedded in the inode and reached through inode->i_mapping. This is the definition in include/linux/fs.h of Linux 5.15, reduced to the fields we use.

struct address_space {
        struct inode *host;                    /* the file these pages belong to */
        struct xarray i_pages;                 /* page number -> struct page */
        unsigned long nrpages;                 /* number of cached pages */
        pgoff_t writeback_index;               /* where writeback continues */
        const struct address_space_operations *a_ops;  /* read and write a page */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
i_pagesAn XArray: a tree that maps a page number to the struct page of the frame that caches it. A lookup for a page that is not cached finds nothing.
nrpagesHow many pages of this file are cached. The fincore command used below reports this count, page by page.
a_opsFunctions supplied by the file system, such as ext4: readpage fills a frame from the disk, and writepages writes dirty frames back. The cache itself knows nothing about disk formats.
hostThe inode.

Each cached frame is a struct page (chapter 7) whose mapping field points back to this address_space and whose index is its page number. Bits in its flags record its state: PG_uptodate when its contents are valid, PG_dirty when it has been written and the disk has not, and PG_writeback while it is being written to the disk.

How much memory is cache

The page cache uses whatever memory nothing else needs. On our machine, with 16 GB of memory:

$ free -m
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           15655        8881         300         294        6473        6197
$ grep -E 'Cached|Dirty|Writeback:' /proc/meminfo
Cached:          5760296 kB
Dirty:              2488 kB
Writeback:             0 kB

Only 300 MB is free, and that is the normal state of a healthy system. 6473 MB is buff/cache, mostly page cache, and the kernel can take it back at any moment, which is why the available column, 6197 MB, is the number that says how much memory a new program could get. Dirty is the part of the cache that has not been written to disk yet, 2.5 MB at that moment.

Measuring the cache

cachefacts counts the cached pages of a file with the fincore utility from util-linux. It uses golang.org/x/sys/unix in Go and the nix crate with the fs feature in Rust, for posix_fadvise.

$ cargo new cachefacts
$ cargo add -p cachefacts nix --features fs

The file must be on a disk-backed file system for the measurement to mean anything. On this machine /tmp is on ext4. drop makes the file’s pages clean with fsync and then asks the kernel to discard them with the advice POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED.

Listing 8.1 The imports of cachefacts, in Go. code/go/cachefacts/main.go

	"fmt"

Listing 8.2 The imports of cachefacts, in Rust. code/rust/cachefacts/src/main.rs

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, Write};
use std::os::unix::fs::FileExt;
use std::path::Path;
use std::process::Command;

use nix::fcntl::{PosixFadviseAdvice, posix_fadvise};

Listing 8.3 Counting and dropping the cached pages of a file, in Go. code/go/cachefacts/main.go

const pageSize = 4096

// cached returns the number of pages of a file that are in the page cache,
// as reported by the fincore utility.
func cached(path string) (int, error) {
	text, err := exec.Command("fincore", "--noheadings", "--output", "PAGES", path).Output()

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(string(text)))
}

// report prints a step and the number of cached pages after it.
func report(step, path string) error {
	pages, err := cached(path)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("%-38s cached pages: %d\n", step+":", pages)

	return nil
}

// drop writes the file's dirty pages to disk and asks the kernel to remove
// the file's pages from the cache.
func drop(file *os.File) error {
	if err := file.Sync(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return unix.Fadvise(int(file.Fd()), 0, 0, unix.FADV_DONTNEED)
}

Listing 8.4 Counting and dropping the cached pages of a file, in Rust. code/rust/cachefacts/src/main.rs

const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

/// Returns the number of pages of a file that are in the page cache, as
/// reported by the fincore utility.
fn cached(path: &Path) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let output = Command::new("fincore")
        .args(["--noheadings", "--output", "PAGES"])
        .arg(path)
        .output()?;

    String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)
        .trim()
        .parse()
        .map_err(|_| io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into())
}

/// Prints a step and the number of cached pages after it.
fn report(step: &str, path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let pages = cached(path)?;
    println!("{:<38} cached pages: {pages}", format!("{step}:"));

    Ok(())
}

/// Writes the file's dirty pages to disk and asks the kernel to remove the
/// file's pages from the cache.
fn drop_pages(file: &File) -> io::Result<()> {
    file.sync_all()?;
    posix_fadvise(file, 0, 0, PosixFadviseAdvice::POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED)?;

    Ok(())
}

run writes 64 pages, drops them, reads 1 byte, reads the whole file, drops the pages again, and reads 1 byte after giving the advice POSIX_FADV_RANDOM.

Listing 8.5 Writes and reads of a file of 64 pages, in Go. code/go/cachefacts/main.go

// run writes a file of 64 pages and reads it in 3 ways, dropping the cached
// pages between the steps.
func run(path string) error {
	file, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREATE, 0o644)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer file.Close()

	if _, err := file.Write(make([]byte, 64*pageSize)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("write of 64 pages", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := drop(file); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("fsync, then FADV_DONTNEED", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	one := make([]byte, 1)

	if _, err := file.ReadAt(one, 0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("read of 1 byte at offset 0", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := io.Copy(io.Discard, io.NewSectionReader(file, 0, 64*pageSize)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("read of the whole file", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := drop(file); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := unix.Fadvise(int(file.Fd()), 0, 0, unix.FADV_RANDOM); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := file.ReadAt(one, 0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return report("dropped, FADV_RANDOM, read of 1 byte", path)
}

Listing 8.6 Writes and reads of a file of 64 pages, in Rust. code/rust/cachefacts/src/main.rs

/// Writes a file of 64 pages and reads it in 3 ways, dropping the cached
/// pages between the steps.
fn run(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .truncate(true)
        .open(path)?;

    file.write_all(&vec![0u8; 64 * PAGE_SIZE])?;
    report("write of 64 pages", path)?;

    drop_pages(&file)?;
    report("fsync, then FADV_DONTNEED", path)?;

    let mut one = [0u8; 1];

    file.read_exact_at(&mut one, 0)?;
    report("read of 1 byte at offset 0", path)?;

    let mut whole = vec![0u8; 64 * PAGE_SIZE];

    file.read_exact_at(&mut whole, 0)?;
    report("read of the whole file", path)?;

    drop_pages(&file)?;
    posix_fadvise(&file, 0, 0, PosixFadviseAdvice::POSIX_FADV_RANDOM)?;

    file.read_exact_at(&mut one, 0)?;
    report("dropped, FADV_RANDOM, read of 1 byte", path)
}
write of 64 pages:                     cached pages: 64
fsync, then FADV_DONTNEED:             cached pages: 0
read of 1 byte at offset 0:            cached pages: 4
read of the whole file:                cached pages: 64
dropped, FADV_RANDOM, read of 1 byte:  cached pages: 1
OutputConclusion
64 pages cached after the writeWritten data is in the cache when write returns.
0 after fsync and DONTNEEDClean pages can be discarded.
4 after a read of 1 byteThe kernel read 4 pages from the disk for a request of 1 byte.
64 after reading the whole fileEvery page that is read stays cached.
1 after a read of 1 byte with FADV_RANDOMWith readahead disabled, a read brings in only the page it needs.

Readahead

Most files are read from start to end. A disk serves 1 large request much faster than many small ones, so the kernel assumes sequential access and reads more pages than were asked for. This is readahead. The first read at the start of a file loads a small window, 4 pages in the measurement. While the reads continue in order, each window is double the size of the last, up to a limit, which is 32 pages on this machine (/sys/block/<device>/queue/read_ahead_kb is 128). A read at an unrelated position starts again with a small window.

A program that knows its access pattern can say so with posix_fadvise. POSIX_FADV_RANDOM turns readahead off for the descriptor, and POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL doubles the limit.

Low-level design: pagecache

TypeFieldsMeaning
diskpages, requests, writtenthe file on disk; counters for requests and pages written

OperationBehaviourDisk requests
read(index)returns a page; on a miss loads a window of pages0 on a hit, 1 on a miss
write(index, value)changes the cached page and marks it dirty0
sync()writes every dirty page1 page written per dirty page
insert(index, page)adds a page; evicts the least recently used page when fulla write when the evicted page is dirty

Modelling the cache

The model reduces the contents of a page to 1 byte and counts requests to the disk.

Listing 8.7 The imports of pagecache, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

	"fmt"

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

Listing 8.9 The disk, a cached page, and the cache, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

// maxWindow is the largest number of pages one disk request reads ahead.
const maxWindow = 8

// A disk holds the pages of a file and counts the requests made to it. The
// contents of a page are reduced to one byte.
type disk struct {
	pages    []byte
	requests int
	written  int
}

// A page is a cached copy of a disk page. dirty is set when the copy has
// been written and the disk has not. used is the time of the last access.
type page struct {
	value byte
	dirty bool
	used  int
}

// A cache maps page numbers to cached pages. next is the page that a
// sequential reader would ask for next, and window is the current number of
// pages to read ahead.
type cache struct {
	disk     *disk
	pages    map[int]*page
	capacity int
	clock    int
	next     int
	window   int
}

func newCache(d *disk, capacity int) *cache {
	return &cache{disk: d, pages: map[int]*page{}, capacity: capacity}
}

Listing 8.10 The disk, a cached page, and the cache, in Rust. code/rust/pagecache/src/main.rs

/// The largest number of pages one disk request reads ahead.
const MAX_WINDOW: usize = 8;

/// Holds the pages of a file and counts the requests made to it. The contents
/// of a page are reduced to one byte.
struct Disk {
    pages: Vec<u8>,
    requests: usize,
    written: usize,
}

impl Disk {
    fn new() -> Disk {
        Disk {
            pages: vec![b'-'; 16],
            requests: 0,
            written: 0,
        }
    }
}

/// A cached copy of a disk page. `dirty` is set when the copy has been
/// written and the disk has not. `used` is the time of the last access.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Page {
    value: u8,
    dirty: bool,
    used: usize,
}

/// Maps page numbers to cached pages. `next` is the page that a sequential
/// reader would ask for next, and `window` is the current number of pages to
/// read ahead.
struct Cache {
    disk: Disk,
    pages: BTreeMap<usize, Page>,
    capacity: usize,
    clock: usize,
    next: usize,
    window: usize,
}

impl Cache {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Cache {
        Cache {
            disk: Disk::new(),
            pages: BTreeMap::new(),
            capacity,
            clock: 0,
            next: 0,
            window: 0,
        }
    }
}

read implements the lookup and the readahead rule. next is the page number that would follow the previous read. A miss at that position doubles the window, and a miss anywhere else sets it to 1 page.

Listing 8.11 Reading through the cache, with readahead, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

// read returns the contents of a page. A page that is cached costs no disk
// request. For a page that is missing, read makes one request for a window
// of pages. The window doubles while the reads are sequential and returns
// to 1 page when they are not.
func (c *cache) read(index int) byte {
	if _, hit := c.pages[index]; !hit {
		if index == c.next {
			c.window = min(2*max(c.window, 1), maxWindow)
		} else {
			c.window = 1
		}

		c.load(index, c.window)
	}

	c.next = index + 1

	return c.touch(index).value
}

// load reads count pages starting at index from the disk in one request.
func (c *cache) load(index, count int) {
	c.disk.requests++

	for i := index; i < min(index+count, len(c.disk.pages)); i++ {
		if _, hit := c.pages[i]; !hit {
			c.insert(i, &page{value: c.disk.pages[i]})
		}
	}
}

// touch records an access to a cached page and returns the page.
func (c *cache) touch(index int) *page {
	c.clock++
	c.pages[index].used = c.clock

	return c.pages[index]
}

Listing 8.12 Reading through the cache, with readahead, in Rust. code/rust/pagecache/src/main.rs

impl Cache {
    /// Returns the contents of a page. A page that is cached costs no disk
    /// request. For a page that is missing, `read` makes one request for a
    /// window of pages. The window doubles while the reads are sequential and
    /// returns to 1 page when they are not.
    fn read(&mut self, index: usize) -> u8 {
        if !self.pages.contains_key(&index) {
            if index == self.next {
                self.window = (2 * self.window.max(1)).min(MAX_WINDOW);
            } else {
                self.window = 1;
            }

            self.load(index, self.window);
        }

        self.next = index + 1;

        self.touch(index).value
    }

    /// Reads `count` pages starting at `index` from the disk in one request.
    fn load(&mut self, index: usize, count: usize) {
        self.disk.requests += 1;

        for i in index..(index + count).min(self.disk.pages.len()) {
            if !self.pages.contains_key(&i) {
                let value = self.disk.pages[i];

                self.insert(i, value);
            }
        }
    }

    /// Records an access to a page and returns the page. A page that is not
    /// cached is created empty.
    fn touch(&mut self, index: usize) -> &mut Page {
        self.clock += 1;

        let page = self.pages.entry(index).or_default();
        page.used = self.clock;

        page
    }
}

write touches only the cache. sync is the model’s fsync.

Listing 8.13 Writing, and writing back, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

// write changes a page in the cache and marks it dirty. It makes no disk
// request.
func (c *cache) write(index int, value byte) {
	if _, hit := c.pages[index]; !hit {
		c.insert(index, &page{})
	}

	p := c.touch(index)
	p.value, p.dirty = value, true
}

// sync writes every dirty page to the disk and returns the number written.
func (c *cache) sync() int {
	before := c.disk.written

	for index, p := range c.pages {
		c.clean(index, p)
	}

	return c.disk.written - before
}

// clean writes one page to the disk if it is dirty.
func (c *cache) clean(index int, p *page) {
	if p.dirty {
		c.disk.pages[index] = p.value
		c.disk.written++
		p.dirty = false
	}
}

Listing 8.14 Writing, and writing back, in Rust. code/rust/pagecache/src/main.rs

impl Cache {
    /// Changes a page in the cache and marks it dirty. It makes no disk
    /// request.
    fn write(&mut self, index: usize, value: u8) {
        if !self.pages.contains_key(&index) {
            self.insert(index, 0);
        }

        let page = self.touch(index);
        page.value = value;
        page.dirty = true;
    }

    /// Writes every dirty page to the disk and returns the number written.
    fn sync(&mut self) -> usize {
        let before = self.disk.written;

        for (&index, page) in &mut self.pages {
            clean(&mut self.disk, index, page);
        }

        self.disk.written - before
    }
}

/// Writes one page to the disk if it is dirty.
fn clean(disk: &mut Disk, index: usize, page: &mut Page) {
    if page.dirty {
        disk.pages[index] = page.value;
        disk.written += 1;
        page.dirty = false;
    }
}

insert enforces the capacity. It evicts the page with the oldest access time, which is the least recently used policy: a page that has not been used for the longest time is the least likely to be needed soon. The kernel approximates this policy with 2 lists of pages, active and inactive, and avoids keeping an exact access time for each page.

Listing 8.15 Inserting a page, and evicting the least recently used, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

// insert adds a page to the cache. When the cache is full it first evicts
// the page whose last access is the oldest. A dirty page is written to the
// disk before it is removed.
func (c *cache) insert(index int, p *page) {
	if len(c.pages) == c.capacity {
		oldest := -1

		for i, candidate := range c.pages {
			if oldest == -1 || candidate.used < c.pages[oldest].used {
				oldest = i
			}
		}

		c.clean(oldest, c.pages[oldest])
		delete(c.pages, oldest)
	}

	c.clock++
	p.used = c.clock
	c.pages[index] = p
}

// held returns the numbers of the cached pages in increasing order.
func (c *cache) held() []int {
	held := make([]int, 0, len(c.pages))

	for index := range c.pages {
		held = append(held, index)
	}

	slices.Sort(held)

	return held
}

Listing 8.16 Inserting a page, and evicting the least recently used, in Rust. code/rust/pagecache/src/main.rs

impl Cache {
    /// Adds a page to the cache. When the cache is full it first evicts the
    /// page whose last access is the oldest. A dirty page is written to the
    /// disk before it is removed.
    fn insert(&mut self, index: usize, value: u8) {
        if self.pages.len() == self.capacity {
            let oldest = self
                .pages
                .iter()
                .min_by_key(|(_, page)| page.used)
                .map(|(&index, _)| index);

            if let Some(oldest) = oldest
                && let Some(mut page) = self.pages.remove(&oldest)
            {
                clean(&mut self.disk, oldest, &mut page);
            }
        }

        self.clock += 1;

        let page = Page {
            value,
            dirty: false,
            used: self.clock,
        };

        self.pages.insert(index, page);
    }

    /// Returns the numbers of the cached pages in increasing order.
    fn held(&self) -> Vec<usize> {
        self.pages.keys().copied().collect()
    }
}

Listing 8.17 The trace, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

// requests reads the given pages through a new cache and returns the number
// of disk requests.
func requests(order []int) int {
	d := &disk{pages: make([]byte, 16)}
	c := newCache(d, 32)

	for _, index := range order {
		c.read(index)
	}

	return d.requests
}

func main() {
	forward := make([]int, 16)

	for i := range forward {
		forward[i] = i
	}

	backward := slices.Clone(forward)
	slices.Reverse(backward)

	fmt.Printf("16 pages read in order: %d disk requests\n", requests(forward))
	fmt.Printf("16 pages read in reverse order: %d disk requests\n", requests(backward))
	fmt.Printf("16 pages read in order, 2 times: %d disk requests\n", requests(append(forward, forward...)))

	d := &disk{pages: []byte("----------------")}
	c := newCache(d, 4)

	c.write(3, 'x')
	fmt.Printf("write of x to page 3: %d pages written, the disk holds %c\n", d.written, d.pages[3])
	fmt.Printf("sync: %d page written, the disk holds %c\n", c.sync(), d.pages[3])

	for _, index := range []int{2, 1, 0, 3} {
		c.read(index)
	}

	c.read(8)
	fmt.Printf("capacity 4, pages 3 2 1 0 3 used, then page 8: cache holds %v\n", c.held())

	c.write(1, 'y')

	for _, index := range []int{0, 3, 8, 12} {
		c.read(index)
	}

	fmt.Printf("write of y to page 1, then pages 0 3 8 12 used: cache holds %v, the disk holds %c\n", c.held(), d.pages[1])
}

/// Reads the given pages through a new cache and returns the number of disk
/// requests.
fn requests(order: impl Iterator<Item = usize>) -> usize {
    let mut cache = Cache::new(32);

    for index in order {
        cache.read(index);
    }

    cache.disk.requests
}

/// Formats page numbers the way Go prints a slice.
fn list(pages: &[usize]) -> String {
    let words: Vec<String> = pages.iter().map(usize::to_string).collect();

    format!("[{}]", words.join(" "))
}

fn main() {
    println!("16 pages read in order: {} disk requests", requests(0..16));
    println!(
        "16 pages read in reverse order: {} disk requests",
        requests((0..16).rev())
    );
    println!(
        "16 pages read in order, 2 times: {} disk requests",
        requests((0..16).chain(0..16))
    );

    cache.write(3, b'x');

16 pages read in reverse order: 16 disk requests
16 pages read in order, 2 times: 4 disk requests
write of x to page 3: 0 pages written, the disk holds -

LineWhat it shows
4 requests in orderWindows of 2, 4, 8 and 8 pages cover 16 pages, as in figure 8.4.
16 requests in reverse orderNo read is sequential, so every miss loads 1 page.
4 requests for 2 passesPass 2 is served from the cache.
