Correspondence with the kernel source. Each file has a struct address_space (include/linux/fs.h) whose i_pages is an XArray from page index to page; that is the cache of the file. filemap_read in mm/filemap.c serves read from it. ondemand_readahead in mm/readahead.c chooses the window, with get_init_ra_size giving the 4 pages of the measurement. Dirty pages are written by the flusher threads in fs/fs-writeback.c, and mm/vmscan.c evicts pages from the inactive list when memory is short.

Writeback and durability

write returns when the data is in the cache. When the data reaches the disk is decided by the kernel’s flusher threads, which wake periodically and write dirty pages. 4 settings under /proc/sys/vm control them, shown here with the values on this machine.

SettingValueMeaning
dirty_writeback_centisecs500The flusher threads wake every 5 seconds.
dirty_expire_centisecs3000A page that has been dirty for 30 seconds is written at the next wake-up.
dirty_background_ratio10When dirty pages exceed 10% of available memory, writing starts at once, in the background.
dirty_ratio20When they exceed 20%, a process that calls write is made to wait and write pages itself.

The last setting is a form of the flow control of chapter 1. A program that writes faster than the disk can absorb fills memory with dirty pages, and at 20% the kernel slows it down to the speed of the disk.

A program for which lost data is unacceptable, such as a database, calls fsync after writing and reports success only after fsync has returned. The call is slow compared with write, since it waits for the disk, and this is the main cost of durability. Opening a file with O_DIRECT bypasses the cache altogether: reads and writes go straight to the disk, for programs that keep a cache of their own.

write returns while the data is still only in memory. Call fsync when the data must survive a power failure.

Eviction

When memory runs short, the kernel frees frames, and the page cache is the first place it looks. It keeps the pages on 2 lists.

A page enters the inactive list when it is first read. If it is used again, it is promoted to the active list. Pages are evicted from the end of the inactive list, and the active list is trimmed into the inactive list to keep the 2 in proportion. The effect is that a page has to be used at least 2 times to be protected, so reading a large file once, as a backup does, does not push out the pages that programs use all the time. /proc/meminfo shows the sizes of the lists as Active(file) and Inactive(file): 3.4 GB and 2.5 GB on this machine.

A clean page is evicted by dropping it. A dirty page has to be written first, which is the reason the kernel writes dirty pages in the background before memory is short. The model above uses a single list with exact access times, which shows the idea with less code.

Inspecting the cache on a live system

CommandShows
free -mmemory used by the cache (buff/cache) and memory a new program could get (available)
grep -E 'Cached|Dirty|Writeback' /proc/meminfothe size of the cache, and the part that is dirty or being written
fincore filehow many pages of a file are cached
syncwrites all dirty pages of the system to disk
echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_cachesas root: discards all clean cached pages, for experiments
cat /sys/block/<device>/queue/read_ahead_kbthe largest readahead window of a device

The complete programs

Listing 8.19 The complete cachefacts, in Go. code/go/cachefacts/main.go

// Command cachefacts measures the page cache for one file: how many of the
// file's pages are held in memory after a write, after the cache is told to
// drop them, and after reads of different kinds.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./cachefacts
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"path/filepath"
	"strconv"
	"strings"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


const pageSize = 4096

// cached returns the number of pages of a file that are in the page cache,
// as reported by the fincore utility.
func cached(path string) (int, error) {
	text, err := exec.Command("fincore", "--noheadings", "--output", "PAGES", path).Output()

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(string(text)))
}

// report prints a step and the number of cached pages after it.
func report(step, path string) error {
	pages, err := cached(path)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("%-38s cached pages: %d\n", step+":", pages)

	return nil
}

// drop writes the file's dirty pages to disk and asks the kernel to remove
// the file's pages from the cache.
func drop(file *os.File) error {
	if err := file.Sync(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return unix.Fadvise(int(file.Fd()), 0, 0, unix.FADV_DONTNEED)
}


// run writes a file of 64 pages and reads it in 3 ways, dropping the cached
// pages between the steps.
func run(path string) error {
	file, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREATE, 0o644)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer file.Close()

	if _, err := file.Write(make([]byte, 64*pageSize)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("write of 64 pages", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := drop(file); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("fsync, then FADV_DONTNEED", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	one := make([]byte, 1)

	if _, err := file.ReadAt(one, 0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("read of 1 byte at offset 0", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := io.Copy(io.Discard, io.NewSectionReader(file, 0, 64*pageSize)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := report("read of the whole file", path); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := drop(file); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := unix.Fadvise(int(file.Fd()), 0, 0, unix.FADV_RANDOM); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := file.ReadAt(one, 0); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return report("dropped, FADV_RANDOM, read of 1 byte", path)
}


func main() {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "cachefacts")

	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	err = run(filepath.Join(dir, "file"))
	os.RemoveAll(dir)

	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

Listing 8.20 The complete cachefacts, in Rust. code/rust/cachefacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures the page cache for one file: how many of the file's pages are
//! held in memory after a write, after the cache is told to drop them, and
//! after reads of different kinds.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p cachefacts
//! ```

use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, Write};
use std::os::unix::fs::FileExt;
use std::path::Path;
use std::process::Command;

use nix::fcntl::{PosixFadviseAdvice, posix_fadvise};

const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;

/// Returns the number of pages of a file that are in the page cache, as
/// reported by the fincore utility.
fn cached(path: &Path) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let output = Command::new("fincore")
        .args(["--noheadings", "--output", "PAGES"])
        .arg(path)
        .output()?;

    String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)
        .trim()
        .parse()
        .map_err(|_| io::ErrorKind::InvalidData.into())
}

/// Prints a step and the number of cached pages after it.
fn report(step: &str, path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let pages = cached(path)?;
    println!("{:<38} cached pages: {pages}", format!("{step}:"));

    Ok(())
}

/// Writes the file's dirty pages to disk and asks the kernel to remove the
/// file's pages from the cache.
fn drop_pages(file: &File) -> io::Result<()> {
    file.sync_all()?;
    posix_fadvise(file, 0, 0, PosixFadviseAdvice::POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED)?;

    Ok(())
}

/// Writes a file of 64 pages and reads it in 3 ways, dropping the cached
/// pages between the steps.
fn run(path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .truncate(true)
        .open(path)?;

    file.write_all(&vec![0u8; 64 * PAGE_SIZE])?;
    report("write of 64 pages", path)?;

    drop_pages(&file)?;
    report("fsync, then FADV_DONTNEED", path)?;

    let mut one = [0u8; 1];

    file.read_exact_at(&mut one, 0)?;
    report("read of 1 byte at offset 0", path)?;

    let mut whole = vec![0u8; 64 * PAGE_SIZE];

    file.read_exact_at(&mut whole, 0)?;
    report("read of the whole file", path)?;

    drop_pages(&file)?;
    posix_fadvise(&file, 0, 0, PosixFadviseAdvice::POSIX_FADV_RANDOM)?;

    file.read_exact_at(&mut one, 0)?;
    report("dropped, FADV_RANDOM, read of 1 byte", path)
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("cachefacts-{}", std::process::id()));

    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;

    let result = run(&dir.join("file"));

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)?;

    result
}

Listing 8.21 The complete pagecache, in Go. code/go/pagecache/main.go

// Command pagecache models the kernel's page cache for one file: pages read
// from a disk are kept in memory, sequential reads fetch pages ahead of the
// reader, writes change only the cached page until a sync, and the page used
// least recently is evicted when the cache is full.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./pagecache
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)


// maxWindow is the largest number of pages one disk request reads ahead.
const maxWindow = 8

// A disk holds the pages of a file and counts the requests made to it. The
// contents of a page are reduced to one byte.
type disk struct {
	pages    []byte
	requests int
	written  int
}

// A page is a cached copy of a disk page. dirty is set when the copy has
// been written and the disk has not. used is the time of the last access.
type page struct {
	value byte
	dirty bool
	used  int
}

// A cache maps page numbers to cached pages. next is the page that a
// sequential reader would ask for next, and window is the current number of
// pages to read ahead.
type cache struct {
	disk     *disk
	pages    map[int]*page
	capacity int
	clock    int
	next     int
	window   int
}

func newCache(d *disk, capacity int) *cache {
	return &cache{disk: d, pages: map[int]*page{}, capacity: capacity}
}


// read returns the contents of a page. A page that is cached costs no disk
// request. For a page that is missing, read makes one request for a window
// of pages. The window doubles while the reads are sequential and returns
// to 1 page when they are not.
func (c *cache) read(index int) byte {
	if _, hit := c.pages[index]; !hit {
		if index == c.next {
			c.window = min(2*max(c.window, 1), maxWindow)
		} else {
			c.window = 1
		}

		c.load(index, c.window)
	}

	c.next = index + 1

	return c.touch(index).value
}

// load reads count pages starting at index from the disk in one request.
func (c *cache) load(index, count int) {
	c.disk.requests++

	for i := index; i < min(index+count, len(c.disk.pages)); i++ {
		if _, hit := c.pages[i]; !hit {
			c.insert(i, &page{value: c.disk.pages[i]})
		}
	}
}

// touch records an access to a cached page and returns the page.
func (c *cache) touch(index int) *page {
	c.clock++
	c.pages[index].used = c.clock

	return c.pages[index]
}


// write changes a page in the cache and marks it dirty. It makes no disk
// request.
func (c *cache) write(index int, value byte) {
	if _, hit := c.pages[index]; !hit {
		c.insert(index, &page{})
	}

	p := c.touch(index)
	p.value, p.dirty = value, true
}

// sync writes every dirty page to the disk and returns the number written.
func (c *cache) sync() int {
	before := c.disk.written

	for index, p := range c.pages {
		c.clean(index, p)
	}

	return c.disk.written - before
}

// clean writes one page to the disk if it is dirty.
func (c *cache) clean(index int, p *page) {
	if p.dirty {
		c.disk.pages[index] = p.value
		c.disk.written++
		p.dirty = false
	}
}


// insert adds a page to the cache. When the cache is full it first evicts
// the page whose last access is the oldest. A dirty page is written to the
// disk before it is removed.
func (c *cache) insert(index int, p *page) {
	if len(c.pages) == c.capacity {
		oldest := -1

		for i, candidate := range c.pages {
			if oldest == -1 || candidate.used < c.pages[oldest].used {
				oldest = i
			}
		}

		c.clean(oldest, c.pages[oldest])
		delete(c.pages, oldest)
	}

	c.clock++
	p.used = c.clock
	c.pages[index] = p
}

// held returns the numbers of the cached pages in increasing order.
func (c *cache) held() []int {
	held := make([]int, 0, len(c.pages))

	for index := range c.pages {
		held = append(held, index)
	}

	slices.Sort(held)

	return held
}


// requests reads the given pages through a new cache and returns the number
// of disk requests.
func requests(order []int) int {
	d := &disk{pages: make([]byte, 16)}
	c := newCache(d, 32)

	for _, index := range order {
		c.read(index)
	}

	return d.requests
}

func main() {
	forward := make([]int, 16)

	for i := range forward {
		forward[i] = i
	}

	backward := slices.Clone(forward)
	slices.Reverse(backward)

	fmt.Printf("16 pages read in order: %d disk requests\n", requests(forward))
	fmt.Printf("16 pages read in reverse order: %d disk requests\n", requests(backward))
	fmt.Printf("16 pages read in order, 2 times: %d disk requests\n", requests(append(forward, forward...)))

	d := &disk{pages: []byte("----------------")}
	c := newCache(d, 4)

	c.write(3, 'x')
	fmt.Printf("write of x to page 3: %d pages written, the disk holds %c\n", d.written, d.pages[3])
	fmt.Printf("sync: %d page written, the disk holds %c\n", c.sync(), d.pages[3])

	for _, index := range []int{2, 1, 0, 3} {
		c.read(index)
	}

	c.read(8)
	fmt.Printf("capacity 4, pages 3 2 1 0 3 used, then page 8: cache holds %v\n", c.held())

	c.write(1, 'y')

	for _, index := range []int{0, 3, 8, 12} {
		c.read(index)
	}

	fmt.Printf("write of y to page 1, then pages 0 3 8 12 used: cache holds %v, the disk holds %c\n", c.held(), d.pages[1])
}

Listing 8.22 The complete pagecache, in Rust. code/rust/pagecache/src/main.rs

//! Models the kernel's page cache for one file: pages read from a disk are
//! kept in memory, sequential reads fetch pages ahead of the reader, writes
//! change only the cached page until a sync, and the page used least recently
//! is evicted when the cache is full.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p pagecache
//! ```

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

/// The largest number of pages one disk request reads ahead.
const MAX_WINDOW: usize = 8;

/// Holds the pages of a file and counts the requests made to it. The contents
/// of a page are reduced to one byte.
struct Disk {
    pages: Vec<u8>,
    requests: usize,
    written: usize,
}

impl Disk {
    fn new() -> Disk {
        Disk {
            pages: vec![b'-'; 16],
            requests: 0,
            written: 0,
        }
    }
}

/// A cached copy of a disk page. `dirty` is set when the copy has been
/// written and the disk has not. `used` is the time of the last access.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Page {
    value: u8,
    dirty: bool,
    used: usize,
}

/// Maps page numbers to cached pages. `next` is the page that a sequential
/// reader would ask for next, and `window` is the current number of pages to
/// read ahead.
struct Cache {
    disk: Disk,
    pages: BTreeMap<usize, Page>,
    capacity: usize,
    clock: usize,
    next: usize,
    window: usize,
}

impl Cache {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Cache {
        Cache {
            disk: Disk::new(),
            pages: BTreeMap::new(),
            capacity,
            clock: 0,
            next: 0,
            window: 0,
        }
    }
}

impl Cache {
    /// Returns the contents of a page. A page that is cached costs no disk
    /// request. For a page that is missing, `read` makes one request for a
    /// window of pages. The window doubles while the reads are sequential and
    /// returns to 1 page when they are not.
    fn read(&mut self, index: usize) -> u8 {
        if !self.pages.contains_key(&index) {
            if index == self.next {
                self.window = (2 * self.window.max(1)).min(MAX_WINDOW);
            } else {
                self.window = 1;
            }

            self.load(index, self.window);
        }

        self.next = index + 1;

        self.touch(index).value
    }

    /// Reads `count` pages starting at `index` from the disk in one request.
    fn load(&mut self, index: usize, count: usize) {
        self.disk.requests += 1;

        for i in index..(index + count).min(self.disk.pages.len()) {
            if !self.pages.contains_key(&i) {
                let value = self.disk.pages[i];

                self.insert(i, value);
            }
        }
    }

    /// Records an access to a page and returns the page. A page that is not
    /// cached is created empty.
    fn touch(&mut self, index: usize) -> &mut Page {
        self.clock += 1;

        let page = self.pages.entry(index).or_default();
        page.used = self.clock;

        page
    }
}

impl Cache {
    /// Changes a page in the cache and marks it dirty. It makes no disk
    /// request.
    fn write(&mut self, index: usize, value: u8) {
        if !self.pages.contains_key(&index) {
            self.insert(index, 0);
        }

        let page = self.touch(index);
        page.value = value;
        page.dirty = true;
    }

    /// Writes every dirty page to the disk and returns the number written.
    fn sync(&mut self) -> usize {
        let before = self.disk.written;

        for (&index, page) in &mut self.pages {
            clean(&mut self.disk, index, page);
        }

        self.disk.written - before
    }
}

/// Writes one page to the disk if it is dirty.
fn clean(disk: &mut Disk, index: usize, page: &mut Page) {
    if page.dirty {
        disk.pages[index] = page.value;
        disk.written += 1;
        page.dirty = false;
    }
}

impl Cache {
    /// Adds a page to the cache. When the cache is full it first evicts the
    /// page whose last access is the oldest. A dirty page is written to the
    /// disk before it is removed.
    fn insert(&mut self, index: usize, value: u8) {
        if self.pages.len() == self.capacity {
            let oldest = self
                .pages
                .iter()
                .min_by_key(|(_, page)| page.used)
                .map(|(&index, _)| index);

            if let Some(oldest) = oldest
                && let Some(mut page) = self.pages.remove(&oldest)
            {
                clean(&mut self.disk, oldest, &mut page);
            }
        }

        self.clock += 1;

        let page = Page {
            value,
            dirty: false,
            used: self.clock,
        };

        self.pages.insert(index, page);
    }

    /// Returns the numbers of the cached pages in increasing order.
    fn held(&self) -> Vec<usize> {
        self.pages.keys().copied().collect()
    }
}

/// Reads the given pages through a new cache and returns the number of disk
/// requests.
fn requests(order: impl Iterator<Item = usize>) -> usize {
    let mut cache = Cache::new(32);

    for index in order {
        cache.read(index);
    }

    cache.disk.requests
}

/// Formats page numbers the way Go prints a slice.
fn list(pages: &[usize]) -> String {
    let words: Vec<String> = pages.iter().map(usize::to_string).collect();

    format!("[{}]", words.join(" "))
}

fn main() {
    println!("16 pages read in order: {} disk requests", requests(0..16));
    println!(
        "16 pages read in reverse order: {} disk requests",
        requests((0..16).rev())
    );
    println!(
        "16 pages read in order, 2 times: {} disk requests",
        requests((0..16).chain(0..16))
    );

    let mut cache = Cache::new(4);

    cache.write(3, b'x');
    println!(
        "write of x to page 3: {} pages written, the disk holds {}",
        cache.disk.written,
        char::from(cache.disk.pages[3])
    );

    let written = cache.sync();
    println!(
        "sync: {written} page written, the disk holds {}",
        char::from(cache.disk.pages[3])
    );

    for index in [2, 1, 0, 3] {
        cache.read(index);
    }

    cache.read(8);
    println!(
        "capacity 4, pages 3 2 1 0 3 used, then page 8: cache holds {}",
        list(&cache.held())
    );

    cache.write(1, b'y');

    for index in [0, 3, 8, 12] {
        cache.read(index);
    }

    println!(
        "write of y to page 1, then pages 0 3 8 12 used: cache holds {}, the disk holds {}",
        list(&cache.held()),
        char::from(cache.disk.pages[1])
    );
}

Summary

  • File contents are cached in memory, page by page. read and write copy between the process and the cache.
  • A write marks the page dirty and returns. The disk is updated later by writeback, or when the program calls fsync.
  • On a sequential read, the kernel loads a window of pages per disk request and doubles the window as the read continues.
  • A clean page can be discarded at once. A dirty page is written to the disk before it is evicted.
  • When memory is needed, pages that have not been used recently are evicted first.
  • posix_fadvise adjusts readahead and can ask the kernel to drop a file’s clean pages.

References

  • posix_fadvise(2), fsync(2) and fincore(1), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/posix_fadvise.2.html
  • R. Love, Linux Kernel Development, 3rd edition, Addison-Wesley, 2010, chapter 16.
  • mm/filemap.c, mm/readahead.c and fs/fs-writeback.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/mm/readahead.c

Event Loops and epoll

An event loop is a program structure in which a single thread waits for activity on many file descriptors at once and handles each descriptor when it is ready. The kernel mechanism behind it on Linux is epoll: the program registers descriptors with an epoll instance and then asks which of them are ready. Network servers, the Go runtime and Rust’s async runtimes are all built on this mechanism.

In this chapter, we will learn how epoll finds the ready descriptors without examining all of them. We will first measure its behaviour on pipes with epollfacts. Then we will write eventloop, a model of the interest list and the ready list, check it against the measurements, and run an event loop on it.

This chapter covers

  • blocking and non-blocking I/O, and why a blocking read on each descriptor does not scale
  • the 3 calls of epoll, and the structure of a server built on them
  • the path from arriving data to the return of epoll_wait
  • the kernel structures: struct eventpoll and struct epitem
  • the interest list and the ready list of an epoll instance
  • why the cost of a wait depends on the number of ready descriptors
  • level-triggered and edge-triggered registrations
  • how a closed peer is reported
  • the structure of an event loop
  • how the Go runtime and Rust’s async runtimes use epoll
  • how to inspect the registrations of a running process

Blocking and readiness

By default a read on a pipe or a socket blocks: if no data is available, the kernel puts the calling thread to sleep until some arrives (chapter 1). A thread that is asleep in a read on 1 descriptor cannot notice that another descriptor has data.

A descriptor can be switched to non-blocking mode with the flag O_NONBLOCK. A read that would have to wait then returns the error EAGAIN immediately. A program could call read on each of its descriptors in a loop and skip those that return EAGAIN, and it would consume a whole CPU doing nothing. What is needed is a single call that sleeps until any of a set of descriptors is ready, meaning that a read or a write on it would not block. That call is the subject of this chapter.

The problem

A server with 10000 connections has to respond to whichever connection sends data next. A blocking read waits on 1 descriptor. The alternatives each have a cost.

ApproachCost
a thread per connection, each blocked in reada stack and a scheduler entry for every connection, and a context switch for every message
select or poll with the full list of descriptorsthe kernel examines every descriptor on every call, including the idle ones
epollthe kernel maintains the list of ready descriptors; a call returns that list

With select and poll, the program passes all its descriptors on each call, and the kernel checks each one. The work per call is proportional to the number of descriptors registered. On a server most connections are idle at any moment, so most of that work finds nothing.

epoll separates registration from waiting. The program registers a descriptor once, with epoll_ctl. From then on the kernel itself records when the descriptor becomes ready. epoll_wait returns the recorded descriptors, and its work is proportional to the number that are ready.

The ready list is filled at the moment of the event. In chapter 1 a write to a pipe woke the readers sleeping on the pipe’s wait queue. Registering a descriptor with epoll adds an entry to that same wait queue, and the entry’s wake-up function puts the registration on the ready list. The writer does this work as part of its write.

The interface

epoll consists of 3 system calls.

CallPurpose
epoll_create1(flags)creates an epoll instance and returns a descriptor for it
epoll_ctl(epfd, op, fd, &event)adds, changes or removes the registration of fd
epoll_wait(epfd, events, max, timeout)sleeps until a registered descriptor is ready, and returns up to max events

A registration and an event are both a struct epoll_event. This is the definition in include/uapi/linux/eventpoll.h.

struct epoll_event {
        __poll_t events;       /* which conditions: EPOLLIN, EPOLLOUT, ... */
        __u64 data;            /* chosen by the program, returned with each event */
};
Bit in eventsMeaning
EPOLLINa read would not block: data is available, or the peer has closed
EPOLLOUTa write would not block: there is room in the send buffer
EPOLLHUP, EPOLLERRthe peer has closed, or an error is pending; always reported, without being requested
EPOLLETmake the registration edge-triggered, explained below
EPOLLONESHOTreport the descriptor once, then disable the registration until it is re-armed

data is how the program recognises an event. The kernel does not interpret it. A program stores the descriptor number or a pointer to its own record of the connection, and gets it back in epoll_wait.

A server on a single thread uses the calls in the following pattern.

The descriptors are in non-blocking mode. epoll reports that a descriptor is ready, and the non-blocking mode guarantees that the handler does not sleep if the situation has changed by the time it reads.

From arriving data to epoll_wait

The claim that epoll_wait does work proportional to the number of ready descriptors rests on 1 mechanism, which we follow for a registered descriptor 7.

  1. At registration, epoll_ctl creates an item for descriptor 7 and adds an entry to the wait queue of the file behind it. A wait queue is the list of sleepers that the file wakes when its state changes (chapter 1). The entry that epoll adds is a function in place of a sleeping thread.
  2. Later, data arrives for descriptor 7. The code that delivers the data, a write by another process or the network stack, wakes the wait queue of the file.
  3. Waking the queue calls the function, ep_poll_callback. It puts the item for descriptor 7 on the ready list of the epoll instance.
  4. It then wakes any thread that is asleep in epoll_wait on this instance.
  5. epoll_wait takes the items from the ready list, asks each file once more whether it is really ready, and copies the events to the program.

No step searches the registered descriptors. The descriptor announces itself at the moment it becomes ready.

The kernel’s structures

An epoll instance is a struct eventpoll, and each registration is a struct epitem. Both are defined in fs/eventpoll.c of Linux 5.15. These are the fields we use.

struct eventpoll {
        struct mutex mtx;                      /* held by epoll_ctl and epoll_wait */
        wait_queue_head_t wq;                  /* threads asleep in epoll_wait */
        struct list_head rdllist;              /* the ready list */
        struct rb_root_cached rbr;             /* the interest list: a tree of epitems */
        /* ... */
};

struct epitem {
        struct rb_node rbn;                    /* its node in rbr */
        struct list_head rdllink;              /* its link in rdllist */
        struct epoll_filefd ffd;               /* the file and descriptor it watches */
        struct eppoll_entry *pwqlist;          /* its entry on the file's wait queue */
        struct eventpoll *ep;                  /* the instance it belongs to */
        struct epoll_event event;              /* the events asked for, and data */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
rbrThe interest list. It is a red-black tree keyed by file and descriptor, so that epoll_ctl finds an existing registration quickly.
rdllistThe ready list: a linked list of the items whose files have reported activity.
wqThe threads that are asleep in epoll_wait. Step 4 wakes them.
rdllinkAn item is on the ready list when this link is in use, which also keeps an item from being added a second time.
pwqlistThe entry of step 1.
eventThe struct epoll_event given at registration.

An epoll instance is itself a file, and the kernel shows its registrations in /proc. This is the session manager of our user account, pid 1203, whose descriptor 4 is an epoll instance:

$ ls -l /proc/1203/fd | grep eventpoll
4 -> anon_inode:[eventpoll]
$ cat /proc/1203/fdinfo/4
pos:	0
flags:	02000002
tfd:       29 events:       19 data:     aaaaf18e8be0  pos:0 ino:b06c sdev:8
tfd:       35 events:       19 data:     aaaaf1953a90  pos:0 ino:b06e sdev:8
tfd:       15 events:       19 data:     aaaaf173f750  pos:0 ino:b049 sdev:8

Each tfd line is an item of the interest list: the descriptor it watches, the events in hexadecimal, and data. 19 is EPOLLIN (1), EPOLLERR (8) and EPOLLHUP (0x10) together. The data values are addresses in the memory of the program, which stored a pointer to its own record of each descriptor.

Measuring epoll

epollfacts uses golang.org/x/sys/unix in Go and the nix crate with the event and fs features in Rust.

$ cargo new epollfacts
$ cargo add -p epollfacts nix --features event,fs

watch creates an epoll instance and a number of pipes, and registers the read end of each pipe for the event EPOLLIN, readability. A registration carries a value chosen by the program, here the number of the pipe, which the kernel returns with each event. ready calls epoll_wait with a timeout of 0, so that it reports the current state without blocking.

Listing 9.1 The imports of epollfacts, in Go. code/go/epollfacts/main.go

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)

Listing 9.2 The imports of epollfacts, in Rust. code/rust/epollfacts/src/main.rs

use std::os::fd::OwnedFd;

use nix::fcntl::OFlag;
use nix::sys::epoll::{Epoll, EpollCreateFlags, EpollEvent, EpollFlags, EpollTimeout};
use nix::unistd::{pipe2, read, write};

Listing 9.3 Creating an epoll instance and registering pipes, in Go. code/go/epollfacts/main.go

// A pipe is the pair of descriptors of one pipe.
type pipe struct {
	reader, writer int
}

// watch creates an epoll instance and n pipes, and registers the read end of
// every pipe for readability with the given extra flags. The number of the
// pipe is stored in the registration and comes back with each event.
func watch(n int, flags uint32) (int, []pipe, error) {
	epoll, err := unix.EpollCreate1(unix.EPOLL_CLOEXEC)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	pipes := make([]pipe, n)

	for i := range pipes {
		var fds [2]int

		if err := unix.Pipe2(fds[:], unix.O_CLOEXEC); err != nil {
			return 0, nil, err
		}

		pipes[i] = pipe{reader: fds[0], writer: fds[1]}
		event := unix.EpollEvent{Events: unix.EPOLLIN | flags, Fd: int32(i)}

		if err := unix.EpollCtl(epoll, unix.EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fds[0], &event); err != nil {
			return 0, nil, err
		}
	}

	return epoll, pipes, nil
}

// ready returns the events that are ready now. A timeout of 0 makes the
// wait return at once.
func ready(epoll int) ([]unix.EpollEvent, error) {
	events := make([]unix.EpollEvent, 16)
	n, err := unix.EpollWait(epoll, events, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return events[:n], nil
}

// release closes an epoll instance and its pipes.
func release(epoll int, pipes []pipe) {
	unix.Close(epoll)

	for _, p := range pipes {
		unix.Close(p.reader)
		unix.Close(p.writer)
	}
}

Listing 9.4 Creating an epoll instance and registering pipes, in Rust. code/rust/epollfacts/src/main.rs

/// The pair of descriptors of one pipe. The write end is an `Option` so that
/// an experiment can close it.
struct Pipe {
    reader: OwnedFd,
    writer: Option<OwnedFd>,
}

/// Creates an epoll instance and `n` pipes, and registers the read end of
/// every pipe for readability with the given extra flags. The number of the
/// pipe is stored in the registration and comes back with each event.
fn watch(n: usize, flags: EpollFlags) -> nix::Result<(Epoll, Vec<Pipe>)> {
    let epoll = Epoll::new(EpollCreateFlags::EPOLL_CLOEXEC)?;
    let mut pipes = Vec::with_capacity(n);

    for i in 0..n {
        let (reader, writer) = pipe2(OFlag::O_CLOEXEC)?;

        epoll.add(
            &reader,
            EpollEvent::new(EpollFlags::EPOLLIN | flags, i as u64),
        )?;

        pipes.push(Pipe {
            reader,
            writer: Some(writer),
        });
    }

    Ok((epoll, pipes))
}

/// Returns the events that are ready now. A timeout of 0 makes the wait
/// return at once.
fn ready(epoll: &Epoll) -> nix::Result<Vec<EpollEvent>> {
    let mut events = [EpollEvent::empty(); 16];
    let n = epoll.wait(&mut events, EpollTimeout::ZERO)?;

    Ok(events[..n].to_vec())
}

/// Writes "hello" to a pipe whose write end is open.
fn send(pipe: &Pipe) -> nix::Result<()> {
    if let Some(writer) = &pipe.writer {
        write(writer, b"hello")?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

level uses the default kind of registration, called level-triggered. It waits before any write, after a write to pipe 1, a second time without reading the data, after reading it, and after closing the write end.

Listing 9.5 Level-triggered events, in Go. code/go/epollfacts/main.go

// level registers 3 pipes level-triggered and waits before a write, after a
// write, again without reading, and after reading.
func level() error {
	epoll, pipes, err := watch(3, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer release(epoll, pipes)

	events, err := ready(epoll)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("3 pipes registered, none written: %d event(s)\n", len(events))

	if _, err := unix.Write(pipes[1].writer, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil || len(events) != 1 {
		return fmt.Errorf("wait after a write: %d events, %v", len(events), err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe %d\n", events[0].Fd)

	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("level-triggered, data not read, wait again: %d event(s)\n", len(events))

	if _, err := unix.Read(pipes[1].reader, make([]byte, 16)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after reading the data: %d event(s)\n", len(events))

	unix.Close(pipes[1].writer)
	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil || len(events) != 1 {
		return fmt.Errorf("wait after a close: %d events, %v", len(events), err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("write end of pipe 1 closed: event has EPOLLHUP %v\n", events[0].Events&unix.EPOLLHUP != 0)

	return nil
}

Listing 9.6 Level-triggered events, in Rust. code/rust/epollfacts/src/main.rs

/// Registers 3 pipes level-triggered and waits before a write, after a write,
/// again without reading, and after reading.
fn level() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (epoll, mut pipes) = watch(3, EpollFlags::empty())?;

    println!(
        "3 pipes registered, none written: {} event(s)",
        ready(&epoll)?.len()
    );

    send(&pipes[1])?;

    if let [event] = ready(&epoll)?.as_slice() {
        println!("write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe {}", event.data());
    }

    println!(
        "level-triggered, data not read, wait again: {} event(s)",
        ready(&epoll)?.len()
    );

    read(&pipes[1].reader, &mut [0u8; 16])?;
    println!("after reading the data: {} event(s)", ready(&epoll)?.len());

    pipes[1].writer = None;

    if let [event] = ready(&epoll)?.as_slice() {
        println!(
            "write end of pipe 1 closed: event has EPOLLHUP {}",
            event.events().contains(EpollFlags::EPOLLHUP)
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}

edge registers a pipe with the flag EPOLLET, edge-triggered, and waits 2 times after a write and again after a further write.

Listing 9.7 Edge-triggered events, in Go. code/go/epollfacts/main.go

// edge registers a pipe edge-triggered and waits 2 times after one write,
// and once more after a second write.
func edge() error {
	epoll, pipes, err := watch(1, unix.EPOLLET)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer release(epoll, pipes)

	var counts [3]int

	for i := range counts {
		if i != 1 {
			if _, err := unix.Write(pipes[0].writer, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		events, err := ready(epoll)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		counts[i] = len(events)
	}

	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, data not read: wait %d event(s), wait again %d event(s)\n", counts[0], counts[1])
	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, after another write: %d event(s)\n", counts[2])

	return nil
}

Listing 9.8 Edge-triggered events, in Rust. code/rust/epollfacts/src/main.rs

/// Registers a pipe edge-triggered and waits 2 times after one write, and
/// once more after a second write.
fn edge() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (epoll, pipes) = watch(1, EpollFlags::EPOLLET)?;
    let mut counts = [0; 3];

    for (i, count) in counts.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        if i != 1 {
            send(&pipes[0])?;
        }

        *count = ready(&epoll)?.len();
    }

    println!(
        "edge-triggered, data not read: wait {} event(s), wait again {} event(s)",
        counts[0], counts[1]
    );
    println!(
        "edge-triggered, after another write: {} event(s)",
        counts[2]
    );

    Ok(())
}

3 pipes registered, none written: 0 event(s)
write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe 1
level-triggered, data not read, wait again: 1 event(s)
after reading the data: 0 event(s)
write end of pipe 1 closed: event has EPOLLHUP true
edge-triggered, data not read: wait 1 event(s), wait again 0 event(s)

OutputConclusion
0 events with nothing writtenA wait reports only descriptors that are ready.
1 event, for pipe 1The event carries the value stored at registration, which identifies the descriptor.
level-triggered: 1 event againA level-triggered descriptor is reported for as long as data remains.
0 events after readingReading the data ends the condition.
EPOLLHUP after the write end is closedThe end of the stream is reported as an event, without being requested.
edge-triggered: 1 event, then 0An edge-triggered descriptor is reported when data arrives and stays silent afterwards, with the data still unread.
1 event after another writeNew data produces a new event.
1000 registered, 1 eventThe wait returns the ready descriptor and no others.

The choice has a consequence for the handler. With a level-triggered registration, a handler may read part of the data and return; the descriptor is reported again. With an edge-triggered registration, a handler has to read until read returns EAGAIN, because no further event will announce the data it leaves behind. Edge-triggered registrations save repeated reports and are used by runtimes that follow this rule strictly.

Modelling epoll

Low-level design: eventloop

TypeFieldsMeaning
pipebuffered, registered, edge, queuedthe bytes waiting; the registration; whether the pipe is on the ready list
kernelpipes, ready, examinedthe pipes; the ready list in order of arrival; a counter of registrations examined
OperationBehaviour
register(index, edge)adds a pipe to the interest list; queues it if it is already readable
write(index, n)adds bytes; puts a registered pipe on the ready list
wait()empties the ready list; returns the pipes that are still readable; queues the level-triggered ones again
scan()examines every registered pipe, as select and poll do
turn(handle)waits, then calls the handler for each ready pipe

A pipe is reduced to a count of buffered bytes. The queued flag keeps a pipe from appearing on the ready list more than once.

Listing 9.11 The imports of eventloop, in Go. code/go/eventloop/main.go

import "fmt"

Listing 9.12 Pipes, the interest list and the ready list, in Go. code/go/eventloop/main.go

// A pipe is the read end of a pipe as epoll sees it: the bytes waiting to be
// read, and its registration. queued is set while the pipe is on the ready
// list.
type pipe struct {
	buffered   int
	registered bool
	edge       bool
	queued     bool
}

// A kernel holds the pipes and one epoll instance. The registered pipes are
// the interest list. ready is the ready list, in the order in which the
// pipes became ready. examined counts the registrations that waits and scans
// have looked at.
type kernel struct {
	pipes    []pipe
	ready    []int
	examined int
}

func newKernel(pipes int) *kernel {
	return &kernel{pipes: make([]pipe, pipes)}
}

Listing 9.13 Pipes, the interest list and the ready list, in Rust. code/rust/eventloop/src/main.rs

/// The read end of a pipe as epoll sees it: the bytes waiting to be read, and
/// its registration. `queued` is set while the pipe is on the ready list.
#[derive(Clone, Default)]
struct Pipe {
    buffered: usize,
    registered: bool,
    edge: bool,
    queued: bool,
}

/// Holds the pipes and one epoll instance. The registered pipes are the
/// interest list. `ready` is the ready list, in the order in which the pipes
/// became ready. `examined` counts the registrations that waits and scans
/// have looked at.
struct Kernel {
    pipes: Vec<Pipe>,
    ready: Vec<usize>,
    examined: usize,
}

impl Kernel {
    fn new(pipes: usize) -> Kernel {
        Kernel {
            pipes: vec![Pipe::default(); pipes],
            ready: Vec::new(),
            examined: 0,
        }
    }
}

write is where a pipe becomes ready, and it is write that queues the pipe. No part of the model searches for ready pipes.

Listing 9.14 Registering, and queuing on a write, in Go. code/go/eventloop/main.go

// register adds a pipe to the interest list. A pipe that is already
// readable goes on the ready list at once.
func (k *kernel) register(index int, edge bool) {
	p := &k.pipes[index]
	p.registered, p.edge = true, edge

	if p.buffered > 0 {
		k.enqueue(index)
	}
}

// enqueue puts a pipe on the ready list unless it is already there.
func (k *kernel) enqueue(index int) {
	if p := &k.pipes[index]; !p.queued {
		p.queued = true
		k.ready = append(k.ready, index)
	}
}

// write adds bytes to a pipe. This is the moment the pipe becomes ready, and
// the writer puts it on the ready list.
func (k *kernel) write(index, n int) {
	k.pipes[index].buffered += n

	if k.pipes[index].registered {
		k.enqueue(index)
	}
}

// read removes up to n bytes from a pipe and returns the number removed.
func (k *kernel) read(index, n int) int {
	n = min(n, k.pipes[index].buffered)
	k.pipes[index].buffered -= n

	return n
}

Listing 9.15 Registering, and queuing on a write, in Rust. code/rust/eventloop/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Adds a pipe to the interest list. A pipe that is already readable goes
    /// on the ready list at once.
    fn register(&mut self, index: usize, edge: bool) {
        let pipe = &mut self.pipes[index];

        pipe.registered = true;
        pipe.edge = edge;

        if pipe.buffered > 0 {
            self.enqueue(index);
        }
    }

    /// Puts a pipe on the ready list unless it is already there.
    fn enqueue(&mut self, index: usize) {
        if !self.pipes[index].queued {
            self.pipes[index].queued = true;
            self.ready.push(index);
        }
    }

    /// Adds bytes to a pipe. This is the moment the pipe becomes ready, and
    /// the writer puts it on the ready list.
    fn write(&mut self, index: usize, n: usize) {
        self.pipes[index].buffered += n;

        if self.pipes[index].registered {
            self.enqueue(index);
        }
    }

    /// Removes up to `n` bytes from a pipe and returns the number removed.
    fn read(&mut self, index: usize, n: usize) -> usize {
        let n = n.min(self.pipes[index].buffered);
        self.pipes[index].buffered -= n;

        n
    }
}

wait takes the ready list and checks each entry again, since the data may have been read in the meantime. The difference between the kinds of registration is a single statement: a level-triggered pipe that is reported is queued again, and an edge-triggered pipe is left off the list until the next write queues it.

Listing 9.16 Waiting, and scanning for comparison, in Go. code/go/eventloop/main.go

// wait empties the ready list and returns the pipes on it that are still
// readable. A level-triggered pipe that is reported goes back on the list,
// so the next wait checks it again. An edge-triggered pipe does not, and is
// reported again only after another write.
func (k *kernel) wait() []int {
	queued := k.ready
	k.ready = nil

	var events []int

	for _, index := range queued {
		p := &k.pipes[index]
		p.queued = false
		k.examined++

		if p.buffered == 0 {
			continue
		}

		events = append(events, index)

		if !p.edge {
			k.enqueue(index)
		}
	}

	return events
}

// scan is the method of select and poll: it examines every registered pipe
// on every call.
func (k *kernel) scan() []int {
	var events []int

	for index, p := range k.pipes {
		if !p.registered {
			continue
		}

		k.examined++

		if p.buffered > 0 {
			events = append(events, index)
		}
	}

	return events
}

Listing 9.17 Waiting, and scanning for comparison, in Rust. code/rust/eventloop/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Empties the ready list and returns the pipes on it that are still
    /// readable. A level-triggered pipe that is reported goes back on the
    /// list, so the next wait checks it again. An edge-triggered pipe does
    /// not, and is reported again only after another write.
    fn wait(&mut self) -> Vec<usize> {
        let queued = std::mem::take(&mut self.ready);
        let mut events = Vec::new();

        for index in queued {
            self.pipes[index].queued = false;
            self.examined += 1;

            if self.pipes[index].buffered == 0 {
                continue;
            }

            events.push(index);

            if !self.pipes[index].edge {
                self.enqueue(index);
            }
        }

        events
    }

    /// The method of select and poll: it examines every registered pipe on
    /// every call.
    fn scan(&mut self) -> Vec<usize> {
        let mut events = Vec::new();

        for (index, pipe) in self.pipes.iter().enumerate() {
            if !pipe.registered {
                continue;
            }

            self.examined += 1;

            if pipe.buffered > 0 {
                events.push(index);
            }
        }

        events
    }
}

// level repeats the level-triggered measurement of epollfacts.

// edge repeats the edge-triggered measurement.
func edge() {
	k := newKernel(1)
	k.register(0, true)

	k.write(0, 5)
	first, second := len(k.wait()), len(k.wait())
	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, data not read: wait %d event(s), wait again %d event(s)\n", first, second)

// many compares the work of a wait with the work of a scan when 1000 pipes
// are registered and 1 is ready.
func many() {
	k := newKernel(1000)

	for index := range k.pipes {
		k.register(index, false)
	}

	k.write(700, 5)

	if events := k.wait(); len(events) == 1 {
		fmt.Printf("1000 pipes registered, pipe 700 written: 1 event, for pipe %d\n", events[0])
	}

	byWait := k.examined
	k.scan()
	fmt.Printf("registrations examined: %d by the wait, %d by a scan\n", byWait, k.examined-byWait)

The loop

An event loop repeats 2 steps: wait for events, then run the handler of each ready descriptor. A handler must return quickly and must not block, because every other descriptor waits while it runs.

Listing 9.20 An event loop on the model, in Go. code/go/eventloop/main.go

// turn is one iteration of an event loop: wait for ready pipes, then run the
// handler for each. It returns the pipes it handled.
func (k *kernel) turn(handle func(k *kernel, index int)) []int {
	events := k.wait()

	for _, index := range events {
		handle(k, index)
	}

	return events
}

// loop registers 4 pipes, writes to 2 of them, and runs an event loop whose
// handler reads at most 4 bytes for each event.
func loop() {
	k := newKernel(4)

	for index := range k.pipes {
		k.register(index, false)
	}

	k.write(2, 5)
	k.write(0, 3)

	handle := func(k *kernel, index int) { k.read(index, 4) }

	fmt.Printf("event loop: turn 1 handles %v, turn 2 handles %v, turn 3 handles %v\n",
		k.turn(handle), k.turn(handle), k.turn(handle))
}

Listing 9.21 An event loop on the model, in Rust. code/rust/eventloop/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// One iteration of an event loop: wait for ready pipes, then run the
    /// handler for each. Returns the pipes it handled.
    fn turn(&mut self, handle: fn(&mut Kernel, usize)) -> Vec<usize> {
        let events = self.wait();

        for &index in &events {
            handle(self, index);
        }

        events
    }
}

/// Formats pipe numbers the way Go prints a slice.
fn list(pipes: &[usize]) -> String {
    let words: Vec<String> = pipes.iter().map(usize::to_string).collect();

    format!("[{}]", words.join(" "))
}

/// Registers 4 pipes, writes to 2 of them, and runs an event loop whose
/// handler reads at most 4 bytes for each event.
fn event_loop() {
    let mut kernel = Kernel::new(4);

    for index in 0..4 {
        kernel.register(index, false);
    }

    kernel.write(2, 5);
    kernel.write(0, 3);

    let handle = |kernel: &mut Kernel, index: usize| {
        kernel.read(index, 4);
    };

    let turns = [
        kernel.turn(handle),
        kernel.turn(handle),
        kernel.turn(handle),
    ];

    println!(
        "event loop: turn 1 handles {}, turn 2 handles {}, turn 3 handles {}",
        list(&turns[0]),
        list(&turns[1]),
        list(&turns[2])
    );
}
