LineWhat it shows
lines 1 to 7The model gives the event counts that epollfacts measured.
1 examined by the wait, 1000 by a scanThe wait looked at the ready list. A scan looks at every registration.
turn 1 handles [2 0]Events are returned in the order the pipes became ready.
turn 2 handles [2]The handler read 4 of the 5 bytes of pipe 2, and a level-triggered pipe with data left is reported again.
turn 3 handles []Nothing is ready. A real loop would sleep in epoll_wait here.

Correspondence with the kernel source. The model corresponds to fs/eventpoll.c. An epoll instance is struct eventpoll, with the interest list in the red-black tree rbr and the ready list in rdllist. A registration is struct epitem. ep_poll_callback is the wake-up function that queues an item when its file becomes ready, and ep_send_events is the loop of wait: it polls each queued item again, copies the event to the program, and adds the item back to rdllist unless EPOLLET is set.

A handler must return quickly. Every other descriptor waits while it runs.

Epoll inside language runtimes

Go and Rust programs rarely call epoll directly, and nearly all of their network I/O goes through it.

The Go runtime has a component called the netpoller. Every socket a Go program opens is put in non-blocking mode and registered, edge-triggered, with a single epoll instance. When a goroutine calls Read and the kernel answers EAGAIN, the runtime parks the goroutine, which costs no thread, and runs another. A wake-up from epoll makes the parked goroutine runnable again. The code reads as if it blocked, and underneath it is the event loop of this chapter.

In Rust, an async runtime such as Tokio does the same for futures. A future that cannot make progress registers its descriptor and returns Pending. The runtime’s reactor calls epoll_wait, and wakes the task that owns a descriptor when its event arrives.

Inspecting epoll on a live system

CommandShows
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | grep eventpollthe epoll instances of a process
cat /proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<n>for an epoll descriptor: every registration, with its events and data
strace -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl -p <pid>the registrations a process makes and the events it receives
cat /proc/sys/fs/epoll/max_user_watchesthe number of registrations a user may hold: 3563520 here

The complete programs

Listing 9.22 The complete epollfacts, in Go. code/go/epollfacts/main.go

// Command epollfacts measures epoll with pipes: which descriptors a wait
// reports, how level-triggered and edge-triggered registrations differ, how
// a closed peer is reported, and how many events a wait returns when 1000
// descriptors are registered and 1 is ready.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./epollfacts
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


// A pipe is the pair of descriptors of one pipe.
type pipe struct {
	reader, writer int
}

// watch creates an epoll instance and n pipes, and registers the read end of
// every pipe for readability with the given extra flags. The number of the
// pipe is stored in the registration and comes back with each event.
func watch(n int, flags uint32) (int, []pipe, error) {
	epoll, err := unix.EpollCreate1(unix.EPOLL_CLOEXEC)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	pipes := make([]pipe, n)

	for i := range pipes {
		var fds [2]int

		if err := unix.Pipe2(fds[:], unix.O_CLOEXEC); err != nil {
			return 0, nil, err
		}

		pipes[i] = pipe{reader: fds[0], writer: fds[1]}
		event := unix.EpollEvent{Events: unix.EPOLLIN | flags, Fd: int32(i)}

		if err := unix.EpollCtl(epoll, unix.EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fds[0], &event); err != nil {
			return 0, nil, err
		}
	}

	return epoll, pipes, nil
}

// ready returns the events that are ready now. A timeout of 0 makes the
// wait return at once.
func ready(epoll int) ([]unix.EpollEvent, error) {
	events := make([]unix.EpollEvent, 16)
	n, err := unix.EpollWait(epoll, events, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return events[:n], nil
}

// release closes an epoll instance and its pipes.
func release(epoll int, pipes []pipe) {
	unix.Close(epoll)

	for _, p := range pipes {
		unix.Close(p.reader)
		unix.Close(p.writer)
	}
}


// level registers 3 pipes level-triggered and waits before a write, after a
// write, again without reading, and after reading.
func level() error {
	epoll, pipes, err := watch(3, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer release(epoll, pipes)

	events, err := ready(epoll)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("3 pipes registered, none written: %d event(s)\n", len(events))

	if _, err := unix.Write(pipes[1].writer, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil || len(events) != 1 {
		return fmt.Errorf("wait after a write: %d events, %v", len(events), err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe %d\n", events[0].Fd)

	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("level-triggered, data not read, wait again: %d event(s)\n", len(events))

	if _, err := unix.Read(pipes[1].reader, make([]byte, 16)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("after reading the data: %d event(s)\n", len(events))

	unix.Close(pipes[1].writer)
	events, err = ready(epoll)

	if err != nil || len(events) != 1 {
		return fmt.Errorf("wait after a close: %d events, %v", len(events), err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("write end of pipe 1 closed: event has EPOLLHUP %v\n", events[0].Events&unix.EPOLLHUP != 0)

	return nil
}


// edge registers a pipe edge-triggered and waits 2 times after one write,
// and once more after a second write.
func edge() error {
	epoll, pipes, err := watch(1, unix.EPOLLET)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer release(epoll, pipes)

	var counts [3]int

	for i := range counts {
		if i != 1 {
			if _, err := unix.Write(pipes[0].writer, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		events, err := ready(epoll)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		counts[i] = len(events)
	}

	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, data not read: wait %d event(s), wait again %d event(s)\n", counts[0], counts[1])
	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, after another write: %d event(s)\n", counts[2])

	return nil
}


// many registers 1000 pipes and writes to 1 of them.
func many() error {
	epoll, pipes, err := watch(1000, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer release(epoll, pipes)

	if _, err := unix.Write(pipes[700].writer, []byte("hello")); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	events, err := ready(epoll)

	if err != nil || len(events) != 1 {
		return fmt.Errorf("wait with 1000 pipes: %d events, %v", len(events), err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("1000 pipes registered, pipe 700 written: 1 event, for pipe %d\n", events[0].Fd)

	return nil
}


func main() {
	for _, experiment := range []func() error{level, edge, many} {
		if err := experiment(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 9.23 The complete epollfacts, in Rust. code/rust/epollfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures epoll with pipes: which descriptors a wait reports, how
//! level-triggered and edge-triggered registrations differ, how a closed peer
//! is reported, and how many events a wait returns when 1000 descriptors are
//! registered and 1 is ready.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p epollfacts
//! ```

use std::os::fd::OwnedFd;

use nix::fcntl::OFlag;
use nix::sys::epoll::{Epoll, EpollCreateFlags, EpollEvent, EpollFlags, EpollTimeout};
use nix::unistd::{pipe2, read, write};

/// The pair of descriptors of one pipe. The write end is an `Option` so that
/// an experiment can close it.
struct Pipe {
    reader: OwnedFd,
    writer: Option<OwnedFd>,
}

/// Creates an epoll instance and `n` pipes, and registers the read end of
/// every pipe for readability with the given extra flags. The number of the
/// pipe is stored in the registration and comes back with each event.
fn watch(n: usize, flags: EpollFlags) -> nix::Result<(Epoll, Vec<Pipe>)> {
    let epoll = Epoll::new(EpollCreateFlags::EPOLL_CLOEXEC)?;
    let mut pipes = Vec::with_capacity(n);

    for i in 0..n {
        let (reader, writer) = pipe2(OFlag::O_CLOEXEC)?;

        epoll.add(
            &reader,
            EpollEvent::new(EpollFlags::EPOLLIN | flags, i as u64),
        )?;

        pipes.push(Pipe {
            reader,
            writer: Some(writer),
        });
    }

    Ok((epoll, pipes))
}

/// Returns the events that are ready now. A timeout of 0 makes the wait
/// return at once.
fn ready(epoll: &Epoll) -> nix::Result<Vec<EpollEvent>> {
    let mut events = [EpollEvent::empty(); 16];
    let n = epoll.wait(&mut events, EpollTimeout::ZERO)?;

    Ok(events[..n].to_vec())
}

/// Writes "hello" to a pipe whose write end is open.
fn send(pipe: &Pipe) -> nix::Result<()> {
    if let Some(writer) = &pipe.writer {
        write(writer, b"hello")?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Registers 3 pipes level-triggered and waits before a write, after a write,
/// again without reading, and after reading.
fn level() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (epoll, mut pipes) = watch(3, EpollFlags::empty())?;

    println!(
        "3 pipes registered, none written: {} event(s)",
        ready(&epoll)?.len()
    );

    send(&pipes[1])?;

    if let [event] = ready(&epoll)?.as_slice() {
        println!("write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe {}", event.data());
    }

    println!(
        "level-triggered, data not read, wait again: {} event(s)",
        ready(&epoll)?.len()
    );

    read(&pipes[1].reader, &mut [0u8; 16])?;
    println!("after reading the data: {} event(s)", ready(&epoll)?.len());

    pipes[1].writer = None;

    if let [event] = ready(&epoll)?.as_slice() {
        println!(
            "write end of pipe 1 closed: event has EPOLLHUP {}",
            event.events().contains(EpollFlags::EPOLLHUP)
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Registers a pipe edge-triggered and waits 2 times after one write, and
/// once more after a second write.
fn edge() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (epoll, pipes) = watch(1, EpollFlags::EPOLLET)?;
    let mut counts = [0; 3];

    for (i, count) in counts.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        if i != 1 {
            send(&pipes[0])?;
        }

        *count = ready(&epoll)?.len();
    }

    println!(
        "edge-triggered, data not read: wait {} event(s), wait again {} event(s)",
        counts[0], counts[1]
    );
    println!(
        "edge-triggered, after another write: {} event(s)",
        counts[2]
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Registers 1000 pipes and writes to 1 of them.
fn many() -> nix::Result<()> {
    let (epoll, pipes) = watch(1000, EpollFlags::empty())?;

    send(&pipes[700])?;

    if let [event] = ready(&epoll)?.as_slice() {
        println!(
            "1000 pipes registered, pipe 700 written: 1 event, for pipe {}",
            event.data()
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> nix::Result<()> {
    level()?;
    edge()?;
    many()
}

Listing 9.24 The complete eventloop, in Go. code/go/eventloop/main.go

// Command eventloop models epoll: an interest list of registered pipes, a
// ready list that a write fills, and a wait that examines only the ready
// list. It repeats the measurements of epollfacts on the model and then runs
// a small event loop on it.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./eventloop
package main

import "fmt"


// A pipe is the read end of a pipe as epoll sees it: the bytes waiting to be
// read, and its registration. queued is set while the pipe is on the ready
// list.
type pipe struct {
	buffered   int
	registered bool
	edge       bool
	queued     bool
}

// A kernel holds the pipes and one epoll instance. The registered pipes are
// the interest list. ready is the ready list, in the order in which the
// pipes became ready. examined counts the registrations that waits and scans
// have looked at.
type kernel struct {
	pipes    []pipe
	ready    []int
	examined int
}

func newKernel(pipes int) *kernel {
	return &kernel{pipes: make([]pipe, pipes)}
}


// register adds a pipe to the interest list. A pipe that is already
// readable goes on the ready list at once.
func (k *kernel) register(index int, edge bool) {
	p := &k.pipes[index]
	p.registered, p.edge = true, edge

	if p.buffered > 0 {
		k.enqueue(index)
	}
}

// enqueue puts a pipe on the ready list unless it is already there.
func (k *kernel) enqueue(index int) {
	if p := &k.pipes[index]; !p.queued {
		p.queued = true
		k.ready = append(k.ready, index)
	}
}

// write adds bytes to a pipe. This is the moment the pipe becomes ready, and
// the writer puts it on the ready list.
func (k *kernel) write(index, n int) {
	k.pipes[index].buffered += n

	if k.pipes[index].registered {
		k.enqueue(index)
	}
}

// read removes up to n bytes from a pipe and returns the number removed.
func (k *kernel) read(index, n int) int {
	n = min(n, k.pipes[index].buffered)
	k.pipes[index].buffered -= n

	return n
}


// wait empties the ready list and returns the pipes on it that are still
// readable. A level-triggered pipe that is reported goes back on the list,
// so the next wait checks it again. An edge-triggered pipe does not, and is
// reported again only after another write.
func (k *kernel) wait() []int {
	queued := k.ready
	k.ready = nil

	var events []int

	for _, index := range queued {
		p := &k.pipes[index]
		p.queued = false
		k.examined++

		if p.buffered == 0 {
			continue
		}

		events = append(events, index)

		if !p.edge {
			k.enqueue(index)
		}
	}

	return events
}

// scan is the method of select and poll: it examines every registered pipe
// on every call.
func (k *kernel) scan() []int {
	var events []int

	for index, p := range k.pipes {
		if !p.registered {
			continue
		}

		k.examined++

		if p.buffered > 0 {
			events = append(events, index)
		}
	}

	return events
}


// level repeats the level-triggered measurement of epollfacts.
func level() {
	k := newKernel(3)

	for index := range k.pipes {
		k.register(index, false)
	}

	fmt.Printf("3 pipes registered, none written: %d event(s)\n", len(k.wait()))

	k.write(1, 5)

	if events := k.wait(); len(events) == 1 {
		fmt.Printf("write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe %d\n", events[0])
	}

	fmt.Printf("level-triggered, data not read, wait again: %d event(s)\n", len(k.wait()))

	k.read(1, 16)
	fmt.Printf("after reading the data: %d event(s)\n", len(k.wait()))
}

// edge repeats the edge-triggered measurement.
func edge() {
	k := newKernel(1)
	k.register(0, true)

	k.write(0, 5)
	first, second := len(k.wait()), len(k.wait())
	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, data not read: wait %d event(s), wait again %d event(s)\n", first, second)

	k.write(0, 5)
	fmt.Printf("edge-triggered, after another write: %d event(s)\n", len(k.wait()))
}

// many compares the work of a wait with the work of a scan when 1000 pipes
// are registered and 1 is ready.
func many() {
	k := newKernel(1000)

	for index := range k.pipes {
		k.register(index, false)
	}

	k.write(700, 5)

	if events := k.wait(); len(events) == 1 {
		fmt.Printf("1000 pipes registered, pipe 700 written: 1 event, for pipe %d\n", events[0])
	}

	byWait := k.examined
	k.scan()
	fmt.Printf("registrations examined: %d by the wait, %d by a scan\n", byWait, k.examined-byWait)
}


// turn is one iteration of an event loop: wait for ready pipes, then run the
// handler for each. It returns the pipes it handled.
func (k *kernel) turn(handle func(k *kernel, index int)) []int {
	events := k.wait()

	for _, index := range events {
		handle(k, index)
	}

	return events
}

// loop registers 4 pipes, writes to 2 of them, and runs an event loop whose
// handler reads at most 4 bytes for each event.
func loop() {
	k := newKernel(4)

	for index := range k.pipes {
		k.register(index, false)
	}

	k.write(2, 5)
	k.write(0, 3)

	handle := func(k *kernel, index int) { k.read(index, 4) }

	fmt.Printf("event loop: turn 1 handles %v, turn 2 handles %v, turn 3 handles %v\n",
		k.turn(handle), k.turn(handle), k.turn(handle))
}


func main() {
	level()
	edge()
	many()
	loop()
}

Listing 9.25 The complete eventloop, in Rust. code/rust/eventloop/src/main.rs

//! Models epoll: an interest list of registered pipes, a ready list that a
//! write fills, and a wait that examines only the ready list. It repeats the
//! measurements of epollfacts on the model and then runs a small event loop
//! on it.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p eventloop
//! ```

/// The read end of a pipe as epoll sees it: the bytes waiting to be read, and
/// its registration. `queued` is set while the pipe is on the ready list.
#[derive(Clone, Default)]
struct Pipe {
    buffered: usize,
    registered: bool,
    edge: bool,
    queued: bool,
}

/// Holds the pipes and one epoll instance. The registered pipes are the
/// interest list. `ready` is the ready list, in the order in which the pipes
/// became ready. `examined` counts the registrations that waits and scans
/// have looked at.
struct Kernel {
    pipes: Vec<Pipe>,
    ready: Vec<usize>,
    examined: usize,
}

impl Kernel {
    fn new(pipes: usize) -> Kernel {
        Kernel {
            pipes: vec![Pipe::default(); pipes],
            ready: Vec::new(),
            examined: 0,
        }
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Adds a pipe to the interest list. A pipe that is already readable goes
    /// on the ready list at once.
    fn register(&mut self, index: usize, edge: bool) {
        let pipe = &mut self.pipes[index];

        pipe.registered = true;
        pipe.edge = edge;

        if pipe.buffered > 0 {
            self.enqueue(index);
        }
    }

    /// Puts a pipe on the ready list unless it is already there.
    fn enqueue(&mut self, index: usize) {
        if !self.pipes[index].queued {
            self.pipes[index].queued = true;
            self.ready.push(index);
        }
    }

    /// Adds bytes to a pipe. This is the moment the pipe becomes ready, and
    /// the writer puts it on the ready list.
    fn write(&mut self, index: usize, n: usize) {
        self.pipes[index].buffered += n;

        if self.pipes[index].registered {
            self.enqueue(index);
        }
    }

    /// Removes up to `n` bytes from a pipe and returns the number removed.
    fn read(&mut self, index: usize, n: usize) -> usize {
        let n = n.min(self.pipes[index].buffered);
        self.pipes[index].buffered -= n;

        n
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Empties the ready list and returns the pipes on it that are still
    /// readable. A level-triggered pipe that is reported goes back on the
    /// list, so the next wait checks it again. An edge-triggered pipe does
    /// not, and is reported again only after another write.
    fn wait(&mut self) -> Vec<usize> {
        let queued = std::mem::take(&mut self.ready);
        let mut events = Vec::new();

        for index in queued {
            self.pipes[index].queued = false;
            self.examined += 1;

            if self.pipes[index].buffered == 0 {
                continue;
            }

            events.push(index);

            if !self.pipes[index].edge {
                self.enqueue(index);
            }
        }

        events
    }

    /// The method of select and poll: it examines every registered pipe on
    /// every call.
    fn scan(&mut self) -> Vec<usize> {
        let mut events = Vec::new();

        for (index, pipe) in self.pipes.iter().enumerate() {
            if !pipe.registered {
                continue;
            }

            self.examined += 1;

            if pipe.buffered > 0 {
                events.push(index);
            }
        }

        events
    }
}

/// Repeats the level-triggered measurement of epollfacts.
fn level() {
    let mut kernel = Kernel::new(3);

    for index in 0..3 {
        kernel.register(index, false);
    }

    println!(
        "3 pipes registered, none written: {} event(s)",
        kernel.wait().len()
    );

    kernel.write(1, 5);

    if let [index] = kernel.wait().as_slice() {
        println!("write to pipe 1: 1 event, for pipe {index}");
    }

    println!(
        "level-triggered, data not read, wait again: {} event(s)",
        kernel.wait().len()
    );

    kernel.read(1, 16);
    println!("after reading the data: {} event(s)", kernel.wait().len());
}

/// Repeats the edge-triggered measurement.
fn edge() {
    let mut kernel = Kernel::new(1);
    kernel.register(0, true);

    kernel.write(0, 5);
    let (first, second) = (kernel.wait().len(), kernel.wait().len());
    println!("edge-triggered, data not read: wait {first} event(s), wait again {second} event(s)");

    kernel.write(0, 5);
    println!(
        "edge-triggered, after another write: {} event(s)",
        kernel.wait().len()
    );
}

/// Compares the work of a wait with the work of a scan when 1000 pipes are
/// registered and 1 is ready.
fn many() {
    let mut kernel = Kernel::new(1000);

    for index in 0..1000 {
        kernel.register(index, false);
    }

    kernel.write(700, 5);

    if let [index] = kernel.wait().as_slice() {
        println!("1000 pipes registered, pipe 700 written: 1 event, for pipe {index}");
    }

    let by_wait = kernel.examined;
    kernel.scan();
    println!(
        "registrations examined: {by_wait} by the wait, {} by a scan",
        kernel.examined - by_wait
    );
}

impl Kernel {
    /// One iteration of an event loop: wait for ready pipes, then run the
    /// handler for each. Returns the pipes it handled.
    fn turn(&mut self, handle: fn(&mut Kernel, usize)) -> Vec<usize> {
        let events = self.wait();

        for &index in &events {
            handle(self, index);
        }

        events
    }
}

/// Formats pipe numbers the way Go prints a slice.
fn list(pipes: &[usize]) -> String {
    let words: Vec<String> = pipes.iter().map(usize::to_string).collect();

    format!("[{}]", words.join(" "))
}

/// Registers 4 pipes, writes to 2 of them, and runs an event loop whose
/// handler reads at most 4 bytes for each event.
fn event_loop() {
    let mut kernel = Kernel::new(4);

    for index in 0..4 {
        kernel.register(index, false);
    }

    kernel.write(2, 5);
    kernel.write(0, 3);

    let handle = |kernel: &mut Kernel, index: usize| {
        kernel.read(index, 4);
    };

    let turns = [
        kernel.turn(handle),
        kernel.turn(handle),
        kernel.turn(handle),
    ];

    println!(
        "event loop: turn 1 handles {}, turn 2 handles {}, turn 3 handles {}",
        list(&turns[0]),
        list(&turns[1]),
        list(&turns[2])
    );
}

fn main() {
    level();
    edge();
    many();
    event_loop();
}

Summary

  • An event loop serves many descriptors from a single thread: wait for events, then handle each ready descriptor without blocking.
  • An epoll instance has an interest list of registrations and a ready list.
  • A descriptor is put on the ready list by the code that makes it ready, such as a write to a pipe. epoll_wait returns the ready list.
  • The work of a wait is proportional to the number of ready descriptors, where select and poll examine every descriptor on every call.
  • A level-triggered descriptor is reported while it is readable. An edge-triggered descriptor is reported when new data arrives, and its handler must read until EAGAIN.
  • A closed peer is reported as EPOLLHUP.

References

  • epoll(7), epoll_ctl(2) and epoll_wait(2), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/epoll.7.html
  • M. Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface, No Starch Press, 2010, chapter 63.
  • fs/eventpoll.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/fs/eventpoll.c

TCP Sockets

A socket is the endpoint of a network connection, held by a process as a file descriptor. Behind the descriptor the kernel keeps the state of the connection: who the peer is, a buffer of data waiting to be sent, and a buffer of data received and not yet read. read and write work on a connected socket as they do on a pipe, and the same descriptor can be registered with epoll.

In this chapter, we will learn what the kernel does for a TCP connection between the calls a program makes. We will first measure a connection on the loopback interface with sockfacts. Then we will write sockmodel, a model of the receiving side: the table that finds the socket for an arriving packet, the accept queue of a listener, and the receive buffer that limits the sender.

This chapter covers

  • the layers between a write and the network
  • the segments of a connection: the handshake, sequence numbers, and acknowledgements
  • the calls that set up a connection: listen, connect and accept
  • the kernel structures: struct sock and struct tcp_sock
  • what identifies a connection, and how many connections share a port
  • the accept queue and its backlog
  • TCP as a stream of bytes without message boundaries
  • the send buffer, the receive buffer, and the window that stops a fast sender
  • how the end of a stream and a closed peer are reported
  • how to inspect the connections of a running system with ss

From write to the network

A network carries packets: blocks of at most about 1500 bytes on Ethernet, each delivered independently, and each of which may be lost, duplicated or delivered out of order. A program wants something else: a stream of bytes that arrives complete and in order. The kernel’s network stack builds the second from the first, in layers.

LayerAddsResponsible for
Socketnothingthe descriptor, the buffers, and blocking
TCPa header with 2 ports, a sequence number, an acknowledgement number and a windowreliability, order, and flow control between 2 programs
IPa header with 2 IP addressesdelivering a packet to the right machine
Devicea frame for the mediummoving the packet to the next machine

An IP address names a machine, and a port is a 16-bit number that names a program on it. The loopback device, with the address 127.0.0.1, delivers packets to the same machine without any hardware, and the programs of this chapter use it.

The segments of a connection

TCP makes an unreliable network reliable by numbering. Every byte of a stream has a sequence number. Each packet of TCP, called a segment, says which bytes it carries. The receiver answers with an acknowledgement: the number of the next byte it expects, which confirms everything before it. The sender keeps each byte until it is acknowledged, and sends it again if no acknowledgement arrives in time. Out-of-order segments are put in order by their numbers, and duplicates are recognised and dropped.

An example with small numbers shows the whole mechanism. The client sends hello, 5 bytes, and its stream is currently at byte 1001.

The acknowledgement is a single number, and it confirms a whole range. This keeps the protocol simple: the receiver always says “the next byte I need is this one”, and whatever went wrong, the sender knows where to continue.

Before any data, the 2 sides have to agree on their starting sequence numbers. This is the handshake, 3 segments marked with the flags SYN and ACK.

  1. SYN: the client proposes its starting number, 1000.
  2. SYN and ACK: the server acknowledges it with 1001 and proposes its own, 5000.
  3. ACK: the client acknowledges 5001. Both sides now know both numbers, and the connection is established.
  4. The client sends 5 bytes, numbered 1001 to 1005.
  5. The server acknowledges 1006 and reports its window, the space left in its receive buffer.
  6. FIN: the client has nothing more to send. This closes its direction of the stream.
  7. The server acknowledges. Its program’s next read returns 0. The server can still send, until it sends a FIN of its own.

All of this is done by the kernels. The programs call connect, write, read and close, and do not see a segment.

Setting up a connection

TCP gives 2 programs a reliable stream of bytes in each direction. A server and a client reach that state through different calls.

CallMade byEffect
socketbothcreates an unconnected socket and returns a descriptor
bindservergives the socket a local address and port
listenservermarks the socket as a listener and sets the length of its accept queue
connectclientexchanges 3 packets with the server’s kernel, the handshake, and returns when the connection is established
acceptserverreturns a new descriptor for an established connection

The handshake is carried out by the server’s kernel. The server program takes no part in it. An established connection waits in the accept queue of the listener until the program calls accept.

A connection is identified by 4 values: the local address, the local port, the remote address and the remote port. A listener and all the connections accepted from it have the same local port. An arriving packet, called a segment in TCP, is matched against the 4 values of the existing connections. A segment that matches none and asks to open a connection, a SYN, is given to the listener on its port.

The kernel’s structures

Behind a socket descriptor is a struct file (chapter 2) whose function table is the socket’s, and behind that a struct sock. For TCP the struct sock is the first part of a larger struct tcp_sock. These are fields from include/net/sock.h and include/linux/tcp.h of Linux 5.15.

struct sock_common {
        __be32 skc_daddr;                      /* remote IP address */
        __be32 skc_rcv_saddr;                  /* local IP address */
        __be16 skc_dport;                      /* remote port */
        __u16 skc_num;                         /* local port */
        volatile unsigned char skc_state;      /* TCP_LISTEN, TCP_ESTABLISHED, ... */
        /* ... */
};

struct sock {
        struct sock_common __sk_common;
        struct sk_buff_head sk_receive_queue;  /* segments received, not yet read */
        int sk_rcvbuf;                         /* limit of the receive queue, bytes */
        struct sk_buff_head sk_write_queue;    /* data written, not yet acknowledged */
        int sk_sndbuf;                         /* limit of the write queue, bytes */
        u32 sk_ack_backlog;                    /* connections waiting for accept */
        u32 sk_max_ack_backlog;                /* the backlog given to listen */
        /* ... */
};

struct tcp_sock {
        u32 rcv_nxt;                           /* next byte we expect to receive */
        u32 snd_nxt;                           /* next byte we will send */
        u32 snd_una;                           /* oldest byte sent and not acknowledged */
        u32 snd_wnd;                           /* the window the peer offered */
        u32 snd_cwnd;                          /* congestion window */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
skc_daddr, skc_dport, skc_rcv_saddr, skc_numThe 4 values that identify the connection.
skc_stateThe state of the connection, shown by ss as LISTEN, ESTAB and others.
sk_receive_queue, sk_rcvbufThe receive buffer and its limit. read takes from this queue.
sk_write_queue, sk_sndbufThe send buffer and its limit. write adds to this queue and blocks when the limit is reached.
snd_una, snd_nxtThe bytes between them have been sent and are waiting for an acknowledgement.
rcv_nxtThe acknowledgement number this side sends.
snd_wndThe peer’s window: this side sends no byte beyond snd_una + snd_wnd.
snd_cwndA second limit that TCP computes itself, to avoid overloading the network between the machines.

The ss command prints these fields for the sockets of a system. Here a server listens on port 9099 and a client has connected to it over loopback:

$ ss -tln 'sport = :9099'
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port
LISTEN 0      1          127.0.0.1:9099      0.0.0.0:*
$ ss -tn 'sport = :9099 or dport = :9099'
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:9099     127.0.0.1:51252
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:51252    127.0.0.1:9099

The first command shows the listener. For a listener, Send-Q is the backlog, 1 here, and Recv-Q is the number of connections waiting for accept. The second shows the connection 2 times, because both ends are on this machine: the server’s socket with local port 9099, and the client’s with the port 51252 that the kernel chose for it. The 4 values of one line are the 4 values of the other, exchanged.

Measuring a connection

sockfacts makes its connections over the loopback address 127.0.0.1, with both ends in the same process. The Go version calls the socket system calls through golang.org/x/sys/unix. The Rust version uses std::net and the nix crate with the socket feature for socket options.

$ cargo new sockfacts
$ cargo add -p sockfacts nix --features socket

listen binds to port 0, which asks the kernel for any free port.

Listing 10.1 The imports of sockfacts, in Go. code/go/sockfacts/main.go

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)

Listing 10.2 The imports of sockfacts, in Rust. code/rust/sockfacts/src/main.rs

use std::io::{self, Read, Write};
use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream};
use std::os::fd::AsRawFd;

use nix::errno::Errno;
use nix::sys::socket::{setsockopt, sockopt};

Listing 10.3 A listener and a client on the loopback interface, in Go. code/go/sockfacts/main.go

// listen returns a TCP socket that listens on a free port of 127.0.0.1, and
// its address.
func listen() (int, *unix.SockaddrInet4, error) {
	listener, err := unix.Socket(unix.AF_INET, unix.SOCK_STREAM|unix.SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	if err := unix.Bind(listener, &unix.SockaddrInet4{Addr: [4]byte{127, 0, 0, 1}}); err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	if err := unix.Listen(listener, 16); err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	address, err := unix.Getsockname(listener)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	return listener, address.(*unix.SockaddrInet4), nil
}

// connect returns a TCP socket connected to an address.
func connect(address *unix.SockaddrInet4) (int, error) {
	client, err := unix.Socket(unix.AF_INET, unix.SOCK_STREAM|unix.SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return client, unix.Connect(client, address)
}

// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EPIPE.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}

// port returns the port of an address.
func port(address unix.Sockaddr, err error) int {
	if inet, ok := address.(*unix.SockaddrInet4); ok && err == nil {
		return inet.Port
	}

	return 0
}

Listing 10.4 A listener and a client on the loopback interface, in Rust. code/rust/sockfacts/src/main.rs

/// Returns a TCP socket that listens on a free port of 127.0.0.1.
fn listen() -> io::Result<TcpListener> {
    TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")
}

/// Returns a TCP socket connected to the address of a listener.
fn connect(listener: &TcpListener) -> io::Result<TcpStream> {
    TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)
}

/// Returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as `EPIPE`.
fn name(error: &io::Error) -> String {
    match error.raw_os_error() {
        Some(code) => format!("{:?}", Errno::from_raw(code)),
        None => error.to_string(),
    }
}

establish calls connect before the server has called accept. Then it accepts and compares the addresses of the ends.

Listing 10.5 Connecting before accept, and the ports of both ends, in Go. code/go/sockfacts/main.go

// establish connects before the server calls accept, and compares the
// addresses of both ends.
func establish() error {
	listener, address, err := listen()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(listener)

	client, err := connect(address)
	fmt.Printf("connect before the server calls accept: succeeded %v\n", err == nil)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(client)

	server, _, err := unix.Accept(listener)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(server)

	fmt.Printf("accept returns a new descriptor: %v, on the listener's port: %v\n",
		server != listener, port(unix.Getsockname(server)) == address.Port)
	fmt.Printf("the client's local port is the server's peer port: %v\n",
		port(unix.Getsockname(client)) == port(unix.Getpeername(server)))

	return stream(client, server)
}

Listing 10.6 Connecting before accept, and the ports of both ends, in Rust. code/rust/sockfacts/src/main.rs

/// Connects before the server calls accept, and compares the addresses of
/// both ends.
fn establish() -> io::Result<()> {
    let listener = listen()?;

    let client = connect(&listener);
    println!(
        "connect before the server calls accept: succeeded {}",
        client.is_ok()
    );

    let client = client?;
    let (server, _) = listener.accept()?;

    println!(
        "accept returns a new descriptor: {}, on the listener's port: {}",
        server.as_raw_fd() != listener.as_raw_fd(),
        server.local_addr()?.port() == listener.local_addr()?.port()
    );
    println!(
        "the client's local port is the server's peer port: {}",
        client.local_addr()?.port() == server.peer_addr()?.port()
    );

    stream(client, server)
}

stream sends ab and cd with separate calls to write, and the server reads 3 bytes and then 1. After that the client closes its socket. The server reads again, and then writes until a write fails.

Listing 10.7 A stream of bytes, and the end of the stream, in Go. code/go/sockfacts/main.go

// readFull reads until buf is full.
func readFull(fd int, buf []byte) error {
	for filled := 0; filled < len(buf); {
		n, err := unix.Read(fd, buf[filled:])

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if n == 0 {
			return errors.New("the stream ended early")
		}

		filled += n
	}

	return nil
}

// stream writes "ab" and "cd" with 2 calls and reads 3 bytes and then 1.
// Then the client closes, and the server reads and writes again.
func stream(client, server int) error {
	for _, part := range []string{"ab", "cd"} {
		if _, err := unix.Write(client, []byte(part)); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	first, second := make([]byte, 3), make([]byte, 1)

	if err := readFull(server, first); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := readFull(server, second); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("writes of \"ab\" and \"cd\", reads of 3 bytes and 1 byte: %q and %q\n", first, second)

	unix.Close(client)

	n, err := unix.Read(server, first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the client closed: read returns %d\n", n)

	for err == nil {
		_, err = unix.Write(server, []byte("x"))
	}

	fmt.Printf("writes to the closed peer: the first is accepted, a later one fails with %s\n", name(err))

	return nil
}

Listing 10.8 A stream of bytes, and the end of the stream, in Rust. code/rust/sockfacts/src/main.rs

/// Writes "ab" and "cd" with 2 calls and reads 3 bytes and then 1. Then the
/// client closes, and the server reads and writes again.
fn stream(mut client: TcpStream, mut server: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> {
    for part in ["ab", "cd"] {
        client.write_all(part.as_bytes())?;
    }

    let (mut first, mut second) = ([0u8; 3], [0u8; 1]);

    server.read_exact(&mut first)?;
    server.read_exact(&mut second)?;

    println!(
        "writes of \"ab\" and \"cd\", reads of 3 bytes and 1 byte: {:?} and {:?}",
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&first),
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&second)
    );

    drop(client);

    let n = server.read(&mut first)?;
    println!("the client closed: read returns {n}");

    let error = loop {
        if let Err(error) = server.write(b"x") {
            break error;
        }
    };

    println!(
        "writes to the closed peer: the first is accepted, a later one fails with {}",
        name(&error)
    );

    Ok(())
}

flow reduces the buffers of a connection, so that the numbers are small, and writes to the client socket in non-blocking mode until the kernel refuses a write. The server does not read during that time. Then the server reads everything, and the client tries again.

Listing 10.9 A sender whose peer does not read, in Go. code/go/sockfacts/main.go

// fill writes blocks to a non-blocking socket until the kernel refuses one
// and returns the number of bytes accepted.
func fill(fd int) (int, error) {
	block := make([]byte, 1024)
	total := 0

	for {
		n, err := unix.Write(fd, block)

		if errors.Is(err, unix.EAGAIN) {
			return total, nil
		}

		if err != nil {
			return total, err
		}

		total += n
	}
}

// flow gives a connection small buffers, fills it while the server does not
// read, lets the server read everything, and fills it again.
func flow() error {
	listener, address, err := listen()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(listener)

	if err := unix.SetsockoptInt(listener, unix.SOL_SOCKET, unix.SO_RCVBUF, 4096); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	client, err := connect(address)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(client)

	if err := unix.SetsockoptInt(client, unix.SOL_SOCKET, unix.SO_SNDBUF, 4096); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	server, _, err := unix.Accept(listener)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(server)

	if err := unix.SetNonblock(client, true); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	sent, err := fill(client)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the server does not read: the client is stopped after %d bytes\n", sent)

	if err := readFull(server, make([]byte, sent)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	again, err := fill(client)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the server has read everything: the client can write again: %v\n", again > 0)

	return nil
}

Listing 10.10 A sender whose peer does not read, in Rust. code/rust/sockfacts/src/main.rs

/// Writes blocks to a non-blocking socket until the kernel refuses one and
/// returns the number of bytes accepted.
fn fill(mut stream: &TcpStream) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let block = [0u8; 1024];
    let mut total = 0;

    loop {
        match stream.write(&block) {
            Ok(n) => total += n,
            Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => return Ok(total),
            Err(error) => return Err(error),
        }
    }
}

/// Gives a connection small buffers, fills it while the server does not read,
/// lets the server read everything, and fills it again.
fn flow() -> io::Result<()> {
    let listener = listen()?;
    setsockopt(&listener, sockopt::RcvBuf, &4096)?;

    let client = connect(&listener)?;
    setsockopt(&client, sockopt::SndBuf, &4096)?;

    let (mut server, _) = listener.accept()?;

    client.set_nonblocking(true)?;

    let sent = fill(&client)?;
    println!("the server does not read: the client is stopped after {sent} bytes");

    server.read_exact(&mut vec![0u8; sent])?;

    let again = fill(&client)?;
    println!(
        "the server has read everything: the client can write again: {}",
        again > 0
    );

    Ok(())
}

accept returns a new descriptor: true, on the listener's port: true
the client's local port is the server's peer port: true
writes of "ab" and "cd", reads of 3 bytes and 1 byte: "abc" and "d"
the client closed: read returns 0
writes to the closed peer: the first is accepted, a later one fails with EPIPE
the server does not read: the client is stopped after 7168 bytes
the server has read everything: the client can write again: true
OutputConclusion
connect succeeds before acceptThe kernel completes the handshake. The connection waits in the accept queue.
a new descriptor on the listener’s portaccept creates a socket for the connection. The listener stays open for further connections.
client’s local port is the server’s peer portBoth ends hold the same 4 values, each from its own side.
abc and dTCP delivers bytes in order and keeps no record of where a write ended.
read returns 0The end of the peer’s stream is reported as on a pipe.
a later write fails with EPIPEThe first write after the close is accepted locally. The peer’s kernel answers it with a reset, and the following write fails.
stopped after 7168 bytesBoth buffers are full. A blocking write would be suspended here.
can write again after the server has readSpace in the receive buffer lets the sender continue.

Row 4 has a practical consequence. A protocol built on TCP has to mark the boundaries of its messages itself, with a length before each message or with a delimiter such as a newline, and a reader has to be prepared to receive part of a message or several messages in a single read.

TCP keeps no message boundaries. A read can return half a message, or 2 messages at once.

Buffers and the window

A write on a socket copies the data into the socket’s send buffer and returns. The kernel transmits from that buffer and keeps each byte until the peer has acknowledged it. On the other side, arriving data is placed in the receive buffer until the program reads it.

The 2 buffers are connected by the window. With every acknowledgement, the receiver reports how much free space its receive buffer has, and the sender transmits no more than that. When the receiving program stops reading, the receive buffer fills, the window becomes 0, the sender’s kernel stops transmitting, the send buffer fills, and write blocks. This is the flow control of a pipe, extended across a network. The 7168 bytes of the measurement are the contents of both buffers at that point.

Low-level design: sockmodel

TypeFieldsMeaning
endpointaddress, portone side of a connection
keyremote, portidentifies a connection: the remote endpoint and the local port
socketreceived, capacity, finishedthe receive buffer; whether the sender has ended its stream
listenerbacklog, queuethe accept queue and its maximum length
stacklisteners, connectionslisteners by port; connections by key
OperationBehaviour
receive(segment)delivers to the matching connection; gives a SYN to the listener; otherwise answers with a reset
deliver(segment)appends data up to the window; records a FIN
accept(port)removes the oldest connection from the accept queue
read(n)removes bytes from the receive buffer; reports the end of the stream

Modelling the receiving side

The model covers the receiving half of TCP and omits transmission, acknowledgements and retransmission.

Listing 10.11 The imports of sockmodel, in Go. code/go/sockmodel/main.go

import "fmt"

Listing 10.12 The imports of sockmodel, in Rust. code/rust/sockmodel/src/main.rs

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};
use std::fmt;

Listing 10.13 Endpoints, sockets, listeners and segments, in Go. code/go/sockmodel/main.go

// An endpoint is an IP address and a port.
type endpoint struct {
	address string
	port    int
}

func (e endpoint) String() string {
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", e.address, e.port)
}

// A socket is one established connection: the bytes received and not yet
// read, the size of the receive buffer, and whether the sender has finished.
type socket struct {
	received []byte
	capacity int
	finished bool
}

// window is the free space of the receive buffer: the number of bytes the
// sender may still send.
func (s *socket) window() int {
	return s.capacity - len(s.received)
}

// A key identifies a connection on this machine: the remote endpoint and the
// local port. With the local address, which the model leaves out, it forms
// the 4 values that identify a TCP connection.
type key struct {
	remote endpoint
	port   int
}

// A listener accepts connections on a port. queue holds the connections that
// are established and have not been returned by accept.
type listener struct {
	backlog int
	queue   []key
}

// A stack is the TCP state of a machine.
type stack struct {
	listeners   map[int]*listener
	connections map[key]*socket
	bufferSize  int
}

// A segment is a packet of TCP. syn opens a connection and fin ends the
// sender's stream.
type segment struct {
	from     endpoint
	port     int
	syn, fin bool
	data     string
}

Listing 10.14 Endpoints, sockets, listeners and segments, in Rust. code/rust/sockmodel/src/main.rs

/// An IP address and a port.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Endpoint {
    address: &'static str,
    port: u16,
}

impl fmt::Display for Endpoint {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{}:{}", self.address, self.port)
    }
}

/// One established connection: the bytes received and not yet read, the size
/// of the receive buffer, and whether the sender has finished.
struct Socket {
    received: VecDeque<u8>,
    capacity: usize,
    finished: bool,
}

impl Socket {
    /// The free space of the receive buffer: the number of bytes the sender
    /// may still send.
    fn window(&self) -> usize {
        self.capacity - self.received.len()
    }
}

/// Identifies a connection on this machine: the remote endpoint and the local
/// port. With the local address, which the model leaves out, it forms the 4
/// values that identify a TCP connection.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Key {
    remote: Endpoint,
    port: u16,
}

/// Accepts connections on a port. `queue` holds the connections that are
/// established and have not been returned by accept.
struct Listener {
    backlog: usize,
    queue: VecDeque<Key>,
}

/// The TCP state of a machine.
struct Stack {
    listeners: HashMap<u16, Listener>,
    connections: HashMap<Key, Socket>,
    buffer_size: usize,
}

/// A packet of TCP. `syn` opens a connection and `fin` ends the sender's
/// stream.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Segment {
    syn: bool,
    fin: bool,
    data: &'static str,
}

receive is the lookup of figure 10.4. The table of connections is consulted first, which is why data for an established connection reaches its own socket while a listener exists on the same port. A SYN for a full accept queue is dropped without an answer. The client’s kernel sends it again after a timeout, which gives the server time to call accept.

Listing 10.15 Finding the socket for a segment, in Go. code/go/sockmodel/main.go

// receive handles an arriving segment and describes the result. A segment
// belongs to the connection with its remote endpoint and local port. Only
// when no such connection exists, and the segment is a SYN, is the listener
// on the port consulted.
func (st *stack) receive(seg segment) string {
	id := key{remote: seg.from, port: seg.port}

	if s, ok := st.connections[id]; ok {
		return s.deliver(seg)
	}

	if !seg.syn {
		return "reset, no connection"
	}

	l, ok := st.listeners[seg.port]

	if !ok {
		return "reset, no listener on the port"
	}

	if len(l.queue) == l.backlog {
		return "dropped, the accept queue is full"
	}

	st.connections[id] = &socket{capacity: st.bufferSize}
	l.queue = append(l.queue, id)

	return fmt.Sprintf("established, accept queue %d", len(l.queue))
}

// deliver puts the data of a segment into the receive buffer, up to the
// window, and records a FIN.
func (s *socket) deliver(seg segment) string {
	if seg.fin {
		s.finished = true

		return "the sender's stream has ended"
	}

	accepted := min(len(seg.data), s.window())
	s.received = append(s.received, seg.data[:accepted]...)

	return fmt.Sprintf("accepted %d, window %d", accepted, s.window())
}

Listing 10.16 Finding the socket for a segment, in Rust. code/rust/sockmodel/src/main.rs

impl Stack {
    /// Handles a segment that arrives from `from` for local port `port`, and
    /// describes the result. A segment belongs to the connection with its
    /// remote endpoint and local port. Only when no such connection exists,
    /// and the segment is a SYN, is the listener on the port consulted.
    fn receive(&mut self, from: Endpoint, port: u16, segment: &Segment) -> String {
        let id = Key { remote: from, port };

        if let Some(socket) = self.connections.get_mut(&id) {
            return socket.deliver(segment);
        }

        if !segment.syn {
            return "reset, no connection".into();
        }

        let Some(listener) = self.listeners.get_mut(&port) else {
            return "reset, no listener on the port".into();
        };

        if listener.queue.len() == listener.backlog {
            return "dropped, the accept queue is full".into();
        }

        let socket = Socket {
            received: VecDeque::new(),
            capacity: self.buffer_size,
            finished: false,
        };

        self.connections.insert(id, socket);
        listener.queue.push_back(id);

        format!("established, accept queue {}", listener.queue.len())
    }
}

impl Socket {
    /// Puts the data of a segment into the receive buffer, up to the window,
    /// and records a FIN.
    fn deliver(&mut self, segment: &Segment) -> String {
        if segment.fin {
            self.finished = true;

            return "the sender's stream has ended".into();
        }

        let accepted = segment.data.len().min(self.window());
        self.received.extend(&segment.data.as_bytes()[..accepted]);

        format!("accepted {accepted}, window {}", self.window())
    }
}

deliver accepts data up to the window. window is the free space of the receive buffer, the value a real receiver reports to the sender.

accept takes connections in the order they were established. read returns the end of the stream only when the buffer is empty and the FIN, the segment that ends the sender’s stream, has arrived, so data that was sent before a close is not lost.

Listing 10.17 Accepting a connection, and reading from it, in Go. code/go/sockmodel/main.go

// accept removes the oldest connection from the accept queue of a port.
func (st *stack) accept(port int) (key, bool) {
	l, ok := st.listeners[port]

	if !ok || len(l.queue) == 0 {
		return key{}, false
	}

	id := l.queue[0]
	l.queue = l.queue[1:]

	return id, true
}

// read removes up to n bytes from the receive buffer. It returns 0 bytes
// with ended set when the buffer is empty and a FIN has arrived.
func (s *socket) read(n int) (data string, ended bool) {
	n = min(n, len(s.received))
	data, s.received = string(s.received[:n]), s.received[n:]

	return data, n == 0 && s.finished
}

Listing 10.18 Accepting a connection, and reading from it, in Rust. code/rust/sockmodel/src/main.rs

impl Stack {
    /// Removes the oldest connection from the accept queue of a port.
    fn accept(&mut self, port: u16) -> Option<Key> {
        self.listeners.get_mut(&port)?.queue.pop_front()
    }
}

impl Socket {
    /// Removes up to `n` bytes from the receive buffer. It returns 0 bytes
    /// with the second value set when the buffer is empty and a FIN has
    /// arrived.
    fn read(&mut self, n: usize) -> (String, bool) {
        let n = n.min(self.received.len());
        let data: Vec<u8> = self.received.drain(..n).collect();

        (
            String::from_utf8_lossy(&data).into_owned(),
            n == 0 && self.finished,
        )
    }
}

	fmt.Printf("read: %q, stream ended %v\n", data, ended)
