fn endpoint(address: &'static str) -> Endpoint {
    Endpoint {
        address,
        port: 5000,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let listener = Listener {
        backlog: 2,
        queue: VecDeque::new(),
    };

    let mut stack = Stack {
        listeners: HashMap::from([(80, listener)]),
        connections: HashMap::new(),
        buffer_size: 8,
    };

    let (a, b, c) = (
        endpoint("10.0.0.1"),
        endpoint("10.0.0.2"),
        endpoint("10.0.0.3"),
    );

    let syn = Segment {
        syn: true,
        ..Segment::default()
    };

    for (from, port) in [(a, 80), (b, 80), (c, 80), (c, 81)] {
        let result = stack.receive(from, port, &syn);
        println!("SYN from {from} to port {port}: {result}");
    }

    if let Some(id) = stack.accept(80) {
        println!("accept on port 80: the connection from {}", id.remote);
    }

    let hello = Segment {
        data: "hello",
        ..Segment::default()
    };

    for from in [b, a, b, c] {
        let result = stack.receive(from, 80, &hello);
        println!("5 bytes from {from} to port 80: {result}");
    }

    let id = Key {
        remote: b,
        port: 80,
    };

    if let Some(socket) = stack.connections.get_mut(&id) {
        let (data, _) = socket.read(4);
        println!(
            "read of 4 bytes on the connection from {b}: {data:?}, window {}",
            socket.window()
        );
    }

    let fin = Segment {
        fin: true,
        ..Segment::default()
    };

    println!("FIN from {b}: {}", stack.receive(b, 80, &fin));

    if let Some(socket) = stack.connections.get_mut(&id) {
        for _ in 0..2 {
            let (data, ended) = socket.read(16);
            println!("read: {data:?}, stream ended {ended}");
        }
    }
}
SYN from 10.0.0.1:5000 to port 80: established, accept queue 1
SYN from 10.0.0.2:5000 to port 80: established, accept queue 2
SYN from 10.0.0.3:5000 to port 80: dropped, the accept queue is full
SYN from 10.0.0.3:5000 to port 81: reset, no listener on the port
accept on port 80: the connection from 10.0.0.1:5000
5 bytes from 10.0.0.2:5000 to port 80: accepted 5, window 3
5 bytes from 10.0.0.1:5000 to port 80: accepted 5, window 3
5 bytes from 10.0.0.2:5000 to port 80: accepted 3, window 0
5 bytes from 10.0.0.3:5000 to port 80: reset, no connection
read of 4 bytes on the connection from 10.0.0.2:5000: "hell", window 4
FIN from 10.0.0.2:5000: the sender's stream has ended
read: "ohel", stream ended false
read: "", stream ended true
LineWhat it shows
lines 1 and 2Connections are established and queued without a call to accept.
dropped, the accept queue is fullThe backlog of 2 is reached.
reset, no listener on the portA SYN for a port without a listener is refused. A client sees this as ECONNREFUSED.
accept on port 80The oldest connection is returned.
5 bytes from 10.0.0.2 and from 10.0.0.1Both connections use local port 80, and each segment reaches its own socket.
accepted 3, window 0The receive buffer of 8 bytes is full. A real sender would have sent only 3 bytes, having been told the window.
reset, no connectionThe SYN of 10.0.0.3 was dropped, so no connection exists for its data.
the reads after the FINThe buffered bytes are returned first. The end of the stream follows.

Correspondence with the kernel source. __inet_lookup_established and __inet_lookup_listener in net/ipv4/inet_hashtables.c are the 2 lookups of receive. A connected socket is struct tcp_sock, with the receive buffer in sk_receive_queue and its limit in sk_rcvbuf. tcp_select_window computes the window, and tcp_data_queue in net/ipv4/tcp_input.c queues arriving data. The accept queue is icsk_accept_queue, limited by the backlog given to listen and by /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn, which is 4096 on this machine.

Inspecting sockets on a live system

CommandShows
ss -tlnthe listening TCP sockets, with their backlog
ss -tnthe established connections, with the bytes waiting in each queue
ss -tniper connection: the congestion window, the round-trip time, and the window
ss -tnpthe process that owns each socket
cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconnthe largest backlog listen may set: 4096 here
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_rmemthe minimum, initial and maximum size of a receive buffer

Recv-Q on an established connection is data that has arrived and that the program has not read. A value that stays high means the program is slow to read, and the sender is being held back by the window.

The complete programs

Listing 10.21 The complete sockfacts, in Go. code/go/sockfacts/main.go

// Command sockfacts measures TCP sockets on the loopback interface: when a
// connection is established, what identifies it, how written bytes arrive,
// what stops a writer whose peer does not read, and how each side learns
// that the other has closed.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./sockfacts
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


// listen returns a TCP socket that listens on a free port of 127.0.0.1, and
// its address.
func listen() (int, *unix.SockaddrInet4, error) {
	listener, err := unix.Socket(unix.AF_INET, unix.SOCK_STREAM|unix.SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	if err := unix.Bind(listener, &unix.SockaddrInet4{Addr: [4]byte{127, 0, 0, 1}}); err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	if err := unix.Listen(listener, 16); err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	address, err := unix.Getsockname(listener)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil, err
	}

	return listener, address.(*unix.SockaddrInet4), nil
}

// connect returns a TCP socket connected to an address.
func connect(address *unix.SockaddrInet4) (int, error) {
	client, err := unix.Socket(unix.AF_INET, unix.SOCK_STREAM|unix.SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0)

	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	return client, unix.Connect(client, address)
}

// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EPIPE.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}

// port returns the port of an address.
func port(address unix.Sockaddr, err error) int {
	if inet, ok := address.(*unix.SockaddrInet4); ok && err == nil {
		return inet.Port
	}

	return 0
}


// establish connects before the server calls accept, and compares the
// addresses of both ends.
func establish() error {
	listener, address, err := listen()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(listener)

	client, err := connect(address)
	fmt.Printf("connect before the server calls accept: succeeded %v\n", err == nil)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(client)

	server, _, err := unix.Accept(listener)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(server)

	fmt.Printf("accept returns a new descriptor: %v, on the listener's port: %v\n",
		server != listener, port(unix.Getsockname(server)) == address.Port)
	fmt.Printf("the client's local port is the server's peer port: %v\n",
		port(unix.Getsockname(client)) == port(unix.Getpeername(server)))

	return stream(client, server)
}


// readFull reads until buf is full.
func readFull(fd int, buf []byte) error {
	for filled := 0; filled < len(buf); {
		n, err := unix.Read(fd, buf[filled:])

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if n == 0 {
			return errors.New("the stream ended early")
		}

		filled += n
	}

	return nil
}

// stream writes "ab" and "cd" with 2 calls and reads 3 bytes and then 1.
// Then the client closes, and the server reads and writes again.
func stream(client, server int) error {
	for _, part := range []string{"ab", "cd"} {
		if _, err := unix.Write(client, []byte(part)); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	first, second := make([]byte, 3), make([]byte, 1)

	if err := readFull(server, first); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := readFull(server, second); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("writes of \"ab\" and \"cd\", reads of 3 bytes and 1 byte: %q and %q\n", first, second)

	unix.Close(client)

	n, err := unix.Read(server, first)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the client closed: read returns %d\n", n)

	for err == nil {
		_, err = unix.Write(server, []byte("x"))
	}

	fmt.Printf("writes to the closed peer: the first is accepted, a later one fails with %s\n", name(err))

	return nil
}


// fill writes blocks to a non-blocking socket until the kernel refuses one
// and returns the number of bytes accepted.
func fill(fd int) (int, error) {
	block := make([]byte, 1024)
	total := 0

	for {
		n, err := unix.Write(fd, block)

		if errors.Is(err, unix.EAGAIN) {
			return total, nil
		}

		if err != nil {
			return total, err
		}

		total += n
	}
}

// flow gives a connection small buffers, fills it while the server does not
// read, lets the server read everything, and fills it again.
func flow() error {
	listener, address, err := listen()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(listener)

	if err := unix.SetsockoptInt(listener, unix.SOL_SOCKET, unix.SO_RCVBUF, 4096); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	client, err := connect(address)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(client)

	if err := unix.SetsockoptInt(client, unix.SOL_SOCKET, unix.SO_SNDBUF, 4096); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	server, _, err := unix.Accept(listener)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	defer unix.Close(server)

	if err := unix.SetNonblock(client, true); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	sent, err := fill(client)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the server does not read: the client is stopped after %d bytes\n", sent)

	if err := readFull(server, make([]byte, sent)); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	again, err := fill(client)

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("the server has read everything: the client can write again: %v\n", again > 0)

	return nil
}


func main() {
	for _, experiment := range []func() error{establish, flow} {
		if err := experiment(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}

Listing 10.22 The complete sockfacts, in Rust. code/rust/sockfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures TCP sockets on the loopback interface: when a connection is
//! established, what identifies it, how written bytes arrive, what stops a
//! writer whose peer does not read, and how each side learns that the other
//! has closed.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p sockfacts
//! ```

use std::io::{self, Read, Write};
use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream};
use std::os::fd::AsRawFd;

use nix::errno::Errno;
use nix::sys::socket::{setsockopt, sockopt};

/// Returns a TCP socket that listens on a free port of 127.0.0.1.
fn listen() -> io::Result<TcpListener> {
    TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")
}

/// Returns a TCP socket connected to the address of a listener.
fn connect(listener: &TcpListener) -> io::Result<TcpStream> {
    TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)
}

/// Returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as `EPIPE`.
fn name(error: &io::Error) -> String {
    match error.raw_os_error() {
        Some(code) => format!("{:?}", Errno::from_raw(code)),
        None => error.to_string(),
    }
}

/// Connects before the server calls accept, and compares the addresses of
/// both ends.
fn establish() -> io::Result<()> {
    let listener = listen()?;

    let client = connect(&listener);
    println!(
        "connect before the server calls accept: succeeded {}",
        client.is_ok()
    );

    let client = client?;
    let (server, _) = listener.accept()?;

    println!(
        "accept returns a new descriptor: {}, on the listener's port: {}",
        server.as_raw_fd() != listener.as_raw_fd(),
        server.local_addr()?.port() == listener.local_addr()?.port()
    );
    println!(
        "the client's local port is the server's peer port: {}",
        client.local_addr()?.port() == server.peer_addr()?.port()
    );

    stream(client, server)
}

/// Writes "ab" and "cd" with 2 calls and reads 3 bytes and then 1. Then the
/// client closes, and the server reads and writes again.
fn stream(mut client: TcpStream, mut server: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> {
    for part in ["ab", "cd"] {
        client.write_all(part.as_bytes())?;
    }

    let (mut first, mut second) = ([0u8; 3], [0u8; 1]);

    server.read_exact(&mut first)?;
    server.read_exact(&mut second)?;

    println!(
        "writes of \"ab\" and \"cd\", reads of 3 bytes and 1 byte: {:?} and {:?}",
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&first),
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&second)
    );

    drop(client);

    let n = server.read(&mut first)?;
    println!("the client closed: read returns {n}");

    let error = loop {
        if let Err(error) = server.write(b"x") {
            break error;
        }
    };

    println!(
        "writes to the closed peer: the first is accepted, a later one fails with {}",
        name(&error)
    );

    Ok(())
}

/// Writes blocks to a non-blocking socket until the kernel refuses one and
/// returns the number of bytes accepted.
fn fill(mut stream: &TcpStream) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let block = [0u8; 1024];
    let mut total = 0;

    loop {
        match stream.write(&block) {
            Ok(n) => total += n,
            Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => return Ok(total),
            Err(error) => return Err(error),
        }
    }
}

/// Gives a connection small buffers, fills it while the server does not read,
/// lets the server read everything, and fills it again.
fn flow() -> io::Result<()> {
    let listener = listen()?;
    setsockopt(&listener, sockopt::RcvBuf, &4096)?;

    let client = connect(&listener)?;
    setsockopt(&client, sockopt::SndBuf, &4096)?;

    let (mut server, _) = listener.accept()?;

    client.set_nonblocking(true)?;

    let sent = fill(&client)?;
    println!("the server does not read: the client is stopped after {sent} bytes");

    server.read_exact(&mut vec![0u8; sent])?;

    let again = fill(&client)?;
    println!(
        "the server has read everything: the client can write again: {}",
        again > 0
    );

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    establish()?;
    flow()
}

Listing 10.23 The complete sockmodel, in Go. code/go/sockmodel/main.go

// Command sockmodel models the receiving side of TCP in the kernel: a table
// of connections keyed by addresses and ports, listeners with an accept
// queue of limited length, and a receive buffer whose free space is the
// window offered to the sender.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./sockmodel
package main

import "fmt"


// An endpoint is an IP address and a port.
type endpoint struct {
	address string
	port    int
}

func (e endpoint) String() string {
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", e.address, e.port)
}

// A socket is one established connection: the bytes received and not yet
// read, the size of the receive buffer, and whether the sender has finished.
type socket struct {
	received []byte
	capacity int
	finished bool
}

// window is the free space of the receive buffer: the number of bytes the
// sender may still send.
func (s *socket) window() int {
	return s.capacity - len(s.received)
}

// A key identifies a connection on this machine: the remote endpoint and the
// local port. With the local address, which the model leaves out, it forms
// the 4 values that identify a TCP connection.
type key struct {
	remote endpoint
	port   int
}

// A listener accepts connections on a port. queue holds the connections that
// are established and have not been returned by accept.
type listener struct {
	backlog int
	queue   []key
}

// A stack is the TCP state of a machine.
type stack struct {
	listeners   map[int]*listener
	connections map[key]*socket
	bufferSize  int
}

// A segment is a packet of TCP. syn opens a connection and fin ends the
// sender's stream.
type segment struct {
	from     endpoint
	port     int
	syn, fin bool
	data     string
}


// receive handles an arriving segment and describes the result. A segment
// belongs to the connection with its remote endpoint and local port. Only
// when no such connection exists, and the segment is a SYN, is the listener
// on the port consulted.
func (st *stack) receive(seg segment) string {
	id := key{remote: seg.from, port: seg.port}

	if s, ok := st.connections[id]; ok {
		return s.deliver(seg)
	}

	if !seg.syn {
		return "reset, no connection"
	}

	l, ok := st.listeners[seg.port]

	if !ok {
		return "reset, no listener on the port"
	}

	if len(l.queue) == l.backlog {
		return "dropped, the accept queue is full"
	}

	st.connections[id] = &socket{capacity: st.bufferSize}
	l.queue = append(l.queue, id)

	return fmt.Sprintf("established, accept queue %d", len(l.queue))
}

// deliver puts the data of a segment into the receive buffer, up to the
// window, and records a FIN.
func (s *socket) deliver(seg segment) string {
	if seg.fin {
		s.finished = true

		return "the sender's stream has ended"
	}

	accepted := min(len(seg.data), s.window())
	s.received = append(s.received, seg.data[:accepted]...)

	return fmt.Sprintf("accepted %d, window %d", accepted, s.window())
}


// accept removes the oldest connection from the accept queue of a port.
func (st *stack) accept(port int) (key, bool) {
	l, ok := st.listeners[port]

	if !ok || len(l.queue) == 0 {
		return key{}, false
	}

	id := l.queue[0]
	l.queue = l.queue[1:]

	return id, true
}

// read removes up to n bytes from the receive buffer. It returns 0 bytes
// with ended set when the buffer is empty and a FIN has arrived.
func (s *socket) read(n int) (data string, ended bool) {
	n = min(n, len(s.received))
	data, s.received = string(s.received[:n]), s.received[n:]

	return data, n == 0 && s.finished
}


func main() {
	st := &stack{
		listeners:   map[int]*listener{80: {backlog: 2}},
		connections: map[key]*socket{},
		bufferSize:  8,
	}

	a, b, c := endpoint{"10.0.0.1", 5000}, endpoint{"10.0.0.2", 5000}, endpoint{"10.0.0.3", 5000}

	for _, seg := range []segment{{from: a, port: 80, syn: true}, {from: b, port: 80, syn: true},
		{from: c, port: 80, syn: true}, {from: c, port: 81, syn: true}} {
		fmt.Printf("SYN from %s to port %d: %s\n", seg.from, seg.port, st.receive(seg))
	}

	if id, ok := st.accept(80); ok {
		fmt.Printf("accept on port 80: the connection from %s\n", id.remote)
	}

	for _, from := range []endpoint{b, a, b, c} {
		fmt.Printf("5 bytes from %s to port 80: %s\n", from, st.receive(segment{from: from, port: 80, data: "hello"}))
	}

	conn, ok := st.connections[key{remote: b, port: 80}]

	if !ok {
		return
	}

	data, ended := conn.read(4)
	fmt.Printf("read of 4 bytes on the connection from %s: %q, window %d\n", b, data, conn.window())

	fmt.Printf("FIN from %s: %s\n", b, st.receive(segment{from: b, port: 80, fin: true}))

	data, ended = conn.read(16)
	fmt.Printf("read: %q, stream ended %v\n", data, ended)

	data, ended = conn.read(16)
	fmt.Printf("read: %q, stream ended %v\n", data, ended)
}

Listing 10.24 The complete sockmodel, in Rust. code/rust/sockmodel/src/main.rs

//! Models the receiving side of TCP in the kernel: a table of connections
//! keyed by addresses and ports, listeners with an accept queue of limited
//! length, and a receive buffer whose free space is the window offered to the
//! sender.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p sockmodel
//! ```

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};
use std::fmt;

/// An IP address and a port.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Endpoint {
    address: &'static str,
    port: u16,
}

impl fmt::Display for Endpoint {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{}:{}", self.address, self.port)
    }
}

/// One established connection: the bytes received and not yet read, the size
/// of the receive buffer, and whether the sender has finished.
struct Socket {
    received: VecDeque<u8>,
    capacity: usize,
    finished: bool,
}

impl Socket {
    /// The free space of the receive buffer: the number of bytes the sender
    /// may still send.
    fn window(&self) -> usize {
        self.capacity - self.received.len()
    }
}

/// Identifies a connection on this machine: the remote endpoint and the local
/// port. With the local address, which the model leaves out, it forms the 4
/// values that identify a TCP connection.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Key {
    remote: Endpoint,
    port: u16,
}

/// Accepts connections on a port. `queue` holds the connections that are
/// established and have not been returned by accept.
struct Listener {
    backlog: usize,
    queue: VecDeque<Key>,
}

/// The TCP state of a machine.
struct Stack {
    listeners: HashMap<u16, Listener>,
    connections: HashMap<Key, Socket>,
    buffer_size: usize,
}

/// A packet of TCP. `syn` opens a connection and `fin` ends the sender's
/// stream.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Segment {
    syn: bool,
    fin: bool,
    data: &'static str,
}

impl Stack {
    /// Handles a segment that arrives from `from` for local port `port`, and
    /// describes the result. A segment belongs to the connection with its
    /// remote endpoint and local port. Only when no such connection exists,
    /// and the segment is a SYN, is the listener on the port consulted.
    fn receive(&mut self, from: Endpoint, port: u16, segment: &Segment) -> String {
        let id = Key { remote: from, port };

        if let Some(socket) = self.connections.get_mut(&id) {
            return socket.deliver(segment);
        }

        if !segment.syn {
            return "reset, no connection".into();
        }

        let Some(listener) = self.listeners.get_mut(&port) else {
            return "reset, no listener on the port".into();
        };

        if listener.queue.len() == listener.backlog {
            return "dropped, the accept queue is full".into();
        }

        let socket = Socket {
            received: VecDeque::new(),
            capacity: self.buffer_size,
            finished: false,
        };

        self.connections.insert(id, socket);
        listener.queue.push_back(id);

        format!("established, accept queue {}", listener.queue.len())
    }
}

impl Socket {
    /// Puts the data of a segment into the receive buffer, up to the window,
    /// and records a FIN.
    fn deliver(&mut self, segment: &Segment) -> String {
        if segment.fin {
            self.finished = true;

            return "the sender's stream has ended".into();
        }

        let accepted = segment.data.len().min(self.window());
        self.received.extend(&segment.data.as_bytes()[..accepted]);

        format!("accepted {accepted}, window {}", self.window())
    }
}

impl Stack {
    /// Removes the oldest connection from the accept queue of a port.
    fn accept(&mut self, port: u16) -> Option<Key> {
        self.listeners.get_mut(&port)?.queue.pop_front()
    }
}

impl Socket {
    /// Removes up to `n` bytes from the receive buffer. It returns 0 bytes
    /// with the second value set when the buffer is empty and a FIN has
    /// arrived.
    fn read(&mut self, n: usize) -> (String, bool) {
        let n = n.min(self.received.len());
        let data: Vec<u8> = self.received.drain(..n).collect();

        (
            String::from_utf8_lossy(&data).into_owned(),
            n == 0 && self.finished,
        )
    }
}

fn endpoint(address: &'static str) -> Endpoint {
    Endpoint {
        address,
        port: 5000,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let listener = Listener {
        backlog: 2,
        queue: VecDeque::new(),
    };

    let mut stack = Stack {
        listeners: HashMap::from([(80, listener)]),
        connections: HashMap::new(),
        buffer_size: 8,
    };

    let (a, b, c) = (
        endpoint("10.0.0.1"),
        endpoint("10.0.0.2"),
        endpoint("10.0.0.3"),
    );

    let syn = Segment {
        syn: true,
        ..Segment::default()
    };

    for (from, port) in [(a, 80), (b, 80), (c, 80), (c, 81)] {
        let result = stack.receive(from, port, &syn);
        println!("SYN from {from} to port {port}: {result}");
    }

    if let Some(id) = stack.accept(80) {
        println!("accept on port 80: the connection from {}", id.remote);
    }

    let hello = Segment {
        data: "hello",
        ..Segment::default()
    };

    for from in [b, a, b, c] {
        let result = stack.receive(from, 80, &hello);
        println!("5 bytes from {from} to port 80: {result}");
    }

    let id = Key {
        remote: b,
        port: 80,
    };

    if let Some(socket) = stack.connections.get_mut(&id) {
        let (data, _) = socket.read(4);
        println!(
            "read of 4 bytes on the connection from {b}: {data:?}, window {}",
            socket.window()
        );
    }

    let fin = Segment {
        fin: true,
        ..Segment::default()
    };

    println!("FIN from {b}: {}", stack.receive(b, 80, &fin));

    if let Some(socket) = stack.connections.get_mut(&id) {
        for _ in 0..2 {
            let (data, ended) = socket.read(16);
            println!("read: {data:?}, stream ended {ended}");
        }
    }
}

Summary

  • A socket is a descriptor for the endpoint of a connection. The kernel keeps a send buffer and a receive buffer behind it.
  • The kernel completes the handshake of a connection and queues it on the listener. accept returns a new descriptor for a queued connection.
  • A connection is identified by local address, local port, remote address and remote port. Connections accepted from a listener share its port.
  • TCP is a stream of bytes. The boundaries of write calls are not preserved.
  • The receiver reports the free space of its receive buffer as the window, and the sender transmits no more than that. A receiver that does not read stops the sender.
  • A closed peer is reported by a read that returns 0. Writing to it fails with EPIPE after the peer’s kernel has answered with a reset.

References

  • tcp(7), socket(7) and listen(2), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/tcp.7.html
  • W. R. Stevens, B. Fenner, A. M. Rudoff, UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1, 3rd edition, Addison-Wesley, 2003.
  • RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293
  • net/ipv4/tcp_input.c and net/ipv4/inet_hashtables.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c

Namespaces

A namespace is a kernel object that gives a group of processes their own instance of a global resource: their own process numbers, their own host name, their own mounted file systems, or their own network interfaces. Processes inside a namespace see and change the instance of that namespace, and processes outside are unaffected. Namespaces are the isolation half of a container. Chapter 12 covers the other half, limits.

In this chapter, we will learn how a process enters a new namespace and what changes for it. We will first measure a child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces with nsfacts. Then we will write nsmodel, a model of nested PID namespaces and of the UTS namespace.

This chapter covers

  • the kinds of namespace and what each isolates
  • how to see the namespaces of a process under /proc
  • the kernel structures: struct nsproxy, struct pid and struct upid
  • how a process is placed in a new namespace: clone flags, unshare and setns
  • the user namespace: why an unprivileged user can be user 0 inside
  • the PID namespace: a process has a number at every level
  • which processes a PID namespace can see
  • the UTS namespace and the host name
  • what the mount and network namespaces isolate

The kinds of namespace

Linux 5.15 has 8 kinds of namespace. Every process is in exactly 1 namespace of each kind, and a child starts in the namespaces of its parent. On a system without containers all processes share 1 namespace of each kind, and the resources appear global.

KindIsolatesA process in a new one sees
pidprocess numbersonly the processes of the namespace, numbered from 1
mntthe list of mounted file systemsa copy of the parent’s mounts, which it can change privately (chapter 13)
utsthe host namea copy of the host name, which it can change
netnetwork interfaces, addresses, routes, portsa loopback interface that is down, and nothing else
useruser and group numbers, and capabilitiesits own numbering of users, mapped to the numbers outside
ipcshared memory segments and message queuesnone of the objects outside
cgroupthe root of the control group treeits own group as the root (chapter 12)
timethe offsets of the monotonic and boot clocksclocks that can be shifted

The kernel shows the namespaces of a process as symbolic links:

$ ls -l /proc/self/ns
cgroup -> cgroup:[4026531835]
ipc -> ipc:[4026531839]
mnt -> mnt:[4026531841]
net -> net:[4026531840]
pid -> pid:[4026531836]
pid_for_children -> pid:[4026531836]
time -> time:[4026531834]
user -> user:[4026531837]
uts -> uts:[4026531838]

The number in brackets identifies the namespace. Processes that show the same number for a kind are in the same namespace of that kind. pid_for_children is the PID namespace that children of the process will be created in, which can differ from the one the process itself is in.

The kernel’s structures

A task refers to its namespaces through struct nsproxy. This is the complete definition from include/linux/nsproxy.h of Linux 5.15, with comments added.

struct nsproxy {
        atomic_t count;                        /* tasks that share this nsproxy */
        struct uts_namespace *uts_ns;
        struct ipc_namespace *ipc_ns;
        struct mnt_namespace *mnt_ns;
        struct pid_namespace *pid_ns_for_children;
        struct net *net_ns;
        struct time_namespace *time_ns;
        struct time_namespace *time_ns_for_children;
        struct cgroup_namespace *cgroup_ns;
};

The structure is a set of pointers, 1 for each kind. Processes that are in the same namespaces share a single nsproxy. The user namespace is absent from the list: it is reached through the credentials of the task, task->cred->user_ns, because it decides what the task is permitted to do.

The PID namespace of a task is recorded in a different place, together with its numbers. These are the definitions from include/linux/pid.h and include/linux/pid_namespace.h.

struct upid {
        int nr;                                /* the number in 1 namespace */
        struct pid_namespace *ns;              /* that namespace */
};

struct pid {
        unsigned int level;                    /* depth of the task's PID namespace */
        struct upid numbers[1];                /* 1 entry per level, 0 to level */
        /* ... */
};

struct pid_namespace {
        struct task_struct *child_reaper;      /* its process 1, which adopts orphans */
        unsigned int level;                    /* 0 for the root namespace */
        struct pid_namespace *parent;          /* the enclosing namespace */
        struct user_namespace *user_ns;        /* the user namespace that owns it */
        /* ... */
};
FieldMeaning
struct pidWhat task_struct.thread_pid points to: the identity of a task in every PID namespace that can see it.
numbersAn array with level + 1 entries. numbers[0] is the number in the root namespace, and numbers[level] is the number in the task’s own namespace.
child_reaperThe first process of the namespace. Orphans of the namespace are given to it (chapter 3).
parent, levelPID namespaces form a tree, and level is the depth in it.
user_nsEvery namespace is owned by a user namespace. A process needs privilege in the owner to change the namespace.

Entering a namespace

A process gets into a namespace in 3 ways.

CallEffect
clone with flags such as CLONE_NEWUTScreates a child that starts in new namespaces of the given kinds
unshare with the same flagsmoves the calling process into new namespaces
setns with a descriptor for /proc/<pid>/ns/<kind>moves the calling process into an existing namespace; this is how docker exec enters a running container

A namespace exists for as long as something refers to it: a process that is in it, or an open descriptor for its /proc link. When the last process leaves, the namespace is destroyed.

User namespaces

Creating a namespace requires a capability. Linux divides the power of the administrator into separate capabilities, and the one needed here is CAP_SYS_ADMIN. There is a single exception: any user may create a user namespace. Inside it, the kernel maps user numbers. The creator can map user 0 inside to its own user number outside, and it then holds all privileges over the resources that the user namespace owns, which include the other namespaces created together with it. Toward everything outside, it remains the unprivileged user it was. This is what lets an ordinary user start a container.

The mapping is written to /proc/<pid>/uid_map, a line of 3 numbers: the first user number inside, the first user number outside, and the count of numbers mapped. In the root namespace every number maps to itself:

$ cat /proc/self/uid_map
         0          0 4294967295

In the namespace that nsfacts creates below, the line is 0 1000 1: user 0 inside is user 1000 outside, and no other number is mapped.

The capabilities a process holds inside a user namespace are checked against the owner of the object it acts on. It may set the host name of a UTS namespace that its user namespace owns. It may not set the clock of the machine, mount a disk, or read a file that user 1000 cannot read, because those belong to the root user namespace.

User 0 inside a user namespace is an ordinary user outside it. The privilege ends at the edge of the namespace.

Measuring namespaces

nsfacts uses golang.org/x/sys/unix in Go and the nix crate with the hostname, sched and user features in Rust.

$ cargo new nsfacts
$ cargo add -p nsfacts nix --features hostname,sched,user

The kernel shows the namespaces of a process as symbolic links under /proc/<pid>/ns. The target of a link, such as uts:[4026531838], names the namespace, and processes with equal targets are in the same namespace.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::env;
use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::process::{self, Command};

use nix::sched::{CloneFlags, unshare};
use nix::unistd::{getgid, gethostname, getpid, getuid, sethostname};

Listing 11.3 Reading the namespaces of a process, in Go. code/go/nsfacts/main.go

// kinds are the namespace types of Linux 5.15, as named under /proc/<pid>/ns.
var kinds = []string{"cgroup", "ipc", "mnt", "net", "pid", "time", "user", "uts"}

// namespaces returns the identity of each namespace of a process. The kernel
// shows it as the target of a symbolic link, such as "uts:[4026531838]".
// Processes are in the same namespace when the targets are equal.
func namespaces(pid string) (map[string]string, error) {
	ids := map[string]string{}

	for _, kind := range kinds {
		id, err := os.Readlink("/proc/" + pid + "/ns/" + kind)

		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}

		ids[kind] = id
	}

	return ids, nil
}

Listing 11.4 Reading the namespaces of a process, in Rust. code/rust/nsfacts/src/main.rs

/// The namespace types of Linux 5.15, as named under `/proc/<pid>/ns`.
const KINDS: [&str; 8] = ["cgroup", "ipc", "mnt", "net", "pid", "time", "user", "uts"];

/// Returns the identity of each namespace of a process. The kernel shows it
/// as the target of a symbolic link, such as `uts:[4026531838]`.
/// Processes are in the same namespace when the targets are equal.
fn namespaces(pid: &str) -> io::Result<HashMap<&'static str, String>> {
    KINDS
        .iter()
        .map(|&kind| {
            let id = fs::read_link(format!("/proc/{pid}/ns/{kind}"))?;

            Ok((kind, id.to_string_lossy().into_owned()))
        })
        .collect()
}

fn hostname() -> io::Result<String> {
    Ok(gethostname()?.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
}

The program runs itself again as a child with the argument inside. The child tries to set the host name to box and prints what it sees.

Listing 11.5 What the child reports, in Go. code/go/nsfacts/main.go

// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EPERM.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}

// inside runs in the child. It tries to change the host name, and prints
// what it sees as key=value lines for the parent to read.
func inside() error {
	outcome := "succeeds"

	if err := unix.Sethostname([]byte("box")); err != nil {
		outcome = "fails with " + name(err)
	}

	host, err := os.Hostname()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	ids, err := namespaces("self")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	uidMap, err := os.ReadFile("/proc/self/uid_map")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("sethostname=%s\nhostname=%s\npid=%d\nuid=%d\n", outcome, host, os.Getpid(), os.Getuid())
	fmt.Printf("map=%s\nuts=%s\npidns=%s\n", strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(uidMap)), " "), ids["uts"], ids["pid"])

	return nil
}

Listing 11.6 What the child reports, in Rust. code/rust/nsfacts/src/main.rs

/// Runs in the child. It tries to change the host name, and prints what it
/// sees as key=value lines for the parent to read.
fn inside() -> io::Result<()> {
    let outcome = match sethostname("box") {
        Ok(()) => "succeeds".to_owned(),
        Err(error) => format!("fails with {error:?}"),
    };

    let ids = namespaces("self")?;
    let uid_map = fs::read_to_string("/proc/self/uid_map")?;
    let uid_map: Vec<&str> = uid_map.split_whitespace().collect();

    println!("sethostname={outcome}");
    println!("hostname={}", hostname()?);
    println!("pid={}", getpid());
    println!("uid={}", getuid());
    println!("map={}", uid_map.join(" "));
    println!("uts={}", ids["uts"]);
    println!("pidns={}", ids["pid"]);

    Ok(())
}

The child is started once in the parent’s namespaces and once in new user, UTS and PID namespaces. The languages create the namespaces differently. Go’s SysProcAttr passes the clone flags and the user mappings to the call that creates the child. unshare of a user namespace is refused in a process with several threads, which a Go program always is. The Rust program is single-threaded, so its helper process calls unshare, writes the mappings to /proc/self/uid_map and /proc/self/gid_map, and then starts the child.

Listing 11.7 Starting the child in new namespaces, in Go. code/go/nsfacts/main.go

// report runs this program again as a child and returns the lines the child
// prints, as a map. With isolate set, the child is created in new user, UTS
// and PID namespaces, and user 0 inside is mapped to the current user.
func report(isolate bool) (map[string]string, error) {
	child := exec.Command("/proc/self/exe", "inside")
	child.Stderr = os.Stderr

	if isolate {
		child.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{
			Cloneflags:  syscall.CLONE_NEWUSER | syscall.CLONE_NEWUTS | syscall.CLONE_NEWPID,
			UidMappings: []syscall.SysProcIDMap{{ContainerID: 0, HostID: os.Getuid(), Size: 1}},
			GidMappings: []syscall.SysProcIDMap{{ContainerID: 0, HostID: os.Getgid(), Size: 1}},
		}
	}

	output, err := child.Output()

	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	seen := map[string]string{}

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader(string(output))); lines.Scan(); {
		if key, value, ok := strings.Cut(lines.Text(), "="); ok {
			seen[key] = value
		}
	}

	return seen, nil
}

Listing 11.8 Starting the child in new namespaces, in Rust. code/rust/nsfacts/src/main.rs

/// Moves this process into new user and UTS namespaces, maps user 0 inside to
/// the current user, and runs the program again as a child. A new PID
/// namespace applies to the children of the process that asks for it, so the
/// child is the first process of that namespace.
fn isolated() -> io::Result<()> {
    let (uid, gid) = (getuid(), getgid());

    unshare(CloneFlags::CLONE_NEWUSER | CloneFlags::CLONE_NEWUTS | CloneFlags::CLONE_NEWPID)?;

    fs::write("/proc/self/setgroups", "deny")?;
    fs::write("/proc/self/uid_map", format!("0 {uid} 1"))?;
    fs::write("/proc/self/gid_map", format!("0 {gid} 1"))?;

    let status = Command::new("/proc/self/exe").arg("inside").status()?;

    process::exit(if status.success() { 0 } else { 1 });
}

/// Runs this program again as a child and returns the lines the child prints,
/// as a map. With `isolate` set, the child is created in new namespaces.
fn report(isolate: bool) -> io::Result<HashMap<String, String>> {
    let mode = if isolate { "isolated" } else { "inside" };
    let output = Command::new("/proc/self/exe").arg(mode).output()?;

    let seen = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)
        .lines()
        .filter_map(|line| line.split_once('='))
        .map(|(key, value)| (key.to_owned(), value.to_owned()))
        .collect();

    Ok(seen)
}

Listing 11.9 Comparing the child with the parent, in Go. code/go/nsfacts/main.go

func run() error {
	mine, err := namespaces("self")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	name, err := os.Hostname()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for _, isolate := range []bool{false, true} {
		seen, err := report(isolate)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		after, err := os.Hostname()

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		fmt.Printf("child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces: %v\n", isolate)
		fmt.Printf("  same UTS namespace as the parent %v, same PID namespace %v\n",
			seen["uts"] == mine["uts"], seen["pidns"] == mine["pid"])
		fmt.Printf("  sethostname %s; host name inside is \"box\" %v, outside unchanged %v\n",
			seen["sethostname"], seen["hostname"] == "box", after == name)
		fmt.Printf("  pid inside is 1 %v; uid inside is 0 %v\n", seen["pid"] == "1", seen["uid"] == "0")

		if fields := strings.Fields(seen["map"]); isolate && len(fields) == 3 {
			fmt.Printf("  uid map: user 0 inside is user %s outside\n", fields[1])
		}
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 11.10 Comparing the child with the parent, in Rust. code/rust/nsfacts/src/main.rs

fn run() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mine = namespaces("self")?;
    let name = hostname()?;

    for isolate in [false, true] {
        let seen = report(isolate)?;
        let get = |key: &str| seen.get(key).map_or("", String::as_str);

        println!("child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces: {isolate}");
        println!(
            "  same UTS namespace as the parent {}, same PID namespace {}",
            get("uts") == mine["uts"],
            get("pidns") == mine["pid"]
        );
        println!(
            "  sethostname {}; host name inside is \"box\" {}, outside unchanged {}",
            get("sethostname"),
            get("hostname") == "box",
            hostname()? == name
        );
        println!(
            "  pid inside is 1 {}; uid inside is 0 {}",
            get("pid") == "1",
            get("uid") == "0"
        );

        let map: Vec<&str> = get("map").split_whitespace().collect();

        if let (true, [_, outside, _]) = (isolate, map.as_slice()) {
            println!("  uid map: user 0 inside is user {outside} outside");
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}
child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces: false
  same UTS namespace as the parent true, same PID namespace true
  sethostname fails with EPERM; host name inside is "box" false, outside unchanged true
  pid inside is 1 false; uid inside is 0 false
child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces: true
  same UTS namespace as the parent false, same PID namespace false
  sethostname succeeds; host name inside is "box" true, outside unchanged true
  pid inside is 1 true; uid inside is 0 true
  uid map: user 0 inside is user 1000 outside
OutputConclusion
ordinary child: same namespacesA child inherits the namespaces of its parent.
ordinary child: sethostname fails with EPERMChanging the host name requires privilege, and the user has none.
new namespaces: different UTS and PID namespaceThe flags gave the child its own instances.
sethostname succeeds, and the host name outside is unchangedThe child is privileged over its own UTS namespace, and the change stays inside it.
pid inside is 1The first process of a PID namespace has number 1 there.
uid inside is 0, mapped to 1000 outsideUser 0 inside the user namespace is the ordinary user outside.

The measurement is clearer with the 2 points of view side by side. Nothing about the child process itself differs between the columns. What differs is the answer the kernel gives when it is asked.

PID namespaces

PID namespaces are nested. A new PID namespace is a child of the namespace in which it was created, and a process in it has a process number in its own namespace and in every namespace above it, up to the root. The numbers are independent of each other.

Visibility follows the nesting. A namespace sees the processes in itself and in the namespaces below it. It has no number for a process in a namespace above it or beside it, so it cannot name such a process in kill or find it under /proc.

The first process of a PID namespace takes the role that process 1 has on the whole machine: it adopts the orphans of its namespace, and when it ends, the kernel ends every other process in the namespace.

Low-level design: nsmodel

TypeFieldsMeaning
pidNamespaceparent, level, lasta namespace, its depth below the root, and the last number it gave out
utsNamespacehostnamethe host name of its processes
processpid, uts, numbersits namespaces; its number in each PID namespace from the root down
OperationBehaviour
fork(parent, newPID, newUTS)creates a child in the parent’s namespaces or in new ones; allocates a number at every level
numberIn(namespace)returns the number of a process in a namespace, when the namespace can see it

Modelling namespaces

The Go version links namespaces with pointers. The Rust version keeps them in vectors owned by a Kernel value and refers to them by index.

Listing 11.11 The imports of nsmodel, in Go. code/go/nsmodel/main.go

import "fmt"

Listing 11.12 PID namespaces, UTS namespaces and processes, in Go. code/go/nsmodel/main.go

// A pidNamespace hands out process numbers. level is its depth below the
// root namespace, which has level 0.
type pidNamespace struct {
	parent *pidNamespace
	level  int
	last   int
}

// allocate returns the next unused number of the namespace.
func (ns *pidNamespace) allocate() int {
	ns.last++

	return ns.last
}

// A utsNamespace holds the host name that its processes see.
type utsNamespace struct {
	hostname string
}

// A process belongs to one namespace of each kind. numbers holds its process
// number in every PID namespace from the root, at index 0, down to its own.
type process struct {
	pid     *pidNamespace
	uts     *utsNamespace
	numbers []int
}

Listing 11.13 PID namespaces, UTS namespaces and processes, in Rust. code/rust/nsmodel/src/main.rs

/// Hands out process numbers. `level` is its depth below the root namespace,
/// which has level 0. `parent` is the index of the enclosing namespace.
struct PidNamespace {
    parent: Option<usize>,
    level: usize,
    last: u32,
}

/// A process belongs to one namespace of each kind, named here by its index
/// in the kernel's tables. `numbers` holds its process number in every PID
/// namespace from the root, at index 0, down to its own.
struct Process {
    pid: usize,
    uts: usize,
    numbers: Vec<u32>,
}

/// The namespaces of a machine. A UTS namespace is the host name that its
/// processes see.
struct Kernel {
    pid_namespaces: Vec<PidNamespace>,
    hostnames: Vec<String>,
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns the next unused number of a PID namespace.
    fn allocate(&mut self, namespace: usize) -> u32 {
        self.pid_namespaces[namespace].last += 1;

        self.pid_namespaces[namespace].last
    }
}

fork walks from the child’s PID namespace up to the root and allocates a number in each. A new UTS namespace starts as a copy of the parent’s, so the child initially sees the same host name.

Listing 11.14 Creating a process, with or without new namespaces, in Go. code/go/nsmodel/main.go

// fork creates a child. By default the child is in its parent's namespaces.
// With newPID it is the first process of a new PID namespace below the
// parent's. With newUTS it gets a copy of the parent's UTS namespace.
func fork(parent *process, newPID, newUTS bool) *process {
	child := &process{pid: parent.pid, uts: parent.uts}

	if newPID {
		child.pid = &pidNamespace{parent: parent.pid, level: parent.pid.level + 1}
	}

	if newUTS {
		child.uts = &utsNamespace{hostname: parent.uts.hostname}
	}

	child.numbers = make([]int, child.pid.level+1)

	for ns := child.pid; ns != nil; ns = ns.parent {
		child.numbers[ns.level] = ns.allocate()
	}

	return child
}

Listing 11.15 Creating a process, with or without new namespaces, in Rust. code/rust/nsmodel/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Creates a child. By default the child is in its parent's namespaces.
    /// With `new_pid` it is the first process of a new PID namespace below
    /// the parent's. With `new_uts` it gets a copy of the parent's UTS
    /// namespace.
    fn fork(&mut self, parent: &Process, new_pid: bool, new_uts: bool) -> Process {
        let (mut pid, mut uts) = (parent.pid, parent.uts);

        if new_pid {
            self.pid_namespaces.push(PidNamespace {
                parent: Some(parent.pid),
                level: self.pid_namespaces[parent.pid].level + 1,
                last: 0,
            });
            pid = self.pid_namespaces.len() - 1;
        }

        if new_uts {
            self.hostnames.push(self.hostnames[parent.uts].clone());
            uts = self.hostnames.len() - 1;
        }

        let mut numbers = vec![0; self.pid_namespaces[pid].level + 1];
        let mut namespace = Some(pid);

        while let Some(current) = namespace {
            numbers[self.pid_namespaces[current].level] = self.allocate(current);
            namespace = self.pid_namespaces[current].parent;
        }

        Process { pid, uts, numbers }
    }
}

numberIn decides visibility. It climbs from the process’s own namespace to the level of the asking namespace and checks that it arrives at that namespace.

Listing 11.16 The number of a process in a namespace, in Go. code/go/nsmodel/main.go

// numberIn returns the number by which a process is known in a namespace. A
// process is visible in its own PID namespace and in every namespace that
// encloses it, and in no other.
func (p *process) numberIn(ns *pidNamespace) (int, bool) {
	own := p.pid

	for own != nil && own.level > ns.level {
		own = own.parent
	}

	if own != ns {
		return 0, false
	}

	return p.numbers[ns.level], true
}

// seen describes a process as a namespace sees it.
func seen(p *process, ns *pidNamespace) string {
	if number, ok := p.numberIn(ns); ok {
		return fmt.Sprintf("pid %d", number)
	}

	return "not visible"
}

Listing 11.17 The number of a process in a namespace, in Rust. code/rust/nsmodel/src/main.rs

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns the number by which a process is known in a namespace. A
    /// process is visible in its own PID namespace and in every namespace
    /// that encloses it, and in no other.
    fn number_in(&self, process: &Process, namespace: usize) -> Option<u32> {
        let level = self.pid_namespaces[namespace].level;
        let mut own = Some(process.pid);

        while let Some(current) = own
            && self.pid_namespaces[current].level > level
        {
            own = self.pid_namespaces[current].parent;
        }

        if own != Some(namespace) {
            return None;
        }

        process.numbers.get(level).copied()
    }

    /// Describes a process as a namespace sees it.
    fn seen(&self, process: &Process, namespace: usize) -> String {
        match self.number_in(process, namespace) {
            Some(number) => format!("pid {number}"),
            None => "not visible".to_owned(),
        }
    }
}

Listing 11.18 The trace, in Go. code/go/nsmodel/main.go

func main() {
	root := &pidNamespace{}
	host := &utsNamespace{hostname: "host"}

	first := &process{pid: root, uts: host, numbers: []int{root.allocate()}}
	shell := fork(first, false, false)
	a := fork(shell, true, true)
	child := fork(a, false, false)
	b := fork(shell, true, true)
	nested := fork(child, true, false)

	rows := []struct {
		name string
		p    *process
	}{{"first process", first}, {"shell", shell}, {"first process of A", a}, {"its child", child},
		{"first process of B", b}, {"nested below A", nested}}

	for _, row := range rows {
		fmt.Printf("%-20s numbers from the root namespace down: %v\n", row.name, row.p.numbers)
	}

	fmt.Printf("the first process of B, seen from the root namespace: %s\n", seen(b, root))
	fmt.Printf("the first process of B, seen from A: %s\n", seen(b, a.pid))
	fmt.Printf("the shell, seen from A: %s\n", seen(shell, a.pid))
	fmt.Printf("the nested process, seen from A: %s\n", seen(nested, a.pid))

	a.uts.hostname = "box"
	fmt.Printf("host name set to \"box\" in A: A sees %q, its child %q, B %q, the shell %q\n",
		a.uts.hostname, child.uts.hostname, b.uts.hostname, shell.uts.hostname)
}

/// Formats numbers the way Go prints a slice.
fn list(numbers: &[u32]) -> String {
    let words: Vec<String> = numbers.iter().map(u32::to_string).collect();

    format!("[{}]", words.join(" "))
}

fn main() {
    let root = PidNamespace {
        parent: None,
        level: 0,
        last: 0,
    };

    let mut kernel = Kernel {
        pid_namespaces: vec![root],
        hostnames: vec!["host".to_owned()],
    };

    let first = Process {
        pid: 0,
        uts: 0,
        numbers: vec![kernel.allocate(0)],
    };

    let shell = kernel.fork(&first, false, false);
    let a = kernel.fork(&shell, true, true);
    let child = kernel.fork(&a, false, false);
    let b = kernel.fork(&shell, true, true);
    let nested = kernel.fork(&child, true, false);

    let rows = [
        ("first process", &first),
        ("shell", &shell),
        ("first process of A", &a),
        ("its child", &child),
        ("first process of B", &b),
        ("nested below A", &nested),
    ];

    for (name, process) in rows {
        println!(
            "{name:<20} numbers from the root namespace down: {}",
            list(&process.numbers)
        );
    }

    println!(
        "the first process of B, seen from the root namespace: {}",
        kernel.seen(&b, 0)
    );
    println!(
        "the first process of B, seen from A: {}",
        kernel.seen(&b, a.pid)
    );
    println!("the shell, seen from A: {}", kernel.seen(&shell, a.pid));
    println!(
        "the nested process, seen from A: {}",
        kernel.seen(&nested, a.pid)
    );

    kernel.hostnames[a.uts] = "box".to_owned();
    println!(
        "host name set to \"box\" in A: A sees {:?}, its child {:?}, B {:?}, the shell {:?}",
        kernel.hostnames[a.uts],
        kernel.hostnames[child.uts],
        kernel.hostnames[b.uts],
        kernel.hostnames[shell.uts]
    );
}
