Correspondence with the kernel source. A process refers to its namespaces through struct nsproxy (include/linux/nsproxy.h), with a pointer for each kind. The numbers of a process are in struct pid (include/linux/pid.h), whose array numbers has an entry for each level, as in the model. pid_nr_ns is the kernel’s numberIn. copy_namespaces in kernel/nsproxy.c handles the clone flags, and zap_pid_ns_processes ends a namespace when its first process ends.

Inspecting namespaces on a live system

CommandShows
ls -l /proc/<pid>/nsthe namespaces of a process
lsnsevery namespace of the system, with the number of processes in it
cat /proc/<pid>/uid_mapthe user mapping of the user namespace of a process
unshare --user --map-root-user --uts --pid --fork shstarts a shell in new namespaces, as nsfacts does
nsenter --target <pid> --uts --pid shstarts a shell in the namespaces of another process, with setns
cat /proc/sys/user/max_user_namespaceshow many user namespaces a user may create: 61507 here

Comparing the links of 2 processes is the quickest way to learn whether they are in the same container.

The complete programs

Listing 11.20 The complete nsfacts, in Go. code/go/nsfacts/main.go

// Command nsfacts measures namespaces. It compares the namespaces of a
// process with those of an ordinary child, and then starts a child in new
// user, UTS and PID namespaces and reports what that child sees.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./nsfacts
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
	"syscall"

	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
)


// kinds are the namespace types of Linux 5.15, as named under /proc/<pid>/ns.
var kinds = []string{"cgroup", "ipc", "mnt", "net", "pid", "time", "user", "uts"}

// namespaces returns the identity of each namespace of a process. The kernel
// shows it as the target of a symbolic link, such as "uts:[4026531838]".
// Processes are in the same namespace when the targets are equal.
func namespaces(pid string) (map[string]string, error) {
	ids := map[string]string{}

	for _, kind := range kinds {
		id, err := os.Readlink("/proc/" + pid + "/ns/" + kind)

		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}

		ids[kind] = id
	}

	return ids, nil
}


// name returns the symbolic name of a system call error, such as EPERM.
func name(err error) string {
	var errno unix.Errno

	if errors.As(err, &errno) {
		return unix.ErrnoName(errno)
	}

	return fmt.Sprint(err)
}

// inside runs in the child. It tries to change the host name, and prints
// what it sees as key=value lines for the parent to read.
func inside() error {
	outcome := "succeeds"

	if err := unix.Sethostname([]byte("box")); err != nil {
		outcome = "fails with " + name(err)
	}

	host, err := os.Hostname()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	ids, err := namespaces("self")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	uidMap, err := os.ReadFile("/proc/self/uid_map")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("sethostname=%s\nhostname=%s\npid=%d\nuid=%d\n", outcome, host, os.Getpid(), os.Getuid())
	fmt.Printf("map=%s\nuts=%s\npidns=%s\n", strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(uidMap)), " "), ids["uts"], ids["pid"])

	return nil
}


// report runs this program again as a child and returns the lines the child
// prints, as a map. With isolate set, the child is created in new user, UTS
// and PID namespaces, and user 0 inside is mapped to the current user.
func report(isolate bool) (map[string]string, error) {
	child := exec.Command("/proc/self/exe", "inside")
	child.Stderr = os.Stderr

	if isolate {
		child.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{
			Cloneflags:  syscall.CLONE_NEWUSER | syscall.CLONE_NEWUTS | syscall.CLONE_NEWPID,
			UidMappings: []syscall.SysProcIDMap{{ContainerID: 0, HostID: os.Getuid(), Size: 1}},
			GidMappings: []syscall.SysProcIDMap{{ContainerID: 0, HostID: os.Getgid(), Size: 1}},
		}
	}

	output, err := child.Output()

	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	seen := map[string]string{}

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader(string(output))); lines.Scan(); {
		if key, value, ok := strings.Cut(lines.Text(), "="); ok {
			seen[key] = value
		}
	}

	return seen, nil
}


func run() error {
	mine, err := namespaces("self")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	name, err := os.Hostname()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for _, isolate := range []bool{false, true} {
		seen, err := report(isolate)

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		after, err := os.Hostname()

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		fmt.Printf("child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces: %v\n", isolate)
		fmt.Printf("  same UTS namespace as the parent %v, same PID namespace %v\n",
			seen["uts"] == mine["uts"], seen["pidns"] == mine["pid"])
		fmt.Printf("  sethostname %s; host name inside is \"box\" %v, outside unchanged %v\n",
			seen["sethostname"], seen["hostname"] == "box", after == name)
		fmt.Printf("  pid inside is 1 %v; uid inside is 0 %v\n", seen["pid"] == "1", seen["uid"] == "0")

		if fields := strings.Fields(seen["map"]); isolate && len(fields) == 3 {
			fmt.Printf("  uid map: user 0 inside is user %s outside\n", fields[1])
		}
	}

	return nil
}


func main() {
	if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "inside" {
		if err := inside(); err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}

		return
	}

	if err := run(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

Listing 11.21 The complete nsfacts, in Rust. code/rust/nsfacts/src/main.rs

//! Measures namespaces. It compares the namespaces of a process with those of
//! an ordinary child, and then starts a child in new user, UTS and PID
//! namespaces and reports what that child sees.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p nsfacts
//! ```

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::env;
use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::process::{self, Command};

use nix::sched::{CloneFlags, unshare};
use nix::unistd::{getgid, gethostname, getpid, getuid, sethostname};

/// The namespace types of Linux 5.15, as named under `/proc/<pid>/ns`.
const KINDS: [&str; 8] = ["cgroup", "ipc", "mnt", "net", "pid", "time", "user", "uts"];

/// Returns the identity of each namespace of a process. The kernel shows it
/// as the target of a symbolic link, such as `uts:[4026531838]`.
/// Processes are in the same namespace when the targets are equal.
fn namespaces(pid: &str) -> io::Result<HashMap<&'static str, String>> {
    KINDS
        .iter()
        .map(|&kind| {
            let id = fs::read_link(format!("/proc/{pid}/ns/{kind}"))?;

            Ok((kind, id.to_string_lossy().into_owned()))
        })
        .collect()
}

fn hostname() -> io::Result<String> {
    Ok(gethostname()?.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
}

/// Runs in the child. It tries to change the host name, and prints what it
/// sees as key=value lines for the parent to read.
fn inside() -> io::Result<()> {
    let outcome = match sethostname("box") {
        Ok(()) => "succeeds".to_owned(),
        Err(error) => format!("fails with {error:?}"),
    };

    let ids = namespaces("self")?;
    let uid_map = fs::read_to_string("/proc/self/uid_map")?;
    let uid_map: Vec<&str> = uid_map.split_whitespace().collect();

    println!("sethostname={outcome}");
    println!("hostname={}", hostname()?);
    println!("pid={}", getpid());
    println!("uid={}", getuid());
    println!("map={}", uid_map.join(" "));
    println!("uts={}", ids["uts"]);
    println!("pidns={}", ids["pid"]);

    Ok(())
}

/// Moves this process into new user and UTS namespaces, maps user 0 inside to
/// the current user, and runs the program again as a child. A new PID
/// namespace applies to the children of the process that asks for it, so the
/// child is the first process of that namespace.
fn isolated() -> io::Result<()> {
    let (uid, gid) = (getuid(), getgid());

    unshare(CloneFlags::CLONE_NEWUSER | CloneFlags::CLONE_NEWUTS | CloneFlags::CLONE_NEWPID)?;

    fs::write("/proc/self/setgroups", "deny")?;
    fs::write("/proc/self/uid_map", format!("0 {uid} 1"))?;
    fs::write("/proc/self/gid_map", format!("0 {gid} 1"))?;

    let status = Command::new("/proc/self/exe").arg("inside").status()?;

    process::exit(if status.success() { 0 } else { 1 });
}

/// Runs this program again as a child and returns the lines the child prints,
/// as a map. With `isolate` set, the child is created in new namespaces.
fn report(isolate: bool) -> io::Result<HashMap<String, String>> {
    let mode = if isolate { "isolated" } else { "inside" };
    let output = Command::new("/proc/self/exe").arg(mode).output()?;

    let seen = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)
        .lines()
        .filter_map(|line| line.split_once('='))
        .map(|(key, value)| (key.to_owned(), value.to_owned()))
        .collect();

    Ok(seen)
}

fn run() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mine = namespaces("self")?;
    let name = hostname()?;

    for isolate in [false, true] {
        let seen = report(isolate)?;
        let get = |key: &str| seen.get(key).map_or("", String::as_str);

        println!("child in new user, UTS and PID namespaces: {isolate}");
        println!(
            "  same UTS namespace as the parent {}, same PID namespace {}",
            get("uts") == mine["uts"],
            get("pidns") == mine["pid"]
        );
        println!(
            "  sethostname {}; host name inside is \"box\" {}, outside unchanged {}",
            get("sethostname"),
            get("hostname") == "box",
            hostname()? == name
        );
        println!(
            "  pid inside is 1 {}; uid inside is 0 {}",
            get("pid") == "1",
            get("uid") == "0"
        );

        let map: Vec<&str> = get("map").split_whitespace().collect();

        if let (true, [_, outside, _]) = (isolate, map.as_slice()) {
            println!("  uid map: user 0 inside is user {outside} outside");
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    match env::args().nth(1).as_deref() {
        Some("inside") => inside(),
        Some("isolated") => isolated(),
        _ => run(),
    }
}

Listing 11.22 The complete nsmodel, in Go. code/go/nsmodel/main.go

// Command nsmodel models 2 kinds of namespace. A PID namespace gives its
// processes their own process numbers, and every process also has a number
// in each enclosing namespace. A UTS namespace holds a host name.
//
// Run it from code/go with:
//
//	go run ./nsmodel
package main

import "fmt"


// A pidNamespace hands out process numbers. level is its depth below the
// root namespace, which has level 0.
type pidNamespace struct {
	parent *pidNamespace
	level  int
	last   int
}

// allocate returns the next unused number of the namespace.
func (ns *pidNamespace) allocate() int {
	ns.last++

	return ns.last
}

// A utsNamespace holds the host name that its processes see.
type utsNamespace struct {
	hostname string
}

// A process belongs to one namespace of each kind. numbers holds its process
// number in every PID namespace from the root, at index 0, down to its own.
type process struct {
	pid     *pidNamespace
	uts     *utsNamespace
	numbers []int
}


// fork creates a child. By default the child is in its parent's namespaces.
// With newPID it is the first process of a new PID namespace below the
// parent's. With newUTS it gets a copy of the parent's UTS namespace.
func fork(parent *process, newPID, newUTS bool) *process {
	child := &process{pid: parent.pid, uts: parent.uts}

	if newPID {
		child.pid = &pidNamespace{parent: parent.pid, level: parent.pid.level + 1}
	}

	if newUTS {
		child.uts = &utsNamespace{hostname: parent.uts.hostname}
	}

	child.numbers = make([]int, child.pid.level+1)

	for ns := child.pid; ns != nil; ns = ns.parent {
		child.numbers[ns.level] = ns.allocate()
	}

	return child
}


// numberIn returns the number by which a process is known in a namespace. A
// process is visible in its own PID namespace and in every namespace that
// encloses it, and in no other.
func (p *process) numberIn(ns *pidNamespace) (int, bool) {
	own := p.pid

	for own != nil && own.level > ns.level {
		own = own.parent
	}

	if own != ns {
		return 0, false
	}

	return p.numbers[ns.level], true
}

// seen describes a process as a namespace sees it.
func seen(p *process, ns *pidNamespace) string {
	if number, ok := p.numberIn(ns); ok {
		return fmt.Sprintf("pid %d", number)
	}

	return "not visible"
}


func main() {
	root := &pidNamespace{}
	host := &utsNamespace{hostname: "host"}

	first := &process{pid: root, uts: host, numbers: []int{root.allocate()}}
	shell := fork(first, false, false)
	a := fork(shell, true, true)
	child := fork(a, false, false)
	b := fork(shell, true, true)
	nested := fork(child, true, false)

	rows := []struct {
		name string
		p    *process
	}{{"first process", first}, {"shell", shell}, {"first process of A", a}, {"its child", child},
		{"first process of B", b}, {"nested below A", nested}}

	for _, row := range rows {
		fmt.Printf("%-20s numbers from the root namespace down: %v\n", row.name, row.p.numbers)
	}

	fmt.Printf("the first process of B, seen from the root namespace: %s\n", seen(b, root))
	fmt.Printf("the first process of B, seen from A: %s\n", seen(b, a.pid))
	fmt.Printf("the shell, seen from A: %s\n", seen(shell, a.pid))
	fmt.Printf("the nested process, seen from A: %s\n", seen(nested, a.pid))

	a.uts.hostname = "box"
	fmt.Printf("host name set to \"box\" in A: A sees %q, its child %q, B %q, the shell %q\n",
		a.uts.hostname, child.uts.hostname, b.uts.hostname, shell.uts.hostname)
}

Listing 11.23 The complete nsmodel, in Rust. code/rust/nsmodel/src/main.rs

//! Models 2 kinds of namespace. A PID namespace gives its processes their own
//! process numbers, and every process also has a number in each enclosing
//! namespace. A UTS namespace holds a host name.
//!
//! Run it from code/rust with:
//!
//! ```text
//! cargo run -p nsmodel
//! ```

/// Hands out process numbers. `level` is its depth below the root namespace,
/// which has level 0. `parent` is the index of the enclosing namespace.
struct PidNamespace {
    parent: Option<usize>,
    level: usize,
    last: u32,
}

/// A process belongs to one namespace of each kind, named here by its index
/// in the kernel's tables. `numbers` holds its process number in every PID
/// namespace from the root, at index 0, down to its own.
struct Process {
    pid: usize,
    uts: usize,
    numbers: Vec<u32>,
}

/// The namespaces of a machine. A UTS namespace is the host name that its
/// processes see.
struct Kernel {
    pid_namespaces: Vec<PidNamespace>,
    hostnames: Vec<String>,
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns the next unused number of a PID namespace.
    fn allocate(&mut self, namespace: usize) -> u32 {
        self.pid_namespaces[namespace].last += 1;

        self.pid_namespaces[namespace].last
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Creates a child. By default the child is in its parent's namespaces.
    /// With `new_pid` it is the first process of a new PID namespace below
    /// the parent's. With `new_uts` it gets a copy of the parent's UTS
    /// namespace.
    fn fork(&mut self, parent: &Process, new_pid: bool, new_uts: bool) -> Process {
        let (mut pid, mut uts) = (parent.pid, parent.uts);

        if new_pid {
            self.pid_namespaces.push(PidNamespace {
                parent: Some(parent.pid),
                level: self.pid_namespaces[parent.pid].level + 1,
                last: 0,
            });
            pid = self.pid_namespaces.len() - 1;
        }

        if new_uts {
            self.hostnames.push(self.hostnames[parent.uts].clone());
            uts = self.hostnames.len() - 1;
        }

        let mut numbers = vec![0; self.pid_namespaces[pid].level + 1];
        let mut namespace = Some(pid);

        while let Some(current) = namespace {
            numbers[self.pid_namespaces[current].level] = self.allocate(current);
            namespace = self.pid_namespaces[current].parent;
        }

        Process { pid, uts, numbers }
    }
}

impl Kernel {
    /// Returns the number by which a process is known in a namespace. A
    /// process is visible in its own PID namespace and in every namespace
    /// that encloses it, and in no other.
    fn number_in(&self, process: &Process, namespace: usize) -> Option<u32> {
        let level = self.pid_namespaces[namespace].level;
        let mut own = Some(process.pid);

        while let Some(current) = own
            && self.pid_namespaces[current].level > level
        {
            own = self.pid_namespaces[current].parent;
        }

        if own != Some(namespace) {
            return None;
        }

        process.numbers.get(level).copied()
    }

    /// Describes a process as a namespace sees it.
    fn seen(&self, process: &Process, namespace: usize) -> String {
        match self.number_in(process, namespace) {
            Some(number) => format!("pid {number}"),
            None => "not visible".to_owned(),
        }
    }
}

/// Formats numbers the way Go prints a slice.
fn list(numbers: &[u32]) -> String {
    let words: Vec<String> = numbers.iter().map(u32::to_string).collect();

    format!("[{}]", words.join(" "))
}

fn main() {
    let root = PidNamespace {
        parent: None,
        level: 0,
        last: 0,
    };

    let mut kernel = Kernel {
        pid_namespaces: vec![root],
        hostnames: vec!["host".to_owned()],
    };

    let first = Process {
        pid: 0,
        uts: 0,
        numbers: vec![kernel.allocate(0)],
    };

    let shell = kernel.fork(&first, false, false);
    let a = kernel.fork(&shell, true, true);
    let child = kernel.fork(&a, false, false);
    let b = kernel.fork(&shell, true, true);
    let nested = kernel.fork(&child, true, false);

    let rows = [
        ("first process", &first),
        ("shell", &shell),
        ("first process of A", &a),
        ("its child", &child),
        ("first process of B", &b),
        ("nested below A", &nested),
    ];

    for (name, process) in rows {
        println!(
            "{name:<20} numbers from the root namespace down: {}",
            list(&process.numbers)
        );
    }

    println!(
        "the first process of B, seen from the root namespace: {}",
        kernel.seen(&b, 0)
    );
    println!(
        "the first process of B, seen from A: {}",
        kernel.seen(&b, a.pid)
    );
    println!("the shell, seen from A: {}", kernel.seen(&shell, a.pid));
    println!(
        "the nested process, seen from A: {}",
        kernel.seen(&nested, a.pid)
    );

    kernel.hostnames[a.uts] = "box".to_owned();
    println!(
        "host name set to \"box\" in A: A sees {:?}, its child {:?}, B {:?}, the shell {:?}",
        kernel.hostnames[a.uts],
        kernel.hostnames[child.uts],
        kernel.hostnames[b.uts],
        kernel.hostnames[shell.uts]
    );
}

Summary

  • A namespace gives a group of processes their own instance of a resource. Linux 5.15 has 8 kinds, and a process is in 1 of each.
  • A child inherits its parent’s namespaces. clone flags and unshare create new ones.
  • An unprivileged user may create a user namespace and be user 0 inside it, with privilege over the namespaces created with it and none outside.
  • A process has a number in its own PID namespace and in every enclosing one. The first process of a PID namespace has number 1 there.
  • A PID namespace sees the processes in itself and below it.
  • A change to the host name stays inside the UTS namespace in which it was made.

References

  • namespaces(7), user_namespaces(7), pid_namespaces(7) and unshare(2), Linux manual pages: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html
  • M. Kerrisk, Namespaces in operation, LWN.net, 2013: https://lwn.net/Articles/531114/
  • kernel/nsproxy.c, kernel/pid_namespace.c and kernel/user_namespace.c, Linux 5.15: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v5.15/source/kernel/nsproxy.c

Control Groups

A control group, or cgroup, is a set of processes that the kernel accounts for and limits as a unit. Where a namespace controls what a process can see, a control group controls how much it can use: how many processes it may contain, how much memory, how much CPU time. Control groups form a tree, and a limit on a group applies to everything below it.

In this chapter, we will learn how processes are placed in a group and how the kernel enforces a limit. We will first create a group and measure 2 limits with cgfacts. Then we will write cgmodel, a model of hierarchical accounting, and follow a fork and an allocation that are stopped by a limit set on a parent group.

This chapter covers

  • the control group file system: groups as directories, settings as files
  • how a process is moved into a group, and where its children start
  • controllers, and which of them a parent passes on to its children
  • the kernel structures: struct cgroup, struct css_set and struct page_counter
  • the checks the kernel makes on fork and on a page fault
  • pids.max: what happens to a fork beyond the limit
  • memory.max: what happens to an allocation beyond the limit
  • hierarchical accounting: a limit covers the whole subtree
  • the CPU and I/O controllers in brief
  • how to read the limits and the usage of a group on a running system

The interface

Control groups have no system calls of their own. The kernel presents them as a file system, mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup. A directory is a group. Creating a directory creates a group, and the kernel fills it with control files.

FileMeaning
cgroup.procsthe processes in the group; writing a pid to it moves that process into the group
cgroup.controllersthe controllers available in this group
cgroup.subtree_controlthe controllers this group passes on to its children
pids.max, memory.maxlimits; the value max means no limit
pids.current, memory.currentthe current usage of the group and its descendants
pids.events, memory.eventscounters of how often a limit was hit

Every process is in exactly 1 group, shown in /proc/<pid>/cgroup. A child process starts in the group of its parent, so a process that has been moved into a group cannot leave the group’s accounting by forking.

A controller is the part of the kernel that accounts for 1 kind of resource: pids, memory, cpu, io. A group has the control files of a controller only when its parent lists that controller in cgroup.subtree_control. On this machine the user’s session is given the memory and pids controllers, which is why the chapter measures those 2.

The group of the shell this chapter was written in, and the controllers available to it:

$ cat /proc/self/cgroup
0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/app-org.gnome.Terminal.slice/vte-spawn-1f7da0d1-a682-46b3-8151-d6603c0e21ae.scope
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers
cpuset cpu io memory hugetlb pids
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice/cgroup.controllers
memory pids

The line in /proc/self/cgroup is a path below /sys/fs/cgroup. Each component is a group, created by the service manager systemd: a group for all users, a group for user 1000, a group for that user’s session manager, and so on down to a group for a single terminal window. The root group has 6 controllers, and the group of user 1000 has received 2 of them.

The counters of a group can be read at any time. For the group of user 1000:

$ cd /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice
$ cat pids.current pids.max
1347
40594
$ cat memory.current memory.max
12315291648
max
$ grep -E '^(anon|file) ' memory.stat
anon 5923209216
file 5730648064

All processes of the user together are 1347 tasks, of 40594 allowed, and use 12.3 GB, with no limit. memory.stat divides the usage by kind: 5.9 GB is anonymous memory of programs, and 5.7 GB is page cache, which is charged to the group whose process first read the file (chapter 8).

The kernel’s structures

A group is a struct cgroup. A task does not point to its group directly. It points to a struct css_set, which holds, for each controller, the state of the group the task belongs to. Tasks in the same groups share a css_set, so fork only has to copy a pointer. These are fields from include/linux/cgroup-defs.h and include/linux/page_counter.h of Linux 5.15.

struct css_set {
        struct cgroup_subsys_state *subsys[CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT]; /* state per controller */
        struct list_head tasks;                /* the tasks that use this set */
        struct cgroup *dfl_cgrp;               /* the group, in the unified tree */
        /* ... */
};

struct cgroup {
        struct cgroup_subsys_state self;       /* links to the parent group */
        int level;                             /* depth in the tree */
        struct kernfs_node *kn;                /* its directory under /sys/fs/cgroup */
        u16 subtree_control;                   /* controllers passed to children */
        struct cgroup_subsys_state *subsys[CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT];
        /* ... */
};

struct cgroup_subsys_state {
        struct cgroup *cgroup;                 /* the group this state belongs to */
        struct cgroup_subsys_state *parent;    /* the same controller, parent group */
        /* ... */
};

struct page_counter {
        atomic_long_t usage;                   /* pages charged: memory.current */
        unsigned long max;                     /* the limit: memory.max */
        struct page_counter *parent;           /* the counter of the parent group */
        /* ... */
};
StructureMeaning
struct cgroupA group: a directory of the control group file system.
struct cgroup_subsys_stateThe state of 1 controller in 1 group. Each controller embeds it in a structure of its own, such as the pids counter or the memory counters. Its parent pointer is what makes accounting hierarchical.
struct css_setThe set of controller states that applies to a task. task_struct.cgroups points to it.
struct page_counterThe memory controller’s counter: a usage, a limit, and a pointer to the counter of the parent group.

Measuring limits

cgfacts needs only the standard libraries. It reads and writes files and starts shell commands.

$ cargo new cgfacts

A group is a path. set and get write and read a control file, and event reads a counter from a file such as pids.events.

Listing 12.1 The imports of cgfacts, in Go. code/go/cgfacts/main.go

import (
	"bufio"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)

Listing 12.2 The imports of cgfacts, in Rust. code/rust/cgfacts/src/main.rs

use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::os::unix::process::ExitStatusExt;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
use std::process::{self, Command};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

Listing 12.3 Reading and writing control files, in Go. code/go/cgfacts/main.go

// A group is the directory of a control group under /sys/fs/cgroup.
type group string

// set writes a value to one of the group's control files.
func (g group) set(file, value string) error {
	return os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(string(g), file), []byte(value), 0)
}

// get reads one of the group's control files.
func (g group) get(file string) (string, error) {
	text, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(string(g), file))

	return strings.TrimSpace(string(text)), err
}

// event returns the counter with the given key from a file of "key value"
// lines, such as pids.events and memory.events.
func (g group) event(file, key string) (string, error) {
	text, err := g.get(file)

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	for lines := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader(text)); lines.Scan(); {
		if fields := strings.Fields(lines.Text()); len(fields) == 2 && fields[0] == key {
			return fields[1], nil
		}
	}

	return "", fmt.Errorf("%s: no line %q", file, key)
}

Listing 12.4 Reading and writing control files, in Rust. code/rust/cgfacts/src/main.rs

/// The directory of a control group under `/sys/fs/cgroup`.
struct Group(PathBuf);

impl Group {
    /// Writes a value to one of the group's control files.
    fn set(&self, file: &str, value: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
        fs::write(self.0.join(file), value)
    }

    /// Reads one of the group's control files.
    fn get(&self, file: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
        Ok(fs::read_to_string(self.0.join(file))?.trim().to_owned())
    }

    /// Returns the counter with the given key from a file of "key value"
    /// lines, such as `pids.events` and `memory.events`.
    fn event(&self, file: &str, key: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
        self.get(file)?
            .lines()
            .filter_map(|line| line.split_once(' '))
            .find(|(name, _)| *name == key)
            .map(|(_, value)| value.to_owned())
            .ok_or_else(|| io::ErrorKind::NotFound.into())
    }
}

create finds a place for a new group. It walks up from the group of the program to the nearest group whose cgroup.subtree_control contains memory and pids, and makes a directory there. An ordinary user can do this because the system’s service manager has given the user ownership of that part of the tree.

command builds a shell command that first writes its own pid to the cgroup.procs of the new group. remove deletes the group. A group can be removed only when it is empty, so remove first writes to cgroup.kill, which ends every process in the group.

Listing 12.5 Creating a group, entering it, and removing it, in Go. code/go/cgfacts/main.go

// create makes a new group. It goes up from the group of this process to the
// nearest group that distributes the memory and pids controllers to its
// children, and creates a directory there.
func create() (group, error) {
	line, err := os.ReadFile("/proc/self/cgroup")

	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	_, path, _ := strings.Cut(strings.TrimSpace(string(line)), "::")

	for dir := filepath.Join("/sys/fs/cgroup", path); dir != "/sys/fs/cgroup"; dir = filepath.Dir(dir) {
		enabled, err := group(dir).get("cgroup.subtree_control")

		if err != nil || !strings.Contains(enabled, "memory") || !strings.Contains(enabled, "pids") {
			continue
		}

		created := filepath.Join(dir, fmt.Sprintf("cgfacts-%d", os.Getpid()))

		return group(created), os.Mkdir(created, 0o755)
	}

	return "", errors.New("no parent group delegates the memory and pids controllers")
}

// command returns a shell script that will run in the group. The shell
// first moves itself into the group by writing its own process number to
// cgroup.procs, and every process it starts afterwards is created there.
func (g group) command(script string) *exec.Cmd {
	return exec.Command("sh", "-c", `echo $$ > "$0/cgroup.procs" && `+script, string(g))
}

// remove ends every process left in the group, waits until the group is
// empty, and deletes it.
func (g group) remove() error {
	if err := g.set("cgroup.kill", "1"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	for {
		current, err := g.get("pids.current")

		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if current == "0" {
			return os.Remove(string(g))
		}

		time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)
	}
}

Listing 12.6 Creating a group, entering it, and removing it, in Rust. code/rust/cgfacts/src/main.rs

impl Group {
    /// Makes a new group. It goes up from the group of this process to the
    /// nearest group that distributes the memory and pids controllers to its
    /// children, and creates a directory there.
    fn create() -> io::Result<Group> {
        let line = fs::read_to_string("/proc/self/cgroup")?;
        let path = line.trim().split_once("::").map_or("", |(_, path)| path);
        let root = Path::new("/sys/fs/cgroup");
        let own = root.join(path.trim_start_matches('/'));

        for dir in own.ancestors().take_while(|dir| *dir != root) {
            let Ok(enabled) = fs::read_to_string(dir.join("cgroup.subtree_control")) else {
                continue;
            };

            if enabled.contains("memory") && enabled.contains("pids") {
                let created = dir.join(format!("cgfacts-{}", process::id()));

                fs::create_dir(&created)?;

                return Ok(Group(created));
            }
        }

        Err(io::Error::other(
            "no parent group delegates the memory and pids controllers",
        ))
    }

    /// Returns a shell script that will run in the group. The shell first
    /// moves itself into the group by writing its own process number to
    /// `cgroup.procs`, and every process it starts afterwards is created
    /// there.
    fn command(&self, script: &str) -> Command {
        let mut command = Command::new("sh");

        command
            .arg("-c")
            .arg(format!(r#"echo $$ > "$0/cgroup.procs" && {script}"#))
            .arg(&self.0);

        command
    }

    /// Ends every process left in the group, waits until the group is empty,
    /// and deletes it.
    fn remove(&self) -> io::Result<()> {
        self.set("cgroup.kill", "1")?;

        while self.get("pids.current")? != "0" {
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
        }

        fs::remove_dir(&self.0)
    }
}

count starts a process in the group and reads pids.current.

Listing 12.7 The kernel counts the processes of a group, in Go. code/go/cgfacts/main.go

// count starts a process in the group and reads the group's process count.
func count(g group) error {
	child := g.command("exec sleep 30")

	if err := child.Start(); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	current, err := g.get("pids.current")

	for err == nil && current != "1" {
		time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)
		current, err = g.get("pids.current")
	}

	child.Process.Kill()
	child.Wait()

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("a process moved into the new group: pids.current %s\n", current)

	return nil
}

Listing 12.8 The kernel counts the processes of a group, in Rust. code/rust/cgfacts/src/main.rs

/// Starts a process in the group and reads the group's process count.
fn count(group: &Group) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut child = group.command("exec sleep 30").spawn()?;

    while group.get("pids.current")? != "1" {
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
    }

    child.kill()?;
    child.wait()?;

    println!("a process moved into the new group: pids.current 1");

    Ok(())
}

limitPids sets pids.max to 4. The shell, which is in the group, then tries to start 6 background commands and prints a line for each success.

Listing 12.9 A limit on the number of processes, in Go. code/go/cgfacts/main.go

// limitPids sets pids.max to 4 and runs a shell that tries to start 6
// background commands and prints a line for each one it started.
func limitPids(g group) error {
	if err := g.set("pids.max", "4"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	started, _ := g.command("for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do sleep 1 & echo started; done 2>/dev/null").Output()
	refused, err := g.event("pids.events", "max")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	fmt.Printf("pids.max 4, a shell starts background commands: started %d, forks refused %s\n",
		strings.Count(string(started), "started"), refused)

	return g.set("pids.max", "max")
}

Listing 12.10 A limit on the number of processes, in Rust. code/rust/cgfacts/src/main.rs

/// Sets `pids.max` to 4 and runs a shell that tries to start 6 background
/// commands and prints a line for each one it started.
fn limit_pids(group: &Group) -> io::Result<()> {
    group.set("pids.max", "4")?;

    let script = "for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do sleep 1 & echo started; done 2>/dev/null";
    let output = group.command(script).output()?;
    let started = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)
        .matches("started")
        .count();

    println!(
        "pids.max 4, a shell starts background commands: started {started}, forks refused {}",
        group.event("pids.events", "max")?
    );

    group.set("pids.max", "max")
}

limitMemory sets memory.max to 32 MiB and memory.swap.max to 0, so that the group cannot move its memory to swap space. It then runs tail /dev/zero. tail keeps the last lines of its input in memory, and /dev/zero supplies bytes without a line end, so the memory of the process grows without bound.

Listing 12.11 A limit on memory, in Go. code/go/cgfacts/main.go

// limitMemory sets memory.max to 32 MiB with no swap and runs a command
// whose memory grows without bound.
func limitMemory(g group) error {
	if err := g.set("memory.max", "33554432"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if err := g.set("memory.swap.max", "0"); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	child := g.command("exec tail /dev/zero")
	child.Run()

	kills, err := g.event("memory.events", "oom_kill")

	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if status, ok := child.ProcessState.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus); ok && status.Signaled() {
		fmt.Printf("memory.max 32 MiB, a command that grows without bound: killed by signal %d, oom_kill %s\n",
			status.Signal(), kills)
	}

	return nil
}

Listing 12.12 A limit on memory, in Rust. code/rust/cgfacts/src/main.rs

/// Sets `memory.max` to 32 MiB with no swap and runs a command whose memory
/// grows without bound.
fn limit_memory(group: &Group) -> io::Result<()> {
    group.set("memory.max", "33554432")?;
    group.set("memory.swap.max", "0")?;

    let status = group.command("exec tail /dev/zero").status()?;
    let kills = group.event("memory.events", "oom_kill")?;

    if let Some(signal) = status.signal() {
        println!(
            "memory.max 32 MiB, a command that grows without bound: killed by signal {signal}, oom_kill {kills}"
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}
a process moved into the new group: pids.current 1
pids.max 4, a shell starts background commands: started 3, forks refused 1
memory.max 32 MiB, a command that grows without bound: killed by signal 9, oom_kill 1
OutputConclusion
pids.current 1The shell moved itself into the group by writing to cgroup.procs, and the kernel counts it.
started 3, forks refused 1The shell and 3 commands are 4 processes. The next fork fails with EAGAIN, and the shell gives up at that point.
killed by signal 9, oom_kill 1When the group could not stay within memory.max, the kernel ended the process with SIGKILL.

The 2 controllers react differently because the resources differ. A fork can be refused with an error, and the program can handle it. An ordinary memory access has no way to return an error. When a group reaches its memory limit, the kernel first tries to free memory inside the group by discarding clean page cache pages and writing out dirty ones. When that is not enough, the OOM killer selects a process in the group and ends it.

At memory.max the kernel ends a process of the group with SIGKILL. Check memory.events when a process disappears without a message.

Hierarchical accounting

The counters of a group include all of its descendants. A process in a child group is counted in the child, in the parent, and in every group up to the root, and a limit at any of those levels can stop it.

The kernel enforces a limit at the moment a resource is requested, by walking up the tree. For the pids controller the moment is fork.

For the memory controller the moment is the allocation of a frame, usually inside a page fault (chapter 7). A page fault cannot return an error to the program, so the kernel has to make room or end a process.

The events are counted hierarchically as well. memory.events of the group of user 1000 on this machine shows oom_kill 16, and those 16 kills include every run of cgfacts made while this chapter was written, 4 levels further down the tree.

This is what makes delegation safe. An administrator sets a limit on a group and hands the subtree below it to a user or to a container. The owner of the subtree can create groups and distribute the resource among them, and cannot exceed the limit set above.

Low-level design: cgmodel

TypeFieldsMeaning
groupparent, pidsMax, memoryMaxa node of the tree and its limits
pids, memoryusage of the group and all its descendants
refused, oomKillsthe counters of pids.events and memory.events
processhome, memorythe group of the process and the memory it holds
OperationBehaviour
spawn(name)fails with EAGAIN when the group or any ancestor is at pidsMax; otherwise counts the process at every level
allocate(amount)charges every level; while a level exceeds memoryMax, kills the largest process in that level’s subtree
kill()removes a process and returns its memory and its place in the count
